## PR #4698 — cmd/cli: proto.Clone MonitorInterfaceRequest in startStream (#4697) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-08)

Branch: `fix/4697-monitor-proto-clone`

## Summary

Fixes a pre-existing `go vet` **copylocks** warning in `cmd/cli/monitor.go`.
The interactive `monitor interface` summary loop's `startStream` closure copied
the request with `reqCopy := *req`, where `req` is a
`*pb.MonitorInterfaceRequest`. That generated proto message embeds
`protoimpl.MessageState`, which contains a `sync.Mutex`, so the shallow struct
copy is a lock copy:

```
cmd/cli/monitor.go:214:14: assignment copies lock value to reqCopy:
  ...MonitorInterfaceRequest contains ...MessageState contains sync.Mutex
```

The warning is pre-existing on `origin/master` (surfaced during the #4694
monitor.go work, **not** introduced by #4696). It is benign in practice —
`reqCopy` only ever has its `SummaryMode` field set per stream and is then read —
but copying a locked type is incorrect.

## Fix

Replace the shallow copy with `proto.Clone(req).(*pb.MonitorInterfaceRequest)`.
This produces a fresh message with no lock copied; the per-stream `SummaryMode`
is set on the clone and the clone pointer is passed straight to
`MonitorInterface` (`proto.Clone` already returns a pointer, so the `&reqCopy`
address-of is dropped). Behavior is unchanged. Added the
`google.golang.org/protobuf/proto` import (already a direct module dependency,
v1.36.11).

## Validation

- `go vet ./cmd/cli/...` — clean (copylocks warning gone; RED: it returns on revert)
- `go build ./...` — passes
- `go test ./cmd/cli/...` — passes
- `gofmt` — clean

No module-doc change needed — internal remote-CLI correctness fix with no
behavior or contract change.

Closes #4697

## PR #4699 — nat: enforce deterministic NAPT64 (IPv6 subscriber, mode 2) on userspace (#4559) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-08)

Branch: `fix/4559-cgnat-ipv6`

## Summary

Completes **#4559** by porting the **IPv6-subscriber / NAPT64 deterministic CGNAT block allocator (mode 2)** to the userspace dataplane. The IPv4 path (mode 1) shipped in #4641; before this change an IPv6-subscriber deterministic pool committed clean but **silently round-robined**, so the subscriber → fixed-port-block mapping (lawful-intercept / CGN audit without per-flow logs) was not enforced for NAT64 traffic.

An IPv6 subscriber now deterministically maps to a **fixed external IPv4 pool address + port block**, reversible from `(external IPv4, port)` back to the subscriber prefix with **no per-flow state**. The subscriber index is the 32-bit word **after** the configured prefix (`/32` → octet offset 4, `/64` → octet offset 8), reproducing the retired-eBPF `nat_pool_alloc_deterministic_v6` (commit `439cd3f`) in Rust.

Mode 2 lives on the **NAT64 forward path** — the only v6→v4 translation. A plain source-NAT rule cannot translate an IPv6 subscriber to a v4 pool, so mode 2 is enforced only when the deterministic source pool is referenced by a `security nat nat64` rule-set with a `/32` or `/64` IPv6 host.

## Implementation

- **`userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs`** — `DeterministicV6`; `deterministic_indices_v6` (IPv6 subscriber → `(ip_idx, block_idx)`); `allocate_deterministic_v6` (mirrors the v4 claim — first free port in the subscriber's block against the shared live-owner map, collision-free, not recycled on release); `reverse_deterministic_v6`.
- **`userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs`** — `allocate_nat64_pool_port_deterministic_v6` wrapper keeping the module-private `TranslatedTuple` out of `nat64.rs`.
- **`userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs`** — `Nat64Prefix.deterministic_v6`, built from the snapshot at `from_snapshots` time (`host_count` derived **pool-bounded** from the parsed pool size — an IPv6 subscriber word far exceeds pool capacity); `allocate_source` routes through the block allocator when set. Out-of-range subscriber **fails CLOSED** (`DeterministicSubscriberOutOfRange`).
- **`pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat64.go`** — `deterministicNAT64V6Fields` computes block params against the **fixed NAT64 port range** (1024-65535 — the range the NAT64 allocator uses, not the source pool's own range); `buildNAT64Snapshots` stamps them.
- **Wire:** 4 additive omitempty fields on `NAT64RuleSnapshot` (Go) + Rust mirror (`#[serde(default)]`, #1961 skew-safe); `protocol_wire_v1.json` regenerated.
- **`pkg/config/compiler_validate_warn.go`** — the #4560 advisory is **narrowed** to residual UNENFORCEABLE cases (`deterministicNAPT64Enforced`): an IPv6-host pool not referenced by a `nat64` rule-set, or an unsupported prefix length. An enforced mode-1/mode-2 pool no longer warns.

## Block-based pool-utilization (#2079) — assessed, DEFERRED

A deterministic pool's exhaustion is **per-subscriber** (each owns a fixed block, cannot borrow another's), so the pool-wide `UsedPorts` numerator does not capture it. A faithful metric needs new allocator block-occupancy state **plus a design decision** (occupied-block ratio vs per-subscriber-block-full events) — not a bounded add. Recorded with rationale in `docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md`.

## Validation

- **RED-on-revert Rust tests:** `deterministic_napt64_v6_fixed_block_per_subscriber_reversible` (allocator level — two subscribers land on their computed external IP + block, a second flow stays in-block on a distinct port, `reverse_deterministic_v6` recovers each, out-of-range fails closed, `/64` word offset) and `napt64_deterministic_v6_routes_through_block_allocator` (through `Nat64State::allocate_source` — **verified RED** with the gate neutralized: panics on the block assertion) + gate-guard companions.
- **Go:** `nat64_deterministic_4559_test.go` (builder wire fields + `deterministicNAT64V6Fields` guards) and advisory-narrowing tests.
- **FULL cargo test 3761/0** (nat subset 668/0); `go test ./pkg/config/... ./pkg/dataplane/...` green (the pre-existing, unrelated `TestOperatorPackagesOnlyUseDocumentedLegacyDataplaneImports` `daemon_ha` allowlist drift also fails on clean `origin/master`).

## Smoke

**Not run — nice-to-have follow-up.** This touches the NAT64 allocation path. A cluster smoke on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0/1` (a deterministic NAPT64 pool + confirm on-wire that a subscriber's translated ports fall in its computed block) would add wire-level proof; the block/IP assignment + reverse mapping are unit-proven and the round-robin path is byte-identical for non-deterministic NAT64 pools.

## Docs

`docs/deterministic-nat-cgnat.md` (mode-2 shipped, block-utilization assessment), `docs/feature-gaps.md`, `docs/vsrx-gaps.md`, `_Log.md`.

Addresses #4559 — the IPv6/NAPT64 mode-2 block allocator is complete; the block-based pool-utilization sub-item (#2079 alarm skips deterministic pools) is assessed and DEFERRED (see above), so #4559 stays OPEN for that follow-up.

`afxdp/forwarding/mod.rs` carried an `IcmpTeRateLimiter` (const `ICMP_TE_MAX_PER_SEC` + struct + impl), every item `#[allow(dead_code)]`. The function returned an owned `String`, so the hot caller `lookup_forwarding_resolution_inner_ecmp` ran `.unwrap_or_else(|| DEFAULT_V4_TABLE.to_string())` — one heap alloc per new-flow FIB resolution just to materialize a `'static` constant. Now returns `Cow<'static, str>`: the default-table remaps (`inet.0`↔`inet6.0`) and the lookup-path default borrow the `'static` `DEFAULT_V*_TABLE` constants (zero alloc); only the rare per-VRF suffix rewrite or a non-canonical passthrough owns a `String`.

Caller updates are mechanical and behavior-identical (`.unwrap_or(Cow::Borrowed(...))`; `.contains(table.as_ref())`; cold build-path `.entry(table.into_owned())` in fib.rs ×2 + the `transport_table` field init in tunnels.rs). **RED-on-revert:** new `canonical_route_table_borrows_default_and_owns_vrf` asserts `Cow::Borrowed(_)` for defaults and `Cow::Owned(_)` for VRF/passthrough — the pre-change `String` return type cannot match those patterns, so the test fails to compile against the reverted signature.

The sibling residual (`session/lookup.rs` `entry.metadata.clone()`) is **not** taken here. Verify-first: `SessionMetadata` is not `Copy` — it carries the load-bearing `policy_counter: Option<Arc<PolicyRuleCounter>>` (#3322 reorder-stable bound hit-counter handle, shared ownership with `PolicyCounterStore`, incremented on the established fast path). All four clone sites (lookup.rs:183/240/281/321) build **owned** return values (`SessionLookup` / `ForwardSessionMatch` / a tuple) that outlive the session-table borrow (the `&mut self.entries` borrow ends before the caller consumes the result). A borrow cannot cross that boundary, and making the type `Copy` would require removing the load-bearing Arc (reintroducing #3322 misattribution) or a return-type split rippling through every lookup caller — neither a LOW-risk change. Per the task guard, no forced lifetime change. **#4675 stays open.**

## PR #4722 — fix(api): deterministic sorted iteration in show-text endpoints (#4712) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

## Problem
`pkg/api/show_text.go` (the `/show-text` REST handler) ranged over Go
string-keyed config maps directly for 12 topics without sorting keys, so
`/show-text` responses came back in randomized order across calls. Go
randomizes map iteration order, so identical active config produced
different orderings request-to-request — breaking config diff/validation
tooling and causing test flakiness (gemini-review-041 Low-13; verified
GENUINE, severity Low — cosmetic, no functional/security impact).

All 12 cited sites iterate `map[string]*...` fields keyed by name, and

`nat-static` / `nat-nptv6` topics iterate slices (`NAT.Static`,
`rs.Rules`) — already deterministic — and were correctly not cited; they
are left unchanged.

Added a generic `sortedKeys[V any](map[string]V) []string` helper (collect
keys, `sort.Strings`, iterate) and routed all 12 map iterations through it.

- `snmp` — `Communities`, `TrapGroups`

- `applications` — `Applications`, `ApplicationSets`

scrambled insertion order for the `applications`, `address-book`, and
`snmp` topics, renders each topic 40× and asserts:

2. entries appear in ascending key order (sorted contract).

## PR #4723 — fix(configstore): resolve master-password across all system stanzas — no plaintext DB leak (#4705) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4705-masterpw-split-system`

Closes #4705

## Summary
`masterPasswordPRF` (`pkg/configstore/crypto.go`) decided whether the config DB
is written encrypted by resolving the PRF via a single first-match
`tree.FindChild("system")`. A `master-password` configured in a **second**
top-level `system {}` stanza was missed, so the whole config DB — secrets
included — was written to disk in **PLAINTEXT** despite the operator configuring
master-password encryption. This is a fail-open at-rest crypto downgrade.

## Reachability proof (verify-first)
Confirmed the split-stanza tree can actually reach the write path:

- **Parser does not merge duplicate top-level stanzas.** `parser.go`
  `parseStatements` appends each `system { ... }` block as its own child →
  `tree.Children` holds two `system` nodes.
- **Loaders feed the raw tree to disk.** `LoadOverride` (`store_command.go`)
  sets `s.candidate = NewParser(content).Parse()` verbatim; `Commit`
  (`store_commit.go`) writes that candidate via `writeActive` → `writeTreeMarked`
  → `maybeEncryptTreeJSON`. `SyncApply` does the same for peer-synced configs.
- **Schema validation accepts duplicates.** `SchemaValidate` →
  `walkSchemaChildren(tree.Children, …)` validates each `system` node
  independently; no dedup/rejection.
- **The compiler already treats it as one system.** `compileSections`
  (`compiler_dispatch.go`) loops over ALL top-level nodes and calls
  `compileSystem(node, &cfg.System, …)` for each — folding every `system` node
  into the same `cfg.System`, so the second stanza's `master-password` **is
  semantically active**. Only the crypto path's first-match lookup disagreed.

## Fix
Resolve the PRF via the **existing** `systemBlocksOf` helper (the same
all-matches walk the dataplane-retirement code uses to see every split
`system {}` block) plus per-node `FindChildren("master-password")`; encrypt if
**any** stanza carries a `pseudorandom-function`. Resolution now fails
**closed** — a master-password anywhere ⇒ encrypted DB. No new bespoke walk;
configstore keeps one consistent multi-stanza-system mechanism.

## Also fixes the #4579 downgrade warning (same root cause)
The #4579 A4-06 "declares a master-password but read back as plaintext" warning
(`db.go` `readTreeMeta`, line ~291) keys off the **same** `masterPasswordPRF`,
so the first-match bug silently defeated it for the split-stanza case too —
a second-stanza master-password DB stored as plaintext read back **without any
warning**. Centralizing the resolution repairs that path. A dedicated
RED-on-revert test asserts the warning now fires.

## Tests — RED on revert
`pkg/configstore/masterpw_split_system_4705_test.go`:

- `TestMasterPasswordSplitSystemStanzaEncrypts` — builds the tree with the
  **real parser** (two `system` stanzas, `master-password` only in the 2nd),

## PR #4724 — fix(config): reject dangling trailing negation in tcp-flags (fail-closed) (#4714) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4714-tcpflags-dangling-neg`

Closes #4714

## Verify-first (what was accepted before)
`ParseTCPFlagsExpression` (`pkg/config/tcp_flags.go`) lexes a firewall-filter
`tcp-flags` expression and tracks `pendingNeg` for a `!` operator, but after the
token loop it only checked `required&forbidden != 0` and `required==0 &&
forbidden==0` — there was **no `if pendingNeg` guard**. A `!` with no flag
operand therefore parsed without error and the negation was silently dropped.

Confirmed on origin/master (`6fa5ab0c6`):

| input | returned | effect |
|-------|----------|--------|
| `tcp-flags "!"` | `(required=0, forbidden=0, ok=false, err=nil)` | no constraint at all |
| `tcp-flags "syn & !"` | `(required=SYN, forbidden=0, ok=true, err=nil)` | trailing `!` dropped — term now matches SYN with **no** ACK exclusion |

The **sole caller** is the #3076 commit-layer guard in `compileFirewall`
(`compiler_firewall.go:268` → `CompileConfig`), so the malformed expression
committed cleanly instead of being rejected — a **fail-open** on a
security-policy input (the intended negated-flag constraint is lost with no
commit error).

## Fix (fail-closed)
Reject a dangling negation with a clear error naming the expression:

- **After the token loop**: `if pendingNeg { return …"dangling negation \"!\" with no flag operand" }` — catches a trailing `!` (`"!"`, `"syn & !"`).
- **In the `&` case**: the same check before resetting `pendingNeg` — catches a `!` standing immediately before a separator with no operand (`"! & ack"`, `"!ack & !"`).

Valid negations are unchanged: `!ack`, `syn & !ack`, `!syn & !ack`,
`(syn & !ack)` all parse to the same masks as before. Double-negation `!!`
(even count → `pendingNeg` ends false) is deliberately **out of scope** — it
cancels to the un-negated flag and is not a fail-open.

## RED-on-revert + over-rejection guard
- `TestParseTCPFlagsExpression`: +3 dangling cases (`"!"`, `"syn & !"`, `"! & ack"`) → expect error.
- `TestParseTCPFlagsDanglingNegation` (new): **5 reject** cases (assert the error names the "dangling negation") + **7 accept** cases that assert the exact `required`/`forbidden` masks for legitimate expressions incl. negations — the over-rejection guard.
- `TestFirewallFilterTCPFlagsCommitReject`: +assert that `tcp-flags "syn & !"` is rejected at **commit**.

RED-on-revert proven: stashing only the parser fix (tests present) makes every
new reject assertion FAIL, e.g.:
```
ParseTCPFlagsExpression([syn & !]): expected error, got req=0x02 forb=0x00 ok=true
tcp-flags "syn & !" (dangling negation) should be rejected at commit (fail-closed), but compiled
```
Restoring the fix → all green. The 7 accept-cases pass with and without the fix
(guarding against over-rejection).

## Gates
- `gofmt -l` clean.
- `go build ./...` clean.

## PR #4725 — fix(api): report current CPU utilization, not since-boot average (#4707) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4707-cpu-current-util`

Closes #4707

## The bug
`pkg/api/metrics_system.go` read the cumulative `/proc/stat` aggregate-cpu
ticks once per scrape and exported them as **gauges** with no previous-tick
state:

```go
// BEFORE (since-boot cumulative average, exported as a "current" gauge)
total := user + nice + system + idle + iowait (+irq+softirq+steal)
sysCPUUser   = (user+nice)/total*100*cpus
sysCPUSystem =  system    /total*100*cpus
```

Because the counters are monotonic-since-boot, that ratio is a **lifetime
average** — it barely moves as uptime grows. A firewall hammered at boot but
idle now still reports high CPU (and vice-versa), so real CPU spikes are
invisible and load alarms silently never fire. The inline comment even
mislabeled it an "instantaneous snapshot". (From gemini-review-041 Medium-13.)

## The fix — inter-scrape delta
Persist the prior aggregate-cpu sample on the collector and report the delta
`(busyΔ / totalΔ)` between consecutive scrapes — the idiomatic Prometheus form
for a gauge implying "current":

```go
// AFTER
delta userPct   = (cur.userNice - prev.userNice) / (cur.total - prev.total) * 100 * cpus
delta systemPct = (cur.system   - prev.system)   / (cur.total - prev.total) * 100 * cpus
```

The `/proc/stat` reading is refactored behind a small seam so the delta logic
is unit-testable without touching `/proc`:

- `parseProcStatCPU(line)` → `cpuSample{userNice, system, total}`; rejects
  per-core `cpuN`/non-cpu lines; tolerates short older-kernel lines.
- `cpuUtilization(prev, cur, cpus)` → per-mode delta %, `ok=false` when totals
  did not advance or a counter went backwards (suspend/hotplug reset) so no
  bogus/negative value is emitted.
- `updateCPUUtilization` folds a sample into collector state and returns
  `emit=false` on the **first** scrape (no predecessor) → nothing published
  that round instead of a bogus 100%.

## Concurrency
New `cpuSamplePrev` / `cpuSampleValid` fields live on the collector and are
guarded by its existing `c.mu`, taken only for the brief read-swap in
`updateCPUUtilization`. Prometheus can call `Collect` concurrently for parallel
scrapers; this mirrors the existing `c.mu`-guarded fairness-throughput window.
The collector is a registered singleton (`newCollector` in `server.go`), so the
prior sample persists across scrapes.

## PR #4727 — fix(config): merge duplicate address-set members instead of dropping earlier ones (#4706) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4706-addrset-merge`

Closes #4706

## Exact trigger (which AST shape)
Two literal `address-set S { ... }` **hierarchical** blocks with the same
name. The hierarchical parser does NOT fold sibling same-name blocks — verified
`NewParser` on a brace config yields **two** sibling `address-set S` nodes,
each with its own member children. `parseAddressBookEntries`
(`compiler_security_addressbook.go`) then processed each independently and did
`ab.AddressSets[as.Name] = as` (last-wins overwrite), so the earlier stanza's
members were silently dropped.

The flat-set `set security address-book global address-set S address ...` path
is **unaffected** — `SetPath` descends into one existing `[address-set,S]` node,
so incremental members already accumulate. That bounds the trigger to duplicate
hierarchical blocks (hand-authored config / `load override`).

## Impact
Silent policy-data-loss / narrowing: a security policy matching `S` matched
FEWER addresses than the operator intended — permitting/denying the wrong set —
with a green `commit` and no warning.

## Before / after
Config: `address-set S { address A1; } address-set S { address A2; }`
- **Before:** `S.Addresses = [A2]` (A1 dropped)
- **After:**  `S.Addresses = [A1, A2]` (union)

## Merge-vs-reject convention chosen
**MERGE (union)** — mirrors the sibling precedent: the `address <name>` case was
explicitly hardened to merge-by-name in **#2222** (documented in `docs/bugs.md`).
`address-set` was the remaining asymmetry. Junos unions same-named
address-sets, so members are unioned with first-seen-order dedup
(`appendUniqueString`). Nested `address-set` references took the same overwrite
path and are fixed too. A single-stanza set compiles identically (no regression).

## Tests (RED-on-revert)
`pkg/config/addressbook_dup_addrset_merge_4706_test.go`:
- `TestDuplicateAddressSetBlocksUnionMembers` — union across two blocks + a
  referencing policy resolves to ALL member prefixes.
- `TestDuplicateAddressSetBlocksUnionNestedRefs` — nested-set refs union.
- `TestDuplicateAddressSetBlocksDedupMembers` — member listed in two stanzas
  appears once.
- `TestSingleAddressSetBlockUnchanged` — no-regression guard.

Reverting the fix to the last-wins overwrite turns the union tests RED
(`address-set S members = [A2], want [A1 A2]`).

## Gates
- `go build ./...` — clean
- `go vet ./pkg/config/` — clean
- `go test ./...` — **53 ok / 3 no-test / 0 fail**

## PR #4728 — fix(config): reject out-of-range BGP peer-as/local-as (no uint32 wrap) (#4713) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4713-bgp-as-range`

Closes #4713

## Problem
The BGP compiler (`pkg/config/compiler_protocols.go`) parsed every
`peer-as`/`local-as` leaf with `strconv.Atoi(v)` then cast to `uint32(n)`,
which **silently wrapped** an out-of-range or negative AS onto a
different-but-valid ASN — the operator's intended AS differed from what was
programmed into frr.conf, with no diagnostic.

Before / after (lenient compile of a persisted/peer-synced config):

| input | pre-fix `PeerAS`/`LocalAS` | post-fix |
|---|---|---|
| `peer-as -1` | `4294967295` (wrapped) → `remote-as 4294967295` | `0` → neighbor skipped (inert) |
| `peer-as 5000000000` | `705032704` (wrapped to a small-looking ASN) | `0` → inert |
| `local-as 5000000000` | `705032704` | `0` → `local-as` omitted |

## VERIFY-FIRST — what was actually still broken
The issue's "commit succeeds" premise no longer holds on the operator path:
**#4589 (already in the issue base `cae466c7b`)** added
`ValidateInteger(1, 4294967295)` on all five BGP AS leaves in
`schema_routing.go`, so the **strict** commit / commit-check path
(`SchemaValidate`) already hard-rejects these, naming field + value
(`integer out of range [1..4294967295] (got -1)`).

The live residual is the **lenient load / peer-sync path**
(`compileTreeLenient` / `CompileConfigLenient`), where `SchemaValidate` is
downgraded to a warning so a persisted or peer-synced config still boots
(#1960). There the compiler still wrapped the bad AS into a valid-looking ASN
and the renderer emitted `remote-as <garbage>` — the leniently-loaded bad
neighbor peered under a wrong-but-valid ASN instead of being **inert**.

## Fix
A shared `parseASNumber(v)` helper — `strconv.ParseUint(v, 10, 32)` (rejects
negatives and > uint32 max at parse) + explicit `n == 0` reject (AS 0 reserved,
RFC 7607) — applied at all **five** parse sites:

- top-level `protocols bgp local-as` (parsed from `child.Keys[1]`)
- group `peer-as` / `local-as`
- neighbor `peer-as` / `local-as`

On a bad value the field is left **unset (0)**, so the FRR renderer's
remote-as-0 skip / local-as-0 omit (#2963) keeps the neighbor inert — the
#2963/#2980 "leniently-loaded bad value is inert" defense-in-depth doctrine,
applied at the parse layer. `compileProtocols` is the SSOT for both the global
and routing-instance BGP scopes, so both are covered.

## Tests (`pkg/config/bgp_as_wrap_4713_test.go`)
- **`TestBGPASWrapLenientInert`** — RED-on-revert core: on the lenient path a
  negative/oversized peer-as/local-as (neighbor + inherited group) must be

## PR #4730 — fix(cli): stream command output to pager instead of buffering (#4709) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4709-cli-pager-stream`

Closes #4709

## Verify-first scope assessment

**Scope: BOUNDED** — no broad interface refactor needed.

`dispatchWithPager` (`pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go`) redirected a `show` command's
`os.Stdout` to an `os.Pipe`, then a goroutine did `io.ReadAll(r)` into one
`[]byte` and `strings.Split` before paging. The full output materialized in
memory first: `show route` (full BGP table) or `show security flow session`
(up to 10M sessions) buffers GBs before printing a byte — OOM risk on a
RAM-constrained firewall.

Crucially, **the pipe seam already existed**. Commands emit output by writing to
`os.Stdout` (redirected to the pipe); the pager is the pipe's consumer. So the
fix is contained to the consumer — I did **not** have to thread an `io.Writer`
through the whole command-dispatch interface. This is the bounded case, so I
proceeded.

**Bounding notes:**
- The pager runs for every `show ` command regardless of TTY (no TTY gate exists
  today); I preserved that. Non-TTY behavior is unchanged — keypresses still
  come from `os.Stdin`.
- The sibling `dispatchWithPipe` (`show ... | match/count/last/...`) has the
  same `io.ReadAll` buffering, but it is **out of #4709's scope** (the issue is
  specifically `dispatchWithPager`). `| count` and `| last` inherently need the
  whole stream; only `match/except/find/no-more` could stream. Noted as a
  related residual, not fixed here.

## Streaming approach

The pager now runs **concurrently** with the command:

- A goroutine reads the pipe **incrementally** via a `lineSource` — a
  `bufio.Reader` with one line of lookahead — and paginates a screenful at a
  time while the command is still running.
- While the pager waits at `--More--`, the pipe fills and the command blocks on
  write, so output is produced **lazily on demand**.
- At most **one page (+1 lookahead line + the OS pipe buffer)** is held at once,
  regardless of total output — the OOM is gone.

Behavior preserved:
- `lineSource` reproduces the old `strings.Split(output, "\n")` + trailing-empty-
  drop semantics exactly: only `\n` is the delimiter (a trailing `\r` stays on
  the line), a `\n`-terminated final line yields no phantom empty line, an
  unterminated final line is its own line.
- Scroll keys unchanged: space = next page, Enter = one more line then a page,
  `q` = quit. Sub-page output prints verbatim with no `--More--` prompt.
- On `q` the pager **drains the rest of the pipe** so the concurrent writer never
  deadlocks on a full pipe.

## PR #4732 — fix(api): stream BGP routes response instead of buffering the full table (#4708) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4708-bgp-routes-stream`

Closes #4708

## Scope assessment — bounded
`bgpHandler` `case "routes"` (pkg/api/routing.go) was the only change site. On CURRENT origin/master (`deee2b0b6`) it rendered every route into one `strings.Builder`, then `writeOK` json-encoded that string into a **second** full copy. On a full internet table (900k+ routes) that materializes a multi-hundred-MB string plus its JSON-escaped copy — ~2x unbounded allocation on a RAM-constrained firewall. The endpoint is a real, operator-reachable REST handler returning the whole table.

No interface change was needed — `GetBGPRoutes` and the `default` BGP-summary path (bounded by peer count) are left untouched.

## Streaming approach
The response is a `TextResponse` envelope: `{"success":true,"data":{"output":"<lines>"}}\n`. The handler now streams that **same** envelope incrementally:

- Write the fixed prefix `{"success":true,"data":{"output":"`.
- For each route, format the line (`%-24s %-20s %s\n`) and JSON-escape it through a fixed-size `bufio.Writer` via a small helper `writeJSONStringFragment` (reuses stdlib `json.Marshal` per line and drops the surrounding quotes).
- Write the suffix `"}}` + `\n`, flushing periodically (every 1024 routes and at the end).

Peak memory is now bounded by the 4KB `bufio` buffer regardless of table size.

## Wire format preserved (byte-equivalent)
JSON string escaping is **per-byte independent** (no cross-byte state), so escaping each line and concatenating is byte-for-byte identical to escaping the joined string. `json.Marshal` and the default `json.Encoder` used by `writeJSON` apply the same HTML-safe escaping. The output has the same `Content-Type` (`application/json`), the same `{"success":true,"data":{"output":...}}` shape, and the same trailing newline `json.Encoder` appends. The tests assert byte-for-byte equality against the pre-change buffered form.

## Test
`pkg/api/bgp_routes_stream_4708_test.go`:
- **Wire-format equivalence** — streamed body is byte-for-byte identical to the buffered golden for a representative table (including a path containing every character `encoding/json` escapes specially: `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `\`) **and** the empty table (valid `{"output":""}`, no nil-panic); all routes present in order.
- **Non-buffering** — a 3000-route table, driven through a recording `ResponseWriter`, streams in bounded chunks: largest single `Write` ≤ 4096, multiple writes, ≥1 incremental `Flush`; still byte-equivalent to the golden.

## Gates

- `go vet ./pkg/api` — clean
- `go test ./...` — **53 ok / 0 FAIL / 3 no-test-files** (pre-existing `pkg/ddns` TestRFC2136 flake did not occur)

## PR #4733 — fix(upgrade): surface RejoinAndConfirm PeerAlive/SyncEstablished errors instead of discarding (#4717) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4717-rejoin-surface-errors`

Closes #4717

## Problem — discarded-error sites
`RejoinAndConfirm` (`pkg/upgrade/kernel_drain.go`) captures `aerr` from
`cl.PeerAlive()` and `serr` from `cl.SyncEstablished()` on every poll, but on a
deadline miss it returned:

```go
return fmt.Errorf("rejoin not confirmed within %s "+
    "(peer-alive=%v sync-established=%v)", deadline, alive, synced)
```

— formatting only the `alive`/`synced` booleans and **discarding** `aerr`/`serr`.
During an ISSU / kernel-roll rejoin, the transport/gRPC cause (e.g. a refused
gRPC dial while xpfd is still restarting) was lost; an operator saw only
`peer-alive=false sync-established=false` and had to correlate syslog to learn
why. (gemini-review-041 Low-2, verified GENUINE, severity Low — observability.)

## Fix — how the errors are now surfaced
Retain the **last non-nil** error from each predicate and wrap it into the
timeout error, **naming which check failed**:

```
rejoin not confirmed within 30ms (peer-alive=true sync-established=false); last sync-established error: dial xpfd gRPC 127.0.0.1:50051: connection refused
```

The base error string is unchanged (existing callers/tests still match); the
underlying cause(s) are appended. This mirrors `DrainAndConfirm`'s timeout in the
same file, which already wraps the last `DrainComplete` error.

## Caller-behavior analysis — happy path preserved, only failure made observable
- **Sole production caller:** `cmd/xpfd/upgrade_kernel.go` (`upgrade kernel rejoin`)
  — on error it prints to stderr and `os.Exit(1)`; on success prints
  `rejoined ...`. The error was already surfaced to the operator; this change
  only enriches its content.
- **No control-flow change.** The function already returned an error on timeout
  and the caller already treated it as fatal. A failed rejoin already STOPPED the
  roll before touching the peer (never-both-down). No new abort is introduced —
  the failure is merely made **observable** instead of silently swallowed.
- **Happy path exact:** `aerr == nil && serr == nil && alive && synced` still
  returns `nil` unchanged. No per-poll logging added (diagnostics live only in
  the terminal error), consistent with `pkg/upgrade`'s no-logger convention.

## Tests — RED-on-revert
- `TestRejoinAndConfirmSurfacesSyncError` — persistent `SyncEstablished` failure
  → asserts the timeout error **names** the sync-established check and **carries**
  the underlying cause.
- `TestRejoinAndConfirmSurfacesPeerAliveError` — persistent `PeerAlive` failure
  → asserts the same for the peer-alive check.
- `TestRejoinAndConfirmSuccessUnchanged` — guard: both checks pass → `nil`.

## PR #4734 — fix(cli): stream show|pipe filters instead of buffering full output (#4731) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4731-pipe-filter-stream`

Closes #4731

## Problem
`dispatchWithPipe` (`show ... | match|except|count|last|find|no-more`,
`pkg/cli/cli_dispatch.go`) did `io.ReadAll` on the **entire** command output and
`strings.Split` it before filtering — buffering the whole output in memory. On a
large `show route | match ...` / `show security flow session | match ...` this is
the same OOM class #4709 (PR #4730) fixed for the interactive pager, applied to
the pipe path. Severity: Low (memory-efficiency; only bites with very large piped
output on a RAM-constrained firewall). Flagged as an explicit residual during
#4709.

## Fix
Reuse the `lineSource` seam #4709 added (bufio.Reader + one-line lookahead,
`strings.Split`-equivalent semantics) and its concurrent `os.Pipe` pattern — do
**not** reinvent. The command writes to a pipe that a filter goroutine consumes
line-by-line while the command runs; the main goroutine runs `c.dispatch(cmd)`
(routing unchanged), closes the writer, then waits on a `done` channel so the
command's exit code is preserved (mirrors `dispatchWithPager`).

New `filterStream(src, out, pipeType, pipeArg)` processes each line as it arrives
with bounded memory:

| Pipe type | Approach | Memory held |
|-----------|----------|-------------|
| `match` / `grep` | write lines containing arg as read | ≤ 1 line |
| `except` | write lines **not** containing arg as read | ≤ 1 line |
| `find` | once a line contains arg, write it + all following | ≤ 1 line |
| `count` | running tally, print `Count: N lines` at end | counter only |
| `last N` | n-wide circular ring buffer (slot `i%n`), replay last `min(count,n)` | n lines |
| `no-more` | write every line as read | ≤ 1 line |

Every filter reads to EOF (arrives when the writer is closed), so no early-return
drain is needed to unblock the producer.

## Semantics preserved
Output is **byte-identical** to the old `io.ReadAll` + `strings.Split` path:
`filterStream` reuses `lineSource`, whose splitting mirrors
`strings.Split(output, "\n")` with the trailing empty element dropped (a
`\n`-terminated final line yields no phantom empty line; an unterminated final
line is its own line; only `\n` is the delimiter so a trailing `\r` stays on the
line). `match` substring-contains, `count` message, `last` default 10 /
`>0`-only parse, `find` first-match-onward — all unchanged.

## Tests (`cli_dispatch_pipe_stream_4731_test.go`, mirrors the #4709 style)
- **Parity:** a `bufferedFilter` reference reproduces the pre-change
  `io.ReadAll`+`strings.Split` path; **every** pipe type × a spread of inputs
  (trailing-newline/none, blank lines, arg absent, empty, single line, CRLF,
  invalid `last` args) asserted byte-identical.
- **Anti-buffering:** a `match` filter emits its needle line after reading

## PR #4735 — perf(config): parse SNMP client CIDRs once instead of per-request (#4711) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4711-snmp-cidr-cache`

Closes #4711

## Problem
`SNMPCommunity.AllowsSource` (`pkg/config/snmp_clients.go`) called
`parseClientPrefix` (`net.ParseCIDR` / `net.ParseIP`) for every configured
`clients` prefix on **every** incoming SNMP v2c packet
(`pkg/snmp/agent.go` `handleV2cPacket`), re-parsing and allocating the same
`*net.IPNet` set on each request instead of using compile-time-known data.
(gemini-review-041 Low-8, perf.)

## Fix — where the parse moved to
The `clients` prefixes are now parsed **once at config-compile time**. In
`pkg/config/compiler_system.go`, after `comm.Clients` is finalized and before
the compiled config is published to the SNMP agent, `compileClientNets` builds
an unexported `[]compiledSNMPClient` (`clientNets`) on the community — each
entry's prefix parsed to a `*net.IPNet` with its prefix length cached.
`AllowsSource` then does an **allocation-free** longest-prefix match over that
set (no per-packet `ParseCIDR`). The cache is written during compilation with
no concurrent readers, and `AllowsSource` never mutates it, so serving is
race-free. `clientNets` is unexported derived state — not marshaled, not
persisted, not part of the config surface.

## Semantics preserved (same allow/deny)
No change to who is allowed/denied — only **when** the parse happens:
- empty `clients` → allow-all (Junos default);
- longest-prefix match wins, honoring the per-entry `restrict` deny;
- `clients` set but source matches no entry → default-deny;
- a malformed prefix is **skipped (inert)** — never a silent allow-all.

## Malformed-CIDR handling
Matches the existing convention: the former per-call code silently skipped an
unparseable entry, so `compileClientNets` skips it too (now once, at compile).
**No** new commit-time rejection is added — a config that loads today still
loads (per #1960). An all-malformed list compiles to a non-nil empty cache and
still default-denies.

## Concurrency
Cache is built at compile time before the config reaches the agent (no
concurrent readers). A community constructed directly (nil `clientNets`, e.g. a
unit test) that never went through the compiler falls back to on-the-fly
parsing for the **identical** decision; the fallback reads only local state, so
it stays race-free, and the real serving path always has `clientNets`
populated.

## Tests
`pkg/config/snmp_clients_4711_test.go`:
- compiled cache populated (bare IP → `/32`, `restrict` flag carried);
- **compiled-vs-fallback parity** over a representative IPv4+IPv6 allowlist
  (CIDRs + bare IP + `restrict`; sources inside and outside each) — same
  allow/deny on both paths;

## PR #4736 — fix(userspace-dp): surface NAT reconcile parse failures instead of silently dropping rules (#4718) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4718-nat-reconcile-surface`

Closes #4718

## Problem
Three NAT snapshot reconcilers in `userspace-dp` dropped a rule/prefix on a
parse failure via a bare `continue`/`{}` with **no diagnostic**, so an
operator debugging a config/sync drift got zero signal that a configured NAT
rule never reached the dataplane (gemini-review-041 Low-3/4/5, all GENUINE).

An unparseable field here is an **internal inconsistency** — the Go
commit-check validates operator config, so it only arises from a
mixed-version peer-sync, a serialization bug, or a missed Go validation edge.
The fix is defense-in-depth: keep dropping **only** the bad rule (so the valid
rules in the same batch still install — failing the whole reconcile on one
malformed rule would take down **all** NAT, a worse availability outcome), but
make the drop **observable**.

## Silent-skip sites fixed (all 3 files)
| File | Function | Sites |
|------|----------|-------|
| `nat/destination.rs` | `DnatTable::from_snapshots` | unparseable destination prefix+address fallback, host destination address, pool address (`:324` / `:330` / `:343`) |
| `nat/static_nat.rs` | `StaticNatTable::from_snapshots` | unparseable `external-ip` / `internal-ip` (`:357` / `:361`) |
| `nat/source.rs` | `parse_match_prefix` | a match prefix parseable as neither CIDR nor bare host IP (`:1375`) — signature gains counter + rule name + axis; fail-closed `*_constrained` behaviour unchanged |

## Surfacing mechanism
Added `NatCounterStore::record_parse_error(detail)`:
- a loud one-line `eprintln!("xpf nat reconcile: dropping rule (unparseable field): …")` **naming the offending rule + field** (journald via stderr — the operator surface), and
- a cumulative `parse_errors` atomic (the **testable seam**; the getter is `#[cfg(test)]`-gated to avoid a dead-code warning until a metrics surface consumes it).

`NatCounterStore` is already threaded by shared reference into all three
builders, so no signature churn on the production callers. This restores the
loud-skip doctrine the NAT64 builder already documents its siblings follow
(`nat64.rs`, #3888); the Go commit gate remains the **primary** defense — this
is the helper-boundary backstop made observable.

## Why not fail-closed-all
Failing the entire forwarding rebuild on one malformed rule would freeze/omit
**every** NAT translation for a single bad rule from a mixed-version peer-sync
— strictly worse than one silently-absent translation. The blast radius is
scoped to the one bad rule, matching the existing NAT64 (#3888) posture.

## Tests (RED-on-revert)
Per reconciler: a batch with one unparseable rule/prefix + valid rules asserts
**(1)** the valid rules install and **(2)** `parse_errors()` is bumped.
Reverting `record_parse_error` to the silent skip leaves the counter `0` → the
surfacing assertion fails. The first cut left the DNAT **pool** site unfixed
and the DNAT test caught it (counter `1`, not `2`) — confirming the seam is
revert-sensitive. An all-valid **guard** per reconciler asserts zero errors
(no false positives).

## PR #4737 — fix(config): redact Secret in YAML marshal/unmarshal (#4710) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4710-secret-yaml-guard`

Closes #4710

## Problem
`config.Secret` (pkg/config/secret.go) enforced a **fail-closed round-trip guard on the JSON path** but had an asymmetric YAML surface:

- `MarshalJSON` redacts a non-empty Secret to the `<redacted>` sentinel.
- `UnmarshalJSON` **REFUSES** that sentinel (`errRedactedSecretIngest`) so a marshalled-then-reloaded compiled config can never silently reload the placeholder as a live secret.
- `MarshalYAML` was already present (defensive, mirrors `MarshalJSON`).
- **`UnmarshalYAML` was missing** — so `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` would decode the literal `<redacted>` straight into a `Secret`, bypassing the guard the moment a YAML config-ingest path is added (LATENT today; gemini-review-041 Medium-8).

## Why this is justified, not premature (verify-first)
- **The yaml dep already exists**: `gopkg.in/yaml.v3 v3.0.1` is in `go.sum` + the module cache (`go mod why` → pulled via `pkg/dhcp` + testify). No **new** third-party dependency is introduced — `go mod tidy` only promotes yaml.v3 to a direct require (**go.sum unchanged**).
- **The project already covers the YAML marshal surface**: `Secret`, `SNMPConfig`, and `SNMPCommunity` all implement `MarshalYAML`. The missing `UnmarshalYAML` is the real asymmetry, matching the JSON path which has both halves.

## Fix
Add `func (s *Secret) UnmarshalYAML(value *yaml.Node) error` mirroring `UnmarshalJSON` **byte-for-byte in behavior**: decode the scalar → reject `SecretRedacted` with the **same** `errRedactedSecretIngest` sentinel → else assign. Type doc updated to "UnmarshalJSON and UnmarshalYAML … refuse the redaction sentinel".

## RED-on-revert test
`TestSecretUnmarshalYAML` drives the **real yaml.v3 encoder/decoder** (not the method directly):
- plain scalar ingests as-is;
- a full `yaml.Marshal` → `yaml.Unmarshal` round-trip of a live Secret is **REFUSED** with `errRedactedSecretIngest`, and never leaks cleartext.
- Neutering the sentinel guard makes the assertion fail (verified); removing the method leaves the yaml import unused and fails the build.

## Validation
- `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...` clean; `go vet ./pkg/config` clean.
- `go test ./pkg/config/...` → green.
- `go test ./...` → green (pre-existing `pkg/ddns` `TestRFC2136` flake unaffected).

## PR #4738 — fix(cluster): stop rg.holdTimer on Manager.Stop to prevent post-stop timer leak (#4716) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4716-holdtimer-stop`

Closes #4716

## Leak scenario
`Manager.Stop()` (`pkg/cluster/manager.go`) stopped only the monitor and heartbeat goroutines — it never iterated `m.groups` to cancel armed per-RG takeover-hold timers. `pkg/cluster/readiness.go` arms `rg.holdTimer = time.AfterFunc(m.takeoverHoldTime, func(){ ... runElection()/electSingleNode() ... })` on a not-ready → ready transition, and the closure guarded only `if !rg.Ready`. A timer armed while `rg.Ready==true` therefore kept running after `Stop()`, fired, took `m.mu`, and ran an election on a quiesced manager. In production `Stop()` is daemon teardown so the election is moot, but the live timer **pins the `Manager` in memory** until `takeoverHoldTime` elapses — goleak / test-teardown flakiness and a lifecycle-invariant violation.

Provenance: gemini-review-041 Medium-12 AND ps-review-040-a5-b1 finding 2 (same bug, both reviewers).

## Fix
In `Stop()`, under `m.mu`: set a new `m.stopped` flag and `Stop()`+nil **every** non-nil `rg.holdTimer` (all RGs). Add an `if m.stopped { return }` guard at the top of the hold-timer closure to cover the race where a timer had **already fired** and is parked on `m.mu` when `Stop()` runs — it acquires the lock after `Stop()` releases it, observes `m.stopped`, and returns without electing. The timer field is guarded by `m.mu` everywhere (armed/cleared in `SetRGReady` under lock), so the cancel loop stays under the same lock — no data race.

## Active path unchanged
Only cleanup on `Stop()` is added. During a running manager `m.stopped` is `false`, so the hold-timer's normal operation — sync-hold release / re-election after the hold window — is untouched. Verified by `TestHoldTimer_StillPromotesWhenRunning`.

## Tests (`pkg/cluster/manager_stop_test.go`)
- **TestStop_CancelsArmedHoldTimer** — deterministic: arms a 1h timer (never fires in-test), calls `Stop()`, asserts `holdTimer==nil`.
- **TestStop_SuppressesHoldTimerElection** — behavioral: the readiness gate blocks the initial election so only a post-hold-window timer could promote; `Stop()` before the short timer fires; asserts no election event and no promotion.
- **TestHoldTimer_StillPromotesWhenRunning** — active-path guard: the timer still fires and promotes on a running manager.

**RED-on-revert:** reverting the `Stop()` cancel-loop + closure guard fails both leak tests (timer left non-nil; election event fires after `Stop()`) while the active-path guard still passes.

## Gates
- `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...` clean
- `go test ./pkg/cluster/...` pass
- `go test -race ./pkg/cluster` pass (9.0s)
- full `go test ./...` green — **53 ok / 0 fail / 3 no-test-files** (pre-existing `pkg/ddns` TestRFC2136 flake did not trigger)

## PR #4739 — fix(cluster): synchronize Monitor.getNlHandle lazy init (race + FD leak) (#4715) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4715-nlhandle-race`

Closes #4715

## Bug (race + FD leak)
`Monitor.getNlHandle()` (`pkg/cluster/monitor.go`) lazily created
`cachedNlHandle` via `netlink.NewHandle()` with **no lock and no
sync.Once**, while `Stop()` writes `cachedNlHandle=nil` under `mon.mu`.

Two concurrent lock-free callers reach `getNlHandle` from **different
goroutines without the lock**:
- `pollInterfaceMonitors` — the poll loop (`poll()` releases `mon.mu`
  before the loop calls it);
- `RGInterfaceReady` — the daemon HA path (`pkg/daemon/daemon_ha.go`; it
  releases `mon.mu` before calling).

Failure scenario: both observe `cachedNlHandle==nil` → both call
`netlink.NewHandle()` → the second write overwrites the first, **leaking
one netlink socket FD**; concurrently `Stop()`'s write **data-races** the
create-and-cache write. Flagged by `go test -race`.

Provenance: gemini-review-041 Medium-11 and ps-review-040-a5-b1 finding 1
(same bug, both reviewers); verified genuine on master.

## Fix (sync mechanism, why)
Guard the **check-create-cache under `mon.mu`** — a mutex, not `sync.Once`,
because the handle is re-created on demand after `Stop()` nils it (`Start()`
calls `Stop()` first), and that lazy-recreate contract must be preserved.
`sync.Once` would permanently bind the first handle and never recreate.

- The test-injection short-circuit (`mon.nlHandle`) stays **before** the
  lock; that field is set once at construction and never mutated, so the
  read is race-free.
- **No deadlock**: neither caller holds `mon.mu` at the call site (both
  release it first), so taking `mon.mu` inside `getNlHandle` is safe.
- Exactly one handle is created under concurrency (no leak); the write can
  no longer race `Stop()`.
- The happy-path return value is unchanged — only creation is synchronized.

**Shutdown safety:** `Stop()` still captures + nils `cachedNlHandle` under
`mon.mu`, then `Close()`s outside the lock. A concurrent `getNlHandle` that
is mid-create while holding `mon.mu` blocks `Stop()` until the handle is
cached, so `Stop()` then closes it — no leak, no torn write.

To make the production creation path testable, `cachedNlHandle` becomes an
`nlHandleCloser` interface (`nlLinkGetter` + `Close()`; `*netlink.Handle`
satisfies it) and creation goes through an injectable `newNlHandle` factory
(`nil` ⇒ real handle). `Stop()`'s `Close()` is unchanged.

## Tests / RED-on-revert
- `TestGetNlHandleConcurrentSingleCreation` — 64 goroutines hammer
  `getNlHandle` with a counting fake factory (1 ms creation delay to widen

## PR #4741 — fix(dataplane): batch/non-blocking ClearAllSessions to avoid HA-watchdog starvation (#4719) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4719-clearsessions-batch`

Closes #4719

## Starvation mechanism
`ClearAllSessions` (`pkg/dataplane/maps_session.go`) cleared the session
table **one syscall per key**: it collected every key with the non-batch
`IterateSessions{,V6}` scan (itself one `GetNextKey`+`Lookup` syscall per
element) and then looped `DeleteSession`/`DeleteSessionV6` with **no
`runtime.Gosched()`**. Against a full table (up to ~10M sessions) that
blocks the controller goroutine for seconds→minutes.

`clear security flow session all` runs on the same process that services
the HA peer watchdog / heartbeat. A multi-second synchronous clear delays
the watchdog → the peer can declare this node dead → **spurious failover /
split-brain**. The batch-delete APIs (`BatchDeleteSessions{,V6}`) and the
yielding batch-lookup iterators (`BatchIterateSessions{,V6}`) already
existed in the same file but were unused by this path.

## Fix (both phases cooperative + batched)
- **Collection** now uses `BatchIterateSessions/BatchIterateSessionsV6`
  (`BPF_MAP_LOOKUP_BATCH`, `runtime.Gosched()` between batches) instead of
  the per-element scan.
- **Deletion** routes v4/v6 keys through new `clearSessionsV4/clearSessionsV6`
  helpers that issue **chunked `BPF_MAP_DELETE_BATCH`** syscalls
  (`sessionDeleteBatchSize = 64` keys/syscall — the same constant the
  `session_store` batch-delete path uses) and **yield between chunks**.
- The `dnat_table` cleanup loops for SNAT sessions now yield every batch.

Chose batch-delete (the PREFERRED option) because the map supports it and
`session_store.go` already establishes the exact chunk pattern on the same
maps — so this mirrors an existing, exercised pattern rather than inventing
a chunk-and-yield scheme.

## Semantics preserved (all cleared, no partial-clear-as-complete)
- Every session is still removed — **both the forward and the reverse**
  conntrack entry that back HA session-sync, plus the dynamic `dnat_table`
  entries for SNAT sessions. WHAT is cleared is unchanged; only HOW.
- Completeness under a concurrent delete: the kernel stops a delete-batch
  at the first missing key (a session GC'd/torn down between collection and
  delete and reports the count deleted so far, so the helper finishes the
  **chunk remainder one key at a time**. Same per-key fallback covers a map
  that can't batch-delete. Never a partial clear reported as complete, and
  no double-count (`cnt` is clamped to the chunk before slicing the
  remainder).

## Test — RED-on-revert
`pkg/dataplane/maps_session_clear_test.go` (real ebpf maps; skips when BPF
map privileges are unavailable, mirroring the `pkg/dataplane/userspace`
helpers):
- Installs 300 **forward+reverse** flows per family, clears, asserts every
  entry (forward AND reverse) is gone and the delete count matches

## PR #4744 — fix(config): reject reversed NAT address/port ranges (#4422) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4422-nat-reversed-range`

Addresses #4422 (umbrella — the "NAT reversed-range" test-coverage slice).

## Verify-first: real gap or already-handled?

**Real gap** in one NAT range site; the sibling sites were already handled.

A source-/destination-NAT rule's `match destination-port <low> to <high>` with `high < low` (e.g. `4000 to 3000`) was **silently accepted at commit and miscompiled**. `parseDNATPortList` required `high >= low` on the range branch and otherwise fell through, splitting the range into its two discrete endpoints — `4000 to 3000` matched only ports `{4000, 3000}`, **not** the contiguous `[3000..4000]` range the operator wrote, with no error and no warning. Both endpoints are valid ports (1..65535), so the existing #3446 out-of-range / non-numeric gate never fired.

Reproduced on origin/master before the fix:
```
CompileConfig err = <nil>          # accepted
DestinationPorts = [4000 3000]     # miscompiled to two discrete ports
```

The **already-handled** sibling reversed ranges (verified, left as-is + pinned by a regression test):
- SNAT pool **address** range → `expandAddressRange` rejects `low > high` ("low address … > high address …").
- SNAT pool **port** range → `validateSourceNATPoolStrict` (#3906) rejects reversed.

## Which NAT sites

`parseDNATPortList` — the `match destination-port` range parser, which feeds **both** the source-NAT and destination-NAT rule paths. Reversed detection is added to all four range-parsing AST shapes (unified single-leaf, set-syntax to-child, hierarchical leaf keys, sibling-node) so it holds across the dual AST shape.

## Fix

- New `NATMatch.ReversedDestinationPortRanges` records a reversed `<low> to <high>` token (third return of `parseDNATPortList`). The two endpoints **still flow through** `ports`, so the lenient load / peer-sync path installs exactly what it did before — **no behavior regression**, matching the #3449 endpoint-preserving precedent.
- `validateNATMatchDestinationPortStrict` hard-rejects a reversed range at commit, naming the rule-set, rule, and the token. Strict on commit / commit-check; downgraded to a warning on the tolerant load / peer-sync path (#1960 no-brick), inheriting the existing `lenientDestNATAddresses` gate.

## RED-on-revert

Disabling the validator's reversed check makes both reject tests fail (`CompileConfig accepted reversed … range`); restoring passes. Additionally, without the parse-time detection the range splits into two ports and `ReversedDestinationPortRanges` stays empty, so the gate has nothing to reject.

## Over-rejection guard

A forward range (`3000 to 4000`), a single-value range (`5000 to 5000`, low == high), a descending **discrete** bracket list (`[ 4000 3000 ]` — two explicit ports, not a range), a single port, and a forward pool address range all still compile clean.

## Tests

- `go build ./...` clean.
- `go test ./pkg/config/...` green (regenerated the #4406 golden baseline — purely additive: the new nil field serializes as `null` in every NATMatch, no value/behavior change).
- Full `go test ./...` green: **53 packages ok, 0 FAIL** (no ddns flake this run).

## PR #4746 — test(config): pin ICMP application type/code attribution (#4422) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4422-icmp-appid`

Addresses #4422 (audit test-coverage slice: "ICMP AppID type/code attribution").

## Verify-first: CORRECT (no bug) → coverage test

The concern: does ICMP application matching (`application junos-ping`,
`junos-icmp-all`, custom `application X { protocol icmp; icmp-type N; icmp-code
M; }`) attribute the ICMP type/code correctly? A swap/drop/mis-range would make
`match application <icmp-app>` match the wrong packets (fail-open / fail-closed).

Traced the full pipeline — it is **correct end-to-end**:

- **Compile** (`pkg/config/compiler_applications.go`): `icmp-type` → `Application.ICMPType`, `icmp-code` → `Application.ICMPCode`, no swap, on both the direct-body and inline-term paths.
- **Wire snapshot** (`capabilities.go` `PolicyApplicationSnapshot` → `protocol.go` json `icmp_type`/`icmp_code` → Rust `policy.rs`): carried verbatim.
- **Match**: the Go simulator `matchSingleApp` checks query TYPE vs `ICMPType` and query CODE vs `ICMPCode` (code only required when constrained); the Rust `policy.rs` `icmp_constraints.find` matches `ctype == ptype && ccode.map_or(true, |c| c == pcode)`. Both fail closed on unknown type/code.
- **Builtins** carry Junos-correct values: `junos-ping`=type 8, `junos-pingv6`=type 128, `junos-icmp-all`/`junos-icmp6-all` unconstrained (pinned in `predefined_icmp_3020_test.go`).

## Gap closed

Existing match-level tests (`icmp_test.go`, `app_junos_ping_3348_test.go`)
exercise only **type-only** apps (junos-ping/junos-pingv6 have `ICMPCode==nil`;
junos-icmp-all is unconstrained). None pins the **icmp-code** dimension through
the end-to-end compile→Match path, and none uses a distinctive `type != code`
pair — so a **type↔code swap** or a silently-dropped code would pass the suite.

## Test (`pkg/policymatch/app_icmp_code_4422_test.go`)

Compiles from flat `set` commands (`ParseSetCommand` + `SetPath`, per CLAUDE.md) and pins:

- **Custom app with both type 3 + code 1** (asymmetric pair): exact type+code permits; transposed **type 1 / code 3 denies (swap catch)**; right type / wrong code denies; right type / omitted code denies; omitted type denies. Also asserts compiled `ICMPType`/`ICMPCode` land in the right fields.
- **Type-only custom app**: matches its type for ANY code, denies wrong type (code not spuriously required).
- **Builtins at the Match verdict surface**: `junos-ping` is code-agnostic echo-request only; `junos-icmp-all` matches every type/code including a nonzero code.

**RED-on-regression confirmed**: injecting a type↔code swap into the compiler
flips the swap-catch assertion; reverting restores green.

- `go test ./pkg/config/... ./pkg/policymatch/...` — pass

## PR #4748 — test(flowexport): unique observation-domain/source-id per flow-monitoring group (#4422) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4422-flowexport-multigroup`

Addresses #4422 — the "flowexport multi-group wire-collision" slice.

## Verify-first: CORRECT (not a bug)

When the config defines multiple flow-monitoring groups (NetFlow v9 / IPFIX
exporters), their exported wire records do **not** collide. #3740 already makes
every exporter stamp a **unique per-group** id derived from the config identity
via `stableExporterID(protocol, InstanceName, TemplateName)`:

- NetFlow v9 → header **SourceID** (RFC 3954 §5.1)
- IPFIX → header **Observation Domain ID** (RFC 7011 §3.1)

`ResolveV9TemplateGroups` / `ResolveIPFIXTemplateGroups` key groups by
`(instance, template)`, so any two distinct groups get distinct ids. Two groups
can never both fall into the degenerate `instance=="" && template==""` → id 1
case: template is the intra-instance group key and instance names are unique map
keys.

The data **template IDs 256/257 are intentionally shared** across groups — that
is RFC-correct, because a template ID is scoped **per** observation domain, so
template 256 under SourceID-A is a different template from template 256 under
SourceID-B. Two groups aimed at one collector are therefore fully
distinguishable; there is no collision to fix.

## Coverage test added

The existing #3740 guards (`exporter_id_3740_test.go`) prove distinctness for
**hand-built** `ExportConfig{}` structs with explicit TemplateName/InstanceName.
None exercise the real path — config → resolver → `NewExporter` → the id written
on the wire. This PR pins that end-to-end:

- `TestNetflowV9MultiGroupWireDistinctFromConfig` — two v9 flow-servers at ONE
  loopback collector referencing two templates (fast/slow) resolve to 2 groups;
  each exporter's wire SourceID is distinct and nonzero, while both data packets
  carry the shared template ID 256.
- `TestIPFIXMultiGroupWireDistinctFromConfig` — the IPFIX equivalent for the
  Observation Domain ID and shared set/template ID 256.

**RED-on-regression verified:** collapsing `stableExporterID` to a constant 1
makes both new tests FAIL with "multi-group wire collision" (both groups stamp
id 1 to one collector); restoring it returns green. A regression that dropped
InstanceName/TemplateName from the resolver's ExportConfig, or collapsed the two
template groups into one, fails the same way.

## Gates

- `go build ./...` — clean
- `go test ./pkg/flowexport/...` — ok (6 collision-relevant tests + full pkg pass)
- `go test ./...` — green, **no failures**

## PR #4749 — test(config): pin per-interface FBF scoping + multi-WAN negative cells (#4422) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4422-pbr-fbf-scoping`

Addresses #4422 — slice **"PBR per-interface FBF scoping + multi-WAN negative cells"** from the test-coverage/observability backlog.

## VERIFY-FIRST: CORRECT (no leak/mis-scope bug) → coverage test

Filter-based forwarding (FBF/PBR) is realized by a `then routing-instance <ri>` term in a firewall filter attached as an interface-unit **INPUT** filter. Two layers keep it per-interface, and both are correctly scoped on current `origin/master`:

- **Kernel ip-rule mirror** (`routing.BuildPBRRules`) builds rules ONLY from filters collected by `collectAttachedInputFilters` — i.e. filters named on some unit's `FilterInputV4`/`V6`. Each attached filter contributes only its own terms, so a filter on WAN1 emits only WAN1's routing-instance table and cannot hijack WAN2's. Output filters and defined-but-unattached filters emit nothing (already covered by the existing `#3430 H1` subtests). The mirror carries **no incoming-interface selector** — a pre-existing **documented** widening for slow-path / `XDP_PASS` traffic; adding an iif selector is a separate, deferred change, **not** a bug in this slice.
- **Fast-path enforcement** (userspace-dp): each interface's `FilterInputV4`/`V6` rides its own `InterfaceSnapshot` (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`), so the per-packet redirect applies to that interface's ingress only. This is the real per-interface FBF boundary.

## Scope analysis
- (a) ge-0/0/0 traffic matching the term → RI-A ✓ (rule scoped to its src + table)
- (b) ge-0/0/0 traffic NOT matching → default/main table ✓ (negative cell: rules stay source-constrained, no catch-all)
- (c) ge-0/0/1 unaffected ✓ (its OUTPUT filter is not FBF; no cross-WAN hijack)

## Tests added (all mutation-verified to bite)
- `TestBuildPBRRules_MultiWANScoping` — two WAN uplinks, each with its own input FBF filter → exactly one rule per filter, each scoped to its own src+table, no cross-WAN hijack, and the negative cell (source outside both subnets matches no rule → falls through to main).
- `TestBuildPBRRules_OtherInterfaceUnaffected` — a routing-instance filter bound as the second WAN's OUTPUT filter contributes no rule → ingress steering never leaks onto the other interface's return path.
- `TestCollectAttachedInputFilters` — only INPUT filters collected, family-split, OUTPUT excluded, dedup across interfaces.

## Deferred dataplane-verify (lab item)
The actual per-packet FBF redirect scoping lives in userspace-dp (Rust), driven by each unit's `FilterInputV4` binding. On-wire verification (WAN1 filter steers only WAN1 ingress; WAN2 return path untouched) is a deferred cluster lab item — not smoke-tested here.

- `go test ./pkg/config/... ./pkg/routing/...` green
- `go test ./...` green — 53 packages ok, no failures (pre-existing `pkg/ddns TestRFC2136` flake did not surface)

## PR #4751 — test(ddns): pin clean provider-transition teardown (#4422) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4422-ddns-provider-transition`

Addresses #4422 (the "ddns provider-transition integration" test-coverage item).

## Verify-first: CORRECT (coverage test only)

The concern: when a DDNS client's **provider** is switched (Cloudflare → Route53, or the provider config is replaced), is the transition handled correctly — old provider torn down, new provider takes over, no stale updates / leaked state / mis-carried creds?

Surface A (the router-address HTTP/rfc2136 DDNS engine, `pkg/ddns/surface_a.go`) already has thorough #3735 coverage for the **un-withdrawable** provider-identity changes:
- **H01** — provider renamed to a different endpoint (old provider *removed* from catalog) → KEEP + orphan alarm
- **H02** — in-place provider mutation (same name, new endpoint) → republish + orphan alarm
- **H03** — removed-binding withdraw after an in-place edit → no wrong-endpoint delete, KEEP + orphan

The **everyday clean transition was untested**: two providers are BOTH defined in the catalog and a binding's `provider` reference is switched A→B, where the old A record is fully withdrawable at A's own (unchanged) endpoint.

### Transition analysis (the clean case)

1. **Pass 1** publishes B at B's endpoint (owned under scope `{pid=B, fqdn=X}`).
2. **Pass 2** sees the old scope `{pid=A, fqdn=X}` as gone-from-config. The provider-aware adopt-in-place guard (`liveByPolicy`/`liveByFP`) does **not** swallow it (A's PolicyID and endpoint fingerprint differ from B's). `classifyOwnedBackend` looks up A's PolicyID in the still-committed catalog → **A is present with a matching fingerprint → `ownedBackendOK`** → a **real DNS delete at A's own endpoint**, rebuilt from A's own catalog entry (A's config/creds, never B's).

Result: A torn down cleanly, B active, **no orphan**, no leaked ownership, no leaked per-scope runtime state (`withdrawOwnedLocked` drops `m.runtime[A]`), and **no double-update** (A gets a withdraw, B gets a publish; neither gets both). Credentials cannot be mis-carried — the backend is rebuilt per provider from its own catalog entry. There are no per-provider goroutines to leak — reconcile is synchronous; only HTTP transports are cached, keyed by source-binding, not creds.

This is the distinguishing input vs the #3735 H01 test, which *removes* prov-a from the catalog so it becomes un-withdrawable → orphan. Here both stay → clean real withdraw.

## Test

`pkg/ddns/surface_a_provider_transition_4422_test.go`:

- **`TestSurfaceAProviderSwitchBothConfiguredCleanHandoff`** — A publishes; binding switched to B with **both** in the catalog. Asserts the withdraw lands at **A's original endpoint** (per-endpoint fake keyed on UpdateServer proves A's config was used, not B's), B published at its own endpoint, `Orphaned==0`, `DeleteOK==1`, `UpsertOK==2`, `Scopes==1`, retired A scope's runtime entry dropped, status shows one published `prov-b` row + no orphan row.
- **`TestSurfaceAProviderUnchangedSteadyStateNoWithdraw`** — steady-state guard: a same-provider forced re-assert republishes and never withdraws/orphans, so the hand-off test can't pass merely because every re-assert withdraws.

**Mutation-verified**: forcing `classifyOwnedBackend` to treat the present provider as gone flips the clean withdraw into an orphan → `ns-a deletes==0` / `Orphaned==0` assertions go RED; reverted → green.

## Gates

- `go test ./pkg/ddns/...` — green
- `go test -race ./pkg/ddns` — green (goroutine-lifecycle clean)
- `go test ./...` — full Go suite green (pre-existing `TestRFC2136` address-in-use flake did not trigger)

## PR #4753 — test(userspace-dp): reject/PBR coverage follow-ups from #4412 (#4499) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `test/4499-rust-reject-pbr-cov`

Closes #4499

## VERIFY-FIRST reconcile against origin/master

Most of #4499 was already landed; this PR closes only the **genuine residual gaps** and documents what was already covered.

**Already covered (no new test needed):**
- **E7** (PBR routing-instance override survives NAT64, no VRF leak), **H1** (output filter on the PBR egress, no bypass), **H6** (IPv6 PBR destination-port fail-closed), **H4 Rust-kernel** (output filter re-evaluated from egress config, never synced session state) — all landed by merged commit `7a320521b`.
- **A2** (reject ICMP type-3/code-13, ICMPv6 type-1/code-1, and TCP RST byte-level) — already comprehensively pinned by `reject_icmp_unreachable_v4/v6_*` (afxdp/tests.rs) and the `build_reject_rst_frame` tests (frame/tcp_tests.rs: flags, seq/ack, ports, MAC/IP swap, checksum, window=0, ext-header). The issue-comment premise ("existing tests assert is_some/is_none not the bytes") was stale.
- **H4 full cross-chassis failover-under-traffic** — a cluster integration test, out of scope for a Rust-only cargo PR (the Rust-kernel property it rests on is pinned).
- Packet-level NAT64 port preservation is already asserted by `translate_v6_to_v4_tcp`.

## Gaps this PR closes

**E2 — reject/deny installs no session, no session-init log.** The poll-loop deny branch calls `deny_reply_and_emit` then sets disposition `PolicyDenied`, never reaching the session-install path — so a denied flow, even one whose policy has `then log session-init`, emits only the `POLICY_DENY` RT_FLOW record and never a session-init (`SessionCreate`) record. The existing `deny_reply_and_emit_*` tests pin only the action byte; the two new tests pin the event **kind** is `PolicyDeny` (not `SessionCreate`) and that exactly one frame is emitted (no trailing session-init):
- `deny_reply_and_emit_reject_logs_policy_deny_kind_not_session_init_4499` — `then reject`: RST enqueued, one `PolicyDeny`/REJECT record, nothing follows.
- `deny_reply_and_emit_plain_deny_silent_logs_deny_no_session_init_4499` — plain `then deny` (no zone `tcp-rst`): silent drop (no reply), one `PolicyDeny`/DENY record, nothing follows. Drives the combined emit path that `deny_reply_no_zone_tcp_rst_is_silent_drop` never exercised.

**A5 — AppCatalog lookup with a NAT64-translated port.** NAT64 copies the L4 header verbatim (only the IP layer changes), so the address-agnostic AppCatalog port resolution yields the same application before and after translation. `nat64_translation_preserves_port_for_appcatalog_lookup_4499` translates a v6 SYN to tcp/80, reads the service port **back out of the translated v4 frame**, and asserts `AppCatalog::lookup_forward` still resolves the app — with a non-80 control and the pre-translation v6 baseline. Reading the port from the translated bytes ties the assertion to `nat64::translate_v6_to_v4`'s port copy.

## Mutation-verified (each new assertion bites)
- E2 kind pins → **RED** when `emit_policy_deny_event`'s `kind` is flipped to `SessionCreate` (both E2 tests fail; A5 unaffected).
- A5 → **RED** when the translated destination port is corrupted (`out[22] ^= 0xff`).
- All reverted; production is byte-identical.

## Production untouched
Only two test files changed (`reject_reply_tests.rs`, `nat64_tests.rs`) plus `_Log.md`. No production source touched — this is coverage, not a fix or refactor. No real bug was uncovered.

## PR #4754 — frr #4484 L-6: write frr.conf 0640 owned root:frr, not world-readable 0644 [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4484-l6-frrconf-mode`

Addresses #4484 (L-6). The opus-172 LOW umbrella stays open to track the remaining Rust/lab/deferred items.

## Problem
`frr.conf`'s xpf-managed section carries routing-authentication secrets — BGP TCP-MD5 passwords and OSPF/IS-IS/RIP authentication keys — but the file was written **0644, world-readable** to every local user. Every other secret-bearing file this daemon writes is 0600/0640. (The `StripManagedSectionFile` zeroize-path comment already flagged the "world-readable (0644) /etc/frr/frr.conf" secret residual.)

## Fix
- Change the two `atomicWriteFile` call sites (`writeManagedSection`, `StripManagedSectionFile`) from `0644` → `0640`.
- 0640 is readable only by owner+group, so on a **fresh** create (no operator file to preserve) install the file **owned `root:<frr-group>`** via `fsatomic.WithOwner`, so the unprivileged frr daemons (group `frr`) keep read access.
- The owner override (`atomicWriteOwnerOpt`) applies **only** when BOTH:
  - the target does not already exist — an existing operator file keeps its own mode AND ownership (`WithPreserveExisting`, no `WithOwner`), so a commit never restamps an operator's chosen owner; AND
  - the process is root and the `frr` group resolves — only root can chown to root:frr, so a non-root xpf (unit tests, dev hosts) skips it and the file lands 0640 root:root (harmless: nothing reads frr.conf without a running FRR).

This mirrors the pkg/dhcpserver **#2450** Kea-memfile ownership fix (own a mode-tightened file by the unprivileged runtime user so it stays readable; best-effort when that user is absent). On a real appliance frr.conf ships from the frr package pre-existing 0640 frr:frr, so the fresh path only fires when the file is genuinely absent — and the root gate keeps the frr suite deterministic and portable regardless of whether the test host has an `frr` group.

## Tests (RED-on-revert verified)
- Updated `TestWriteManagedSection_PreservesExistingMode` fresh-file assertion `0644`→`0640`.
- New `frrconf_mode_4484_test.go`: fresh-mode `0640` (FAILS on revert to 0644), operator-mode preservation, and the owner-override decision matrix (fresh+resolves → apply, existing → preserve, group-absent → skip).

## Validation
`go build ./...` clean; `go test ./...` clean (pre-existing pkg/ddns port-bind flake ignored); `gofmt`/`go vet` clean. Documented in `pkg/frr/README.md`.

## PR #4755 — cluster #4484 L-9: show control-link auth engaged vs dual-accept [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4484-l9-controllink-auth-show`

Addresses #4484 (L-9). The opus-172 LOW umbrella stays open to track the remaining Rust/lab/deferred items.

## Problem
The #4107 control-link HMAC authentication runs in a deliberate **dual-accept** grace during a rolling upgrade and only **engages** enforcement once both nodes carry the key and are observed signing. But no operator surface revealed which state the link was in, so a control link silently degraded to dual-accept — a peer that stopped signing, a half-configured key — was invisible.

## Fix
Add `controlLinkAuthStatus()` and render an `Authentication:` line in `FormatControlPlaneStatistics` (`show chassis cluster control-plane-statistics`). The posture is a tri-state derived from the **same two facts** `syncAuthDecision` / `heartbeatAuthDecision` gate on:

| Local key | Peer authenticated | Rendered |
|---|---|---|
| no | — | `dual-accept (no control-link key configured)` |
| yes | yes | `engaged (peer authenticated; unauthenticated frames rejected)` |
| yes | no | `dual-accept (key configured; peer not yet authenticated)` |

Because it reuses `ControlLinkAuthKey()` presence + `HeartbeatPeerAuthSeen()`, the line tracks the **real enforcement decision** rather than a separate estimate, and it inspects only `len(key)` so the secret is never rendered. No new gRPC RPC or cmdtree command is needed — the show command already exists; this only adds a line to its render (the deferral in the earlier #4484 PR over-estimated the scope as "new gRPC + CLI cmdtree wiring").

## Tests (RED-on-revert verified)
`controllink_auth_status_4484_test.go`: the three states, that the key bytes never leak into the string, and that the `Authentication:` line is wired into `FormatControlPlaneStatistics` (removing the line FAILS the render test).

- unrepresentable matches marked `<unrepresentable — snapshot fails closed>`
  (#3406/#3367).

## PR #4757 — fix(userspace-dp): clamp IPv4 datagram end (L-3) + redact syn-cookie key in Debug (L-7) (#4484) [MERGED] (merged 2026-07-09)

Branch: `fix/4484-l3l7-rust`

Addresses #4484 (umbrella stays open). Drives two genuine Rust residuals in one PR, one commit each (bisectable).

## L-3 — clamp IPv4 datagram end to frame length (fail-closed self-DoS)

**Verify-first (origin/master):** `tcp_segment_consumed_len` in
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/tcp.rs` derived the IPv4 datagram end from
the header's `total_len` field (`ip_datagram_end = parsed.l3 + total_len`,
via `checked_add`) with **no** `.min(frame.len())` clamp. `total_len` is
attacker-controlled; `frame_l4_offset` validates only the IHL, so an
inflated `total_len` passes parsing and reaches this site. The value flows
into `payload_len = ip_datagram_end.saturating_sub(tcp_data_start)`, which
feeds the no-ACK RST's `ack = seq + seg_len` — so an inflated `total_len`
produces an over-large ack the SYN-SENT peer discards, degrading the
`reject`/RST leg to a silent drop (fail-closed self-DoS).

**Fix:** clamp the derived datagram end to `frame.len()` after the
address-family match (bounds the v4 `total_len` path — the reported
residual — and the v6 `payload_len` path). No-op for well-formed packets.

**RED-on-revert:** `reject_rst_v4_inflated_total_len_..` — a SYN frame
claiming `total_len=1200` in a real 54-byte frame acks `seq+1` with the
clamp; removing the clamp yields `seq+1161` (1261 vs 101) → test FAILS.
**Guard:** `reject_rst_v4_exact_total_len_unchanged_by_clamp` — a
well-formed `total_len==46` / 60-byte SYN+6-payload frame still acks
`seq+1+6` (clamp is a no-op).

## L-7 — redact syn_cookie_master_key in Debug (secret leak)

**Verify-first (origin/master):** `ForwardingState`
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types/forwarding.rs`) derives `Debug`; the field
`syn_cookie_master_key: Option<[u8; 16]>` had no hand-redaction, so the
auto-derived `Debug` prints the 16-byte SYN-cookie master key in
cleartext. The sibling secrets in this file (`TunnelEndpoint` /
`WgRuntimePeer` WG keys) hand-implement `Debug` with `<redacted>`.

**Fix:** wrap the field in a `SynCookieMasterKey(Option<[u8; 16]>)`
newtype whose manual `Debug` redacts (`Some(<redacted>)` / `None`, never
the bytes). `ForwardingState` keeps `#[derive(Debug)]`, so every other
field renders unchanged and no future field silently drops from Debug (a
hand-written 67-field impl would be large and drift-prone). Read/write
sites access `.0` (`forwarding_build/mod.rs`,
`worker/loop_body/{mod,setup}.rs`).

**RED-on-revert:** `syn_cookie_master_key_debug_redacts_the_secret_in_forwarding_state`
— formatting a `ForwardingState` with a non-None key asserts the raw
bytes never appear and the field renders `Some(<redacted>)`; deriving
`Debug` on the newtype re-leaks `Some([171, 171, ...])` → test FAILS.
**Guard:** the same test asserts sibling fields (`local_v4`) still render.
