## PR #6673 — config: accumulate both sides of five fail-open multi-value leaves (#6659) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-12)

Branch: `fix/6659-multivalue-leaf-arms`

Advances #6659 (the fail-open subset; the remaining value-drop sites follow in a second PR).

## What this fixes

Five compiler arms read only ONE side of a dual-shape multi-value leaf, so a
bracketed list or a packed statement silently compiled to one value — or to none.
CLAUDE.md already states the rule ("a compiler reading a multi-value leaf MUST
read `child.Keys[1:]` AND `child.Children` and accumulate"); these arms did not.

This PR takes the **fail-open** subset only. Each site here either widens what a
rule matches, or lets an invalid value escape the commit gate that exists to
reject it. The pure value-drops (CoS, ntp, api-key, key-exchange, archive-sites,
shared-umem, RA dns, vlan-id-list) are a separate PR so they can be reviewed at a
different depth.

## Verified firsthand, not pattern-matched

Every site below was confirmed on current master by compiling the config and
reading the output, not by inspecting code shape. That surfaced three corrections
to the issue's own table:

| issue says | actually |
|---|---|
| `attributes-match` packed form compiles zero constraints | true only for the **packed leaf**; the block and flat-set forms already worked |
| CoS `code-points` is one of the three fail-opens | **not a fail-open** — its validator reads `Keys` and correctly rejects a bogus code point in either slot. (It has a real bug — the hierarchical block loses the *entire* classifier, worse than "zero code points" — but it is a value-drop, and it is in PR 2.) |
| proxy-arp is high severity alongside the fail-opens | the DROP is a **pure value-drop**. But proxy-ARP addresses had no commit-time validator at all, and *widening the read is what makes one necessary* — the fold below adds it, covering **every slot including the first**, not just the tail the read widened. |

The fail-open set is therefore **one match-widening** (`attributes-match`) plus
**three gate-escapes** (`flow flag`, static-NAT `destination-address`,
`forwarding-table export`) — not the three the issue names.

## The one-sidedness runs in BOTH directions

This is the property that makes the class recur, and it defeats the obvious fix
strategy:

- some arms read `Children` and **never** `Keys[1:]` — `attributes-match` and
  `then change-configuration commands` here, which is why their **packed-leaf**
  spellings compiled to nothing while the block spellings worked;
- other arms read `Keys[1:]` and **never** `Children` — the CoS `code-points`
  collector (PR 2) reads `Keys` plus the inline tail, so its hierarchical
  **block** spelling is the broken one, and it loses the entire classifier.

Anyone auditing this class by grepping for "looks like a `nodeVal` call" finds
only the first direction and leaves the mirror image untouched. The check that
works is per-shape: compile BOTH the bracketed/packed spelling AND the
hierarchical block spelling and compare. Every test here does that, and the
statement is repeated in the code comment at each reader adoption site so the
next auditor meets it where the work happens.

**#5173 must stay OPEN** when this merges. Deliberately not a close keyword.

> **Reachability, stated narrowly after a correction.** `flags == 0` in the

> planned-but-not-live binding read back as absent and the old raw-queue
> fallback fired with an unbounded `rx_queue_index`.
>
> An earlier revision of this body claimed that happens on "every RG
> transition". **That is false and is retracted.** An unarmed binding leaves
> `ctrl.Enabled=0` and `lib.rs:405` returns before any binding lookup; a normal
> data-RG transition keeps standby bindings armed, and `update_ha_state` touches
> HA runtime/session state rather than binding readiness. What survives is the

> transition", still a real reachable path rather than a latent one. The

> overstated it; this is the accurate middle.


## The defect

AF_XDP delivery is queue-bound: the kernel's `xsk_rcv_check` drops a redirect
whose target socket is bound to a different `(netdev, queue)` than the packet
arrived on. `select_userspace_queue` nonetheless returned
`rx_queue_index % queue_count`, where `queue_count` is the planner's global
**minimum** RX-queue count across every interface.

So a packet arriving on a queue at or above that minimum was reduced onto a
different queue's socket and **silently dropped by the kernel** — on any box
whose interfaces have asymmetric RX-queue counts, which the global-minimum
planner *guarantees* whenever one interface has more queues than the smallest.

The raw-queue fallback meant to catch exactly this only fired when the reduced
target was **absent**. In steady state the planner had created a binding for
every queue below the minimum, so the reduced target existed and the fallback
did not run — but see the note at the top: `flags == 0` also covers planned-but-
not-live bindings, so on every bringup and RG transition it DID run, with an
unbounded index. RSS restriction does not save it: best-effort,
mlx5-only, skipped for `workers == 1` and `workers >= queues`.

**The comment above the defect asserted the invariant the code then broke** —
"Keep the XDP handoff on the ingress queue" — which is presumably how it
survived. It now describes what the code actually does.

carrying the *mechanism*, as opposed to the operator note in
`docs/host-inbound-service-matrix.md` — still described only the bracketed form.

The lexer discards `[` and `]` (#2419), so

```
interfaces { [ ge-0/0/0 ge-0/0/1 ] { host-inbound-traffic {...} } }
interfaces {   ge-0/0/0 ge-0/0/1   { host-inbound-traffic {...} } }
```

parse to the same multi-key node and fan identically. A reader consulting the AST
shape table to work out **which spellings reach `len(Keys)>1`** — the question the
whole safety argument turns on — would previously have concluded, wrongly, that
brackets were required. The table now carries the bare row.

## 2. Strengthen the rationale for excluding a nested extra membership

Both the doc and the test comment called `[ a b ] { c; host-inbound {...} }`
excluding `c` a *defensible judgement call*. Codex's review of #6670 supplied a
stronger reason, and it is worth recording because a future reader could otherwise
decide the judgement call goes the other way:

> `c` is a nested CHILD, not a bracket PEER, and its AST position is
> indistinguishable from the flat-set membership tail that caused #6389
> (`set ... interfaces [ a b ]` nests `b` as exactly this kind of child).

So applying the body to `c` would restore the forbidden children-fan and re-open
the original leak by another route. The exclusion is **forced by the fix's own
invariant**, not chosen.

Rounds 1 and 2 argued about whether the fallback could hand an "unzoned" `st0.0`

it. **That map never had an effect at runtime, because it could not: it was built
from `InterfaceSnapshot.zone`, and the Go builder has already propagated.**

snap name="st0.0" linux="st0"   ifindex=42 parent=42 zone=""      hw=""
snap name="st0.1" linux="st0.1" ifindex=43 parent=42 zone="vpnb"  hw=""

own `Zone` is non-empty in both zone-ref spellings. So `ifindex_own_zone_id` and
`ifindex_to_zone_id` were **the same map on every producible snapshot**.

section and `_Log.md` entry made about "own vs propagated" is corrected.

then passed **vacuously** over the empty slice: the gates that exist
specifically to protect zone membership were inert against a membership list
that never arrived. Downstream `UserspaceBoundLinuxInterfaces`
(`pkg/dataplane/userspace/interfaces.go`) skips any interface with `Zone == ""`,
so the interface was never AF_XDP-bound and every policy naming that zone never
applied to its traffic.

The with-body variant was worse than a drop: `prop.Children` there holds the
member's **body**, so the loop ran once with the `host-inbound-traffic` node
mistaken for a member — the real member dropped **and** its body keywords
compiled as phantom interface names.

### Measured differential (compileZones, at the parent SHA)

| variant | BLOCK spelling | COMPACT-LEAF spelling |
|---|---|---|
| single | `[ge-0/0/1.0]` | `[]` |
| multi | `[ge-0/0/0.0 ge-0/0/1.0]` | `[]` |
| with body | `[ge-0/0/0.0]` + `hib[ge-0/0/0.0]={ssh}` | `[host-inbound-traffic system-services ssh]`, no override |

## Reachability (honest bound)

Hierarchical text ingest only — `load override` / `load merge` / the persisted
config file / HA `SyncApply`. **Not** reachable from the `set` CLI (`SetPath`
always descends the `interfaces` container and stores each member below it —
pinned by `TestZoneInterfaces6525FlatSetNeverReachesCompactLeaf`), and
`show configuration | display set` round-trips safely. Those are still the boot
path and the peer-sync path.

## The fix

`zoneInterfaceMemberNodes` **normalizes** the compact shape onto the block
shape: it synthesizes one member node carrying `prop.Keys[1:]` with
`prop.Children` as that member's body. Every spelling then takes the identical

## PR #6815 — userspace-dp: cap lenient SNAT aggregate bitmap at apply boundary (#6812) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6812-snat-aggregate-bitmap-cap`

## Summary

opus-review-001 **R73 (High)**: the #5877 aggregate cardinality gate hard-rejects an over-budget source-NAT config at strict commit but downgrades to a warning on the tolerant load / peer-sync path (#1960 no-brick) — and a tolerated over-budget config still reached the Rust apply boundary, which built every pool's per-address occupancy bitmap **eagerly**. `PortAllocator::new` ran for every pool-mode rule with `total_pool > 0` **before** the reuse maps were consulted and even when `pool_failure` was already set, with no aggregate cap at the final allocation boundary. Three full-range /16 pools materialise **12,683,575,296 bitmap bits (~1.48 GiB)** — enough to stall or OOM the dataplane on an upgrade boot or HA convergence, while processing exactly the legacy config the tolerant path exists to recover.

The fix caps the aggregate at the apply boundary on both sides, and makes the two sides answer the *same* question in the *same* order.

- **Rust apply boundary** (`userspace-dp/src/nat/source.rs`): `parse_source_nat_rules_with_previous` splits into parse + `resolve_pool_allocators` — **reuse-before-build** (a same-config re-apply no longer builds and discards a full bitmap per pool), **nothing built for a failed pool**, and the Go-mirrored budgets (1024 pools / 1,048,576 addresses / 2^33 port slots, one shared `allocator_capacity` formula) charged per distinct allocator key. Reused keys **consume budget but are always accepted**, so a no-op re-apply preserves last-good state while a two-step apply cannot creep past the cap one generation at a time. A non-fitting new key fails every referencing rule closed with the `OverBudget` variant (`source_nat_pool_over_budget`) and builds no bitmap; first-fit admission means a refused key consumes nothing, so a later smaller pool still installs.
- **Go tolerant snapshot poison** (`pkg/config`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat_source.go`): the #5877 validator's referenced-pool walk is extracted into `sourceNATAggregateReferencedCharges` — one source of truth for scoping and saturating charge arithmetic, with the strict validator keeping its exact messages on top of it — and `SourceNATAggregateOverBudgetPools` runs the same first-fit admission. The snapshot builder marks rules referencing a non-fitting pool `PoolUnusable` with reason `aggregate_over_budget`: a tolerated config degrades per-pool with an actionable signal instead of silently forcing the eager bitmap.
- **Wire + status contract**: `aggregate_over_budget` maps to `OverBudget`; an older helper's catch-all maps the unknown reason to `InvalidPool` — still fail-closed, wire-skew safe, no protocol change. With failed pools building no allocator, the pool status view would have reported the default 1024-65535 range for exactly the pools an operator is debugging, so the configured range now rides on the rule (`pool_port_low`/`pool_port_high`), read by both `source_nat_pool_statuses` and the allocator key.
- **Strict-vs-lenient split unchanged**: strict commit / commit-check (and the #5876 peer-effective view) still hard-reject the over-budget aggregate; the tolerant path warns and boots — it just no longer materialises the over-budget allocator state.

## What the review rounds changed

Seven hostile-review rounds landed on top of the original cap. They are not cosmetic — most found a way the two sides could still disagree:

1. **Failed pools must not charge the budget** (Codex F1-F4). The Go poison walk charged pools the Rust side never builds an allocator for, so it refused a pool the dataplane admits — a fail-closed OVER-rejection on the one path that exists to recover a broken box.
2. **The budget must ask the runtime's question, not a proxy for it.** A fifth unusability class (`some_member_fails`) meant the Go-side host-count sum and the Rust all-or-nothing verdict disagreed. The walk now consults `SourceNATPoolUnusableReason`, the runtime's own predicate.
3. **The shared verdict needs a shared grammar.** Pool-member CIDR acceptance is now pinned cross-language by `snat_pool_grammar_v1.json`, read by the Rust expander, the Go grammar predicate, and `pkg/nat`.
4. **First-fit order is part of the contract.** The Go walk's charge order must equal the builder's emitted order, or the two halves poison different pools. Both are stable-sorted on one shared `SourceNATScopeTier` (#4161 interface > zone > routing-instance).
5. **Round-4 amendment**: the pool network-base mask had no witness; the migration "option" was not one.
6. **The tie-break guards could not see the rule they forbid.** All three same-tier fixtures declared rule-sets in ascending suffix order, so within a tier config order and ascending NAME order were the same sequence and a `(tier, Name ASC)` tiebreak — precisely the rule an earlier round removed — was GREEN on all three. Re-cut descending. Separately, `expandPoolV4` accepted a non-canonical mask (`10.0.0.0/016`) that every other layer refuses, so the deterministic-CGNAT surface answered a forward-mapping query with a 65,536-address fiction for a pool that translates nothing.
7. **That round-6 tripwire could not fire.** The precondition asked whether the *whole* declared name sequence was non-decreasing; these fixtures interleave two tiers (`if00 zn00 if01 zn01 …`) and `"zn00" > "if01"`, so the sequence is non-monotonic in both directions and the `t.Fatal` was unreachable. Reproduced: with the loops re-cut ascending the test passed against pristine production *and* against the `(tier, PoolName ASC)` mutation. Replaced with a per-tier predicate, now present in all three fixtures. Round 6's commit message claimed this precondition worked; that claim is retracted in `_Log.md` and the plan. One further claim narrowed: the canonical-mask fix was justified as "already refused at commit and poisoned on the tolerant path" — the first conjunct is over-broad, because `validateSourceNATPoolAddressGrammarStrict` walks rule references rather than the pool table, so an *unreferenced* pool carrying `10.0.0.0/016` compiles strict-clean. It is still unusable, which is what carries the conclusion.
8. **The same blindness one nesting level in, and an assertion that admitted empty success.** Round 7 de-correlated the rule-SET names and left the RULES inside each rule-set declared `r0` then `r1` — config order and ascending name order at once — so a within-rule-set `Rule.Name` sort left the builder fixture entirely GREEN. Rules now declare descending, assertion (3) reads the DECLARED sequence out of the compiled config instead of re-deriving `r%d`, and the round-7 tripwire gained a rule-level sibling. Every other generated name in these fixtures was enumerated against "could a production sort key on it"; there is no fourth level. The walk side had no rule-level assertion at all (one rule per rule-set everywhere), so it gained one. Separately, the shared-grammar reject half fired only for `nil error && nonempty output`, which admits EMPTY SUCCESS — exactly what a per-member skip produces on a single-member pool: turning the `netip.ParsePrefix` refusal into a `continue` left it GREEN. It now requires a non-nil error per row plus a mixed-member half in both orders. Finally, this PR's own "same order" claim about the Rust resolver is corrected: `resolve_pool_allocators` reserves REUSED allocator keys before admitting NEW ones, so the sequences coincide only on a first apply. The Go/Rust *agreement* claim is unaffected — the Go poison travels on the wire and a poisoned pool reaches neither Rust phase.
9. **The anti-coincidence property, asked of the STRUCT rather than of a remembered list.** Round 8 permuted the rule and pool NAMES of its new walk-side fixture and then generated the match address and the pool member address from the loop index — so both ascended, and a `Match.SourceAddress` sort in the charge walk left the *entire* `pkg/config` suite green. Rounds 7 and 8 had each fixed an ascending coincidence by re-cutting the fixture DESCENDING, which trades one monotone direction for the other and left five reverse cells blind. Both fixtures now emit a PERMUTATION at every level (three rules per rule-set — two cannot be de-correlated from both directions). **Round 10 then found that the closure claim was itself still a list:** both fixtures manually enumerated the helper CALLS, so a column with no call stayed silent, and three real ones were — `CounterID` (the builder passed nil for the ID map, so every emitted ID was zero while production supplies populated FNV-derived IDs), pool CARDINALITY, and port CAPACITY. Measured against the whole `pkg/dataplane/userspace` suite at the round-9 head, all three of `(tier, CounterID)`, `(tier, len(PoolAddresses))` and `(tier, PortLow)` are GREEN; all three are RED now. `sweepAxes6812` reflects over every field of the value the production comparator reads — recursing into nested structs and pointers, `.len` per slice, and a HARD FAILURE for any kind with no order-preserving key encoding — so adding a field to `SourceNATRuleSnapshot` or `NATPool` reds the fixture instead of silently widening the blind set. **The constant exemption was also wrong as applied:** a stable sort on a constant cannot permute anything, but that is only costless when the column is invariant for all PRODUCTION inputs, and these were fixture-constant. Constants must now be REGISTERED as either an admitted blind spot or a provable non-axis; the split is printed by `go test -v` — 25 columns guarded (6 by hand in round 9), 74 named holes, 9 provable non-axes. What reflection still cannot close — keys derived from fields by arithmetic — is stated, with the derived keys declared as fields of one wrapper struct. Four claim corrections ride along: the round-8 "order equality holds ONLY on a first apply" was too categorical and now carries the `charge(A)`-bound proof; the mixed-member two-order rationale was false for its own mutation; "Rust's pendings are exactly A" is false with a shared pool (pendings are per-RULE — corrected to distinct-key granularity); and the Rust `charged ONCE` fail-on-revert named a line that phase-one reservation had made a no-op (measured GREEN), replaced by phase 1's distinct-key dedup (measured RED).

## Hot-path shape

No packet-path change. The resolve pass runs once per config apply; per pool-mode rule it adds one allocator-key construction (already allocated pre-change) and three `saturating_add`s. A same-config re-apply now does strictly LESS work — no per-pool bitmap construction and drop.

## PR #6820 — config/nat: bind the #5628 gate's tolerant-path safety claim [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5717-config-parity`

Advances #5717 (C-CONFIG cohort). Deliberately **not** `Closes` — see "Why this is not
`Closes`" at the bottom.

> **Round 7 rescoped this PR.** Rounds 5 and 6 were reverted. Read "Round 7: what changed
> and why" before reviewing against an older comment thread — several earlier findings are
> about code that is no longer here.

## What this PR does

The #5628 gate hard-rejects a NAT rule whose `then` block carries zero or 2+
mutually-exclusive translation actions at strict commit, but only WARNS on the tolerant
load / peer-sync path (#1960 no-brick). Its contract comment justified that leniency with
two claims about what the dataplane does next. **Neither was bound by a test, and one was
false.**

**Claim 1 — a contradiction is safe because "off-precedence governs (off wins → exempt)".**
True, and load-bearing: it is the only thing stopping a leniently-loaded contradiction from
publishing an authored EXEMPTION as a TRANSLATION. The precedence is decided in Rust on
both paths — `rule.off`'s early return in `nat/source.rs`, the `off`-only branch of
`DnatEntry::to_outcome` — and the Go `isOff` short-circuit in `nat_destination.go` is
CANONICALIZATION, not the decision. Both halves are now pinned, on both sides of the
language boundary. The claim was also over-quantified: `interface` + `pool` carries no
`off`, and interface mode wins there. The comment now says so.

**Claim 2 — "a leniently-loaded actionless rule is inert (installs nothing)".** False in
the way that matters. The SNAT builder EMITS the actionless rule and the Rust matcher's
`else` arm continues, so matching traffic falls through to a later **broader** rule and is
translated by it (DNAT reaches the same outcome by skipping the rule). Where NO later rule
matches, the packet leaves untranslated — a different disposition, pinned separately.

### Operator-visible changes (scoped)

Two rejection strings, emitted verbatim at strict commit and wrapped into a `cfg.Warnings`
entry on the tolerant path (`compiler_uniformgates_firewall_nat2.go`):

- The **zero-action** rejection now states both fall-through outcomes ("translated by a
  later broader rule if one matches, otherwise left untranslated"), replacing wording that
  presumed a later rule exists.
- The **2+-action** rejection no longer claims "the compiler would silently pick one by
  packed-key/child order". That mechanism stopped being used at #5628 for the shapes that
  make this message fire, and was contradicted 116 lines earlier in the same file. It now
  says what happens: every authored action is published and the DATAPLANE resolves the rule
  by a fixed precedence (`off` > `interface` > `pool` for SNAT, `off` > `pool` for DNAT).
  The precedence clause is per-kind, so a destination-NAT rule is not told `interface` beats
  `pool`.

No compiled forwarding artifact changed. The two Rust files are `#[cfg(test)]` modules
(`nat/mod.rs:32-40`), so nothing enters the helper binary. **No cluster smoke owed.**

## PR #6825 — fix(ha): scope HA capability/debt state to its real owner (#5718 C-HA) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-12)

Branch: `fix/5718-ha-hardening`

Closes #5718.

Implements the five items the #5718 audit comment confirmed still
unimplemented on master. C01b/C01c shipped earlier in PR #6376 and are
untouched here.

**STEP-0 re-verification.** The audit was written against `8a69bef9a`;
this branch re-verified every item against current `origin/master`
`ad9591177` before writing code, following the issue's own method note
that a naive item-ID grep hits `docs/reviews/**`, `docs/issues/**` and
`_Log.md` for 100% of items and falsely reads as "all fixed". All five
were still live at the cited file:line.

## What each item was

| Item | Defect |
|---|---|
| `C01a` | `peerHeartbeatAckEver` was `SessionSync`-lifetime, so a peer **downgrade** left the capability latched against a peer that can never satisfy it |
| `A6-b01-C1` | `heartbeatZeroSlots` cast to `uint32` **before** clamping, so `1<<32` narrowed to 0 and zero-initialised nothing |
| `A7-b01-C001` | `networkd.Clear` recorded no reload debt and short-circuited on an empty glob, so the second `Clear` reported a success it had not achieved |
| `A7-b02-C01` | `Manager.Close()` nil-dereferenced on the partial test-manager constructors whose comments promised it nil-guarded them |
| `D-A6-b00-C1` | The user app-set NAT guard was membership-only, so a duplicated member masked a missing one |

### C01a — the heartbeat-ACK capability is peer-incarnation scoped

`peerHeartbeatAckEver` latches when the connected peer replies
`syncMsgHeartbeatAck`. That latch is what switches two paths from
"assume healthy" to "enforce": the `receiveLoop` missed-heartbeat
teardown (two read deadlines with no traffic closes the connection) and
`PeerHealthy()`'s silence window, which `computeUserspaceTransferReadiness`
consults before allowing a manual failover.

It was never cleared, so it outlived the peer incarnation that earned
it. On a peer downgrade — new build acks, peer rolls back to a build
that never acks — the stale latch turns a healthy old peer into
connection churn every two read deadlines plus a permanent "session sync
disconnected" failover block.

It is now cleared in `handleDisconnect`'s **full**-disconnect block,
directly beside `clockSynced` — the sibling peer-incarnation capability
that was already reset correctly, same reason and same place. It is
deliberately **not** cleared on a partial disconnect: one fabric link
dropping while the other holds is the same peer process, and resetting
there would disarm both enforcement paths on every link blip. Both
directions are pinned by tests (see the scope control below).

The durable management cert (#1916 D6) bakes **two** identities into its SANs at
first generation — the HTTPS bind host and the kernel host name — and is
deliberately never re-minted (a re-mint churns remote clients' TOFU pins).
#6378 closed the silence for the bind host only.

A later `set system host-name` leaves the cert's DNS SAN naming the **old**
host. Renaming a firewall does not move its management IP, so the bind-host
check does not fire either — an operator connecting by the new name got a bare

This is **live breakage**, not hygiene. SANs are the only thing a modern client
matches on; CN-only fallback left Go's verifier in 1.15 and browsers/curl years
earlier. The handshake failed before and still fails — what changes is whether
the operator can see why, and that the remedy (`rm -rf /etc/xpf/tls`) appears in
the failure path instead of being undocumented.

## Half 1 — `pkg/api`: what the LOAD path now says, and what it declines to say

`generateSelfSignedCertAt`'s load-success path calls `warnStaleLoadedCert`,
which parses the leaf ONCE and warns per uncovered identity, each line naming
the identity **and** the cert's DNS/IP SANs — so an operator re-mints or
dismisses in one read. All checks share `certCoversHost`, the same strict
`x509.VerifyHostname` classification a remote client applies.

- **`certHasNoSANs` is reported first and is TERMINAL.** A pair persisted by an
  older build (or placed by an operator) can carry no subjectAltName at all, and
  then it covers NOTHING — even `https://localhost` fails. The per-identity

  carries the loopback SANs, which is true only of certs this mint path
  produced; without this check the most broken certificate possible was the one

separate, operator-visible decision; see "What is deliberately not here".

## STEP-0 changed the shape of this fix twice

**The obvious fix would have broken working configs.** `security log stream
facility` is already enum-validated against `syslogFacilities`
(`schema_security.go:688`), so reusing that enum for `system syslog` looks free.
It is not — **`any` is absent from that list but IS honoured here**
(`daemon_system.go:941,975` special-case it into the rsyslog wildcard `*`), so
the naive gate hard-rejects `set system syslog host <h> any info`.

**The vocabularies do not match at all.** Junos names facilities
`authorization`, `kernel`, `interactive-commands`, `conflict-log`, `pfe`.
`ParseFacility` knows only the BSD/rsyslog spellings (`auth`, `kern`, …). I built
a commit-time gate keyed on the mapped set and **reverted it**, because its own
over-rejection test rejected *this issues own worked example*:

```
host 192.0.2.10 { daemon info; authorization critical; }
```

That is valid Junos which silently forwards under **local0** today. Closing the
name set requires first deciding the Junos→BSD mapping, and that decision changes
which facility records leave under — operator-visible, and the half of #5797 that
wants a converged plan.

**A second defect the issue does not describe.** The `file` and `user`
destinations never touch `SyslogClient`: the daemon builds an rsyslog selector
`<facility>.<severity>` and writes a managed drop-in (`daemon_system.go:953,985`).
#4902 belted the file NAME and user TOKEN on that exact line against
leniently-loaded / peer-synced values but left **the two selector tokens
unchecked** — a newline or metacharacter in either escapes the selector and
injects rsyslog configuration. Same threat model, one field short.

## What ships

- **`ParseFacilityChecked`** returns the "was this recognized" bit that
  `ParseFacility` discards, wired into the host client with a warning. The
  substituted code is **deliberately unchanged** — a visibility split, not a
  behaviour change.
- **`syslogSelectorTokenSafe`** shape-checks facility+severity on the file/user
  render path and skips the destination rather than writing an unsafe drop-in.
  A **shape** check on purpose: `[A-Za-z0-9-]` admits the entire legitimate Junos
  vocabulary *including names the mapper cannot resolve*, so the belt cannot
  pre-empt the mapping decision by silently dropping valid destinations.

## PR #6832 — fix(afxdp): ring-guard base cursor + defer zone-counter prune to build success [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5716-afxdp-api-hardening`

Closes #5716

Completes #5716 — codex-review-182 cohort **C-RUST**. That bucket has exactly two ledger rows (`git show origin/master:docs/reviews/archive/codex-review-182.md | grep 'COHORT C-RUST'` → lines 181, 325). **Both were re-verified still live on `origin/master` `ad959117748`** — the issue was only ever verified against `fc479ca65`, so neither turned out to be a stale fixed-not-closed row. Both are fixed here.

Four review rounds have landed on this branch. This body describes the tree **as it now stands**; where a round replaced an earlier round's shape, only the surviving shape is described.

## 1. Ring guards reusable after a terminal op without advancing the base cursor (`A1-b03-C01`)

All four AF_XDP guards in `userspace-dp/src/xsk_ffi.rs` stayed usable after `commit()`/`release()` while `base_idx` stood still, so a guard reused across that boundary aliased the slots it had just handed the kernel:

| Guard | Pre-fix behaviour on reuse |
|---|---|
| `WriteTx::commit` | second `insert()` restarts at `base_idx + 0`, **overwrites** just-submitted descriptors |
| `WriteFill::commit` | same — hands the kernel two RX slots pointing at **one UMEM frame** |
| `ReadComplete::release` | post-release `read()` **re-reaps** completion addresses already returned |
| `ReadRx::release` | sticky `released` flag seals the guard; post-release reads are **never releasable**, `Drop`'s `cancel(peeked - read_count)` under-cancels, `cached_cons` stays permanently ahead of `*consumer` — RX slots leaked for the life of the socket |

Each terminal op now advances `base_idx`. `ReadRx` drops the sticky flag for the advance-and-reset shape `ReadComplete` already used.

**This is API hardening, not a live-path fix.** Every production call site is `create -> insert/read* -> commit/release -> drop` and none crosses a terminal op (audited: `bind.rs` `prime_fill_ring` — its retry loop builds a *fresh* guard per attempt — `tx/rings.rs` reap+refill, `tx/transmit`, `cos/queue_service` ×4, `poll_descriptor`). The single-use path is behaviourally unchanged: the advance decrements `peeked` by the same amount it zeroes from `read_count`, so `Drop` still cancels exactly the peeked-but-unread remainder.

## 2. A rejected forwarding build mutated the live shared zone-counter store (`Z3-C01`)

`ZoneCounterStore` is `Arc`-backed, so the build's carry-forward `clone()` is a **handle on the live map**, not a copy. Binding a candidate to it mutates it **two** ways, and both ran mid-builder, ahead of the fallible `filter_state` and `cos` steps:

- `reconcile` **prunes** the blocks for zones the candidate no longer configures. Both real preflights pass `Some(&self.forwarding)` and on `Err` discard the build — but the live store had already lost the removed zones' totals, so `show security zones` traffic statistics (and REST / Prometheus behind them) reset on a commit that was never applied.
- `ZoneCounterSlotMap::build` **get-or-creates** a block per configured zone. A rejected build therefore left a zero-valued block behind for a candidate-only zone. `snapshot()` omits all-zero rows, so operator-visible counts stay correct and nothing looks wrong — the map just grows by one orphaned block per rejected commit that adds or renumbers a zone, raising the cost of every snapshot, clear and reconcile. Reachable from ordinary config churn.

### The fix is structural, not a moved statement

Round 1 deferred the prune to the last statement before `Ok(state)`. **That shape did not survive review, and is not what merges.** A source-order comment is not a guard, and it was measured not to be one: moving the NPTv6 `?` step below the prune left the entire pre-existing Rust suite green (4280 of 4281 — the single failure was the new zone-block assertion, reporting a different defect).

`build_forwarding_state_with_policy_counters_and_previous` is now a thin wrapper over

- a private `build_fallible_forwarding_state` holding **every** `?` step, which touches no live *zone-counter* state, plus
- a private, infallible `attach_zone_counters` that runs **only after** the `?`.

A fallible step added anywhere in the inner builder is above the `?` by construction, so it cannot become the "step below the prune" that reintroduces the bug. A zone present in both configs keeps its **same** atomic block, which is what stops the #5163 lock-free per-slot fold resetting across a slot renumber.

### The integrity belts are not the whole rejection surface (round 5)

The split above is necessary and it holds — but "the build returned `Ok`" is not "the apply committed". A build can succeed and the apply still be rejected afterwards, by a worker-thread spawn failure (#4952) or an incomplete queue bind (#5143). Measured with live zones `{100,200}` carrying folded traffic, candidate `{100,300}`, and `force_worker_spawn_fail = 1`:

```
before rows=[100, 200] tracked=[100, 200]
reconcile is_err=true variant=WorkerSpawn
after  rows=[100]      tracked=[100, 300]
```

Zone 200's cumulative totals, destroyed for a configuration that never brought up a single worker. The two bring-up failure arms are **not** interchangeable, and the one that matters is the one that keeps reporting: `WorkerBindIncomplete` calls `stop_inner`, which defaults `coord.forwarding`, so the coordinator's own view goes empty; `WorkerSpawn` returns **without** it, leaving the candidate state published — so `show security zones` keeps serving rows from a store whose history for the removed zone is already gone.

`research/5798-frag-assoc-authority` — **both** of its elements, since neither

Defect **LIVE**; nothing has fixed it. `Nat64FragKey` was still exactly

`} else if let Some(hit) = …consult… { hit } else { <input filter / PBR / zone policy> }`,
so a hit returned the first fragment's whole `SessionDecision` before any

Three things the issue body understates, all verified firsthand:

   `.or_else(|| nat_consult_forward_fragment_assoc(…))` to the same arm, so the

machinery at consult time.

*(Search note: `gh pr list --search "5798 in:body"` returns only RFC-5798 VRRP
false positives — the RFC number collides with the issue number.)*

## Element 1 — authority + protocol in the key

`Nat64FragKey` gains the upper-layer protocol and a new `FragAuthority`
(effective logical ingress ifindex + VLAN, effective ingress zone after any
fabric/tunnel override, routing instance). One SSOT helper,
`frag_ingress_authority`, resolves it for **both** install and consult and
mirrors `prerouting_ingress_scope` field for field — the key must derive from
exactly the ingress inputs enforcement uses, or "same key ⟺ same domain" does not
hold and the fix leaks at the seam.

Authority **in the key** (not validated in the value) is **fail-closed by
construction**: a cross-domain fragment computes a *different* key, misses, and
falls through to full enforcement under its own real identity. There is no window
in which a wrong decision is returned and then rejected.

## PR #6838 — config: reject login classes carrying unenforced deny regexes [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5831-rbac-inert-regex-reject`

Advances #5831 — the **fail-closed half** only. Per-command deny
*enforcement* stays open on #5831.

## The defect

`pkg/cli/permissions.go` `checkPermission` is coarse: it matches a required
permission against the class's mapped bucket set and consults **none** of the
four regex sub-statements a custom `system login class` accepts. All four were
"recognized, not enforced". So

```
set system login class limited permissions all
set system login class limited deny-commands "request system zeroize"
```

committed cleanly and could still zeroize the box — a config asserting the verb
was denied, on a box where it was allowed. A security restriction accepted as
inert state is strictly worse than a refused one.

Confirmed on `ad9591177`: `pkg/cli` has **zero** references to any of the four
fields. One correction to the issue's framing — `compiler_system.go` does more
than parse them: `loginClassAdvisoryWarnings` already emitted a `WARNING ...
MORE PERMISSIVE` advisory (#4304 FIX 2). So this is not "silently ignored", it
is "warned about and still ignored". This PR upgrades that warning to a
rejection.

## Directionality — the four fields are NOT symmetric

| Leaf | Junos direction | If xpf ignores it | This PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allow-commands`, `allow-configuration` | **additive** — grants *in addition to* the permission bits | class gets a **subset** of what was written — fail-**closed** | accepted, advisory kept |
| `deny-commands`, `deny-configuration` | **restrictive** — subtracts from the permission bits | denied verbs stay **allowed** — fail-**open** | **rejected at commit** |

Ignoring an additive grant cannot widen anything, so rejecting the allow-\*
half would break configs that are already safe. Junos precedence cuts the same
way: `allow-commands` **wins** over `deny-commands`, so a class pairing them is
a deny-with-exceptions — rejecting on deny-presence alone still catches it, and
no allow leaf makes a deny leaf safe to drop.

## The gate keys off PRESENCE, not value

`deny-commands ""` and a valueless `deny-commands` both flatten to the empty
string — indistinguishable from an absent leaf, so a `!= ""` test accepts them.
But an empty POSIX regex matches every command, i.e. **denies everything** — the
most restrictive thing an operator can write and the most dangerous to drop.
Presence is recorded at parse into `LoginClass.DenyLeavesPresent`, inside the
existing switch, which inherits its dual-AST-shape coverage (the leaf carries
its name in `Keys[0]` in both the flat-set and hierarchical-block shapes; both
are tested).

## PR #6843 — api: restore the per-zone traffic Prometheus surface (#3651) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-06)

Branch: `fix/3651-zone-prom-surface`

Advances #3651.

## The gap

#3651 shipped the per-zone traffic populate path end to end — the Rust helper
accounts ingress/egress packet+byte volume per zone on the forward path
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/zone_counters.rs`), publishes it in
`ProcessStatus.zone_traffic_counters`, and `syncBPFCountersLocked` mirrors each
row into the Go-side offset map via `SetZoneCounterOffset`. `show security
zones` and REST `/security/zones` picked that up immediately.

The Prometheus collector, deleted by the #3643 HIDE, was never brought back
with it. For a period the firewall reported live per-zone volume on the two
interactive surfaces and nothing at all on the one an operator actually alerts
on. That gap is this PR.

## What changed

`xpf_zone_packets_total` / `xpf_zone_bytes_total` are live again, sourced from
the offset map. Labels are unchanged from the pre-#3643 family (`zone`,
`direction` ∈ `{ingress,egress}`), so dashboards and recording rules written
before the gap keep working.

**The reason #3643 dropped the metrics no longer holds; the reason it was RIGHT
to drop them constrains this collector.** The old collector read a dense
`MaxZones*2` per-CPU BPF array indexed by zone id. Stable-hash zone ids live in
`[1,65533]` (#3075) while `MaxZones` is 64, so essentially every real zone OOB'd
the bounded `Lookup` and the error branch bumped `xpf_counter_read_errors_total`
once per zone **per scrape** — a permanent false alert on the #3345 signal. This
collector's only read is `dp.ReadZoneCounters`, which since #3643 keys a sparse
`map[uint16][2]CounterValue` and never indexes anything by position; a large id
is an ordinary map miss.

**New: `xpf_zone_counters_unpopulated_zones`, and omission instead of
zero-fill.** The helper's status snapshot is sparse and drops all-zero rows
(`ZoneCounterStore::snapshot`), so `ErrCounterNotPopulated` cannot distinguish
three states: a pre-#3651 helper, a zone past the helper's 63 assignable
hot-path slots whose traffic genuinely goes uncounted, and a zone that is merely
idle. Publishing `0` would be correct only for the last and would silently
understate the first two as "no traffic" — an authoritative zero over an
unknown. So the samples are omitted and this gauge carries the count. It is
emitted on every path (0 when healthy) so `> 0` is alertable and its absence
means the scrape did not run. It counts exactly the zones REST reports
`per_zone_counters_available:false` for, and that coherence is asserted, not
just claimed.

Unpopulated deliberately does **not** bump `xpf_counter_read_errors_total` — it
is a legitimate steady state, and routing it there is precisely the false alert
#3643 removed the family to stop. A genuine read failure still skips the samples
and bumps, per #3345/#3408.

## PR #6851 — sessions: stop rendering policy_id 0 as the first configured policy (#4626) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-06)

Branch: `fix/4626-policy-id-zero`

## Summary

- `policy_id` 0 is overloaded: `compilePolicies` assigns `policySetID*MaxRulesPerPolicy + i`, so the first rule of the first zone-pair genuinely has id 0 — and the userspace dataplane stamps 0 on every session **no policy admitted**. `publish_conntrack.rs` says so at the stamping site: "`0` stays the value for non-policy-forwarded sessions".
- That population is host-inbound, neighbor-seed, fabric and tunnel installs, every pre-#3056 session, and **every session synced from an older HA peer during a rolling upgrade** — the peer's whole table.
- Six session-row render sites indexed `CompileResult.PolicyNames` directly, where key 0 holds the first configured policy. `show security flow session`, REST `/sessions` and gRPC `GetSessions` therefore all reported that a specific policy admitted traffic it never saw. REST and gRPC had **no** numeric fallback, so the wrong name went unconditionally into a structured field automation consumes.
- Adds `dataplane.SessionPolicyName`, which takes both reserved ids (0 and `DefaultPolicySentinelID`) before consulting the map, and routes all six sites through it. Unreserved ids resolve exactly as a direct index did, including `""` for an absent id, so each caller keeps its existing not-found behaviour.

## Scope — this does not close L01 as the issue words it

#4626 L01 asks to **reserve the id space** so real policies start at 1. That is a cross-plane change (userspace-dp `policy.rs`, the #3056 stamping path, runtime-id assignment, HA wire compatibility), it has no approved research plan, and **it cannot fix the case that matters most**: an older HA peer keeps sending a bare 0 for its entire table throughout the upgrade window regardless of the local id space. A render-side guard is required either way and is not made redundant by that work.

This PR removes the misattribution. The id-space half of L01 stays open.

## Why `unattributed` rather than a policy name

The wire value is ambiguous and nothing else on the session disambiguates it — `SessionValue`'s flag bits are NAT-only (`SessFlagSNAT`/`DNAT`/`StaticNAT`/`NAT64`/`NPTV6`), with no host-inbound, fabric or tunnel marker. So every possible rendering is wrong for one of the two populations.

Under-claiming is the safer error on a security surface: an operator who sees `unattributed` investigates, whereas one who sees a real policy name on a host-inbound session may leave a rule in place believing it is load bearing. It is also the direction already chosen for this identical overload on the **behavioral** path — `deletedPolicyRuntimeIDs` excludes id 0 as a documented "fail-SAFE under-clear". The display should not claim a precision the wire cannot support while the enforcement path refuses to.

The numeric id is still shown beside the name on every surface (`Policy name: unattributed/0`; REST/gRPC carry `policy_id` as its own field), so nothing is hidden.

## Test plan

- [x] `dataplane.SessionPolicyName` unit tests — fixture deliberately **occupies id 0** with a real policy, which is the whole defect; a fixture without it passes against broken code.
- [x] REST `sessionEntryV4`/`V6` and gRPC `sessionEntryV4`/`V6` driven directly (4 of 6 render sites).
- [x] AST canary covering all six sites plus any seventh added later, with its scope stated explicitly.
- [x] Over-rejection controls: an admitted session still names its policy; the #3057 `default-policy` sentinel still renders.
- [x] Full `pkg/dataplane`, `pkg/api`, `pkg/grpcapi`, `pkg/cli`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/logging`, `pkg/refactoraudit` suites pass. No existing golden asserted the old attribution.
- [ ] Cluster/smoke not run — display-layer change, and smoke is scheduled centrally.

### Mutation matrix

Snapshot-and-write-back restore with a byte-for-byte verify; every mutant required to **compile** before scoring, so no RED is a build break.

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Revert the CLI pair (`printV4`/`printV6`) | RED |
| Revert the REST pair | RED |
| Revert the gRPC pair | RED |
| Revert all six at once (= master) | RED |
| Guard consults the map FIRST, falls back to the pseudo-name | RED |
| Drop the reserved-zero arm | RED |
| Blank every policy name | RED |

The map-first mutation is the one worth naming: it still looks like a guard and guards nothing whenever a first policy exists. The `LOAD-BEARING` comment on that arm exists for it.

The two CLI sites are bound **only** by the AST canary — they are closures printing to real stdout behind a live dataplane, so no cheap behavioural test reaches them. That limit is stated in the canary rather than left implicit.

## PR #6858 — class-of-service: add `show class-of-service rewrite-rule` (#6848) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6848-cos-show-rewrite-rule`

Closes #6848

Advances #4228 (Gap 7 residual).

## The gap

`show class-of-service` had `interface`, `classifier`, `scheduler-map` and
`forwarding-class`. `rewrite-rule` — the fifth Junos CoS show command — was
never wired.

It matters more now than when #4228 was written. At that point `rewrite-rules`
held only `dscp`, so the missing command hid one table. Since then the config
models three more families — `ieee-802.1` (#4228 Gap 4), `inet-precedence` and
`exp` (#4316) — and **all three are accepted-but-inert**: they commit clean and
have no runtime effect, because the dataplane rewrites DSCP on egress only.

So an operator could configure four kinds of rewrite rule, three of which do
nothing, with **no command to display any of them**. The only signal was a
commit-time advisory that scrolls past once.

## Enforcement is a column, not a footnote

```
Rewrite rule: rw-dscp, Code point type: dscp, Enforced: yes
  Forwarding class  Loss priority  Code point
  best-effort       low            000000
  premium           low            101110

Rewrite rule: rw-pcp, Code point type: ieee-802.1, Enforced: no (accepted for
Junos compatibility; the dataplane rewrites dscp only)
  Forwarding class  Loss priority  Code point
  premium           high           101
```

Rendering an inert rule identically to an enforced one would reproduce, inside
the command built to expose the problem, exactly the silence that made it worth
fixing. The marker names what the operator loses rather than only that a flag is
off.

## The four families do not carry equal data

`dscp` and `ieee-802.1` compile to full entry lists. `inet-precedence` and `exp`
record only rule **names** — the compiler builds no runtime structure because
nothing consumes one. Those render `Code points not modeled` rather than an
empty table, which would imply a fidelity the config does not have.

`TestShowTextCoSRewriteRuleNameOnlyFamiliesAreProducible6848` authors such a
rule **with** a code point in real `set` syntax and asserts the value does not
surface — so if the compiler ever starts modeling those entries, the test fails
and says to render them, rather than leaving a view that quietly under-reports

## PR #6861 — config: reject tunnel mode ipip at commit instead of accepting a dead tunnel (#4785) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-12)

Branch: `fix/4785-ipip-reject`

## Summary

IPIP (ip-in-ip, proto-4/41) parses, compiles, creates a Tuntap routing anchor and reaches the dataplane snapshot — and then passes no traffic in either direction. The userspace helper is the only supported runtime and has no IPIP primitive:

- **inbound**: `forwarding_build/tunnels.rs` enters an endpoint into `gre_decap_index` only when `tunnel_mode_kind(&endpoint.mode) == TunnelKind::Gre`. `tunnel_mode_kind` maps `gre`/`ip6gre` and `wireguard`; `ipip` falls to `TunnelKind::Unknown`, so it is never indexed and a received proto-4 frame has nothing to decap against.
- **outbound**: `TunnelKind::Unknown` is the egress encap dispatcher's fail-closed drop arm, as that enum's own doc states.

Before this, the config committed green with only the #4788 advisory: a configured, UP interface that carries nothing and no error to act on. This converts the advisory into a commit gate — the "reject, don't guess" resolution.

`validateIpipTunnelUnimplementedStrict` is wired in `compiler_tailgates.go` beside `validateTunnelOuterFamilyStrict`, whose shape it mirrors: strict on commit / commit-check, downgraded to a warning on the tolerant load / peer-sync paths via the new `lenientIpipTunnelMode` opt.

## ⚠️ Behaviour change: a config that commits today will stop committing

An operator with an IPIP stanza currently commits successfully and gets a dead tunnel. After this they get a hard commit error. That is the point, but it is a real change and it is worth being precise about the blast radius:

- The gate evaluates the **whole candidate config**, not the delta. So an operator whose *active* config already carries an IPIP stanza cannot commit **any** change — including an unrelated one — until they remove or convert it. This is how every strict gate in this file behaves, but it is the part an operator actually feels.
- `mode ipip` is **not only written explicitly**. `compileInterfaces` infers it from an `ip-*` interface name (and `gre` from `gr-*`), so a config that never types "ipip" is affected. The error message names the inference.
- The gate keys on the compiled **mode**, not the interface name, so `ip-0/0/0 tunnel mode gre` still commits. A name-keyed gate would take working GRE tunnels down — that is mutation M7 below.

## No-brick (#1960) — checked, not assumed

- `Store.Load` and `Store.SyncApply` compile through `compileTreeLenient` → `CompileConfigLenient` → `lenientCompileOpts()`. The new opt is set there, so an already-committed IPIP config still **boots**, with a warning. Pinned by `TestIpipTunnelWarnsOnTolerantPath_4785`.
- **The commit-confirmed rollback path does not reach this gate**, so no check was added there. `CommitConfirmed` stashes `s.confirmPrevCfg = s.compiled` — the already-compiled active config, by reference — `PromoteRollback` returns that value, and the daemon applies it directly via `applyConfigLocked(prevCfg)`. No compile runs on that path. Scoped precisely: this is a statement about *that* path, not a claim that no rollback target anywhere is ever recompiled. A check there would have guarded nothing, so stating the reasoning is the honest alternative to adding a decorative one.

## Pre-existing tests

Three tests (`TestIPIPTunnelSetSyntax`, `TestIPIPTunnelExplicitMode`, `TestIPIPTunnelWithRoutingInstance`) compiled IPIP through `CompileConfig` and expected success. Their subject is field parsing and mode inference, not commit acceptance, so they now compile through `CompileConfigLenient` — the path that still accepts this config — each with a note saying why. They double as the tolerant-path canary: M4 and M5 below are caught by them.

A first pass over-applied that switch to three *passing* GRE tests (`TestGRETunnelRoutingInstanceDestination`, `TestPointToPointFlag`, `TestInterfaceLevelTunnelLinuxName`); those were reverted to strict `CompileConfig`, which is the stronger assertion and the one they want.

## Test plan

- [x] Strict rejection driven through the real entry point (`CompileConfig`), covering the inferred `ip-*` case, explicit `mode ipip` on a `gr-*` interface, and unit-level tunnels.
- [x] Tolerant path warns and still compiles, preserving the stanza.
- [x] Over-rejection guard: GRE by prefix, explicit `mode gre` on an `ip-*` interface, unit-level GRE, an `ip-*` interface with no tunnel stanza, and a config with no interfaces.
- [x] Determinism: 50 runs assert the lowest sorted name is reported first (Go map order is randomized, and both HA nodes must report identically); lenient path reports every offender.
- [x] Full `go test ./pkg/... ./cmd/...` passes.
- [ ] Cluster/smoke not run — config-layer change, and smoke is scheduled centrally.

### Mutation matrix

Snapshot-and-write-back restore with a byte-for-byte verify; every mutant required to **compile** before scoring.

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| Unwire the gate | RED |
| Wire it, swallow the error | RED |
| Hardcode lenient (old behaviour dressed as a gate) | RED |
| Hardcode strict (loses the #1960 downgrade) | RED |
| Never set the tolerant opt (same brick, other route) | RED |

## PR #6862 — test(ha): scope sync-import refusal counters per Coordinator [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-06)

Branch: `fix/6819-ha-counter-scoping`

Closes #6819

## The defect

Seven `#[test]` fns in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha_tests.rs` used **process-global** `AtomicU64` statics as their before/after baseline. Cargo runs tests concurrently in one process, so one test's intentional stale-generation install, stale-generation delete, or over-ceiling import bumped a global another test was asserting had **not** moved.

Measured at pristine `origin/master` ad9591177, full `cargo test --release`, each run bounded at 900 s:

```
SEQUENCE[before]: FAIL FAIL HUNG FAIL FAIL
suite: 0 PASS / 4 FAIL / 1 HUNG
#6819 participant tests failed in 5 of 5 runs
```

That is 5-of-5, not the issue's 3-of-5, because of a scoring detail worth reusing: **the trailing `failures:` block never prints on a wedged run**, so scoring off that block alone counts a wedged run as *clean* — and the run that hung had already failed a #6819 test before wedging. Score off the union of the `failures:` block and the per-test `... FAILED` lines, which survive the wedge. Any harness measuring flake rate against this suite has that bug until it does the same.

## Why the issue's suggested fix wouldn't have worked

The issue offers "make the assertions DELTA-based" as option 2. **They already are** — every one captures `let before = ...` and asserts `before + 1`. That is not sufficient, because a concurrent test's increment lands *inside* the capture window. Recomputing a delta over shared state still observes the other writer. Only a per-instance home removes the dependency, which is the issue's option 3.

## The fix

Three counters move out of `afxdp/bpf_map/metrics.rs` onto `SessionManager`, beside the existing per-instance `export_seq`:

| was (process-global) | now (per-Coordinator) | |
|---|---|---|
| `SESSION_INSTALL_STALE_IGNORED` | `sessions.install_stale_ignored` | #2170 |
| `SESSION_DELETE_STALE_IGNORED` | `sessions.delete_stale_ignored` | #2170 |
| `SYNCED_IMPORT_CAP_DROPS` | `sessions.import_cap_drops` | #5674 |

Every bump site (`ha/session_import.rs:82`, `:118`, `:278`) and every read site (`coordinator/status.rs:207`, `:214`, `:227`) already held a `&self` `Coordinator`, so there are no signature or call-graph changes. This mirrors an existing convention: `Coordinator` already documents three test seams as *"per-instance, NOT a process-global … so parallel tests never race."*

**`ha_tests.rs` is untouched** — no assertion weakened, relaxed or deleted, no `--test-threads=1`, no `#[serial]`, no `>=` tautology.

### The single-Coordinator invariant is load-bearing

"No production behaviour change" rests entirely on production building exactly one `Coordinator`. A second one would silently convert three process-wide sums into three per-instance tallies, so this was established exhaustively rather than by inspecting the obvious site:

- Every `Coordinator::new()` call site enumerated; all but one are under `#[cfg(test)]`. **Two do not live in `*_tests.rs` files and so don't look like tests at a glance**: `coordinator/reconcile/snapshot.rs:801` (inside the `cfg(test)` module opening at `:643`) and `worker/launch.rs:292/301/355` (inside the one opening at `:287`).
- The sole non-test construction is `server/lifecycle.rs:315`, in the one-shot startup initializer of the shared `ServerState` — not in a loop, not in a re-entrant function.
- No `impl Default for Coordinator`, and no struct-literal construction: `Coordinator {` matches only `impl` blocks.
- The `afxdp` field holding it is never reassigned outside tests, so no restart path swaps in a fresh `Coordinator` mid-process.

So the per-instance counters have exactly the lifetime the statics had — created once at startup, never replaced, live until exit. gRPC and Prometheus values are identical.

### Scope note: three counters, not two

`import_cap_drops` is included deliberately rather than deferred. It sits three lines below the other two in the same static block, is asserted in the same `== before + N` form by two tests that **both** bump it (ha_tests.rs:789/806/849/912), and failed in the same measured run. Deferring it would leave the gate red for the identical reason.

## PR #6864 — dataplane: observe-only arm-coverage proof (#5275 PR1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-06)

Branch: `fix/5275-arm-failclosed`

Advances #5275 — **PR1 of a phased fix**. This PR **gates nothing**.

## The defect (re-verified on current master)

A config that COMPILES but whose dataplane fails to ARM degrades a cold-booted firewall to a policy-free router:

- ownership, VIP/RA/Kea, VRRP and `enableForwarding` are all published in `initManagers` (`daemon_run_bringup.go:47`, forwarding at `:215`) **before** the arm at `:414`;
- an attach failure surfaces through `d.dp.ApplyConfig` as an **ordinary #5679 deferred error** — `compileErrorMustAbortApply` matches only `IsRequiredProtocolGateError` — so the apply tail still publishes.

## Why observe-only first

"Armed" today is materially weaker than the proof the eventual gate will apply. `attachUserspaceShimXDP` treats a **native** XDP attach failure as a warning: it detaches and re-attaches in **generic (skb) mode**, and only a *generic* failure returns an error. A box therefore reports itself armed while running the whole shim on the fallback path — and iavf SR-IOV VFs have **no native XDP support at all**, so that is a supported steady state, not a misconfiguration.

That is a known population which a stricter proof could silently fail closed, on a boot path, where nobody is watching. So this PR measures the divergence rate across real deployments before the gate is ever load-bearing. `ArmCoverageReport.WouldGate` is a diagnostic; no caller branches on it.

## Coverage is three-valued — a correction to the plan

The converged plan (§5/D1) specifies strict program-instance identity "on every mapped attach point (**native or generic**)". That binary is wrong.

Under the userspace shim a **VLAN sub-interface is never attached** — both attach loops skip it and it is recorded in `Manager.VlanSubInterfaces` — because the parent's XDP sees VLAN-tagged frames before kernel VLAN demuxing, and attaching the child breaks IPv6 NDP under generic-mode `XDP_PASS`. Policy *is* enforced, at a different attach point.

Implemented literally, the plan's proof fails on every VLAN sub-interface. The loss cluster runs `reth0.50`/`reth0.80`; the standalone VM runs VLAN 50. It would fail-close essentially every real deployment. The opposite shortcut — skip VLAN children unconditionally — would pass a surface whose coverage was never checked.

| Kind | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `direct` | A shim instance is attached here. **Native and generic both count.** |
| `delegated` | No attach expected here by design; the **parent** covers it, and the parent is **resolved**. |
| `uncovered` | Nothing here and no proven delegate — including a failed readback. |

Both decisions are written into the definition **and pinned by tests**, deliberately, because an implicit behaviour survives only until someone "tightens" it — and the tightening flips a supported deployment to fail-closed with nobody intending it.

`CoverageUncovered` is the iota **zero** value so an unpopulated entry reads as not-covered: a partially-built report can only ever be more conservative.

The skb-mode population is measured by reading the attach mode back from the KERNEL (`RTM_GETLINK` -> `LinkAttrs.Xdp.AttachMode`), not from compile bookkeeping. An earlier draft recorded a `fallbackGenericIfindexes` field on the compile result; fold round 1 deleted it, because the native->generic fallback happens once and the `m.xdpLinks` entry survives every later compile, so `AttachXDP` short-circuits on "already attached" and the per-compile record is empty from compile #2 onward while the box is still on skb-mode — it would have reported "went native" on exactly the iavf SR-IOV population it exists to count.

## Validation

`TMPDIR=/tmp go test ./pkg/dataplane/... ./pkg/daemon/...` — all six packages **ok**, exit 0. `gofmt` + `go vet` clean on every touched file (`pkg/dataplane/constants.go` is gofmt-unclean on `origin/master` too and was left alone).

### Mutation proofs

Six mutations, each snapshotted and restored byte-for-byte with sha256 verification, scored from real `go test` exit codes. All produced **assertion** failures with `go vet` exit 0:

| Guard reverted | RED |
|---|---|
| generic fallback treated as NOT armed | the fallback test — this is the fail-close-a-supported-deployment bug |
| delegated branch removed (VLAN child demands its own attach) | the delegation test |
| delegation ASSUMED rather than resolved | the resolved test |
| failed instance readback treated as covered | two tests |
| surface ordering unsorted | the determinism test |

## PR #6865 — cluster: require an authenticated session-sync peer when keyed (#5078 PR1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-06)

Branch: `fix/5078-syncauth`

First of several PRs for #5078. Covers **Blocker 2 only** (plan §3.10). No wire-format change, and — as of r2 — **no config-surface change either**.

## Why this is separable, and first

Blocker 2 is exploitable with **no PSK and no reflection**. A keyed node dual-accepted an unkeyed peer whenever the sticky downgrade guard had not yet armed — a window open on *every fresh boot*, since "before the guard arms" is exactly when a node starts. That peer's first frame, consumed by the handshake read, executed **before** the connection was installed, and `syncMsgFence` on that path reaches `OnFenceReceived` and disables every routing group. The same connection then displaced the legitimate peer's, and arming the guard later did not evict it.

## Changes

**A keyed node requires an authenticated peer.** `syncAuthDecision` no longer consults `peerAuthSeen` for the unkeyed-peer branch. It cannot: the entire exposure is the pre-arm window, so a predicate that only fires *after* arming can never cover it. That is the shape of the old bug, not just its location — which is why this is a removal rather than a reordering.

**The pre-admission frame mechanism is deleted, not reordered.** With the dual-accept grace gone, `pendingFrame`'s only producer sits behind a decision that always rejects, so the mechanism is unreachable. `pendingFrame`, `performSyncHandshake`'s third return value, and the call site are removed — unreachable code that mutates cluster state before admission is one edit from being live again. The legacy arm rejects **unconditionally** and consults `syncAuthDecision` only for the reason string, so re-introducing a grace in the decision cannot silently reopen the path.

## r2: the migration window was removed, and its justification was wrong

r1 shipped `authentication-migration-window`. The gate found three MAJORs, **all against that knob** — it bounded admission but not connection *lifetime*; an admitted peer could re-arm it through config-sync; and its in-memory arming granted a fresh interval on every restart.

The root cause was my justification. I claimed a rolling key rollout would **deadlock** without it, since config-sync delivers the key over this channel and keying the primary first strands it from the unkeyed secondary. **That was wrong.** `authentication-key` is an ordinary config leaf, so the operator commits it locally on each node; two unkeyed nodes still dual-accept unchanged, so sync works until the first node is keyed and is authenticated once the second is. The gap is a brief operator-controlled sync outage, not a deadlock.

A convenience that needs three guards of its own does not belong inside the fix that closes the hole. It is removed entirely — leaf, typed field, compiler arm, manager state, provider method, alarm — and `golden_4406.json` is **byte-identical to master again**.

What remains is the property a security appliance should have: **a node must possess the key to join a keyed cluster.** A fresh or RMA node is keyed locally as part of the same bootstrap that gives it its node-id.

**Rollout procedure:** commit `authentication-key` locally on each node. Session sync is down between the two commits, so avoid a failover in that gap; key the standby first if you want the primary serving throughout.

## Net diff

Five files: `pkg/cluster/{sync_auth.go, sync_auth_test.go, sync_conn.go, README.md}` and `_Log.md`. No config, no wire format, no schema.

## Plan reference rot (for the next PR)

The plan's premises are all live — `sync_auth.go` is byte-identical to the base it was written against — but `sync_conn.go` was refactored -1506/+692 into five files, so its citations were stale. **Corrected in place on `research/5078-syncauth-reflection` (`2d2390dfd`)**, nine references fixed and three left marked unverified rather than guessed. #5303 pre-closed most of §3.11.

## Both-sides check (Go + Rust)

Nothing in `userspace-dp/` references `syncMagic` or the sealed frame format; `session_sync.rs` encodes deltas that ride as payload **inside** the Go frame. This leg is Go-only. To be re-grepped before any framing change.

## Test plan

- [x] `syncAuthDecision` matrix rewritten for the fail-closed policy
- [x] `TestSyncAuthHandshakeKeyedNodeRejectsLegacyPeer` — replaces a green test that asserted the **opposite** ("so the stream stays legacy-compatible (no brick)" — the vulnerability written down as a requirement). Replaced rather than deleted, with the reason recorded in the replacement
- [x] Mutation: restore the grace → `legacy_peer_rejected_when_keyed` + `unkeyed_peer_rejected_when_keyed` RED, build+vet rc=0 first, snapshot restored and `sha256sum -c` verified
- [x] **No runtime mutation for the pre-admission half, deliberately.** That path is gone from the type system, so reordering it is a build break, not an assertion RED — claiming a mutation there would be dressing up a compile error. r1's version of that test had itself gone vacuous when its fixture changed, which is how the unreachability was found
- [x] `go vet ./...` clean; `gofmt` clean
- [ ] **`make test-failover` — NOT run.** Session-sync changes require it; scheduled separately

**Known unrelated flake:** a whole-repo run intermittently reds `pkg/ddns`. Established as not from this change — `pkg/ddns` and `pkg/config` are byte-identical to master here and `pkg/ddns` does not import `pkg/cluster` — measured 0/8 on branch and 0/8 on master standalone, and filed as #6867 rather than re-run to green.

## PR #6866 — daemon: route external dataplane consumers through a revocable facade (#5275 PR2) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5275-facade`

Advances #5275 — **PR2 of a phased fix**, stacked on #6864. This PR **gates nothing**.

> Base is `fix/5275-arm-failclosed` (PR1), not master. Retarget to master once PR1 merges.

## The defect

`d.dp = nil` does not contain the backend. gRPC, REST and the CLI capture a backend **alias at construction** and hold it for the process lifetime, so they keep a live handle after the daemon has dropped its own. Several methods they reach are mutators — `SetForwardingArmed`, `SetQueueState`, `SetBindingState` via the CLI's `userspaceDataplaneControl` path — that **never traverse the apply gate**. On bootstrap-exit, management already holds the backend when a later arm fails.

Every external consumer now holds a shared **revocable facade** instead. Revoking it stops all of them at once, atomically and stickily.

## What this PR does NOT do

The facade is constructed **LIVE** and nothing revokes it in production. Deliberate: pure indirection, behaviour-identical, cannot leave the system half-armed. The plan's "starts SEALED, opened at the final arm proof" is a change to the *constructor* and the *release path*, and belongs with the PR that gates. `Revoke()` is implemented and tested here so the mechanism is proven before anything depends on it.

## Scope came from the audit, not the plan's wording

§7 says "gRPC/REST/CLI capture backend aliases" as if one shape. `runtime_probes.go` declares **three separate structural mirrors** — `grpcDataPlane`, `apiDataPlane`, `cliDataPlane` — that overlap heavily but are not the same set. The facade satisfies their **union** (27 unique methods); each mirror keeps its own compile-time drift check at its own assignment site.

Going the other way: `PolicySchedulerActiveStateFn` *looks* like a capture but is a **closure over `d`** that re-reads `d.dp` per call. It is already revocable and already fails closed (#3414), so it is deliberately left alone. Of 164 `d.dp` references across 28 files, only the construction sites are the problem.

## No interface embedding — on purpose

Embedding would make the facade ~10 lines, and it is wrong in a way review would not catch: **an embedded interface silently forwards every method not overridden**, so a method later added to the backend bypasses the gate *by default*, and the failure direction is open. Explicit delegation makes a new backend method a **compile error** until someone decides its gate behaviour. The verbosity is the point; the reasoning is in the file so a future "simplify this" has to argue with it.

## Fail-safe details

- `setDataplane` replaces direct `d.dp` assignment at all five sites and **revokes the outgoing facade** rather than only repointing the field — a consumer constructed earlier still holds the old object.
- `facadeClosed` is the iota **zero**, so a zero-valued or forgotten facade grants nothing; a nil facade fails closed rather than panicking.
- `newDataplaneFacade` returns **nil** for an absent/unsuitable backend, preserving today's nil-DP semantics exactly. A non-nil facade over nothing would flip consumers' nil checks — a behaviour change in a PR whose whole claim is that it makes none.

## Validation

`TMPDIR=/tmp go test ./pkg/daemon/... ./pkg/dataplane/... ./pkg/cli/... ./pkg/grpcapi/... ./pkg/api/... ./pkg/configstore/...` — all green, exit 0. `gofmt` + `go vet` clean.

The #1451 retirement import-allowlist canary caught both new files; it and its docs table are updated. That canary is path-keyed, so it fires on any new `pkg/dataplane` importer by design.

### Mutation proofs

Four mutations, snapshotted and restored byte-for-byte with sha256 verification, all **assertion**-RED with `go vet` exit 0:

| Guard reverted | RED |
|---|---|
| **gRPC re-pointed at the raw backend** (the exact pre-facade code) | the completeness test |
| `setDataplane` repoints without revoking | the captured-handle test |
| `live()` ignoring revocation | three tests |
| a direct `d.dp` assignment sneaking back in | the assignment-discipline test |

The first is the one that matters. Such a change **compiles and passes every behavioural test** while silently reinstating the un-revocable alias — the facade still works perfectly for whoever still holds it. That is why the completeness test scans the construction sites rather than only exercising behaviour.

**No cluster or smoke validation:** changes no forwarding behaviour and gates nothing.

## PR #6869 — daemon: fold activeClusterTransport under the comms epoch guard [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6290-cluster-transport-lock`

`activeClusterTransport` was written by `startClusterComms` while holding neither `clusterCommsMu` nor `applySem`, and read by `applyTailReconciles` step 20 under `applySem`.

## The issue's "NOT a race today" is wrong

#6290 reasoned that the boot `startClusterComms` completes before the gRPC/HTTP servers accept commits, so the write is visible before any reader. That accounts for the wrong readers — `applyConfig`'s own doc lists **DHCP callbacks, config-poll, dynamic feeds, event engine, in-process CLI commits, CLI auto-rollback, cluster sync recv**, none of which are the gRPC or HTTP servers.

The DHCP one is live *before* the write:

```
daemon_run_bringup.go  dhcp.New(..., d.onDHCPAddressChange, ...)   callback wired
daemon_run_bringup.go  boot d.applyConfig(cfg)
 -> daemon_apply_routing.go  reconcileDHCPClients(cfg)             client goroutines START
daemon_run.go          d.startClusterComms(ctx)                    the WRITE happens here
```

A lease arriving in that window runs `onDHCPAddressChange` → `applyConfig` → step 20, which **reads** the field. The DHCP client goroutines were created *before* the write, so goroutine creation orders them the wrong way and supplies no happens-before; `applySem` cannot bridge it because a semaphore only excludes participants that take it, and the boot writer does not hold it at the write. This is the mirror of #5113 on `mgmtVRFInterfaces` — written under `applySem`, read by this same callback without it — which `daemon.go` already documents as "a real Go data race".

The callback itself runs on a runtime timer goroutine, not on a DHCP client goroutine: `pkg/dhcp/dhcp.go` arms it via `time.AfterFunc(2s, …)`. The conclusion is unaffected — `AfterFunc` happens-before `f`, so the callback inherits the client goroutine's happens-before set as of the `scheduleRecompile` call, and that set does not contain the boot write.

## Fix

`setActiveTransportIfCurrent(gen, key)`, epoch-gated like `publishSessionSyncIfCurrent` rather than a bare locked store: the same window admits two concurrent `startClusterComms` calls (boot + a DHCP-driven restart from step 20), and an ungated store lets the loser land last, leaving the transport key describing a superseded epoch while `clusterCommsGen` names the live one. Step 20 now takes ONE `activeTransport()` snapshot, which serves six uses — the non-zero test, the inequality test, and its four `old_*` log fields (the four `new_*` fields come from the locally-computed `newTransport` and were never shared state).
