## PR #7118 — daemon: fail the HA fence when the rg_active clear fails [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6371-fence-verdict`

## The defect

`watchClusterEvents`' demotion branch cleared `rg_active` and then called
`d.signalFailoverActuated(ev.GroupID)` **unconditionally**. The `SetRGActive`
error path only logged a WARN and fell through to that same call, and
`signalFailoverActuated` consulted no applied state, so `waitFailoverActuated`
released the remote-failover applied-ack **even when the clear had FAILED** —
telling the peer to promote while this node may still have been forwarding for
the redundancy group. That is the two-owner window #5640 was written to close,
reopened by its own error path. `git log -S'signalFailoverActuated' --
pkg/daemon/` returns exactly one commit (`e5c61b59d`, #5640): nothing had
fenced the failure path since it was introduced.

## The fix

The fence barrier now carries a **verdict**, not bare completion.

- `failoverActuation{done, resolved, err}` replaces the plain `chan struct{}`.
  `err` is written under `failoverActuateMu` *before* `done` is closed, so every
  observer of the close also observes the verdict.
- The demotion branch records the `SetRGActive` error and resolves through the
  new `signalFailoverActuationFailed` instead of `signalFailoverActuated`.
- `waitFailoverActuated` returns that verdict, so `handleRemoteFailover`
  downgrades the ack to `failoverAckFailed` (existing code) and the peer
  **holds** instead of joining a split-brain.

Resolving with a failure rather than staying silent is deliberate: silence would
park the waiter for its whole `failoverActuateTimeout` on a fence already known
not to have landed, delaying the peer's failover by seconds for no gain.

A resolved barrier is now **left in the map** for `waitFailoverActuated` to
consume, where the old success-only path deleted it at signal time. With
deletion, a resolution landing before the waiter arrives reads as "never armed",
which `waitFailoverActuated` maps to success — discarding exactly the failure
verdict this path exists to deliver. A re-arm replaces the entry, so the map
stays bounded by the RG count.

## Why the refactor

`cluster.Manager` exposes only a receive-only `Events()`, so the demotion branch
was unreachable from any test — the fix would have been unbindable. The
per-event body is split out as
`handleClusterEvent(ctx, ev, vrrpTimer) *time.Timer`: pure movement, with the
VRRP debounce timer (the only loop-carried state) threaded through the argument
and return value, and the dual-active `continue` becoming `return vrrpTimer`.

## Validation

Five new tests drive the real path. `TestFailoverActuation_*` primes RG1 to
cluster-primary, arms the barrier, calls `cluster.ManualFailover` (what

## PR #7119 — config: compile fab0 members from every AST shape [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6694-fabric-member-interfaces`

## Problem

`interfaces { fab0 { fabric-options { member-interfaces [ ge-0/0/0 ge-0/0/1 ]; } } }`
compiled an **empty** member list. `compiler_interfaces.go` descended `miNode.Children`
only, and the hierarchical bracket spelling — the idiomatic Junos one for a two-member
fabric — carries every name on the node's own `Keys` with no children at all.

`fab0` is the chassis-cluster fabric: session sync, config sync, IPsec SA sync and the
cross-chassis forwarding path that keeps TCP alive across a VRRP failback all ride it. A
fabric with zero compiled members cannot form, the commit is green, and the symptom appears
only under HA.

## Finding the issue did NOT describe

The same `Children`-only descent also emptied the plain single-value hierarchical spelling
`member-interfaces ge-0/0/7;`. A **one-member fab0 authored in a config FILE** (load merge,
day-0 import, rescue config) lost its member too. Flat `set` is unaffected in that shape,
which is why the existing flat-set cluster tests never caught it. Same site, same one-line
fix, so it is folded in here rather than filed separately.

## Enumeration — six spellings, measured

| spelling | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `member-interfaces { a; b; }` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` |
| `member-interfaces [ a b ];` | `[]` | `[a b]` |
| `member-interfaces a;` | `[]` | `[a]` |
| `member-interfaces a; member-interfaces b;` | `[]` | `[a b]` |
| `set ... member-interfaces <a>` (x2) | `[a b]` | `[a b]` |
| `set ... member-interfaces [ a b ]` | `[a]` | `[a b]` |

Four of six spellings were broken.

## Why not `firewallMatchValues`

The SSOT helper reads `Keys[1:]` of the node plus **`Keys[0]` of each child**. The
flat-set bracket list for this leaf files every name on **one child's Keys**, so
`firewallMatchValues` would still have dropped all but the first. That difference exists
because the schema node is a plain `children: nil` leaf with no `args` and no `multi`,
unlike the leaves the SSOT helper was written for. `fabricMemberValues` descends the whole
subtree and takes every non-empty key; the caller now iterates `FindChildren` rather than
`FindChild` because repeated hierarchical statements land as sibling nodes.

## Validator obligation (docs/config-schema.md #6659 rule)

Widening a multi-value read cannot turn a previously clean commit into a rejection here:
the only validator that reads `FabricMembers` is the fab0/fab1 shared-member overlap check
in `compiler_validate_warn.go`, and it appends a **warning**. That check was previously
vacuous for bracket-authored fabrics — nothing to compare — so this fold **arms** it rather
than tightening it.

## PR #7122 — config: read every child of a routing-policy from-protocol block [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6689-policy-from-protocol`

## Problem

`from { protocol { bgp; ospf; static; } }` compiled to **`[bgp]`** alone. A term written
to filter three protocols filtered one.

`collectProtocolList` descended a single-child **chain** — `Children[0]` at each level —
which is the right shape for the flat-set bracket list but not for a brace block. A nested
block leaves the node with `Keys=["protocol"]` and files one leaf child per protocol as
**siblings**, so the chain walk reached the first and stopped. The chain is one child deep
at every level; the block is N children wide at one level.

Fails **OPEN**: with `then reject` the operator meant to exclude BGP, OSPF and static; the
compiled policy excluded BGP alone, so the OSPF and static routes meant to be filtered were
accepted and installed. No diagnostic — `show configuration` renders the authored list back
intact.

## Enumeration — five spellings, measured

| spelling | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `from { protocol { bgp; ospf; static; } }` | `[bgp]` | `[bgp ospf static]` |
| `from { protocol [ bgp ospf static ]; }` | all three | all three |
| `from { protocol bgp; protocol ospf; ... }` | all three | all three |
| `set ... from protocol [ bgp ospf static ]` | all three | all three |
| `set ... from protocol <X>` (x3) | all three | all three |

## Promotion analysis (docs/config-schema.md #6673 rule)

Every token below a routing-policy `protocol` node is a protocol name — Junos has no
per-protocol option keyword on this leaf — so unlike `system ntp server` (#6690) the full
descent cannot promote an identifier into the value list. Blank tokens are skipped, since
every value returned is installed as an FRR `match source-protocol` line.

## Validator analysis (docs/config-schema.md #6659 rule)

The routing-policy `from protocol` value domain is **unvalidated at commit in every
spelling** — unlike the identically-named firewall-filter leaf, which
`filterProtocolResolvable` checks. There is therefore no one-sided validator to widen
alongside the read.

What the fold does change is that a token authored in the block spelling now reaches the
`pkg/frr` renderer, where the other four spellings already delivered it and where
`sanitizeFRRValue` already applies. So this makes five spellings agree rather than opening
a new path. The absent value-domain gate is filed as **#7121** rather than bundled here,
because adding one is a new commit rejection, not a bug fix.

copied `delta.session_id`. So every session recovered through the
`drain_session_deltas` polling fallback (used whenever the binary event stream
is down) or the owner-RG resync export imported id 0, and the peer minted a
fresh local id: the originating node's SESSION_CREATE and the peer's
post-failover SESSION_CLOSE carried different ids — exactly the cross-node
correlation #5212 exists to provide, absent precisely in the full-resync
recovery window.

## The fix

`#[serde(rename = "rt_flow_session_id", default)] rt_flow_session_id: u64`,
populated from `delta.session_id`. The **Go consumer field already existed** for
the binary leg (`SessionDeltaInfo.RTFlowSessionID`, `json:"rt_flow_session_id"`),
so nothing downstream changes: the id flows on into
`SessionValue{,V6}.RTFlowSessionID` → the cluster sync wire →
`build_synced_session_entry` as it already did from the binary frame.

The delta→JSON conversion is extracted from `flush_session_deltas` as
`afxdp::session_delta_info` — pure movement. That function needs live BPF map
fds, per-binding shared state and an event-stream handle, so nothing could test
what this leg actually puts on the wire.

## No protocol-version bump — and why

`ProtocolVersion` (8) is the **config-snapshot** contract: `apply_snapshot` and
`bump_fib_generation` gate on exact equality, and every required-protocol gate
dispatched from `ensureRequiredSnapshotProtocolLocked`
(`ErrScopedGlobalZoneSet…`, `ErrEgressZone…`, `ErrSecureTunnel…`, …) is a
snapshot feature. This field is on the `drain_session_deltas` control RPC, which
that version does not govern.

Against the v4/#5488 rule — an additive field needs the bump when a peer that
IGNORES it behaves differently in a way that matters — this one degrades in
**both** directions to 0: an older helper omits the key and `serde(default)`
decodes 0; an older daemon ignores a key it does not know. 0 is the pre-existing
"no id carried" sentinel that falls back to a fresh local allocation, i.e. the
pre-#6312 behaviour of this leg. No coverage change, no fail-open. This is the
same reasoning the sibling `SessionSyncRequest.session_id` field already carries
in tree from #5212.

## Scope

Sub-item 1 of the issue only. Sub-item 2 — the `emit_open_delta_with_origin`
comment that overstated the owner-RG path — was already tightened on master; it

Two `scripts/image` defects that block the Tier-1 validation gate — and
therefore block any signed bake — with unrelated causes but the same effect.
Split into two commits.

## 1. `test_bake_base_pin.py` still asserts the pre-respin digest (#7125)

`5fb53d7a1` bumped `PINNED_BASE_SHA256["26.04"]` to Canonical's 2026-08 respin

at master:

```
AssertionError: '9dc7c536…' != '3ee4f67f…'
  passed=49  skipped=0  failed=1
```

The duplication is deliberate — it is what makes a trust-anchor move visible in
a diff — so the fix moves the expectation rather than removing it, and records
the provenance next to it. The digest was **re-verified here, not taken on
trust**: Canonical's `SHA256SUMS` + detached `SHA256SUMS.gpg` for 26.04 verify
against the UEC Image Automatic Signing Key

#7114, a separate PR). Scenarios **a, b, c, d PASS**; `e` dies before booting:

```

"xpf-image-<run>-e" conflict between "extranic0" and "eth0" because both are
connected to same network
```

incus registers one DNS record per instance per managed network, so the second
NIC on `xpf-image-net` is refused at device-add time — and scenario `e` needs
three NICs on one network to prove the node-1 positional naming (`em0` +
`ge-7/0/N`). `nictype=bridged parent=xpf-image-net` does **not** dodge it:
incus resolves the parent bridge back to the managed network and refuses
identically (verified by hand).

Fix: create the harness-owned network with `dns.mode=none`, and `set` it on a
network left behind by an earlier run (the name is fixed and outlives runs).
DHCP is unaffected and no scenario resolves an instance by DNS.

## PR #7128 — test(config): gate the multi-value spelling differential [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `test/2419-spelling-differential-gate`

Infrastructure. **`Closes` nothing** — the fourteen allowlisted issues stay open on their
own merits.

## Why

Three instances of one defect shape turned up in a single 131-issue range (#6690, #6694,
#6689), on top of the fourteen #6659 enumerates and the three in #6714. Fixing them one
report at a time will keep finding them one report at a time.

For every value-bearing leaf in `setSchema` the gate authors a two-element list in all five
spellings the grammar admits and requires the compiled config to agree:

```
dropped(spelling) := compile(spelling, [v1]) == compile(spelling, [v1 v2])
```

Behavioural, not syntactic, and encoding-independent — it does not care whether the value
lands as a string, an int, a bitmask or a packed byte slice.

## Why a gate and not a lint

There is no single correct reader to lint **for**. `pkg/config` now has at least six
accumulating readers — `firewallMatchValues`, `multiLeafAuthoredValues`,
`proxyARPAddressValues`, `eventMultiWordLeafValues`, `fabricMemberValues`, and
`ntpServerValues`, the last of which must additionally skip per-value option **keywords**.

A rule matching "reads `Keys[1]`" would flag compliant code, and would **miss the #7126
sites entirely**: both of those read `Keys[1:]` AND `Children` exactly as
`docs/config-schema.md` instructs, and still drop, because reading `Children` is not the
same as reading every KEY of each child. A differential asks whether the compiler disagrees
with **itself**, which is the actual defect.

## Calibration

Detects all three of #6690/#6694/#6689 at their pre-fix commit `d2b32cf71`; detects none at
master; base→master delta is exactly those three with nothing new appearing. Calibrated
against confirmed defects before being trusted on code nobody had inspected.

## Three ways the harness was itself wrong

Recorded in the test file, not just here — each is a general trap, and two made whole
subtrees report zero while looking healthy.

1. **A sweep that cannot find the bug you already have is a sweep that reports zero.** A
   wildcard-named level was emitted at the wrong brace depth, so the compiler never saw the
   object, every spelling compiled empty, and the differential reported *agreement*. It
   silently suppressed every finding under every wildcard-rooted subtree — including #6694,
   known to be there at the time.
2. **"Did the literal token survive" is blind to transformed encodings** (CoS `code-points`
   → a packed byte slice) **and to rejected synthetic values**. That is why #6697 was missed

## PR #7130 — validate: make scenario e assert what the daemon actually contracts [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/7129-scenario-e-assertions`

Follow-on to #7127. With the device-add failure fixed there, scenario `e`
finally launches — and immediately fails two of its own assertions. Both are
the scenario's, not the daemon's.

```
FAIL: em0 not present — daemon did not enter cluster naming mode for a
node-id-present image
```

## 1. `/etc/xpf/node-id` does not select cluster naming

The scenario wrote a day-0 config with **no `chassis cluster` stanza** and then
asserted that the node-id file alone makes the daemon assign `em0` +
`ge-7/0/N`. It does not, and is not meant to:

- `namingParamsFromConfig` → `clusterMode = cfg.Chassis.Cluster != nil`
- `hasNodeIDFile()` feeds only `computeBootClass` (bootstrap vs normal)
- the #4179 comment in `daemon_run_bringup.go` states it outright: a node-id
  node with a cluster-less config runs **STANDALONE** naming and re-names when
  the real cluster config arrives

So the daemon was right — `fxp0`, `ge-0-0-0`, `ge-0-0-1`, no `em0` — and the
scenario was asserting something nothing promises.

The config now carries a cluster stanza. `authentication-key` is part of the
minimum, not decoration: the cluster control channel fails OPEN without a PSK,
so a stanza without one is rejected by the real commit-check gate. Verified
against that gate:

```
$ xpfd check-config -node-id 1 scenE.conf      # no authentication-key
FAIL … chassis cluster: no authentication-key configured …
rc 2
$ xpfd check-config -node-id 1 scenE.conf      # with it
PASS (strict commit-check: parse + schema + compile + device-map preflight)
rc 0
```

The key is a throwaway literal — the VM peers with nothing and the scenario
asserts naming only.

## 2. `ip link show ge-7/0/0` can never match

Kernel link names use dashes: `enumerateAndRenameInterfaces` assigns
`ge-{FPC}-0-{idx-2}`, i.e. `ge-7-0-0`. `ge-7/0/0` is what
`show interfaces terse` prints, not what the kernel calls the link. This
assertion would have failed even after fix 1.

A factory boot of the appliance image — no day-0 config drive — left every NIC

console. Tier-1 validation scenario `a` fails on it, and because that gate is
fatal the bake writes artifacts but never signs them.

Reproduced firsthand at `70d2d819f` against the previously baked
`…-gf93215641` qcow2 (`validate.py a --keep`):

```
$ incus exec … -- ip -br link
lo      UNKNOWN  …
enp5s0  DOWN     10:66:6a:03:e4:96 <BROADCAST,MULTICAST>

(empty)                          (empty)             (nothing)

WARN "bootstrap lifeline: no IPv4/IPv6 default route found; cannot identify a
```

**The code.** The scenario is not stale, and this is not a design call:

  the shipped contract as *"invalid/missing medium → loud journal log +
  factory bootstrap (fxp0 DHCP)"*, and says in as many words:
  *"the no-config boot is the existing, proven fxp0-DHCP bootstrap. M1b

- **Issue #1922** (M1b, the lifeline itself) opens with *"The appliance image
  relies on the existing fxp0-DHCP factory bootstrap"* and scopes the
  PCI-keyed lifeline as *"needed for foreign-host installs, **not the pinned
  image**"*.
- `79941ada7` (#1922, 2026-06-16) nevertheless replaced the unconditional
  `writeBootstrapFxp0Network()` with the default-route-gated lifeline, and so
  regressed exactly the case it promised not to touch. Three docs still assert
  the pre-#1922 behaviour.

The guard itself is right and stays. On a **foreign** host xpf is a guest,
installed from the `.deb`, and the operator's own network configuration is what
keeps the box reachable — refusing to touch a NIC is correct there. The
appliance has no such configuration: the bake purges cloud-init and deletes
every netplan / `interfaces.d` file, so a factory boot has no route, no
address, and no `.network` anywhere. There is nothing to preserve, and
refusing leaves the box dark.

## PR #7133 — config: fail closed on an unconsumed source-NAT port-range token [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6688-natsrc-port-range-tail`

## What

`parseSourcePoolPortRange` matched the legacy `low <lo> high <hi>` shape at `len(toks) >= 4` and the Junos `<low> to <high>` shape at `len(toks) >= 3`, then discarded whatever the match did not consume. #5457 validated the endpoints the grammar read; it never bounded how many tokens the grammar read.

`port range 1000 2000` therefore fell through to the bare `<low>` case and compiled `PortLow == PortHigh == 1000` — a pool the operator sized at 1001 ports provides ONE and commits clean. The second slot was never parsed, so `port range [ 1000 99999 ]` and `port range [ 1000 notaport ]` committed clean as well.

## Why not "make `[ low high ]` mean low..high"

`port range` is **not a value list** — it is a compound value TAIL. The lexer strips `[`/`]` before the compiler observes anything, so `port range [ 1000 2000 ]` and a mistyped bare `port range 1000 2000` arrive as the SAME token slice `["1000","2000"]` (measured, not assumed). Accepting that as `[1000,2000]` would invent a two-token `range <low> <high>` grammar Junos does not have, and would silently redefine the mistyped bare form too.

Each shape now matches at an EXACT arity and an unconsumed token fails closed through the existing #5457 channel: the raw spec lands in `PortRangeInvalidSpec`, `validateSourceNATPoolStrict` hard-rejects naming it, and `SourceNATPoolPortRange` marks the pool unusable on the tolerant load / peer-sync path.

## Reproduced matrix (before the fix)

Site `security nat source pool <*> port range`, from the #2419 spelling-differential gate's own `spellingVerdicts`:

| value pair | A hier-bracket | B hier-block | C hier-repeat | D set-bracket | E set-repeat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| smallint (101,202) | drop | inert | keep | drop | keep |
| bigint (40961,40962) | drop | inert | keep | drop | keep |
| word / cidr / ipv6 / iface / dscp / proto | keep | inert | keep | keep | keep |

The numeric pairs are the ones whose second slot is a *valid port*, which is exactly when the discard is silent — the non-numeric pairs already reached `PortRangeInvalidSpec` and so differed.

After the fix, all four compared spellings are `keep` for every pair (B stays inert under the gate's synthetic parent path).

## Allowlist row

The `security nat source pool <*> port range` row is removed from `knownSpellingInconsistencies` in this PR, as the gate requires. It went stale because the defect is **fixed**, not because coverage dropped: the site is still enumerated and compared (4 of 5 spellings carry a verdict). It was deliberately NOT moved to `notAValueList` — the agreement is now a real property of the compiler.

## Validation

- `go test -count=1 ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/dataplane/...` exit 0.
- Mutation proof: reverting the arity hunk alone leaves `go build ./...` and `go vet ./pkg/config/` at exit 0 and reds `TestParseSourcePoolPortRangeUnconsumedTail_6688`, `TestSourceNATPoolPortRangeTailFailsClosed_6688` and `TestSourceNATPoolPortRangeSpellingsAgree_6688` as ASSERTIONS, plus the gate itself with an unexpected-inconsistency hit. The over-reject control `TestSourceNATPoolPortRangeValidUnaffected_6688` stays GREEN under the same mutation.
- Go-only in `pkg/config`. `PortRangeInvalidSpec` is `json:"-"` and never crosses the wire, so nothing reaches the Rust helper binary — no cluster smoke is owed.

## Behaviour change to call out

A persisted config carrying `port range 1000 2000` (or trailing junk) previously booted with a one-port pool; it now warns on the tolerant path and the pool installs nothing. That is the #5457 fail-closed posture applied to a spec that was already mis-compiling.

Closes #6688

## PR #7134 — config: validate every vlan-id-list value, not slot 0 alone [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6687-vlan-id-list-every-value`

## The defect

`bridge-domains <bd> vlan-id-list` was read with `nodeVal`, which selects the
first authored value and nothing else. The parse and range checks that follow
that read are the leaf's **only** validator — `setSchema` declares no typed
validator for it — so reading slot 0 alone was not merely a value drop, it was
a **gate escape**:

| authored | committed | compiled |
|---|---|---|
| `vlan-id-list [ 10 99999 ]` | **CLEAN** | `VlanIDs=[10]` |
| `vlan-id-list [ 10 notanumber ]` | **CLEAN** | `VlanIDs=[10]` |
| `vlan-id-list 99999` | REJECTED *"out of range (1-4094)"* | — |

The bracketed list is the idiomatic Junos spelling of this leaf, so the
unvalidated path was the common path.

## Measured, at 22e17c2de, `[ 10 20 ]` in all five spellings

| spelling | compiled `VlanIDs` |
|---|---|
| A hierarchical bracket `vlan-id-list [ 10 20 ];` | **`[10]`** |
| B hierarchical block `vlan-id-list { 10; 20; }` | **`[10]`** |
| C hierarchical repeated | `[10 20]` |
| D flat-set bracket `set … vlan-id-list [ 10 20 ]` | **`[10]`** |
| E flat-set repeated | `[10 20]` |

The leaf is `multi: true`, so the flat-set bracket list is absorbed onto the
node's own `Keys` and the hierarchical block puts one value per child. `nodeVal`
reads neither the tail past slot 1 nor any sibling past the first.

## The fix

The read goes through `multiLeafAuthoredValues`, the documented reader for a
`multi: true` leaf (`Keys[1:]` **and** one value per child). Empty tokens are
skipped by this caller, because `vlan-id-list;` carries no id and is not a parse
error.

**Severity split.** Widening the READ without widening the TOLERANCE would turn
a config the old gate ACCEPTED into a boot failure after upgrade: the bad id is
already persisted in the config DB and the tolerant load path would refuse the
whole config. So the check is split the way every other AST-level gate in this
compiler is split — strict (commit / commit-check) hard-rejects naming the
value, lenient (tolerant load / peer-sync, the new `lenientBridgeDomainVlanID`)
warns and drops that one id. A leniently-loaded config carries exactly the VLAN
set master compiled; only the warning is new.

The check stays in the compiler rather than moving to a typed `validator` in
`setSchema`: a strict schema gate firing first would mask whether the compiler's
own loop ever widened, which is the mask the issue's acceptance criteria call

## PR #7135 — config: read every value of four system multi-value leaves [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6692-system-multivalue-leaves`

## Reproduced matrix (before any fix)

From the #2419 spelling-differential gate's own `spellingVerdicts`, identical for **all eight** of the gate's value pairs — so the drop is shape-driven, not domain-driven:

| Site | A hier-bracket | B hier-block | C hier-repeat | D set-bracket | E set-repeat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `system archival configuration archive-sites` | drop | keep | keep | drop | keep |
| `system services ssh key-exchange` | drop | drop | keep | drop | keep |
| `system services web-management api-auth api-key` | drop | drop | keep | drop | keep |
| `system dataplane shared-umem interface` | drop | drop | keep | drop | keep |

`archive-sites` differs on B because its reader already walked `Children`; the other three read neither side past slot 0.

## Does one shared reader fix all four? No — three, and the fourth would have shipped a secret to scp

- **`key-exchange`, `shared-umem interface`** → `firewallMatchValues`. Every value they return is installed and an empty token means absence. `key-exchange` now matches the `ciphers`/`macs` siblings converted in #4305/#4902.
- **`api-key`** → `multiLeafAuthoredValues`, **not** `firewallMatchValues`. An EMPTY value is load-bearing here: a quoted-empty `api-key ""` authenticates any request presenting the empty token, so it must still reach `validateAPIAuthNoEmptySecretsStrict` to be hard-rejected (#5636). An empty-skipping reader would make an empty key in a non-zero slot *vanish*, silently withdrawing an operator-visible security rejection. The `multiLeafAuthoredValues(n)[0] == nodeVal(n)` invariant keeps slot 0 byte-identical.
- **`archive-sites`** → neither. Its tail interleaves a `password <secret>` MODIFIER with the URLs, so accumulating it wholesale would promote the keyword AND the secret into `ArchiveSites`, where runtime archival hands each entry to `scp <src> <dest>` — the symmetric #6673 hazard the pre-existing comment at that read site named by number. New grouping reader `archiveSiteEntries`, same `<value> [modifier ...]` shape as `firewallPrefixListRefs`. Its five AST shapes were **measured**, not assumed, and are recorded in its doc comment.

## The #4589 gate escape is CLOSED, not armed

The leading-dash check (CWE-88, `must not begin with '-'`) ran on slot 1 alone, so a `-oProxyCommand=` member authored past the first was both dropped and unchecked — the bracket form ACCEPTED what the same token authored alone REJECTED. It now runs over **every** entry `archiveSiteEntries` returns. Widening the read without widening the gate is exactly what the pre-fix comment warned would ship a live argv injection; both moved in this commit.

## Validator coverage for the widened reads

- `key-exchange` declares a schema `validator` (`ValidateSSHAlgorithm`), and `validateMultiValueLeaf` already walks `Keys[1:]` AND every child's `Keys[0]`. `TestSSHKeyExchangeValidatorCoversEverySlot_6692` pins a rejection in a NON-ZERO slot plus an over-reject control.
- `api-key` has no schema validator; its check is the #5636 empty-secret gate, which the widened read now feeds every authored slot.

## Allowlist rows

All four `knownSpellingInconsistencies` rows removed in this PR. Measured after the fix: **all five** spellings are COMPARED and all report `keep` at every site — coverage went UP, not down.

- `go test -count=1 ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/daemon/ ./pkg/api/ ./pkg/configstore/ ./pkg/dataplane/...` exit 0; `go build ./...` and `go vet ./pkg/config/` exit 0.

| narrow ONLY the leading-dash GATE (read left widened) | 0 | 0 | `LeadingDashGate` **only** |
| stop separating the `password` modifier | 0 | 0 | `PasswordIsNotASite` **only** |

## PR #7136 — config: read every key of every child on two plain value lists [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/7126-flatset-bracket-child-keys`

## The predicate, not two special cases

`routing-options rib-groups <g> import-rib` and `event-options policy <p> events`
both read the leaf's own `Keys[1:]` **and** its `Children` — exactly what
`CLAUDE.md` and `docs/config-schema.md` prescribe — and both still dropped every
value past the first when the operator authored a bracket list through the
flat-set path. **Reading `Children` is not the same as reading every KEY of each
child.**

`SetPath` files a bracket list differently depending on the schema flag:

| schema | `set … <leaf> [ v1 v2 ]` becomes |
|---|---|
| `multi: true, children: nil` | `Keys=["<leaf>","v1","v2"]` — the tail absorber runs |
| **`multi: false, children: nil`** | `Keys=["<leaf>"]` with **ONE child** `Keys=["v1","v2"]` |

`child.Name()` is `Keys[0]`, so the second row keeps `v1` and discards the rest.
The hierarchical parser puts the list on the node's own tail instead, which is
why both sites survived every brace-authored test and bit only `set` /
`load set` / the CLI.

## Measured at 22e17c2de, `[ a b ]` in all five spellings

| site | A hier-bracket | B hier-block | C hier-repeat | D set-bracket | E set-repeat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `import-rib` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | **`[a]`** | **`[a]`** | `[a b]` |
| `events` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | `[a b]` | **`[a]`** | `[a b]` |

So `import-rib` needed **two** reads widened, not one — the issue records D, and
C drops as well because repeated hierarchical statements land as SIBLING nodes
and `FindChild` consulted only the first. Both are now `FindChildren` +
`plainListValues`.

Neither drop is one an operator can see: `import-rib` is the inter-VRF
route-leak membership list (the second table's leak simply never happens, and
`show configuration` renders the full list back), and `events` is an event
policy's trigger set (the automation silently never runs for part of what was
authored).

## Not in the issue: the import-rib drop is also a GATE ESCAPE

The #2226 cross-reference check iterates `ImportRibs`, so a rib named in a slot
the compiler never read could never be rejected:

```
set routing-options rib-groups rg1 import-rib [ inet.0 does-not-exist.inet.0 ]   -> committed CLEAN
set routing-options rib-groups rg1 import-rib [ does-not-exist.inet.0 inet.0 ]   -> "references an undefined rib"
```

The newly visible tail entries land on #2226's **existing** tolerant-path

`inert` is worse than it looks and is not visible from the issue text: the block shape carries no `Keys[1]` at all, so `dns-server-address { a; b; }` compiled **nothing** — not a truncation, a total drop. Confirmed under mutation: `B-hier-block: compiled DNSServers [], want [2001:db8::53 2001:db8::54]`.

After the fix, all five spellings are `keep`.

## Fix

`firewallMatchValues` — it reads both sides of the AST and skips empty tokens, which is right here because **every value it returns is installed**: the sender folds them into ONE RFC 8106 `RecursiveDNSServer` option, so an empty token legitimately means absence rather than a selection.

## Validator coverage for the widened read

`dns-server-address` declares a schema `validator` (`ValidateIPv6Address`, #2497) and, being `multi: true` with `children == nil`, is dispatched to `validateMultiValueLeaf`, which walks `Keys[1:]` **and** every block-child. `TestRADNSServerValidatorCoversEverySlot_6695` pins a rejection in a NON-ZERO slot (`[ 2001:db8::53 8.8.8.8 ]`) with an over-reject control beside it — so a malformed address cannot ride the widened read onto the wire.

## The wire assertion the issue asks for

`pkg/ra/sender_marshal_rdnss_6695_test.go` drives the real Junos text through `CompileConfig` into the sender's own `buildRA`, marshals, re-parses, and asserts the RDNSS option's `Servers` list. A dropped address is invisible in the option COUNT (the sender emits one option holding every server), so the assertion is on the list, not the count.

## Allowlist row

Removed in this PR. After the fix **all five** spellings are compared and all report `keep`, so gate coverage of this site went UP — the previously inert block spelling now carries a verdict.

## Validation

- `go test -count=1 ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/ra/ ./pkg/daemon/` exit 0; `go build ./...` and `go vet ./pkg/config/ ./pkg/ra/` exit 0.
- Mutation proof (revert the single read to `nodeVal`): `go build` and `go vet` both exit 0, and the reds are ASSERTIONS —
  - `TestRADNSServerMultiValue_6695` (A, B, D)
  - `TestRADNSServerThreeAddresses_6695`
  - `TestBuildRA_6695_EveryRDNSSServerOnWire` — 3 of 4 subtests; `flat-set-repeated` is the control that always worked
  - `TestSchemaSpellingDifferentialGate` fires the unexpected-inconsistency hit for the removed row
  - `TestRADNSServerValidatorCoversEverySlot_6695` stays **green**, because it guards the validator, not the read
- Go-only in `pkg/config` (plus a `pkg/ra` test) — nothing reaches the Rust helper binary, so **no cluster smoke is owed**.

Closes #6695

## PR #7138 — config: read every CoS code-point spelling [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6697-cos-code-points-spellings`

Closes #6697

## What was actually broken

Measured across all five spellings **before** fixing anything, because the
issue's own count had been wrong twice. With **domain-valid** values
(`ef`/`af11` for DSCP, `3`/`5` for the 0..7 domains), at `22e17c2de`:

| family | A hier-bracket | B hier-block | C hier-repeat | D set-bracket | E set-repeat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `classifiers dscp` | keep [46,10] | **ABSENT** | keep | keep | keep |
| `classifiers ieee-802.1` | keep [3,5] | **ABSENT** | keep | keep | keep |
| `classifiers inet-precedence` | keep [3,5] | **ABSENT** | keep | keep | keep |
| `rewrite-rules dscp` | 46 | **ABSENT** | 46 | 46 | 46 |
| `rewrite-rules ieee-802.1` | 3 | **ABSENT** | 3 | 3 | 3 |

"ABSENT" = the whole classifier / rewrite-rule compiled to nothing, not a
truncated list — the compiler stores one only with `len(Entries) > 0`. This is
why every assertion in the new test reports ABSENT and WRONG-VALUES as separate
failures: "the entry has 2 code points" would pass **vacuously** here.

Two corrections to the issue, both now measured:

1. **Five families, not the two in the title.** `inet-precedence` classifiers
   and both `rewrite-rules` families are reached too.
2. **The bracket / repeated / flat-set spellings were never truncating.** The
   uniform-drop the earlier sweep reported at those sites was a gate artifact —
   see "The gate was wrong twice" below. The single live defect was the
   hierarchical **block** spelling, in all five.

A third defect fell out of the same read: the two rewrite readers also never
read the inline tail, so `loss-priority low code-point ef;` — **the spelling
Junos itself emits** — compiled to nothing.

And because each reader's per-value domain check runs on the tokens it reads,
the unread shape was a **gate escape**, not just a value drop:
`code-points { totally-bogus; }` committed CLEAN where `code-points
[ totally-bogus ]` was rejected.

## The fix

All five readers now share `coSCodePointTokens`, which returns the leaf node's
tail, **every key** of each of its children (reading `Children` is not the same
as reading every KEY of each child — the #7126 shape), and the inline
`loss-priority low code-points ef;` tail. Every caller still runs its own
per-value check over every token returned, so the escape closes with the drop.

`inet-precedence` classifiers were made live by #6847/PR #6877 today; its fifth
reader has the identical shape and is widened here in the same pass, as that
PR's comment on the issue asked. Nothing else in the tree reads these leaves

## PR #7140 — dataplane: guard the helper control-socket stale unlink; type the control-socket leaf [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5839-control-socket-stale-unlink`

Closes #5839

The control-socket half of userspace helper bring-up still removed its stale
socket with a bare `_ = os.Remove(cfg.ControlSocket)`. The path is
operator-supplied (`system dataplane control-socket`) and xpfd runs as root, so
that unlink deleted whatever filesystem object the path named — a regular file,
a symlink, a directory entry, or the **live socket of a running helper** — and
discarded the failure when it could not.

The sibling EVENT-socket half was hardened in #5273 (`7c00ef1bd`,
`removeStaleEventStreamSocket`). This PR extracts that logic into
`removeStaleUnixSocket` (new `pkg/dataplane/userspace/stale_socket.go`) so
stale-socket removal has ONE implementation — an explicit #5839 invariant — and
points the control socket at it.

## Which of the four checks apply

All four. Assessed individually, not copied:

| Check | Applies to the control socket? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `Lstat`, not-exists tolerated | **Yes** | A first boot has no socket. `Lstat` rather than `Stat` so a symlink is judged on its own inode instead of being followed into an unlink of its target. |
| `os.ModeSocket` gate | **Yes** | This is the data-destruction case, and the path is operator-supplied. A regular file / directory / FIFO / device / symlink is preserved and refused. |
| `/proc/net/unix` liveness probe | **Yes — this is the one that matters** | Unlinking a live listener's socket does not stop that listener; it keeps serving an unreachable inode while a second process binds a fresh socket at the same name. For the control socket the surviving helper becomes undialable — including by the #1993 boot armed-probe, which resolves forwarding state through exactly this path — while the new helper cannot claim the AF_XDP queues the first still holds. The probe is non-invasive by design: dialing would, on the event socket, make the daemon accept the probe as its new helper and drop the real one. |
| Non-ignored `os.Remove` | **Yes** | A failed unlink (EACCES, EROFS) must fail bring-up rather than proceed into a bind that fails more confusingly. |

**Judged INAPPLICABLE: the sidecar `flock`.** `EventStream.Start` holds one
across its call, which serializes daemon-side *owners* of the socket it binds.
xpfd does not bind the control socket — the Rust helper does
(`remove_stale_socket`, `userspace-dp/src/server/lifecycle.rs`), and it does not
participate in the flock protocol. A daemon-side lock there would serialize
nothing, and making it meaningful would be a cross-binary protocol change (and
would move the Rust binary, owing a smoke). Not attempted.

## Ordering: the guard alone would have been an availability regression

`ensureProcessLocked` stops generation N before it prepares generation N+1. So
the guarded removal **on its own** would have converted "silently delete a
regular file and continue" into "tear down forwarding, then fail" — worse than
the bug for a misconfigured path. `preflightHelperPaths` therefore runs the
DETERMINISTIC checks — control/event/state must name distinct paths, and neither
socket path may already exist as a non-socket — BEFORE the stop, via
`stopForNewGenerationLocked`. A config that could never bring up a new
generation now leaves the previous one, and its forwarding, running.

The liveness check is deliberately NOT hoisted: the control socket is live
precisely until the helper holding it is stopped. An inconclusive `Lstat` in the
preflight is left to the post-stop path rather than turned into a new failure on
a code path that previously had none.

## PR #7141 — userspace-dp: recover poisoned WireGuard engine locks instead of panicking the worker [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6422-wg-lock-poison`

## What

Convert every **production** lock acquisition under
`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/` from `.unwrap()` to the tree-wide
poison-tolerant idiom `unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`.

`std` marks a `Mutex`/`RwLock` **poisoned** the moment a thread panics
while holding its exclusive guard, and every later acquisition then
returns `Err`. With `.unwrap()` that converts ONE contained panic — the
#925 worker supervisor contains it — into a panic on **every subsequent
acquisition of that lock**. For an `Arc`-shared engine that is a
permanent outage, not a transient one: the supervisor restarts the
worker, the restarted worker touches the same lock, and panics again.

## Population, measured at the base commit

| file | sites |
|---|---|
| `wg/cookie.rs` | 7 |
| `wg/engine.rs` | 21 |
| `wg/handshake_session.rs` | 19 |
| `wg/peer.rs` | 10 |
| `wg/tai64n.rs` | 3 |
| `wg/timers.rs` | 8 |
| **total** | **68** |

Composition: **29 `Mutex::lock()` + 39 `RwLock::read()/write()`**.
Reproduces the count in the issue comment exactly, including the method
note: a single-line grep reports **64**; four sites wrap `.lock()` /
`.read()` and `.unwrap()` across source lines (3 in engine.rs, 1 in
handshake_session.rs) and need a newline-tolerant match.

**60 converted. 8 deliberately left panicking** — see below.

## Which sites should still panic, and why

The eight `#[cfg(test)]` accessors:

| file | fn |
|---|---|
| cookie.rs | `set_rng_fail_for_test`, `source_table_len_for_test`, `source_contains_for_test` |
| engine.rs | `set_keepalive_for_test`, `force_current_for_test` (×2 sites) |
| handshake_session.rs | `try_reserve_pending_for_test`, `pending_count` |

They are compiled out of the shipped helper binary, so they cannot cause
the production failure this issue describes; and in a **test** build a
poisoned lock is *evidence of a panic that the test should surface*, not
a condition to paper over. Converting them would make an
already-broken test report a misleading pass. Every production site is
converted.

## PR #7142 — cluster: key the HA failover fence barrier by request (#6177 items 2+3) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/6177-failover-fence-barrier-identity`

Addresses **#6177** items 2 and 3. **Item 1 stays open** — see below — so this
PR deliberately does not carry a close keyword.

## Item 2 — barrier bookkeeping was delete-by-key (fixed)

The barrier that gates a remote-failover applied-ack on the local demotion
actually actuating (#5640; verdict-carrying since #7118/#6371) was one slot per
redundancy group. `disarmFailoverActuation` deleted `failoverActuateWait[rgID]`
by key with no check that the entry was still the barrier the caller armed, and
`waitFailoverActuated`'s expiry called it.

The responder handles every failover request on its own goroutine
(`go s.handleRemoteFailover`, `pkg/cluster/sync_conn_read.go:410`), so two
transfer-out cycles for one RG can overlap. An older request's expiry then
deleted the slot a newer request had just armed → the newer wait found no
barrier → `waitFailoverActuated` returned `nil`, which encodes "the fence
actuated" → the node replied `failoverAckApplied` for a demotion it had not
performed. That is the two-owner window #5640 exists to close, reached through
the bookkeeping rather than through the ack path. (The issue predicted a
spurious `failoverAckFailed`; at HEAD the missing-barrier case reads as
SUCCESS, so the consequence is the unsafe direction, not the safe one.)

Fix: key the map by `failoverActuationKey{rgID, reqID}`. The request id is the
peer's own `SessionSync.failoverSeq` value — already on the wire, already handed
to `OnRemoteFailover` for the #5079 lease — and now also reaches the wait, so
`WaitFailoverApplied` / `WaitFailoverAppliedBatch` gain a `reqID` parameter.
**No wire change.** A peer that sends no request id supplies 0 and degrades to
exactly the previous one-slot-per-RG behaviour.

Identity is checked as well as the key: `armFailoverActuation` returns the
barrier it stored and `disarmFailoverActuation` removes the entry only while it
is still that barrier, so a superseded handle (a duplicate request message
re-using one request id) cannot evict a live one either.

The demotion event carries no request id — it reports that *this node* finished
demoting the RG, which is what every in-flight request for that RG is asking —
so `resolveFailoverActuation` fans its verdict out across the RG's entries.

## Item 3 — barrier lifecycle had no direct test (fixed)

#7118 added `daemon_ha_actuation_6371_test.go`, which covers the VERDICT legs
(success / dataplane rejection / parked waiter / unarmed RG) through
`handleClusterEvent`. It does not touch the lifecycle: the bounded-wait expiry,
the disarm path, the map cleanup, the batch wait, or double-resolve. Seven new
tests in `daemon_ha_actuation_barrier_6177_test.go` drive the barrier API
directly and cover exactly those.

## Item 1 — RETH VIP-removal window: STILL LIVE, left open

## What

`Manager.FenceStatus()` (`pkg/cluster/failover.go`) returns the configured
peer-fencing action plus the `EventFence` history — and had **zero non-test
callers**. Every fence decision taken on a heartbeat timeout was recorded to the
event history and rendered nowhere, so it was reachable only by grepping
journald.

This adds a `Peer fencing:` block to `Manager.FormatInformation`, which is the
single render behind `show chassis cluster information` on **both** operator
surfaces — the local CLI (`pkg/cli/cli_show_cluster.go`) and the gRPC remote CLI

reaches both.

```
Peer fencing:
  Action: disable-rg
  Attempts:
    Aug 21 09:14:02  Fence disable-rg sent to peer
    Aug 21 09:31:47  Fence failed: peer not connected
```

`Action` is the **currently committed** value, `disabled` when the leaf is
absent. That distinction is deliberate: the event history outlives a config
change, so after an operator removes `peer-fencing` the past attempts must stay
visible without the surface implying fencing is still armed. The whole block is
suppressed when fencing was never configured and never fired, matching the
conditional style of the neighbouring `Install fence:` and
`Interface monitoring events:` sections.

#72's three acceptance criteria at `a77d5568c`:

## PR #7150 — cluster: report the takeover hold in cluster status [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/103-takeover-hold-status`

Partial for #103 — item 5 of its proposed fix. **#103 stays open**; the walk of
all five sub-conditions and what is left is below.

## The defect

`IsReadyForTakeover(holdTime)` is TWO conditions: `rg.Ready` AND
`ReadySince + holdTime` elapsed. Both status renders keyed their
`Takeover ready:` line on `rg.Ready` alone. Inside the hold window that printed
`Takeover ready: yes` while `runElection`, `electSingleNode` and the four
`failover.go` gates were all declining to promote the RG — a status line that
contradicts the election, with nothing naming the hold. `takeoverHoldTime` was
rendered by no surface at all.

Repro before the fix (throwaway probe, `takeover-hold-time 5000`, fresh
`SetRGReady(0, true, nil)`, peer alive):

```
ready-but-holding state: secondary (hold remaining ~5s)
rendered status line: "  Takeover ready: yes"
```

## The fix

`RedundancyGroupState.TakeoverHoldRemaining` + `Manager.TakeoverHoldTime`, and
both renders keyed on the property election gates on:

```
Takeover ready: no (takeover hold: 3.2s of 5s remaining)
```

`show chassis cluster information` also prints the configured
`Takeover hold time:`. A NOT-ready RG is untouched — the hold is not what blocks
it, and naming the hold there would bury the real reason.

`DefaultTakeoverHoldTime` is 0, so with `takeover-hold-time` unset both renders
are byte-identical. That bounds the change onto clusters that configured a hold,
which matters for `pkg/upgrade`'s pre-demotion precheck: it parses the first
token after `Takeover ready:` and treats `no` as a blocker. That reading is the
intended semantics there — the precheck documents itself as conservative and a
holding RG genuinely cannot take over yet.

Also corrects two stale docs: `docs/bugs.md` and `docs/phases.md` both said the
hold defaults to 3s. It shipped at 3s in `91a57cf` and was changed to 0 in
`cd4dbe9`, a bodyless commit with no recorded rationale.

| 1a | required interfaces exist and are up | **covered** — `Monitor.RGInterfaceReady` (`pkg/cluster/monitor.go`) reports `interface X missing` / `X down`. Skips only interfaces whose FPC slot maps to the PEER node, which cannot exist locally. |

## PR #7151 — dataplane: stop discarding the recompile FIB generation bump [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/7149-fibgen-bump-error`

`CompileConfig` ended a recompile with a bare `dp.BumpFIBGeneration()`,
dropping both results. On the live userspace path that is not a harmless
discard.

## Why this call in particular

`CompileUserspaceShim` compiles against `userspaceShimCompileDataplane`
(`pkg/dataplane/loader.go`), whose ~55 `DataPlane` overrides are all no-ops —
`TestPrePassFakeIsNoMorePermissiveThanProduction_4960` asserts exactly that.
Diffing every `dp.<Method>` the compiler calls against that override set leaves
three that are NOT overridden and therefore promote to the embedded `*Manager`:

| method | consequence |
|---|---|
| `IsLoaded` | runs before any mutation, cannot report a mid-apply failure |
| `GetPersistentNAT` | returns a pointer, no error |
| `BumpFIBGeneration` | **real bpffs map write — the only compiler dataplane call on this path that can genuinely fail** |

Measured, driving the production shim directly:

```go
dp := userspaceShimCompileDataplane{Manager: &Manager{}}
gen, err := dp.BumpFIBGeneration()
// -> gen=0 err="dataplane not armed: fib_gen_map"
```

`(*Manager).BumpFIBGeneration` warns on two of its three failure branches; the
`registryFresh` / not-armed branch returns `ErrDataplaneNotArmed` with **no log
at all**. So on that branch the failure was completely silent.

## Why it matters

`userspace/manager_compile.go` builds the snapshot it is about to hand the
helper with `m.readFIBGeneration()`, which re-reads the very `fib_gen_map` this
bump writes. A failed bump leaves the map at its old value → the published
snapshot carries the OLD FIB generation → the helper's `session.fib_gen`
comparison still matches → **established flows keep the cached next-hop
(ifindex + DMAC/SMAC) that the recompile may have just invalidated**, until they
age out, with the apply reporting success throughout.

## Why it is reported, not returned

This site runs *after* `compileZones` has mutated the host and *before* the new
snapshot is published. Propagating would manufacture a fresh instance of the
exact half-applied shape #4960 exists to prevent. The other two production
callers each pick the treatment their own path supports — the ip-monitoring
actuator retries via `pendingFIBBump` (#1844/#3757 H3), the route-leak commit
tail fails the commit closed for want of a retry owner (#5696 M19) — and neither
is available here. Failing an apply closed *after* the dataplane has been asked
is the apply-transaction half of #4960 (`research/4960-apply-txn`, twice

## PR #7152 — cluster: refuse a reflected session-sync handshake nonce [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5078-nonce-reflection-guard`

Advances #5078. **Does not close it** — see "What this does NOT fix".

## Measured defect

A PSK-less attacker that echoes every byte back completes the session-sync auth
handshake. Fixture at `origin/master` `a77d5568c`, whose entire algorithm is
"read a frame, write it back verbatim":

```
REPRO RESULT: mode=1 keylen=32 err=<nil>
VULNERABLE: pure byte-echo authenticated with NO PSK; frameKey=9256908c...
```

`mode=1` is `syncAuthAuthenticated`. The attacker holds no key and computes no
HMAC.

**Why it works.** `syncAuthProof` is `HMAC(key, tag ‖ challenge)` — no role, no
node identity, no transcript — and the accept test is
`hmac.Equal(peerProof, syncAuthProof(key, localNonce))`. The mirror gets our
HELLO back as the peer HELLO with `peerNonce == localNonce`; we compute
`HMAC(key, tag ‖ localNonce)` and, because the proof is written *before* the
peer's is read, send it first; the attacker replays that exact value. Since
`syncDeriveFrameKey` sorts the two nonces canonically the session key is
undirected too, so our own sealed frames verify when reflected into
`receiveLoop`.

## Change

`syncCheckPeerNonce` refuses a peer nonce **equal to our own** or **all zero**,
before any proof is emitted. The ordering is deliberate: the proof we write *is*
the value the echo replays, so a check placed after it would already have handed
over the answer.

## What this does NOT fix

The two-connection variant relays a proof computed over connection α's local
nonce onto connection β. There the nonces on each connection differ, so nothing
here fires — and because both nodes share **one** PSK, that oracle can be the
**peer node**, which no per-node nonce bookkeeping could see either. Closing it
requires role + identity + transcript bound into the proof: a new proof
construction and a keyed↔keyed wire flag-day.

That limitation is stated in the commit message, in both test doc comments, and
in `pkg/cluster/README.md`, so a green suite here is not misread as the
reflection issue being fixed. #5078 stays open.

## Why no migration window

This is what makes the piece separable from the rest of #5078 at all. It adds no
field, bumps no version, and changes **not one emitted byte**. It only *narrows*

`xsk_ffi::Umem::new` is `unsafe` on one stated precondition — the caller's
`area` must be "a valid, page-aligned mmap'd region that **outlives this
Umem**" (`userspace-dp/src/xsk_ffi.rs:387-389`). `WorkerUmemInner`
(`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem/mod.rs`) owns both halves of that pair and
declared `area: MmapArea` before `umem: Umem`. Rust destroys struct fields in
DECLARATION order, so teardown ran `munmap` first and `xsk_umem__delete`
second: the pages were released while the libxdp UMEM object was still
registered against them.

Latent rather than a live UAF — `bridge_xsk_umem_delete` -> `xsk_umem__delete`
does not read the user area, and the kernel pins UMEM pages while the fd is
open. But that mitigation is an **unpinned external library's implementation
detail**, not an invariant this repo controls. This box links `libxdp 1.6.3-1`
(`dpkg -l libxdp1`), while the original refutation was reasoned about 1.6.0.
The correct order costs two lines.

## Pinning the order

Rust has **no compile-time drop-order assertion** — there is no `const` fact to
hang a `const _: () = assert!(..)` on, and `ManuallyDrop` + a hand-written
`Drop` would trade a latent bug for two live `unsafe` calls whose only job is to
restate what declaration order already says. Neither was invented; the order is
pinned by **observation** instead.

`crate::drop_order_probe` is a `cfg(test)`-only recorder that both destructors
append to, and `umem/tests/drop_order.rs` asserts the sequence on the **real**
`WorkerUmemInner` (via `WorkerUmem::new_for_test`) and on the `WorkerUmemPool`
wrapper production actually constructs. The recording sites are the production
`Drop` impls, so the test watches the shipped teardown path, not a mirror.

The probe is allocation-free on purpose (fixed thread-local array + `try_with`,
not a `Vec`): it runs inside `Drop`, and this crate installs a counting global
allocator under `cfg(test)` that other tests assert against.

## Validation

The test was written against the **unfixed** field order and observed the defect
directly:

```
left:  [MmapArea, Umem]     <- a77d5568c (origin/master): munmap first
right: [Umem, MmapArea]
```

Both cases red before the swap, green after. `make test-rust` green end to end
(4453 + 60 + 8 + 22 + 31 + 1 + 2 passed, 0 failed, `$?` = 0).
`make build-userspace-dp` clean — the probe compiles to nothing outside
`cfg(test)`.

## PR #7166 — cluster: size transfer grace from live heartbeat timing [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5081-live-heartbeat-timing`

Fixes the non-auth half of #5081.

## The bug

`transferCommitGracePeriodLocked` (`pkg/cluster/failover.go`) sized the
manual-transfer grace from `Manager.hbInterval` / `Manager.hbThreshold` — the
**desired** values, which `UpdateConfig` rewrites on every commit. Dead-peer
detection runs on a different set of numbers: the snapshot `StartHeartbeat`
handed the receiver. Nothing restarts the heartbeat when only the timing
changes (`clusterTransportKey` keys on endpoint fields; `RestartHeartbeat` is
reached only from the VRF-rebind path), so after
`set chassis cluster heartbeat-interval` a node sizes a window against timing
its wire is not using.

The dangerous direction is a commit that **shortens** the configuration:

| | desired | live |
|---|---|---|
| timing | 3 × 100 ms | 5 × 1000 ms |
| dead-peer declared at | 300 ms | **5 s** |
| grace computed | 0.6 s + 5 s slack → **10 s floor** | **15 s** |

The grace exists to suppress exactly that peer timeout during a manual
transfer, and at 10 s it can expire before the 5 s-armed timeout is re-armed by
the next transfer step — so the transfer takes a spurious peer-death failover.

`FormatInformation` (`pkg/cluster/status.go`) had the same defect in reporting
form: it rendered the desired values, telling the operator the new timing was
in effect while the wire was still on the old one.

## The fix

`liveHeartbeatTimingLocked` returns what the running receiver is actually
using, falling back to the desired values when no heartbeat is running
(standalone, pre-bringup, or between stop and start — there is no live cadence
to be wrong about there, and the next `StartHeartbeat` adopts exactly those).
The receiver's `threshold`/`interval` are written once in
`newHeartbeatReceiver` and never mutated; only the `m.hbReceiver` pointer is,
under `m.mu`, so the read is race-free.

The grace is sourced from it, and status renders the live values plus a
`Heartbeat pending restart: configured interval N ms, threshold M (not applied
to the running heartbeat)` line when they diverge. When they agree — every
steady state, and every standalone or pre-bringup manager — the render is
byte-identical to before, pinned by
`TestFormatInformation_NoPendingLineWhenTimingApplied_5081`.

**Applying** a committed timing or PSK change to live comms is the other half

## PR #7170 — xdp: stop diverting transit ESP and non-native GRE to the kernel [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/304-esp-gre-destination-gate`

Fixes the live half of #304.

## The gap

The AF_XDP shim tested only the protocol number before handing a packet to the
kernel (`userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs`):

```rust
if parsed.protocol == PROTO_ESP { return Ok(cpumap_or_pass(ctrl)); }
if parsed.protocol == PROTO_GRE && !native_gre { return Ok(cpumap_or_pass(ctrl)); }
```

No destination predicate, anywhere, in either branch. A **transit** ESP or
non-native GRE packet — addressed to a host beyond this firewall, not to the
firewall itself — was handed to the kernel too, and the kernel forwards it:
`ip_forward=1`, every nft chain is `policy accept`, no `hook forward` rule
exists, and there is no tc/clsact qdisc anywhere. The packet leaves the box
having had **no zone policy evaluated at all**.

Two things in the same file already say this is wrong:

- The sibling **WireGuard** branch immediately below carries an
  `is_local_destination` gate its own comment calls **MANDATORY** — "a
  port-only match would shunt TRANSIT/DNAT UDP that happens to use the WG port
  to the kernel, bypassing the userspace policy engine". Same shape, opposite
  treatment.
- `is_degraded_local_or_control` already gates ESP on
  `is_interface_nat_destination`, gates GRE on native-GRE plus an inner
  `PASS_TO_KERNEL`, and drops other transit. The **degraded** path was
  adjudicating what the healthy path waved through — which also refutes any
  claim that ESP must always reach the kernel.

## The fix

Delete both protocol-only returns. ESP and non-native GRE now fall into the
ordinary session-miss classification, whose `is_local_destination` arm already
cpumaps a locally-terminated tunnel, so kernel XFRM and the kernel GRE device
keep working unchanged.

The one case that arm cannot see is a tunnel endpoint sitting on an address
**interface-mode SNAT owns** — `is_local_destination` deliberately returns
false for an interface-NAT member, and that is the common WAN deployment. It is
handled by reusing the `is_interface_nat_destination` call the session-miss
path already makes, rather than adding a second map lookup. GRE reaching that
arm is necessarily non-native (the native-GRE classifier is the other branch),
so no native-GRE flow is affected.

A remote destination now continues to the AF_XDP redirect and is adjudicated by
the worker, where the #5620 `owns_configured_ip` gate is **table-scoped**:

## PR #7182 — dataplane/userspace: detach XDP/TC only after the snapshot is accepted (#5485) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/5485-attach-rollback`

## The defect

`userspace.Manager.Compile` mutated kernel XDP/TC attachment state twice per
apply, and until this PR both halves ran BEFORE `apply_snapshot`:

1. `CompileUserspaceShim(cfg)` **attaches** the shim to the new candidate set.
2. `syncInterfaceAttachments(result, snap)` **detaches** XDP and TC from every
   ifindex the new snapshot no longer adjudicates. Both detach errors were only
   `slog.Warn`ed.
3. Only then did the function take `m.mu`, program the classifier maps, and
   publish. `m.lastSnapshot` — the authority every fail-closed path in this
   package calls "the retained snapshot" — advances only on success.

Every failure between step 2 and a landed publish left the kernel on the NEW
interface set while the retained authority (and the helper's applied snapshot)
was still the OLD one.

**The detach half is a policy bypass, not just an outage.** Both pre-publish
failure modes drive the shim to `ctrl.Enabled=0` — `programBootstrapMapsLocked`
programs it disabled, and `publishSnapshotFailClosedLocked` disables it on the
same-plan path (#4959) — and a disabled ctrl DROPS transit on every interface
that still carries the shim, because `degraded_ctrl_disabled_action` runs
*before* the ingress-map test in `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs`. An interface that
has already been detached is outside that fail-closed surface entirely: no XDP
program at all, so with `ip_forward=1` its traffic goes straight into the Linux
stack, unadjudicated by xpf, while the daemon reports the previous-good snapshot
as enforced.

## Mechanism chosen: (a) re-sequence

`syncInterfaceAttachments` now runs only at the points where the new snapshot
has become the retained authority. `Compile` is split at the `m.mu` boundary
into `Compile` (attach + build) and `applyCompiledSnapshot` (publish, advance
the authority, then reconcile the attachment set), which is also what makes the
invariant unit-testable. There are **two** acceptance points and both reconcile:
the published path (`m.lastSnapshot = snap` after `publishSnapshotFailClosedLocked`)
and the deferred-publish branch, which also advances `m.lastSnapshot` and returns
nil. The call is placed immediately after each acceptance rather than at the tail
of the function, because `applyHelperStatusLocked`, the HA sync and the forwarding
sync can all fail *after* the snapshot is already the authority and must not
strand a stale attachment.

```rust
## PR #7183 — syslog: scope a host selector to the facility its client emits [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-21)

Branch: `fix/5797-syslog-selector-facility`

Advances #5797 — the bounded, provable half. The architecture half (a source
facility on the event envelope, per-facility routing, the eight design
invariants) is split to a successor; see the close comment on #5797.

## The defect

A Junos `system syslog host <h>` may carry several independent
`<facility> <severity>` selectors, and Junos evaluates them **independently**:
each facility keeps its own threshold. xpf folded every selector of a host into
one `SyslogClient.MinSeverity` with `MoreRestrictiveMinSeverity`, so a selector
naming a facility that destination's client **never emits** still filtered every
record it did.

The issue's own example:

```
host 192.0.2.10 {
    daemon info;
    authorization critical;
}
```

Junos forwards daemon records at info-or-higher. xpf took the more restrictive
of `{info, critical}` and filtered the whole destination at critical — silently
dropping the daemon notice/info records the operator had asked for by name.

`daemon info; authorization none` is the same defect at full magnitude. `none`
outranks everything in `minSeverityRestrictRank`, so **one** selector naming a
facility this client can never emit silenced the destination outright, emergency
included.

## The fix, and why it is keyed on the code

A selector can only match a record whose facility it names, and every record a
client sends carries the one facility it stamps. So the threshold is computed
only from the selectors that can match:

- the `any` wildcard, which matches everything;
- selectors resolving to the stamped facility code.

The key is the numeric **code**, not the authored name, because the code is what
appears in the wire PRI. Every Junos name xpf's mapper does not know resolves to
local0, so a host that really does stamp local0 stays constrained by them — the
selector and the emitted record genuinely share a facility on the wire.
`TestSyslogSelector_UnmappedNameSharingLocal0Applies` pins that boundary, which
is what stops the change from degenerating into "ignore names I do not
recognize" and dropping a real operator restriction.

Junos more-specific-wins: an exact selector for the stamped facility displaces
the wildcard. Two selectors naming the **same** facility are a genuine conflict

## PR #7184 — dataplane: transmit a session pair under one sessionMu hold (#5698) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/5698-pair-transmit`

## Summary

- The forward and reverse halves of a locally-created session pair were built under ONE uninterrupted `m.mu` hold (#5007), then transmitted by `syncSessionRequestsLocked`, which drops `m.mu` once and **loops** calling `requestSessionSync` — and that helper took and released `m.sessionMu` around **each** round trip. `m.sessionMu` was therefore FREE between the forward's reply and the reverse's dial.
- Any other session-socket mutation (operator clear, policy invalidation, GC delete, stale-session reconciliation) could land in that gap. A generation-0 forward delete arriving there removes BOTH halves in the helper, and the pair's already-built explicit reverse then re-creates a **standalone reverse-only permit** — return traffic permitted with no forward session behind it.
- `syncSessionRequestsLocked`'s doc comment asserted the opposite and was false: *"Sending both requests under a single unlock also keeps the pair's transmit contiguous."* `m.mu` and `m.sessionMu` are independent locks. That sentence is deleted and replaced with what the unlock actually buys (the "socket I/O must not block snapshot publishes" property and the #5007 one-snapshot build).
- `requestSessionSync` splits into the per-request locking wrapper plus `requestSessionSyncLocked` (unlocked inner, caller holds `sessionMu`). Dial timeout, round-trip deadline, and `errSessionHelperUnreachable` transport wrapping are unchanged.
- New `syncSessionPairLocked` drops `m.mu` as before, takes `m.sessionMu` **once** for the whole group, sends every request through the unlocked inner, releases it, reacquires `m.mu`. The #5380 transport fast-fail is preserved by factoring the loop into a single `sendSessionSyncBatch` that both transmit paths drive, so the two cannot drift on error handling.

## Scope of the fix — read this before assuming more

**This closes the Go-side interleaving window ONLY.** The pair's transmit is now *contiguous*, not *atomic*: if the pair's **second** request fails at the transport layer, the helper is left with a half-installed pair and nothing rolls the first half back. That residual needs a helper-side pair transaction on the wire and is going to a successor issue — it is deliberately out of scope here, and is stated as such in `syncSessionPairLocked`'s doc comment and in `docs/session-sync-architecture.md`.

No Rust, no wire/protocol change.

## Why only the pair path

Every other caller of `syncSessionRequestsLocked` keeps per-request locking **on purpose**. A bulk delete chunk is up to `sessionHelperDeleteChunk` (256) requests; holding `m.sessionMu` across a chunk that large would starve live session installs for minutes — the exact harm #5380's fast-fail exists to bound. `sessionPairMaxRequests` (2) makes that structural rather than conventional: an over-cap group logs and falls back to the per-request path rather than trading a rare interleave for a multi-minute install stall.

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./...` → rc=0
- [x] `go vet ./pkg/dataplane/...` → rc=0
- [x] `go test -count=1 ./pkg/dataplane/...` → rc=0
- [x] `go test -count=1 -race -run 'Session' ./pkg/dataplane/userspace/...` → rc=0
- [x] New `TestSessionPairTransmitIsContiguous_5698` + `..._V6_5698` + `TestSessionPairOversizedGroupFallsBack_5698`

### Why the new test is deterministic in both directions

The test drives the **real** mirrors against a fake session socket, with three competing `requestSessionSync` goroutines and a 2ms hold on every reply. Both knobs are load-bearing, and the test file says so at length so nobody "simplifies" them away:

- **Green** needs no probabilistic argument. With the fix `sessionMu` is never released between the halves, so an interleave is *impossible*, not merely improbable.
- **Red** is forced by Go's mutex starvation mode. A one-shot race does **not** fail reliably: on the first `Unlock` the runtime only *wakes* the waiter, and the unlocking goroutine (the pair loop) barges and re-acquires for the reverse before the woken competitor is ever scheduled. The first draft of this test did exactly that and **passed against the unfixed code**. Go also clears the starving bit on a hand-off to the *last* waiter, so a single competitor keeps dropping the mutex back into barge-friendly normal mode — hence >1 competitor. With two or more waiters queued the starving bit survives the hand-off, `Lock`'s fast path stays disabled, and the interleave is forced on every pair.

### Mutation proof — one mutation, one line per cell, `$?` read directly

| Mutation | rc | Failing assertion |
|---|---|---|
| `mirrorSessionPairV4` → `syncSessionRequestsLocked` | 1 | `33 session-sync request(s) interleaved BETWEEN the pair's forward and its reverse (first: "competitor-delete" at position 6)` — **V4 cell only**, V6 stayed green |
| `mirrorSessionPairV6` → `syncSessionRequestsLocked` | 1 | same assertion, **V6 cell only**, V4 stayed green |
| over-cap branch returns an error instead of falling back | 1 | `helper received 0 of 3 requests from an oversized group` |

Base RED reproduced 5/5 runs; fixed GREEN 5/5 runs. The arrival order under the bug is a textbook signature — exactly three competitor deletes wedged between every forward and its reverse:

```
[... forward competitor-delete competitor-delete competitor-delete reverse ...]
```

## Docs

`docs/session-sync-architecture.md` gains a **#5698 invariant** section next to the existing #5007 one: why the `m.mu` unlock says nothing about session-socket ordering, why the pair path takes `sessionMu` once, why the bulk paths deliberately do not, and the un-closed residual. `pkg/dataplane/README.md` needed no change — it documents the shim/Manager layer and makes no claim about session-socket locking or pair transmit atomicity.

## PR #7185 — api: don't certify a zero under an nft fence [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/5719-fence-zero-not-authoritative`

## The defect

`pkg/nftables.ReadHostInboundDenyCounters` returned `(nil, nil)` for two
different kernel states and documented it as "no enforcement means no denies,
not an error". That is true for one of them and false for the other:

| kernel state | `inet xpf_hostinbound` | `xpfhi_*` counters | old return |
|---|---|---|---|
| real policy loaded | present | >=1 | non-empty — distinguishable |
| **cold-boot fail-closed FENCE (#5644 M37)** | **present, actively DROPping** | **none** | `(nil, nil)` |
| table absent | absent | — | `(nil, nil)` |

The fence is counter-less BY DESIGN — `buildHostInboundFencePayload` /
`buildHostInboundFenceNetlink` render the mandatory admits plus catch-all DROPs
with "NO per-service accepts, NO named counters".

So while a fence enforced — the appliance DEGRADED and actively dropping
host-bound traffic — REST `/api/v1/statistics/global` published
`host_inbound_kernel_denies: 0` with `host_inbound_kernel_denies_unavailable`
absent/false: an **authoritative** zero asserting "the kernel host-inbound path
saw no denies", published in exactly the window an operator reads that field to
find out. It contradicted the #3345 / #3681-H05 "counter unavailable != zero"
contract that the same function's own comment cites for the netlink-failure
case.

## The fix

`ReadHostInboundDenyCounters` now returns a `HostInboundTableState`
(`Absent` / `Counterless` / `Counted`) alongside the rows. `pkg/api/stats.go`
routes `Counterless` onto the **existing** `HostInboundKernelDeniesUnavailable`
channel — the already-documented "this zero is not authoritative" marker,
exactly as it already does on a netlink read failure — and
`collectHostInboundKernelDenies` bumps `xpf_counter_read_errors_total` for the
same state, keeping the two surfaces consistent (there is no series to omit:
no counter object exists to label).

The discriminator is **"the table carries no named counter OBJECT"**, not "the
deny slice came back empty". That distinction is load-bearing: a real
generation declares the three #4759 ICMP/ND ACCEPT counters unconditionally, so
the one legitimate ruleset with no per-zone catch-all DROP (a junos-host
program-only generation) still reads `Counted` and is not false-alarmed. The
weaker `len(rows) == 0` form flags it — proved by a mutation cell below.

Two states stay **AUTHORITATIVE**: an absent table (no enforcement really is no
denies), and real deny counters that merely READ zero (the counter objects
exist, so `GetObjects` returns them with `Packets: 0` and the read is
`Counted`). Verified before relying on it and pinned by its own test row.

## PR #7186 — config: warn on unadjudicated WireGuard plaintext [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/5618-wg-plaintext-warn`

Closes #5618

## What this does — and what it does NOT do

This makes the WireGuard forward-zone-policy bypass **OPERATOR-VISIBLE at commit
time**. It does **NOT** enforce policy on decapsulated plaintext. The
decapsulated inner packet still goes straight to the `wgN` TUN and is still
forwarded by the Linux kernel with no zone policy, no session, no NAT and no
screen. Enforcement — re-injecting the inner packet into the AF_XDP
forward/zone-policy pipeline on the tunnel's logical interface, the model native
GRE decap already follows — is an architectural change tracked by a successor
issue filed separately.

## The defect

`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/coordinator/wg_control/dispatch.rs` writes authenticated
WireGuard plaintext straight to the `wgN` TUN via
`slowpath::write_packet_nonblocking`. Its own comment states the consequence:
"the kernel routes/firewalls it (NOT the AF_XDP policy engine — the AllowedIPs
gate inside `try_decap` is S2a's inner-src control)."

`wgN` rows are `Tunnel=true`, so the `Tunnel` arm of `netdevExclusionClasses`
makes `userspaceSkipsIngressInterface` exclude them from the
ingress-adjudication map and the AF_XDP binding plan. xpf force-enables
`ip_forward=1` and installs only nftables `hook input` chains, so the plaintext
is kernel-forwarded with no xpf authority. `allowed-ips` is a cryptographic
peer/source ownership gate on the inner SOURCE address — no destination, no
zone-pair, no application, no direction.

Today an operator can write `set security zones security-zone vpn interfaces
wg0.0`, commit it cleanly, and read it as enforced. It is not.

## What this adds

`warnWireGuardPlaintextUnadjudicatedAST` (`pkg/config/compiler_wireguard_plaintext_warn.go`),
the exact analogue of the shipped #5619 IPsec advisory:

- **It cannot reject.** No error return, no `lenient` flag — the #1960 no-brick
  property is structural, not a convention. A box already running a route-based
  WireGuard tunnel can still commit an unrelated change.
- **ONE aggregated advisory per commit**, naming every affected tunnel.
- **Fires whenever a WireGuard tunnel is configured**, not only when one carries
  a zone — an unzoned interface resolves to zone id 0, which a `from-zone any
  to-zone any permit` rule matches (#6682), so unzoned is not a mitigation.
- **Two groups, worded differently.** A ZONED tunnel escalates (the operator was
  told something specific and untrue); an unzoned one is a plain statement of
  the gap.
- **Runs on every compile path** — strict commit, lenient restart/peer-sync, and
  both HA node views — because the operator who most needs telling is the one
  who never re-commits after an upgrade.
```
