Mirror the cluster arm, which is what the issue asks for.
`watchUserspaceEventStreamCallbacks` keeps the 500 ms cadence and the
first-wire behaviour of the helper it replaces, but never returns: it
re-resolves the provider and the stream from the #2114 cell each tick and
re-installs on the same **instance-identity** predicate the fallback loop
uses, so an unreplaced stream is never re-wired.

`wireUserspaceEventStreamCallbacks` is unchanged and still used by
`daemon_ha_sync.go`, where a bounded 5 s wire is followed by
`eventStreamFallbackLoop` taking over the re-install.

### Shutdown join

The arm now blocks for the life of `ctx` where it used to return, and
`daemon_run.go` registers that goroutine on the run WaitGroup.

## PR #7248 — cluster: re-check the config epoch after the synced install writes (#6368) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6368-config-epoch-install-race`

`configEpochStale` and `PutClusterSynced*` are not one critical section. The
check reads `max(applyingConfigGen, lastAppliedConfigGen)`; the write lands
several statements later, on the `receiveLoop` goroutine, while
`configApplyLoop` runs on its own. A receiveLoop descheduled across that gap
passes the check against the pre-fence threshold and lands its write **after**
the deleted-policy sweep that was supposed to invalidate the session.

## The one place I disagree with the issue

It filed this as *"practically impossible timing — the entire beginConfigApply +
sweep would have to fit inside a single install's check→Put gap (a few
instructions)"*. The gap is not a few instructions. The racing party must fit
`beginConfigApply` plus the whole of `OnConfigReceived` — which **compiles and
promotes a config and runs `clearSessionsForDeletedPolicies` inside it** — into
the window, and a GC pause or a loaded box is enough to deschedule a goroutine
across that. So the probability is low but the mechanism is ordinary, and the
consequence is not self-limiting: what survives is a stale PERMIT that no later
sweep re-examines. It lives until the next config apply, which on a quiet box
may be never, and on a standby it is exactly what that node forwards on after a
failover.

## Fix — act-then-verify, not a lock

The install re-reads the threshold after a successful write and rolls the
session back (`DeleteWithCompanions*`, reason `cluster-stale` — the same
primitive and reason the stale bulk reconcile uses) when it has gone stale.

Serializing the check with the write would hold a mutex across dataplane I/O on
the bulk-install hot path, which the **#2198 F3 non-atomicity note refuses on
exactly those grounds**. Re-reading two atomics costs one load per install and
detects precisely the case the pre-check cannot see.

The rollback introduces **no new semantic**: `configEpochStale` never consults
policy, it refuses on epoch alone, so applying its verdict a moment later is the
guard's own decision rather than a fresh judgement about the session. The
per-key generation is deliberately **not** recorded for a rolled-back install,
so the peer's next re-sync of that key is admitted instead of refused as stale.

## Tests

Drive the real apply layer and land the concurrent config apply **inside** the
dataplane write, through a new `onSetV4`/`onSetV6` hook on `mockSweepDP` (nil
for every existing test) — the only way to place the event in that window
without depending on the scheduler.

| cell | asserts |
|---|---|
| v4 / v6 rollback | the session does not survive; the late refusal is counted; the per-key recv-gen high-water did **not** advance |
| uncontended install | a current-epoch install with no racing apply still lands (the fix cannot be satisfied by rolling back everything) |
| apply that is not newer | an apply raising the fence to 11 leaves an epoch-12 session alone — pins the rollback to the staleness predicate, not to "an apply happened" |

## PR #7249 — userspace-dp: follow the selected WG peer on the tx_ifindex>0 dispatch (#6345) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6345-wg-dispatch-peer-route`

`resolve_forward_target_ifindex` early-returned `decision.resolution.tx_ifindex`
whenever it was > 0, so #6308's peer-route SSOT reached only the
`tx_ifindex == 0` branch.

For a WG transit-egress flow whose transport table **does** carry a default
route, that stored value is the DEFAULT-route parent — while `wg_encap_frame`
builds the outer L2/VLAN/src against the **selected peer's** more-specific route
(#6306). With one underlay the two name the same NIC and nothing changes. With
several — a peer reachable over a different NIC than the default route's —
dispatch targeted one NIC while the bytes carried another egress's L2: a frame
emitted on the wrong wire, carrying a source MAC and VLAN belonging to a
different segment.

## Fix

Consult the peer-route resolution **first**, on both branches; `tx_ifindex`
becomes the fallback rather than the short circuit. Dispatch NIC and frame L2
are then the same NIC by construction.

If the peer's NIC has no XSK binding the dispatcher drops. That is deliberate
and it is the better of the two outcomes: a drop is visible and bounded, while
the alternative puts a frame with a foreign source MAC and VLAN onto a segment
it does not belong to.

**The fast path is unchanged in cost.** The resolver's first act is
`decision.resolution.tunnel_endpoint_id == 0 -> None`, so a plain forward pays
one integer compare and then takes `tx_ifindex` verbatim exactly as before. The
doc comment claiming the resolution runs ONLY on the `tx_ifindex == 0` path is
corrected rather than left standing — it is the load-bearing claim this change
invalidates.

## Tests

| cell | asserts |
|---|---|
| `wg_transit_egress_dispatch_follows_peer_route_over_tx_ifindex_6345` | `tx_ifindex` set to a different physical bind than the peer route resolves to → dispatch follows the **peer** |
| `non_wg_forward_keeps_the_tx_ifindex_fast_path_6345` | anti-over-reject: a non-tunnel decision still takes `tx_ifindex` verbatim, so a future refactor cannot quietly route every forward through the peer resolution |

The existing #6308 single-underlay assertion is unchanged and still green —
there the two resolutions agree, which is precisely why the common case is
untouched.

## Verification

- Mutation-proven by restoring the **verbatim** pre-fix ordering (`tx_ifindex`
  short circuit before the peer resolution): the multi-underlay cell reds, the
  anti-over-reject cell stays green, post-restore green.
- Full `cargo test --manifest-path userspace-dp/Cargo.toml --release --bins
  --tests -- --test-threads=1`: **4484 + 60 + 8 + 22 + 31 + 1 + 2 passed, 0
  failed** (rc=0).

## PR #7251 — test(cos): verify the CLI transcript, not the session exit status [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6440-cos-apply-cli-transcript-gate`

## The defect

`apply-cos-config.sh` exited **6** on `loss:xpf-userspace-fw0` with "no
shaper/scheduler binding" and auto-rolled-back. Because `make cluster-deploy`
wipes CoS and this script is how it gets re-applied, every CoS-dependent
measurement after such a run was silently taken against **un-applied config**.

The script drives the CLI by piping a heredoc into it and gated each phase on
that command's **exit status**. That gate is structurally unable to detect a
failure. The piped-stdin form of the CLI is a **REPL, not a batch runner** —
`cmd/cli/main.go`:

```go
err = c.dispatch(line)
if err != nil {
    if err == errExit { break }
    if err == context.Canceled { continue }
    fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "error: %v\n", err)   // print and CONTINUE
}
```

A failed command prints one line to stderr, the loop moves to the next heredoc
line, and `main` returns normally — **exit status 0**. Only
`cli -c "<one command>"` `os.Exit(1)`s on a dispatch error.

So a `load merge` that failed left a candidate holding ONLY the script's
`delete class-of-service ...` lines. Deleting is a **valid** candidate, so
`commit check` passed and `commit` committed the deletes — wiping CoS instead
of re-applying it. Neither the phase-1 nor the phase-2 gate could fire; the
first check that inspected anything was the phase-3 output grep, which blamed
a missing shaper binding for a failure two phases upstream.

Both the exit-4 ("commit check failed") and exit-5 ("commit failed") paths were
**dead code** for per-command failures.

## Three further defects on the same root cause

1. **The rollback reassurance was unverified.** Every rollback site ran
   `... <<'EOF' || true` and then announced `live state reverted` from the
   `then` branch of an `if` on the session exit status — i.e. unconditionally.
   The script could report a clean revert over a rollback that never happened.
   #6440 recorded exactly that reassurance.
2. **The two `cli -c` readbacks discarded their exit status** with `|| true`.
   That form's status *is* meaningful, so an unreachable xpfd produced an error
   transcript that failed the shaper grep and exited 6 blaming CoS — the
   misdiagnosis this issue was filed on.
3. **No daemon-readiness wait** between a deploy (which restarts xpfd) and the
   first CLI call. The issue's follow-up comment recorded a commit-check dying
   on connection-refused for this reason.

## PR #7252 — docs: regenerate the refactoring heatmap [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/refactor-audit-regen-2`

`pkg/refactoraudit` is red on master again — for two files unrelated to the previous regeneration in #7235.

Measured firsthand at `origin/master` `e5403832e`:

```
entered the audit (now >=1500 LOC):
  [WATCH]    pkg/dataplane/types.go
changed tier (crossed 2000 LOC):
  pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go: [WATCH] -> [REFACTOR]
```

I confirmed both sizes independently rather than trusting the assertion text: `pkg/dataplane/types.go` is **1501** lines — it crossed the floor by **exactly one line** — and `pkg/grpcapi/server_sessions.go` is **2197** after `0053f3533` ("filter sessions by the recorded ingress interface", +251/-47) pushed it through 2000. `tcp_segmentation.rs` from #7235 is still correctly present at 1582, so that fix landed and held.

## The second regeneration in an hour is the actual finding

This unblocks `go test ./...`, but it is a treadmill and should be read as one.

The artifact is a generated snapshot of a **repo-global** property, so it is only valid for the tree it was generated from. On a board landing several PRs an hour it can go stale between authoring and merge — #7235 was authored against a head that no longer existed by the time it landed. A PR author who did everything right still lands red, and the file that reds them is usually one they never touched.

`types.go` at **1501** is the sharpest illustration: a one-line addition anywhere in the repo flipped a gate for unrelated authors.

**#6617 already relaxed this gate once for exactly this reason** — from a byte-for-byte compare to an audit-content compare, after measuring master byte-stale in 26 of 40 first-parent commits. The content compare has the same flaw one level up: it is narrower, but any file crossing a threshold anywhere still reds it globally.

Filed separately as a gate-design issue rather than worked around here. The plausible fixes are regenerating at merge time, or letting the gate tolerate a bounded lag — both are decisions for whoever owns the gate, not something to smuggle into a regeneration PR.

## The change

Generated with the committed generator, not edited by hand:

```
bash scripts/refactoring-audit.sh > docs/refactoring-audit-current.txt
```

## Validation

- Failure reproduced first at `origin/master` `e5403832e` with none of this change.
- Both file sizes verified independently (1501, 2197).
- After regeneration: `go test -count=1 ./pkg/refactoraudit/` **rc=0**.

Exit codes read from `$?` directly, never through a pipe.

Docs-only: one generated artifact, no `.go`, no `.rs`, no compiled artifact. No cluster smoke owed.

## PR #7255 — cluster: source the bulk window from table-truth (#6031) [CLOSED] (closed 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6031-cold-prime-table-truth`

Closes #6031

## The residual, at HEAD

`BulkSync` delimits the authoritative cold-prime snapshot the peer's
`reconcileStaleSessions` runs against. Since #5085 removed the empty-bulk
reconcile skip, a session merely **absent** from that window is treated as
stale and **deleted**.

But the window was sourced from `s.sessions.ForEachV4/V6` — which on the
userspace dataplane walks the shim `sessions`/`sessions_v6` BPF maps. Those are
a best-effort **display mirror** the Rust helper publishes via
`publish_bpf_conntrack_entry` so `show security flow session` can render
zone/interface info — not the helper's authoritative in-process `SessionTable`.
The mirror can drift:

- publication is gated at table cap and on `install_failed` (`session_glue/mod.rs`),
- the periodic refresh lags,
- and it carries no per-session **origin**, so it also echoes peer-owned imports
  back at their owner (`ShouldSyncZone` is only a zone-level approximation).

A transiently under-populated mirror at cold-prime therefore reconciles **live
peer-owned sessions** away on the standby.

## The fix

`SessionSync.BulkSessionSource`, resolved **before** the epoch is taken so a
failure aborts without opening a window. Three cases — the middle one is why
this is not a plain getter:

| returns | BulkSync does |
|---|---|
| snapshot (possibly **empty**) | frames exactly that set. Empty is an authoritative "I own nothing", which the peer must reconcile against |
| `(nil, nil)` | falls back to the store walk — no authoritative source exists (no userspace runtime, no committed config), so nothing regresses |
| `(nil, err)` | **aborts** |

The abort is the load-bearing choice. Falling back on an export failure would
reconcile the peer against exactly the mirror this change decided is not
authoritative, and an under-populated window deletes live sessions. A skipped
bulk is recoverable: every `doBulkSync` caller re-arms and retries
(`handleNewConnection`'s `needColdPrime` latch, the #4090 survivor re-drive, the
#82 sweep re-drive).

**A source, not an override.** `BulkSyncOverride` runs *before* `BulkSync`, so a
window framed there would still be followed by the mirror-sourced one the
receiver actually reconciles against — which is why the issue's "rewire the
override" sketch would not have closed the residual. Exactly one
`BulkStart → sessions → BulkEnd` window is written, same epoch, same #3912
record-then-send discipline, same #5272 completion gate. **No wire change.**

## PR #7256 — deploy: run the #1864 verifier pre-flight on the standalone deploy too [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6493-standalone-verify-dataplane`

Closes #6493

## What was wrong

`grep -rn verify-dataplane test/incus/*.sh` matched **only** `cluster-setup.sh`. The standalone deploy — `make test-deploy` / `test/incus/setup.sh deploy`, the canonical single-VM flow in the README and the CLAUDE.md Quick Start — pushed a new `xpfd` and started it with no proof that its embedded AF_XDP shim is accepted by that VM's BPF verifier.

Nothing else in the deploy can catch it. `incus file push` succeeds; `deploy_verify_pushed_sha` compares **bytes**; `deploy_verify_running_xpfd` proves only that systemd launched the pushed image. All three pass for a binary whose shim loads nothing — the VM comes up config-only with no dataplane, the deploy reports success, and the failure surfaces later as a forwarding mystery. That is the 2026-06-10 #1864 incident mode, and the standalone VM is the *higher*-risk venue for it: it is where `make generate` shim iteration happens, against a VM kernel independent of the build host's.

## What this does

Extracts the #1869 gate from `cluster-setup.sh` into `deploy-lib.sh` as `deploy_verify_dataplane_preflight` (+ `deploy_preflight_cleanup`) and calls it from **both** paths, rather than growing a second hand copy that drifts.

The cluster path's behaviour is unchanged: same staged `/tmp/xpfd.preflight`, same worker-core-complement CPU mask with the `taskset` probe and the nice-only fallback, same abort-before-touching-the-old-daemon on REJECT. The only visible difference is that diagnostics now name the remote-qualified instance (`loss:xpf-userspace-fw0`) rather than the bare VM name.

In `setup.sh` the call sits above the bpfrxd migration, the pin reconcile, `systemctl stop xpfd`, the pkills and the binary push — so a REJECT aborts with the old daemon still running and forwarding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `setup.sh deploy` runs the same `verify-dataplane` preflight (push to /tmp, CPU-complement mask with probe fallback, `nice -19`) **before** `systemctl stop xpfd`, aborting with the old daemon untouched on REJECT.
- [x] Shared logic lives in `test/incus/deploy-lib.sh`; both callers use it. Not a second copy.
- [x] `make test-deploy-lib` covers REJECT-aborts-before-any-stop/push, PASS-proceeds, and preflight-binary-cleanup.

## Validation

`./test/incus/deploy-lib-selftest.sh` (`make test-deploy-lib`) — **27 passed, 0 failed, rc=0** (9 new cases).
`scripts/run-selftests.sh` — **50 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed, rc=0** (unchanged from baseline).

### Mutation proofs

Exit codes read from `$?`, never through a pipe. One line mutated per run; `git checkout --` restore verified clean (`git status --porcelain` empty) and rc back to 0 between each.

| # | Mutation (one line) | rc | Cell that reddened |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | REJECT `die` → `warn` | 1 | `verifier REJECT MUST hard-fail (this is the #1864 mode)` + `REJECT must not return 0` |
| M2 | move the `setup.sh` call below `systemctl stop xpfd` | 1 | `pre-flight at :625 runs AFTER stop(:624)` |
| M3 | drop `deploy_preflight_cleanup` from the REJECT path only | 1 | `staged candidate left behind after REJECT` |
| M4 | delete the `setup.sh` call entirely (the pre-fix state) | 1 | `no deploy_verify_dataplane_preflight call — the standalone deploy has NO verifier gate` |

## A note on the two structural cases

The function can be perfect and the gate still useless if a caller runs it after the daemon is stopped, so two cases read the **real** `setup.sh` / `cluster-setup.sh` and assert the call precedes every destructive step in its function (M2/M4 above).

That check found a defect in its own first draft, which is worth flagging for review: the call sites are documented with prose that *names* the destructive steps ("...runs before `systemctl stop xpfd`..."), so the unanchored sweep matched the **explanation of the invariant** instead of the code that would break it, and reported a correctly-ordered gate as mis-ordered. The comment-skipping line filter in `_first_line_matching` is therefore load-bearing, not tidiness.

## Scope

- **Does not reach the Rust helper.** Shell only; no `userspace-dp`/`userspace-xdp` source, no `.o` movement, no binary artifact.
- **No cluster time used.** Every assertion above is hermetic (the existing fake-incus mock in `deploy-lib-selftest.sh`); the loss cluster was not touched, deployed to, or smoked.

the session mirror had to read the HA state machine and vice versa, and the
file's lock-discipline invariants (#5007 one-snapshot build, #5698 pair-transmit

Each declaration was copied **by exact source line range by a script, never

No moved body is non-identical, so there is nothing to justify individually.

## PR #7262 — daemon(nft): give the cold-boot fence its own drop scope [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6492-fence-lifeline-zoneless`

> **Findings coverage:** A **fixed**, B **fixed**, C (`daemon_nft.go:235`,
> `installLo0ColdBootFence` — the #6489 whole-table re-render) **subsumed, and
> proven subsumed** — see "Finding C" below. `Closes #6492` covers all three.

## Problem

The #5644 host-inbound and #6476 lo0 cold-boot fences both rendered their drop
set from `BuildZoneHostInboundViews` + `BuildUnzonedHostInboundAddrs` — the
address scope the **real** ruleset uses. A fence is the real table with every
per-service ACCEPT removed, so reusing that scope unchanged is wrong in two
independent directions.

**Finding A — lifeline lockout.** The view builders exclude lifeline
*interfaces* (fxp0 / em0 / fab\* / the configured control+fabric links), not
lifeline address *values*. When the same IP is also configured on a non-lifeline
interface — a topology xpf explicitly accepts
(`pkg/config/dup_host_local_address_3718_test.go`) — the non-lifeline snapshot
re-adds it, and the fence drop carries **no `iifname` qualifier**, so it renders
as a bare `ip daddr <mgmt-ip> drop`. Every NEW management connection to that
address dies for the whole fence window. The real table is unaffected: its
per-service accepts precede the catch-all DROP.

**Finding B — zone-less fail-open.** Both builders return nothing when the config
declares no security zone, because the real host-inbound default-deny is a
zone-model construct. Host-inbound / lo0 filters are independently valid without
zones (`compiler_filter_ref_3296_test`), so on a zone-less-but-addressed router a
failed cold-boot lo0 install produced an accept-policy fence shell with **ZERO
drops** — the exact fail-open the fence exists to prevent.

## Fix

`dpuserspace.BuildFenceAddrSets` derives a **fence-only** scope and is the single
input to both fence sites:

- **Narrower:** withholds any address that also lives on a lifeline interface,
  reported at WARN by `logFenceWithheld` (it is a real coverage hole while the
  fence is up, so it is not applied silently).
- **Wider:** derives the drop set from the firewall-local **addresses** — every
  non-lifeline interface address from the canonical snapshot builder plus every
  configured VRRP virtual address (a VIP is live only on the RG master, #3172) —
  rather than from zone membership. **No "are there zones?" branch**: the address
  walk is identical either way and simply yields more than the zone views do when
  zones are absent or incomplete. That also closes the same-shape hole for a VIP
  on an unzoned interface in a *zoned* config.

The narrowing is deliberately **not** applied inside `BuildZoneHostInboundViews`
— that would relax the real table's default-deny, a fail-open. Because the
fence's coverage now differs from the real ruleset's `desiredDrop` in both
directions, `installHostInboundColdBootFence` records `hostInboundCoveredAddrs`
from the fence's own sets so the #5789 day-2 gap check describes what the

## PR #7263 — cli: surface the day-0 config-import verdict as `show system bootstrap-import` [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6496-bootstrap-import-show`

Closes #6496

## What was wrong

The #4184 work records the boot-time config-import outcome (`ok` / `loaded-from-db` / `no-config` / `import-failed` + error detail) and emits a `BOOTSTRAP_IMPORT_FAILED` event — but rendered it in exactly one place: the `/health` JSON on the loopback REST API. `grep -rn "bootstrap_import_status\|BootstrapImportStatus" pkg/cmdtree pkg/grpcapi proto` returned nothing.

The operator that feature exists for is standing at a fresh box on day zero with the `cli` prompt open, asking the exact question the status answers. They could not get it from the CLI they were in — they had to know to leave it and `curl 127.0.0.1:8080/health`, documented only in the bare-metal device-map doc, not in the general day-0 flow.

## What this does

`show system bootstrap-import` on the operational tree, the in-process console CLI, the gRPC `ShowText` dispatcher, and the remote `cli` client. **No proto change was needed** — `ShowText(topic)` already exists.

```
> show system bootstrap-import
Bootstrap configuration import:
  Status:   import-failed
  Meaning:  a configuration file was present but could NOT be applied — see Error below
  Recorded: 2026-08-21 14:02:11 UTC
  Error:    day-0 config REJECTED by commit-check: ...

  The box is in the lifeline-safe bootstrap state; the running
  configuration is NOT the one on the day-0 medium. ...
```

**Rendering is single-sourced** in a new leaf package `pkg/bootstrapshow`, in the `pkg/natshow` idiom. Two renderings of one recorded fact that disagree is *always* a bug, never a legitimate difference — so this is single-sourced rather than duplicated-and-cross-checked, and both call paths are asserted byte-identical to it.

That package also owns the **status vocabulary**; `pkg/daemon`'s four unexported constants become aliases of it. The renderer maps each status to a meaning and reports anything else as `unrecognized status`, so a status recorded but never taught to the renderer would surface to the day-0 operator as the CLI not understanding its own daemon. Aliasing makes that unreachable, and a test asserts every recordable status renders without the marker.

**The error detail is rendered here, deliberately.** `/health` withholds it (#5031): that endpoint is unauthenticated and an import error quotes the offending config, which can echo a submitted secret. The CLI/gRPC paths are authenticated, so they are the *only* surfaces that can answer "why didn't my config apply" with the reason — the point of the command. Topic sits at `PermView`, matching the coarse model the rest of `show` uses and matching `login`, which renders login configuration at the same level.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Renders status, error detail, and timestamp via the gRPC path, matching the /health payload (same recorded snapshot, one conversion).
- [x] `docs/install-images.md` day-0 troubleshooting references the command **and** the /health field.
- [x] `import-failed` remains non-503 on /health (untouched), and the CLI rendering is likewise informational — `Render` has no failure return; a test asserts non-failure statuses never render the remediation block.

## Two of the repo's own gates were load-bearing

`TestEveryShowTextTopicHasAPermission_5278` required the authz entry, and `TestShowTextTopicAuditCoverageIsComplete` required the topic to join the #6532 fabric secret-render sweep. The second is worth a reviewer's attention: **`ShowText` is reachable from the peer chassis over the fabric**, not only from loopback. That is not a new disclosure class here (an HA peer already receives the full config over config-sync), but it is why the topic is *audited* rather than assumed safe.

## PR #7264 — cluster: roll back the transfer-out override on a failed commit [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6527-transfer-commit-rollback`

`commitRequestedPeerFailover` arms `peerTransferOutOverride` — which also
forces `peerGroups[rgID].State` to `SecondaryHold` — and only then runs the
election, returning an error when the local RG did not reach primary. The
**batch** request path aborted on that error; the **single-RG** path returned
it bare and leaked the override.

### Why it is persistent, not a blip

`applyTransferCommitOverridesOnPeerStateLocked` re-forces the peer to
`SecondaryHold` on every subsequent heartbeat **with no time bound** — unlike
`peerTransferCommitGraceUntil`, which expires in the same helper — and nothing
else clears the map on the requester side. So `electRG` keeps taking its "Peer
transfer out" arm and self-promotes this node as soon as whatever failed the
election clears. Both chassis then hold the RETH VIP and virtual MAC
indefinitely.

### Reachability

No exotic fault needed. `RequestPeerFailover` releases `m.mu` around the fabric
round-trip, and `commitRequestedPeerFailover`'s re-check is
`IsReadyForTakeover`, which reads `Ready`/`ReadySince` and never looks at
weight. An interface-monitor debt landing in that window passes the readiness
gate and then loses the election on `electRG`'s "Local weight 0" arm — the
ordinary case of a monitored link dropping mid-failover.

### Fix

Call `abortRequestedPeerFailover` on the commit error, matching the batch path.
The rollback is reqID-matched and a no-op on the two error returns that precede
the override, so it is safe on every commit failure.

### Test

Binds the **agreement** between the two request paths rather than either copy:
one table drives `RequestPeerFailover` and `RequestPeerFailoverBatch` through
the same commit-time election failure and asserts identical post-conditions
(override + snapshot maps empty, peer state restored from the snapshot, this
node not primary), then recovers the monitor and delivers another peer-primary
heartbeat to assert the dual-primary does not appear later either. The election
is failed through `SetMonitorWeight`, the same entry point `pkg/routing/monitor.go`
and the interface-monitor poll use.

## PR #7265 — daemon/HA: re-arm the rg_active retry after an out-of-band write [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6530-fence-rearm-rg-retry`

`rgStateMachine`'s retry predicate in `reconcileRGState` is
`tr.Changed || s.NeedsApply()` — the desired value moved, or the last apply did
not converge. But `applied`/`applyPending` are advanced only by `MarkApplied`
and `ApplyIfCurrent`, and **neither has a path that SETS `applyPending`**: both
only CLEAR it, when `applied == active`.

That makes the retry structurally blind to any writer that changes `rg_active`
in the dataplane without going through the state machine's transition path.
After such a write the machine still believes `desired == applied`, the 2s
reconcile pass does nothing, and nothing else re-arms it. Forwarding stays
wherever that second writer left it — a **blackhole with no retry**, not a
glitch the next tick repairs.

`fenceAllRedundancyGroups` is the instance that surfaced this: a received peer
fence writes `SetRGActive(rg, false)` directly, so a fenced primary never came
back, because the pass that exists precisely to restore it could not see that
anything had changed. The fence is opt-in on the **sending** node
(`set chassis cluster peer-fencing disable-rg`) but the **receiving** side is
wired unconditionally, so a node with no fencing configured is still exposed to
a peer that has it.

### Fix — the class, not the call site

Add `rgStateMachine.InvalidateApplied()` and have the fence call it after each
write.

- It arms the retry **unconditionally** rather than recording the value
  written: a write that returned an error may still have partially landed, so
  "not known to have converged" is the only honest reading, and forcing a
  re-drive is the fail-closed one at a cost of at most one idempotent re-apply.
- It sets `applied = !active` rather than only flipping `applyPending`,
  preserving the invariant `reconcileLocked` relies on (`applyPending` is true
  exactly when `applied != active`).
- It deliberately does **not** bump the epoch: `ApplyIfCurrent` already fails
  routinely and `recordRGActiveAppliedIfCurrentOrStable` falls back to
  `MarkApplied`, so a bump would not stop a concurrent in-flight apply from
  stamping over it. Ordering between two unsynchronised writers is not
  resolvable here; what this guarantees is that the machine never *silently*
  believes a convergence it did not observe. That bound is documented rather
  than papered over.
- `daemon_run_shutdown.go`'s `SetRGActive(false)` is the one deliberate
  non-caller — the daemon is exiting, there is no later reconcile pass to arm.

`getOrCreateRGState` now lazily allocates `d.rgStates`: `New()` always makes the
map, but the fence path reaches it from `Daemon` literals that minimal test
constructions build, and a nil-map write panics.

### Validation

- `go vet ./pkg/daemon` clean.

## PR #7266 — cluster/dhcpserver: converge a failed Kea apply without a transition [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6535-kea-apply-converger`

In cluster mode every driver of the Kea applier is an **edge**.
`applyRethServicesForRG` and `clearRethServicesForRG` run only under
`if tr.Changed`, `applyDirectVIPOwnership` only on an ownership change, and the
commit path only when an operator commits. The async apply worker logs an error
and drops it — it does not retry.

So a failover whose Kea apply failed left the wrong node serving: **persistent
dual-DHCP** when the demoting node's stop failed and both Kea instances stayed
up, or **no-DHCP** when the promoting node's start failed and neither did.
Recovery required another RG transition or a commit, neither of which happens on
its own.

RA — the other per-RG service those same two functions own — already has a
per-pass converger (`reconcileClusterRAServices`, #5861) built on the rule that
the applied marker advances only on a verified success, so a transient error is
retried on a later pass rather than latched as converged. This gives Kea the
same thing.

### Implementation

- `dhcpserver.Manager` records whether each **completed** apply attempt
  converged (`applyFailed`, cleared only by a success) and exposes
  `ClaimApplyRetry`, which grants a spaced retry window when it did not. A
  superseded apply (`gen <= lastAppliedGen`) never ran, so it deliberately
  leaves the marker alone.
- `lastAppliedGen` itself still advances on failure. A retry allocates a fresh
  generation and is never blocked by the superseded guard, so leaving that
  ordering invariant untouched keeps the #1835 coalescing reasoning intact.
  (The issue proposed changing it; measured against the code, it buys nothing
  and risks the concurrency invariant. Noting the divergence explicitly.)
- The retry state lives under **its own mutex**, not `m.mu`. `m.mu` is held for
  the whole apply body — a 15s-bounded systemctl shell-out — and the caller is
  the daemon's 2s reconcile pass, which must not block behind a restart still
  in flight. Lock order is `m.mu -> retryMu`; only the tail of `apply` takes
  both. (The first draft guarded it with `m.mu` and deadlocked the reconcile
  pass in test; the test still pins the ordering.)
- `reconcileClusterDHCPServices` is the converger, called from
  `reconcileRGState` beside its RA counterpart. Retries are spaced 30s because
  re-driving a permanently broken Kea (missing binary, bad unit) on every 2s
  tick is a continuous restart loop.
- `desiredClusterDHCPConfig` **single-sources** the desired state the commit
  path, both transition edges, and the converger derive from (config, current
  master-RG set). Single-sourced rather than bound with an agreement test: a
  divergence between the converger and an edge is always a bug, since the
  converger runs every pass and would fight the edge indefinitely. All three
  call sites now go through it; each was already computing exactly this, so
  the refactor is behaviour-preserving.

## PR #7267 — dataplane: drop dead eBPF NAT record construction (#6420) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6420-dead-ebpf-nat-records`

## Summary

- `compileNAT` / `compileStaticNAT` / `compileNAT64` (`pkg/dataplane/compiler_nat.go`) built `SNATValue`, `SNATValueV6`, `SNATEgressValue`, `NATPoolConfig`, `DNATValue`/`DNATValueV6`, static-NAT and `NAT64Config` records and handed them to `SetSNATRule` / `SetDNATEntry` / `SetNATPoolConfig` / `SetSNATEgressIP` / `SetStaticNATEntryV4/V6` / `SetNAT64Config`/`Count` and the stale-NAT deleters. **None of that reached a map on any production path.** Deleted the construction; kept every value that escapes the function.
- `compiler_nat.go`: **1428 → 1066 lines** (594 deleted / 199 added across the PR).
- `compileNPTv6` is deliberately untouched — see *Deferred* below.
- New `TestNATCompilerCallsNoDataplaneNATWriter_6420` binds the deletion from the side a counter cannot.

## The sink is a no-op on every production path

`SetSNATRule` / `SetDNATEntry` each have **three** implementations:

| site | receiver | behaviour | production? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `loader.go` | `userspaceShimCompileDataplane` | `return nil` (every NAT setter + every stale-NAT deleter) | **yes — the only one** |
| `compiler_validate_4960.go` | `discardingDataPlane` | discards by construction (#4960 pre-pass) | yes, but discarding is its contract |
| `maps_nat.go` | `(*Manager)` | real eBPF map write | **no — unreachable** |

The `maps_nat.go` writers are reached only via `Manager.Compile` → `CompileConfig(m, ...)`. Traced, not assumed:

- `RegisterRuntimeBackend` has exactly **one** call site in the tree (`userspace/manager.go`, `TypeUserspace`); `backendRegistry` has none. So `NewDataPlane`/`NewRuntimeDataPlane` can never hand back a `*dataplane.Manager`.
- `NewDataPlane`/`NewRuntimeDataPlane` hard-reject `TypeEBPF` with `ErrEBPFBackendRetired` (#1373/#1476).
- The only production `dataplane.New()` is `userspace.New()`'s `bpfShim`, and the only methods called on it are `CompileUserspaceShim`, `LastCompileResult`, `SelectUserspaceXDPShimEntryProgram`, `XDPLinks`/`TCLinks`/`DetachXDP`/`DetachTC`.
- `LegacyDataPlaneAdapter` embeds `dataplane.DataPlane` (= that shim) but **shadows** `Compile` and `ApplyConfig` with the userspace ones, so no caller falls through to `(*dataplane.Manager).Compile`.

The one production compile is `Manager.CompileUserspaceShim`, which passes `userspaceShimCompileDataplane`. `loader.go` already says so in a comment: *"The compiler's shim dataplane methods are no-ops"*.

## What was kept, and why

Everything that escapes `compileNAT` — this is where a deletion goes wrong, so it was enumerated rather than eyeballed:

| kept | escapes via | read by |
|---|---|---|
| `result.PoolIDs`, `result.NextPoolID` | `ApplyResult` | `show security nat source pool`, `pkg/api/nat.go`, `pkg/api/metrics_nat.go`, `pkg/grpcapi/server_nat.go`, `pkg/cli/cli_show_nat.go`; and `compileNAT64` continues the sequence |
| `result.NATCounterIDs` (source + dest + static) | `ApplyResult` **and** `buildSnapshotWithSchedulerStateAndNATCounters` | every operator NAT surface's translation-hit counters |
| `result.AddrIDs` / `nextAddrID` (`_snat_match_<cidr>`) | `CompileResult` | pinned as a measured determinism dimension by `TestPrePassDoesNotPerturbIDAssignment_4960` |
| persistent-NAT table (`ClearPoolConfigs`, `SetPoolConfig`, `RegisterNATIP`) | `dp.GetPersistentNAT()` — **not** shadowed by the shim, so this is the file's one live dataplane effect | conntrack GC, `show security nat source persistent-nat-table` |
| every rejection | `error` | unknown zone/pool, DNAT match/pool address that is a prefix not a host, mixed-family static NAT, non-/96 NAT64 prefix, empty NAT64 source pool — all surfaced by the #4960 pre-pass before the first host mutation |

Consequently the interface-SNAT branch still resolves the egress zone's addresses (whether *any* resolves decides if the rule consumes a pool ID), the named-pool branch still parses pool addresses (they feed `RegisterNATIP`), and the DNAT application match is still resolved (its `slog.Warn`s are operator diagnostics).

`TestNATCompilerCallsNoDataplaneNATWriter_6420` arms **every** retired NAT writer to return an error and then requires the compile to validate **clean**, on both `isValidationPass` arms (the marker gates only logs, not writes, so a write reintroduced inside a gated block would be invisible to the pre-pass arm alone). A counter can only observe a call that happens; this observes its absence.

## PR #7269 — refactoraudit: gate the growth you caused, not the global snapshot's drift (#7253) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/7253-split-audit-gate`

## Summary

`TestHeatmapNotStale` fused two different properties into one fatal assertion, and only one of them is a gate:

- **modularity** — "this file is growing past the point where it should be split". Aimed at the author of the growth, actionable by them, worth interrupting them for.
- **freshness** — "the committed global snapshot disagrees with the tree". Aimed at whoever merges next, not actionable by them, not worth interrupting anyone for — and unable to stay true from authoring to merge.

This PR implements the decision recorded on #7253 (option 3): keep the first as a hard gate derived from the PR's own diff, demote the second to a job.

- **Hard half** — `TestTouchedFileCrossedModularityThreshold` + `scripts/refactoring-audit-touched.sh`. Reds when a file **the branch touches** went from below 1500/2000 LOC at its merge base to at-or-above in the working tree. It never reads `docs/refactoring-audit-current.txt`, so no unrelated file can flip it and regenerating the artifact cannot silence it. Structurally silent on master (empty changed set).
- **Demoted half** — `TestGlobalHeatmapFreshnessAdvisory` reports drift and never fails on it; `scripts/refactoring-audit-refresh.sh` / `make audit-refresh` regenerates and commits the artifact so freshness converges through a job.
- **Escape hatch** — `docs/refactoring-audit-accepted.txt`, a hand-written record of a `When NOT to refactor` decision with its reason. Never generated, so it cannot go stale from someone else's commit.
- **`make audit-check`** now exits 0 on every kind of staleness and reserves exit 1 for a malformed artifact, so its verdict still agrees with what the suite actually does — the property its own comment says must hold.
- **One source of truth** — the audited roots, the two floors and `audit_is_audited_path` moved into `scripts/refactoring-audit-lib.sh` so the generator and the touched probe cannot answer "is this path audited?" two ways. Generator output is byte-identical after that refactor.

The modularity signal is **not** deleted: `tcp_segmentation.rs` entering the audit at 1582 LOC was a correct catch, and the touched-file gate still makes it — to the author who caused it.

## Why the freshness half stopped being a gate

The heatmap is a snapshot of a repo-**global** property, so any file crossing a threshold anywhere flips it for everyone. **#7235, #7252 and #7254 each regenerated it inside one hour**, for different files, and **#7252 was already stale by the time it merged** — merged, master re-tested, still red on the same two files, fourth regeneration needed. `pkg/dataplane/types.go` crossed the floor at **exactly 1501 lines**. #6617 had already narrowed the same class once (byte-compare → content-compare, after measuring master byte-stale in **26 of 40** first-parent commits) without changing its shape.

## Changed-set mechanism, and what it gets wrong

`git diff --name-only <merge-base> --` (working tree included, so uncommitted growth counts) plus untracked files, where `<merge-base>` is `git merge-base origin/master HEAD`. Diffing the **merge base** rather than the base-ref tip is what keeps master's own commits out: a file master grew — or shrank — after the fork is not in the branch's diff at all.

Stated so nobody has to rediscover them:

- a **stacked branch inherits its parent PR's changed set** (the merge base against master is the parent's fork point) — point the child at its parent with `XPF_AUDIT_BASE_REF=<parent>` or argv[1];
- **after a branch merges `origin/master` into itself** the merge base moves forward, so a crossing master caused is attributed to master and the branch goes silent on it — intended, but it means a crossing first appearing in a merge is announced to nobody; the refresh job records it;
- it is a **whole-branch** view, not a last-commit view. Deliberate: the rejected alternative, `HEAD~..HEAD`, misses every crossing introduced before the last commit, which is most of them on a multi-commit branch.

**Undeterminable changed set fails loudly.** No git, no such base ref, no common ancestor (shallow/grafted clone) → the probe exits 3 naming the reason and the test fails. It never prints an empty set, because empty reads as "nothing crossed" — the one wrong answer a broken probe must not give. Matches the existing fixtures in this package, which `t.Fatal` when their source is unreadable.

## Test plan

- [x] `TestTouchedGateIsNotASnapshotCompare` — **the deliverable that keeps the split from being cosmetic.** Shows the two mechanisms disagreeing in **both** directions, including the decisive case: a perfectly fresh artifact where the branch's own crossing still reds. No snapshot compare can produce that red — there is no drift to restrict — so the hard half is provably not the old shape wearing new clothes.
- [x] `TestTouchedSetIsLocalToTheBranch` — real scripts, throwaway git repo, four commits: base + heatmap, a sibling PR growing a file, the branch forking and growing its own, master then splitting a third file after the fork. The global compare is red on two files; the gate blames exactly one, the branch's own.
- [x] `TestBranchTouchingNothingAuditedIsSilent` — acceptance criterion 2 literally: a docs-only branch does not red however stale the artifact is.
- [x] `TestTouchedSetSeesUncommittedAndUntrackedGrowth` — the probe measures the working tree, like the generator.
- [x] `TestUndeterminableBaseFailsLoudly` — unresolvable ref and orphan branch both exit non-zero, print no rows, and name the reason.
- [x] `TestThresholdCrossingCases` — the crossing predicate, including 1499→1500 crossing and 1500→1501 not, 2119→2448 not, new file at 1582 yes.
- [x] `TestRefreshJobConvergesTheGlobalArtifact` / `TestRefreshJobRefusesAnEmptyHeatmap` — the demoted half regenerates, commits, commits only the artifact on a dirty tree, is idempotent, and refuses an empty generation.
- [x] `TestAcceptedCrossingIsTheOnlyEscape` / `TestAcceptedFileWellFormed` — an entry silences its own file at its own tier and nothing else; a reasonless or non-audited entry is rejected.
- [x] `TestAuditedPathPredicateAgreesWithGenerator` / `TestShellFloorsMatchGoConstants` — the two users of the audited-path decision, and the two spellings of 1500/2000, bound together.

**Exit codes (read from `$?` directly, never through a pipe):** `go build ./...` rc=0 · `go vet ./pkg/refactoraudit/...` rc=0 · `go test -count=1 ./pkg/refactoraudit/...` rc=0 · `go test -count=1 ./...` rc=0 (62 packages) · `shellcheck` clean on all five audit scripts · `make audit-check` up-to-date, and STALE→0 / malformed→1 verified by perturbing a scratch copy.

One earlier full-suite run showed `pkg/ddns` failing with `bind: address already in use` — the known **#7009** flake, reproduced again standalone on an unchanged tree, and green in the clean run.

## PR #7270 — image: assert the #1930 A/B slot registration in the Tier-1 gate [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6494-tier1-ab-slot-assert`

Closes #6494

## What was wrong

`grep -n "efibootmgr\|xpf-A\|xpf-B\|BootOrder\|kernel-promote" scripts/image/validate.py` returned **nothing**. The Tier-1 gate signs `validated: true` into the image manifest without ever checking that the #1930 LANE-1 A/B kernel-slot substrate came up in the guest.

The bake stages `/boot/efi/EFI/{xpf-A,xpf-B}` and enables the two oneshots, and hard-asserts the signed shim is present. What it *cannot* assert offline is the half that only happens in-guest: UEFI `Boot####` variables live in the target's firmware NVRAM, which `virt-customize` cannot write, so registration is a first-boot oneshot on the real machine.

That oneshot is deliberately **non-fatal on every failure path** — a read-only or no-efivars platform must still boot ("degraded, not bricked") — and nothing downstream re-read its outcome. So a regression in the ESP disk/part parse, the loader-path match, or the `efibootmgr` write shipped a fully validated image whose verify-gated kernel channel was silently unavailable, and the operator found out when `xpfd upgrade kernel arm` exited 2 with `ErrKernelChannelUnavailable`.

## What this does

Scenario A now asserts in-guest: both oneshots ran and exited 0; both slots registered exactly once, each pointing at its own `\EFI\<slot>\shimx64.efi`, both reachable in BootOrder; and the promotion gate logged its ordinary-boot path.

The three slot properties are reported **separately** because they have three different causes — exactly-once (a duplicate makes `BootNext` ambiguous: the live #1930 bug, from a label guard anchored at `$`), its-own-loader (a label-only match chainloads the wrong thing), and in-BootOrder (a slot the firmware never reaches is not registered in any sense the channel can act on). The verdict regexes deliberately mirror `xpf-uefi-slots`' own shell regexes: a gate that disagreed with the script about what "registered" means would certify a state the script would not accept.

Both oneshots are `WantedBy=multi-user.target` and deliberately **not** ordered `Before=xpfd` (a hanging `efibootmgr` must never block the #1922 mgmt lifeline), so xpfd being active does not imply they have finished — the assertion waits for each to leave `activating` rather than racing it.

## One correction to the issue's acceptance criteria

> - [ ] Same scenario asserts ... (or the promote journal line "promotion gate: clean").

**That line is unreachable in scenario A.** `promotion gate: clean` (`xpf-kernel-promote:646`) is emitted only after the gate has exec'd xpfd to run the promote verb. On a factory boot with nothing armed the script exits 0 much earlier at `:591`, logging `no armed kernel candidate recorded`. Requiring the former would fail **every good image**.

The gate asserts `ExecMainStatus=0` **plus that ordinary-boot line** instead, which together prove the unit *executed* rather than being skipped by a Condition — which is what an operator is relying on when they arm a candidate later. Flagging it rather than quietly substituting.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Asserts `efibootmgr` lists both `xpf-A` and `xpf-B` each exactly once, each pointing at `\EFI\<slot>\shimx64.efi`, and both in BootOrder.
- [x] Asserts both services ran with `ExecMainStatus=0` — with the promote-line substitution above, stated explicitly.
- [x] A deliberately-broken registration FAILS the gate — see M1/M2/M3/M6 below (each fixture is a broken registration).

## Validation

`scripts/run-selftests.sh` — **51 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed, rc=0** (50 at baseline; the new test file is auto-discovered by the `scripts/image/test_*.py` glob).

Verdicts are pure functions over captured command output, in the existing `_qemu_img_verdict` idiom, so the acceptance criterion is testable without a hypervisor. 16 hermetic cases: missing slot, neither slot, duplicate, right-label/wrong-loader, registered-but-not-in-BootOrder, no BootOrder line, the bare (non-`File()`) loader rendering, hex-id case differences between the entry line and BootOrder, empty output, and never-ran vs ran-and-failed vs timed-out for the oneshot verdict. Two are structural — the verdicts can be perfect and prove nothing if scenario A never calls them.

### Mutation proofs

`python3 -m py_compile` checked green before each run so every red is an assertion, not a syntax error. Exit codes from `$?`. One line per mutation; restore verified (`git status --porcelain` empty, rc back to 0).

| # | Mutation (one line) | py_compile | rc | Cell that reddened |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | stop requiring the slot be in BootOrder | 0 | 1 | `registered_but_absent_from_bootorder_fails`, `bootorder_id_case_is_ignored` |
| M2 | drop the exactly-once rule | 0 | 1 | `duplicate_slot_fails` |
| M3 | match the label only, ignore the loader path | 0 | 1 | `right_label_wrong_loader_path_fails` |
| M4 | stop distinguishing never-ran from ran-and-failed | 0 | 1 | `never_ran_is_distinguished_from_failed` |
| M5 | drop the `assert_ab_kernel_channel` call from scenario A | 0 | 1 | `scenario_a_calls_the_ab_assertion` |
| M6 | anchor the entry regex at `$` (the live #1930 miss) | 0 | 1 | 5 cells incl. both PASS fixtures |

## PR #7271 — docs(nat64): cite RFC 6052 §3.1 for the non-global rule, not §2.2 [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6521-rfc6052-section-citation`

Closes #6521

## The claim that was wrong

The #6475 destination-eligibility work cited **RFC 6052 §2.2** for the normative rejection of a NAT64 prefix embedding a non-global IPv4 address — 17 occurrences across 11 files.

§2.2 is *IPv4-Embedded IPv6 Address Format*. It defines prefix lengths and the u-byte. **It states no translation rule and names no address ranges.** The normative language is in **§3.1**, *Restrictions on the use of the Well-Known Prefix*:

> The Well-Known Prefix MUST NOT be used to represent non-global IPv4 addresses, such as those defined in [RFC1918] or listed in Section 3 of [RFC5735]. Address translators MUST NOT translate packets in which an address is composed of the Well-Known Prefix and a non-global IPv4 address; they MUST drop these packets.

The citation was uniformly wrong because it was inherited from the original issue text, which mis-cited.

## Two places needed more than the section number

Swapping `§2.2` → `§3.1` mechanically would have left two statements still false.

**1. `embedded_v4_is_non_global` claimed the section "names RFC 1918 private space as non-global".** No section of RFC 6052 enumerates the non-global ranges. §3.1 defines them *by reference* — RFC 1918, or RFC 5735 §3. The comment now says that, and notes that each screened class is cited to its own defining RFC (1122, 3927, 5771, 1112) rather than to the reference chain. Every class screened is an RFC 5735 §3 entry, so the provenance now actually holds up.

**2. The screen header read as if §3.1 mandated the behaviour for every prefix.** It said a NAT64 prefix "MUST NOT translate" a non-global embedded address, with the Well-Known Prefix and any configured Pref64 held to one bar.

**§3.1 is normative only for the Well-Known Prefix** `64:ff9b::/96`. Holding every configured Pref64 to it is **stricter than the RFC requires**. The original prose hinted at this in a parenthetical, but with the section number corrected the sentence would have read as a restatement of the standard. It now marks the broader application as a deliberate hardening choice — which is what it is, and worth a reader knowing before they "fix" it to match the RFC.

## Scope and safety

- **Comments and documentation only.** No behaviour change.
- **No operator-facing text moves.** Before editing I classified all 16 non-log hits: **0 were outside a comment or markdown**. A claims-only change can still move the binary when the claim lives in a string literal — none here does.
- **`_Log.md`'s 2026-07-24 #6475 heading is deliberately left mis-cited.** The log is append-only and records what was believed at the time; rewriting a past entry would falsify the record. A new dated entry carries the correction, placed at the chronological top, with the heading count verified +1 against `HEAD~`.

## Files

`docs/feature-coverage.md`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/format/status_test.go`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/protocol_binding.go`, `userspace-dp/src/FEATURES.md`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/binding_state/mod.rs`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/mod.rs`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker/mod.rs`, `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs`, `userspace-dp/src/nat64_tests.rs`, `userspace-dp/src/protocol/binding.rs`

## Validation

```
go build ./...                    rc=0
go vet ./pkg/dataplane/...        rc=0
cargo check --tests --bins        rc=0
residual §2.2 citations           1  (the _Log.md historical heading, intended)
```

**No cluster time owed.** No `userspace-dp` executable statement changes, no shim `.o` movement, no protocol change.

## PR #7272 — nftables(lo0): fail closed on a malformed filter address token [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6512-lo0-addr-fail-closed`

## Problem

The lo0 kernel mirror dropped an unparseable `source-address` /
`destination-address` token **per-token** and installed the surviving subset.
#3433 chose that so an ALL-malformed positive list resolved to "constrained +
empty → match nothing", which is fail-closed. The per-token drop is wrong for the
two shapes #6512 filed, in **opposite** directions:

- a **partially** malformed POSITIVE list installs a **NARROWED** rule — a
  `discard`/`reject` term enforcing a smaller address set than the operator
  wrote, with the dropped range accepted by fall-through;
- an **EXCEPT** list narrowed to empty takes `lo0AddrScope`'s empty-except arm,
  which drops the predicate entirely, so the direction becomes **UNCONSTRAINED**
  and the rule matches every address.

The second shape is why **"skip the bad entry" cannot be the fix**: for an except
set an empty list *means* match-everything, so removing entries widens the match.

## Fix

Both builders now refuse the token:

- `filterFamilyAddrs` (`pkg/nftables/netlink_lo0.go`, the **production** builder,
  reached via `InstallLo0` → `buildLo0FilterNetlink`) returns an error;
  `buildLo0TermNetlink` turns it into `nlPlan.fail`, so the transaction aborts and
  the prior ruleset is retained.
- `nftFamilyAddrs` (`pkg/daemon/daemon_nft.go`, the parity **oracle**) keeps the
  token verbatim so `nft -f -` rejects the whole payload.

That is exactly the posture both already had for an unrepresentable port / DSCP
token (#6405). Wrong-family literals and `any`/empty placeholders are still
dropped — those are legitimate and match the userspace matcher.

**Detection is on the TOKEN, not on the #6463 `AddressUnrepresentable` marker.**
That marker is derived from `term.UnknownAddresses`, which records malformed
**literal** tokens only. Verified firsthand: a malformed entry inside a
referenced `policy-options prefix-list` reaches the lowering with the marker
unset **and is not rejected at strict commit either** —
`validateFirewallPrefixListReferencesStrict` validates that the *reference*
resolves, not that its *entries* parse. So this shape reaches the mirror on the
**ordinary commit path**, not only the lenient / peer-sync path; the branch this
PR adds is on "does this token parse", which varies on both paths.

## #1960 no-brick

Fail-closed is not fail-to-boot. The install error makes `applyLo0Filter` install
the #6476 cold-boot fail-closed fence (lifelines exempt, mandatory L3 / return
traffic admitted) and the boot apply logs+discards the error, so an
already-persisted config still loads — it just does not get a kernel filter that
differs from what the operator wrote. On the strict **commit** path the commit

## PR #7274 — image: assert Secure Boot in the Tier-1 gate instead of inheriting it [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6497-tier1-secureboot-assert`

Closes #6497

## What was wrong

`grep -n "secureboot\|mokutil\|lockdown" scripts/image/validate.py` returned **nothing**. The production posture is UEFI Secure Boot ON (`test/incus/setup.sh:265-273`, #1943), and the Tier-1 gate — the only thing between a bake and a release signature — proved nothing about it.

The incus scenarios **inherited** SB from the incus default rather than setting it, and the plain-QEMU leg deliberately preferred a non-secboot OVMF with no SB-on variant at all. A default flip, a profile override, or a hypervisor without the MS db silently degraded the whole gate to SB-off — and still passed.

This is more than "the image is signed". The #1930 A/B substrate makes lockdown-sensitive design choices nothing automated exercised: `scripts/image/grub.d/09_xpf` documents that `regexp` may be unavailable under Secure-Boot lockdown and that the slot selector must be a GRUB *script* so GRUB can parse it there. The only SB-on validation of that chain was a one-time manual probe on a hand-staged stock VM, not the baked artifact.

## What this does

**1. `launch()` sets `-c security.secureboot=true` explicitly.** It is the incus default today, but a gate must not inherit the property it exists to assert.

**2. Scenario A asserts the guest actually booted under SB**, from three independent readings so a *missing* reading is distinguished from the property being false:

- byte 4 of the `SecureBoot` EFI variable — authoritative and **package-free** (an efivarfs file is 4 attribute bytes then the value);
- `mokutil --sb-state` when present — deliberately *not* required, because `mokutil` is **not in `bake.py`'s `RUNTIME_PACKAGES`**, so asserting through it alone would turn a package-set change into a fake Secure Boot regression;
- `/sys/kernel/security/lockdown` as corroboration — it never *overrides* a definite "off", since lockdown can also be forced from the cmdline.

**No readable source at all is a FAIL, not a pass.** A gate that cannot observe the property has not asserted it — which is exactly how SB-off shipped green.

**3. The plain-QEMU leg prefers an SB-ENFORCING firmware pair** (secboot `OVMF_CODE` **and** MS-keyed `OVMF_VARS`, so the Canonical-signed shim verifies with no MOK enrollment). Both halves are required and each is asserted separately: a non-secboot CODE build ignores SB even with MS keys present, and a secboot CODE build with plain VARS has no db for the shim to verify against. With no enforcing pair on the host the leg still runs SB-off for bootability coverage but says so in the log, the boot line, and its PASS line.

The fallback was never the defect — presenting it as Secure Boot proof was. The retired comment read *"plain-QEMU bootability is proven fine with SB off"*: true, and being counted as something it is not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Explicit `-c security.secureboot=true`; scenario A asserts the guest reports SB enabled (`mokutil --sb-state` **and/or** lockdown — implemented as efivar-primary with both as corroboration, for the package-set reason above).
- [x] The QEMU scenario gains an SB-on variant, with an explicit **logged** fallback when secboot OVMF is unavailable — never a silent SB-off pass presented as bootability proof.
- [x] A regression that breaks boot under SB fails the gate: scenario A fails on a definite "off" *and* on an unobservable posture; the QEMU leg boots under enforcing firmware, so a broken shim→grub→kernel chain fails to reach `day-0 config installed`.

## One existing test had to be rewritten, not left alone

`test_non_secboot_code_preferred_over_secboot` asserted the preference this change inverts. Left in place it would **not have gone red — it would have gone vacuous**: `_OVMF_CODE_CANDIDATES` no longer contains a secboot entry at all, so its `first_plain < first_sb` comparison still passes while testing nothing.

Replaced with the property that list still has: no secboot or MS-keyed build may leak into the SB-OFF fallback, which would make the "SB-off" leg silently SB-*something* and defeat the honest reporting this change adds.

## Validation

`scripts/run-selftests.sh` — **51 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed, rc=0** (50 at baseline). 18 hermetic cases over the two pure functions; `find` is injected into the firmware chooser so the preference order is asserted independently of which OVMF packages the test host has.

### `py_compile` is NOT a sufficient green for this file

A first draft bound `find=_find_first` as a **default argument** with `_find_first` defined further down the file. `python3 -m py_compile` returned **0** — it checks syntax, not import — and the module raised `NameError` on import. Every mutation below therefore uses a real **module import** as the green check (`IMPORT rc=0` recorded per run), not `py_compile`. Flagging it because the brief specified `py_compile`, and for this file it would have certified a broken module.

### Mutation proofs

Exit codes from `$?`. One line per mutation; import green verified before each; restore verified (`git status --porcelain` empty, rc back to 0).

## PR #7276 — daemon(nft): do not let a vacated lo0 filter claim enforcement [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6529-lo0-vacated-enforced`

## Problem

`applyLo0Filter` stored `lo0Enforced = true` on **any** successful `InstallLo0`,
including one whose spec compiled to an empty `policy accept` chain. That flag is
the #6476 cold-boot fence's skip gate, so a **vacated** filter permanently
suppressed the fence: every later failed install took the day-2 retention branch
on the premise that a real operator filter still governs every local address, and
the host input path stayed open.

The in-code comment already stated the intended trust model — *"Only a retained
REAL filter is trusted to govern every local address … with lo0Enforced true no
fence is installed."* A vacated real filter is also `policy accept`, and one
boolean cannot tell the two apart.

## Fix

The discriminator that **can** tell them apart is the **rendered rule count**.
`Installer.InstallLo0` now reports it alongside its error, taken from
`nlPlan.rules` — the actual build — so it can never drift from the lowering the
way a second, daemon-side "does this spec enforce anything?" predicate would.
`replaceTable` returns the count; the fence and host-inbound installers discard
it.

**A term count is not sufficient.** Zero rendered rules is reachable through three
doors:

1. a filter **name** that resolves to no filter (`toNftLo0Spec`'s map lookup
   silently yields no terms) — the issue's headline path;
2. a filter with no terms;
3. a filter whose **every term lowers to zero rules** — a Junos match-nothing
   scope, e.g. an unresolved `from source-prefix-list`.

Door 3 *has* terms and would pass a term-count gate. All three arrive through
`opts.lenientFirewallRefs` on `Store.Load` at boot or `Store.SyncApply` on HA
peer-sync.

A zero-rule install **Stores false** rather than merely skipping the Store: on a
peer-sync a vacated generation atomically *replaces* a live real filter, so
leaving the stale `true` would keep suppressing the fence through a different
door. That mirrors the no-filter teardown (#5790 parity).

It deliberately does **not** install a fence — fencing on a *successful* install
would deny host-bound traffic on a clean commit. The gate being false is what
matters: the next failed install fences from the then-current snapshot, which is
the issue's second acceptance criterion.

## Readers of the flag

`lo0Enforced` has exactly **one** reader — the `!lo0Enforced` fence gate in
`applyLo0Filter` — so tightening when it is set changes no other consumer. The

The three duplicate-name gates — `validateDuplicateNamedBlockAST` (#5180),

while the byte-identical duplicate authored **inline** is hard-rejected:

Same config, same compiled shape, opposite verdict, decided by where the
operator happened to write it.

A pre-expansion per-group-body scan was tried and **withdrawn** in PR #6491. It
false-rejects a legitimate apply-groups FRAGMENT config: fragments of one named
object authored across repeated group roots COALESCE under `mergeNodes` during
`ExpandGroups` — two `interfaces` roots each contributing a unit, a screen
profile split into ICMP and TCP halves, a NAT rule split into `match` and
`then` — and a sibling-scan cannot model that same-pass coalescing.

Run the **same three scanners** on a group-**expanded** clone, where the
coalescing has already happened. A fragment pair is one node by then and reports
nothing; a genuinely duplicated pair is still two siblings and reports.

## PR #7278 — daemon: split startClusterComms into focused builders (#6428) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `refactor/6428-start-cluster-comms`

Closes #6428

## Summary

- `Daemon.startClusterComms` was a **602-line** constructor wiring the whole cluster-comms stack. Thirteen sub-constructions move **verbatim** into a new `pkg/daemon/daemon_ha_comms_wiring.go`; the constructor drops to **233 lines** and keeps only the control-flow spine.
- **Pure code motion.** All 13 moved bodies are byte-identical modulo indentation, verified mechanically by an independent verifier (below) — not by eye.
- The ordering contract that a 602-line constructor encodes implicitly is now **written down**, on `startClusterComms` itself and in `pkg/daemon/README.md`.
- Five blocks were **deliberately not extracted** — each carries a `return` out of the constructor goroutine.
- Second commit: the moved wiring turned out to be **entirely unbound by tests**. 17 of the 30 sites are now bound and mutation-proven; the other 13 are reported, not quietly relocated.
- `daemon_ha_sync.go` leaves the refactor-audit `[WATCH]` tier; artifact regenerated.

## The builders

| Builder | Owns |
|---|---|
| `resolveClusterVRFDevice` | which VRF device the cluster sockets bind to |
| `startHAWatchdogHeartbeat` | the 500ms `ha_watchdog` tick goroutine (#3917 live-RG re-read) |
| `clusterSyncTransport` | control-link vs fabric transport selection |
| `wireSessionSyncTransportRefs` | auth provider, transport label, gRPC peer addresses |
| `startFabricGRPCListeners` | the `grpcSrv` poller + fabric listener(s) |
| `wireSessionSyncConfigCallbacks` | `OnConfigReceived`, `OnConfigApplyHealth` |
| `wireSessionSyncPeerCallbacks` | connect / bulk / forward-installed / disconnect / `BulkSnapshotSource` |
| `wireSessionSyncFailoverCallbacks` | remote-failover request + commit (single and batch), actuation barriers |
| `wireClusterPeerFailoverHooks` | cluster `Manager` → sync senders, readiness/lease/timeout hooks |
| `wireClusterFenceCallbacks` | outbound fence sender + inbound fence handler |
| `wireUserspaceEventStreamForSync` | event-stream callbacks, returns the wired stream |
| `startClusterSyncAuxLoops` | IPsec SA sync, config-sync reconcile, DHCP lease sync |
| `startFabricForwardingLoops` | `fabric_fwd` populate (fab0/fab1) + netlink state monitor |

## Ordering dependencies — and how each extraction preserves them

Every extraction is called at the **exact sequence point** the moved block occupied, so order is preserved by construction. The dependencies found while reading the whole function:

1. **`beginClusterCommsEpoch` must run first.** It bumps `clusterCommsGen` and installs the cancellable sub-context that every goroutine below captures and every publish presents. Anything spawned earlier would capture a stale/nil context.
2. **`resolveClusterVRFDevice` before both goroutine spawns.** The heartbeat goroutine takes `vrfDevice` as an argument; the constructor goroutine uses it for the gRPC listeners and `ss.SetVRFDevice`.
3. **`syncRGStrictVIPOwnershipMode` before the heartbeat goroutine.** Once VRRP starts driving `rg_active`, the strict-VIP-ownership mode must already be set, or there is a window where `rg_active` follows cluster-primary *intent* instead of VIP ownership. Left as a one-line call at its original position.
4. **`clusterCommsWG.Add(1)` executes on the caller's stack, never inside the goroutine.** If it moved inside, `stopClusterComms`'s `Wait()` could return before the constructor registered. The `Add`/`go func`/`defer Done()` shape is untouched.
5. **Inside the constructor:** resolve → build `ss` → `publishSessionSyncIfCurrent` → **all** wiring → `ss.Start`. Every `ss.On*` callback, cluster-`Manager` hook and `SetVRFDevice` must be installed *before* `Start`, which spawns the accept/connect goroutines whose first connection runs the authoritative cold-prime bulk. All six wiring builders sit strictly between the publish gate and the retry loop.
6. **`wireUserspaceEventStreamForSync` before the `ss.Start` retry loop** — its return value selects which drain loop the loop launches on success.
7. **`ss.SetRuntime` + `IsPrimaryFn` before `ss.Start`** (#82) and `StartSyncSweep` *after* — inside the retry loop, untouched.
8. **`startClusterSyncAuxLoops` runs unconditionally after the retry loop** — these loops still start when every `Start` attempt failed. Preserved by not making the call conditional.
9. **Fabric refresh channels published before `startFabricForwardingLoops`**, and each loop is handed its **own channel by value** (#4038/#4958).

### Capture semantics: by-reference → by-value

Extraction turns closure captures into parameters. That is only safe if no moved closure observes a *later* mutation of a captured variable. Checked mechanically: every one of `vrfDevice, syncIface, syncPeerAddr, syncTransport, syncIP, syncLocal1, ss, cc, commsCtx, commsGen, fabRefreshCh, fabRefreshCh1, wiredStream` is **single-assignment before its moved consumer runs** (`grep` for every assignment site in the original function body). Every call site also passes each argument **under the identifier it binds**, so the moved bodies see identical values under identical names — and the compiler proves nothing was silently dropped, since a lost capture is an undefined identifier.

### Goroutine lifecycle — a finding, not a fix (#7257)

`clusterCommsWG.Add(1)` appears **exactly once** in the tree. `stopClusterComms` joins **only** the session-sync constructor; the other **ten** goroutines this path spawns (`startHeartbeatWithRetry`, the watchdog ticker, the gRPC listener poller and its inner listener, `eventStreamFallbackLoop`/`runUserspaceEventStream`, `syncIPsecSAPeriodic`, `configSyncReconcileLoop`, `populateFabricFwd{,1}`, `monitorFabricState`) are context-cancelled but never joined.

## PR #7279 — userspace-dp: namespace session ids by cluster node (#6311) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6311-session-id-node-bit`

Closes #6311

## The defect

The stable session id was `worker_id << 48 | counter` with **no node
discriminator** (`alloc_session_id` / `set_worker_id`). Both HA nodes run the
**same** worker set (queue indices 0..N on the 6-queue mlx5 VF) and both
per-worker counters start at 1.

Under #5212 a standby **adopts** the primary's id verbatim
(`upsert_synced_with_origin`), so an adopted `(w<<48)|c` collided with the
importing node's OWN worker-`w` id `(w<<48)|c`. In **active/active** — a
supported, tested mode (`test-active-active`) — low-counter collisions early
after boot were essentially guaranteed. It also **regressed pre-#5212 same-node
uniqueness**: before adoption every import got a fresh local id, so a node's own
RT_FLOW stream was internally unique.

`session_id` is a metadata-only stamp (RT_FLOW correlation + the
`show security flow session` mirror id), never a lookup key or slab handle, so
there was no forwarding / security / memory impact — but a duplicate correlation
stamp defeats the feature's own "one id per logical session" goal.

## The fix

The high-16 namespace is now `node_bit << 15 | worker_id`.
`set_worker_id(worker_id)` becomes
`set_session_id_namespace(node_id, worker_id)` — one call carrying both halves,
so a caller cannot set one and forget the other (no compatibility wrapper, on
purpose: a revert then has to *state* a node id rather than silently omit one).

An adopted id carries the **originating** node's bit and by construction can
never equal an id the importing node mints. That is also why
`upsert_synced_with_origin` still does **not** reconcile `next_session_id`
against an adopted id — the two namespaces are disjoint, so a later local alloc
cannot re-hand-out an adopted value. **Node 0's layout is bit-for-bit the
pre-change one.**

Two invariants are enforced at worker setup (config time, where
`docs/engineering-style.md` prefers crash-start):

- **The #6198 control-plane reservation survives the re-partition.** `0xFFFF` is
  now node-bit-1 plus worker `0x7FFF`, and the assert moved onto the **combined**
  namespace — which is what keeps it meaningful after the split. The 6198 test
  had to name node 1 explicitly: a worker id of `0xFFFF` no longer reaches that
  assert at all (it trips the narrower worker-range one first), and leaving it
  would have quietly turned the guard into a test of a different assertion.
- **A worker id above `0x7FFF` is REFUSED, not masked.** Masking would carry into
  the node bit and mint ids inside the **peer's** namespace — a silent cross-node
  collision, strictly worse than the counter aliasing the old 16-bit mask
  prevented. Unreachable today (`MAX_NAT_HOLDER_WORKERS` = 128 bounds worker ids

## PR #7281 — routing: never tear down proxy-ARP on a failed iface resolution [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-22)

Branch: `fix/6536-proxyarp-unresolved-debt`

## Problem

`ReconcileProxyARP`'s returned `(iface -> families)` "enabled" set is the daemon's memory of the interfaces whose proxy responder sysctl it must eventually tear down, and it is the **only** input to the #2475 teardown diff. An interface that drops out of it is **disabled** — a destructive `proxy_arp`/`proxy_ndp` write to `0` — and **forgotten**, which also loses the #4955 `NTF_PROXY` orphan sweep for it.

Two different conditions produced that same absence:

- **(a)** proxy-arp is no longer configured on the interface — teardown is correct;
- **(b)** the interface's kernel identity would not resolve on this pass — `net.InterfaceByName` in `proxyARPIfaceMap` (daemon layer), or `netlink.LinkByIndex` inside `ReconcileProxyARP` (dataplane layer).

(b) is transient — an `ENOBUFS`/`EMFILE` netlink hiccup, a VLAN netdev mid-recreate — and says nothing about the config. Every ifindex that reaches the sysctl step was built from `cfg`, so it is *by construction* still configured.

## Reproduced at `origin/master`

Driving the real entry point `(*Daemon).reconcileProxyARP` twice with the SAME config, failing only the ifindex resolution on the second pass:

```
after pass 1: enabled=map[lo:map[2:{}]]
after pass 2: enabled=map[] disabled=[map[lo:map[2:{}]]]
```

The responder is disabled for `lo` while `lo` is still configured for proxy-arp, and `lo` is dropped from the remembered state so no later pass can tear it down either.

## Fix

Distinguish the two conditions at both layers rather than teaching the consumer to guess.

- `proxyARPIfaceMap` now returns `(byJunos, names, unresolved)` — the ifindex -> Linux netdev name mapping it resolved, plus the names it could not resolve at all.
- `ReconcileProxyARP` takes that mapping and uses it as the **fallback key** when `LinkByIndex` fails, so the entry stays in the enabled set *and* the sysctl is still re-asserted under the name the caller resolved the ifindex from.
- The unresolved names come back as **debt**: `reconcileProxyARP` carries their prior `(iface -> families)` state forward into the enabled set (`retainUnresolvedProxyResponders`) before the diff runs.

The retention is debt, not a leak — the next reconcile that resolves the interface either re-asserts it (still configured) or tears it down through the normal diff once it really leaves the config. `TestReconcileProxyARP_UnresolvedDebtIsRedeemed` binds that.

The GARP name lookup in the add loop deliberately keeps the old drop-on-failure behaviour: its only cost is a skipped gratuitous ARP, which self-heals, so the fallback is scoped to the destructive site. `netlink.LinkByIndex` is wrapped in a `linkByIndexSeam` package var so the transient can be injected without deleting a real netdev.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] An unresolvable ifindex does NOT result in a sysctl disable.
- [x] Fail-on-revert test with a transient resolution failure.

## Validation

`go vet ./pkg/daemon ./pkg/dataplane` clean. Full `go test -count=1 ./pkg/dataplane` (ok, 19.5s) and `./pkg/daemon` (ok, 38.2s) green.

Mutations, one at a time, exit codes read from `$?` directly:

| mutation | vet | result |
|---|---|---|
| drop the `retainUnresolvedProxyResponders` call (daemon) | 0 | rc=1 — `still-configured-but-unresolvable` **RED**, `genuinely-removed-from-config` **PASS** |
| disable the `ifaceNames` fallback branch (dataplane) | 0 | rc=1 — `caller-supplied-name-retains-entry` **RED**, `no-fallback-name` **PASS** |
