## PR #8092 — vrrp: self-frame check consults the interface's address SET [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7334-self-frame-addr-set`

Closes #7334

`resolveLocalIPv4` selects **one** address — the lowest non-VIP IPv4 — and stores it as the snapshot. The four receive-path self-checks compared a frame's source against that single value.

So the self-check **also failed with a non-nil snapshot**: a self-advert sent from address A bypassed the comparison once the selected source had become B. `resolveEqualPriorityMaster` then compared `peerCmp` (our own **old** source A) against `localCmp` (our own **new** source B) and stepped down whenever `A > B` — **a coin flip, and a self-inflicted master-down.**

#6560 fixed the two delivery paths and named this residual explicitly. The comparison is the last line of defence if a delivery path is ever re-opened.

## The selection and the set are different things, deliberately

| | purpose | shape |
|---|---|---|
| `localIP` / `localIPv6` | the **send** source | one deterministic address (the lowest), so it does not flip on unrelated secondary-address churn — #2528's whole point |
| `localAddrSet` / `localAddrSetV6` | the **self-check** | every address we might have sent from, *including one the selection has since moved off* |

Both are recomputed from a single `reresolveLocalAddrs` read, so the set can never lag the selection — with a cell asserting they clear together.

## It fails open, and that bounds the risk

An unresolved set means *not ours*, so the frame is accepted. That is the #2528 RETH-MAC flush window, when `programRethMAC`'s link DOWN has removed every kernel address. **A frame we cannot classify must still be able to be a peer's advert** — dropping it would be the self-inflicted master-down this change exists to prevent. The fix's failure direction is bounded by the same rule as the bug's.

## The MAC alternative was not taken

The issue offers comparing the frame's source MAC against `vi.iface.HardwareAddr`. That covers only the AF_PACKET path, whereas the address set covers **all four** call sites including the raw-socket receivers — and it would introduce an L2 identity the package currently does not use at all (`grep HardwareAddr pkg/vrrp/*.go` non-test is still zero hits).

## The matrix caught my tests binding the wrong thing

My first ten cells called `isLocalAddr` directly. Unwiring a receive call site escaped **every one of them** — and "the check exists but consults the wrong thing" is the shape of this very defect. Four cells now drive the real `parseAfPacketIPv4`/`IPv6` and assert on `rxCh`, which is what an admitted advert actually reaches.

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| revert to the single selected address | RED | **RED(3)** |
| fail CLOSED on an unresolved set | RED | **RED(7)** |
| set not recomputed with the selection | RED | **RED(1)** |
| families cross | RED | **RED(1)** |
| v4 parse site unwired | RED | **RED(1)** |
| v6 parse site unwired | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

One mutation is **INERT rather than uncovered**: removing the explicit `To4()` from `canonicalVRRPAddr` changes nothing, because `net.IP.String()` performs the same check internally. Kept so the intent is visible at the call site rather than inferred from the standard library — with a comment saying *why* the mutation is inert, so the next reader does not delete it, see nothing red, and conclude the canonicalisation is untested.

## Gates

- `go test -count=1 ./...` — **69 packages ok, 0 `--- FAIL`, rc=0**
- **`make test-failover` on the loss userspace cluster — 17 passed, 0 failed.** Owed because this is VRRP code, run under the `/tmp/xpf-cluster.lock` cell.

One gate run failed on `TestArrivalIfindexDetector`, which captured an **INFO** line from an unrelated test's address-watcher goroutine. Not reproducible in isolation on either this branch (5/5) or `origin/master` (8/8); the full suite passed 69/69 on re-run with the same tree. Filed as **#8091** rather than re-run-and-forget.

## PR #8093 — nat: warn that a pool-utilization alarm cannot fire on an address-only pool [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7361-addr-only-alarm-advisory`

Closes #7361

**The defect is real and confirmed.** `used_ports` is a popcount over the allocator's occupancy bitmaps; `reserve_address_only` never touches occupancy — it records ownership in `live.address_only_owners`. So for a `port no-translation` pool `UsedPorts` is permanently 0, the utilization percentage is permanently 0, and the raise-threshold cannot be crossed.

**The harm is not the missing percentage.** The configuration reads as *working*: `show` renders the alarm, and 0% utilization is indistinguishable from a healthy pool. The alarm's silence looks exactly like the silence of a pool with plenty of headroom.

## I did not implement the fix the issue asks for, deliberately

#7361 proposes `capacity = AddressCount`, `used = distinct addresses currently allocated`. That models an exhaustion mode this pool class does not have.

Addresses are handed out round-robin (`reserve_address_only_roundrobin`) and freely **reused** across flows with different destination tuples — an address-only pool exhausts on **reverse-identity collision**, not on running out of addresses. So:

> **A one-address pool would report 100% utilization after its first flow and stay there while serving thousands more.**

That is not a warning. It is an alarm that fires on the first packet and never clears — worse than the current silence, because it trains operators to ignore the alarm that *does* work on port-bearing pools. On a two-address pool it would sit at 50% or 100% with no relation to headroom.

This replaces a never-fires alarm with a **statement that it cannot fire**, which fixes the stated harm, invents no percentage, and cannot false-positive. If a genuine early warning is wanted for this class, the signal is the **denial rate** (the `AllocatorExhausted` / collision path) — a different mechanism with its own threshold semantics, deserving its own specification.

The issue's acceptance criterion *"an address-only pool crossing raise-threshold RAISES"* presumes the percentage model and is not met, on purpose. Flagging that rather than shipping through it.

## Warn, never reject

The combination is valid — `port no-translation` and a global `pool-utilization-alarm` are each legitimate, and the alarm applies correctly to every other pool. #4316 accept-with-advisory, and the tolerant load / peer-sync path must keep booting (#1960).

## The monitor side

It stops evaluating such a pool and records the reason (`InapplicableReason`). **No syslog** — this is not an alarm transition, and raising one would be a permanent alarm on a healthy pool, exactly the failure mode the proposed denominator would produce. A pool raised while port-bearing and later switched to `no-translation` has its latched state dropped **without a clear syslog**, because a CLEAR would claim utilization fell below the threshold and that is not what happened.

## Mutation matrix

| cell | expect | result |
|---|---|---|
| never warns | RED | **RED(2)** |
| warns on every pool | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the threshold gate | RED | **RED(1)** |
| drop the referenced gate | RED | **RED(1)** |
| deterministic not skipped | RED | **RED(1)** |
| unwired from `ValidateConfig` | RED | **RED(1)** |
| comment reword (negative control) | GREEN | **GREEN** |

**Two escaped first, and both were fixture problems worth naming.**

The threshold gate was uncovered because the only fixture without a raise-threshold had **no alarm stanza at all** and returned one line earlier at the nil check. I measured that the in-between state is reachable — `clear-threshold 50` with no raise compiles leniently to `RaiseThreshold: 0` — *before* writing the cell.

The deterministic fixture used a bare `deterministic ...` path that never populated `pool.Deterministic` (it lives under `port deterministic`), so it asserted the skip against a pool that was not deterministic. It failed **loudly** rather than passing vacuously, which is the good direction — but it is the same class as any fixture that does not reach the condition it names.

## PR #8094 — grpcapi: the #8057 validity check was weaker than its PR claimed [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7172-5a-validity-check-was-too-weak`

**Self-reported defect in merged code**, found while authoring cut 5a-2. Test-only; no shipped mapping was wrong.

## The overstated claim

#8057's body says every entry is checked to be "a real, already-canonical operational command". **That is too strong.**

`cmdtree.Canonicalize` returns `CanonicalOK` for `show interfaces zzbogus`, because `interfaces` carries a dynamic child and **value slots absorb arbitrary words**. So an entry naming a command nobody can run passed the check — provided the garbage landed in a value slot rather than at a keyword position.

The mutation run against #8057 (`show zzbogus nonexistent`) reds because nothing under `show` matches. That is why the hole did not surface: **the top level has no value slot to absorb anything. One level down it does.**

## `Canonicalize` is not wrong and is not changed

Absorbing operator data into value slots is exactly what it must do for a command an operator typed — `show interfaces ge-0/0/0` has to canonicalize. The mismatch is that *this table* holds argument-free command paths, so the stricter rule belongs to the table's validity check, not to the shared canonicalizer where it would break the callers cut 1 exists for.

## The fix

Every word must name a real node. Verified as a **paired result**:

- rejects `show interfaces zzbogus` and `show route zzbogus`
- accepts **all 40 current entries unchanged** — so no shipped mapping was wrong

Mutation: `GetInterfaces` → `show interfaces zzbogus` now reds `TestEveryMappedCommandIsCanonical7172` by name (build-clean).

## How it surfaced

The candidate-generation pass for 5a-2's 98 topics produced obvious nonsense that *resolved* — `show interfaces address book`, `show route alarms`. That is the tell, and I would not have seen it by re-reading the check. Generating a large batch of candidates against a validator is a cheap way to find out what the validator actually accepts, as opposed to what its author believes it accepts.

## Gate

`go test ./... -count=1` — **rc=0, 69 packages, 0 named FAILs**.

Refs #7172, #8057.

## PR #8095 — ddns: state the fingerprint's no-credential claim precisely [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7405-fingerprint-credential-claim`

Closes #7405

`BackendFingerprint`'s doc comment claimed the persisted digest "carries NO credentials", justified by listing the four `config.Secret`-typed fields that are excluded. The list is right; the headline is broader than the list supports. It is a claim about field *types*, and it reads as a guarantee about the hashed *values*.

`Server` is documented as accepting a full base URL, so `https://user:pw@host/` is a legal value, and it is hashed. `Server` is a plain `string`, not a `Secret`, so nothing redacts it on the way in.

### What I measured before deciding

| question | answer |
|---|---|
| is the digest persisted? | yes — `/var/lib/xpf/dhcp-ddns-state.json` |
| is it logged? | **no** — zero call sites |
| is it exported off-box? | no — not on any API or proto surface |
| which hashed inputs can hold userinfo? | **only `Server`**. `UpdateServer` is host/host:port, no scheme. `URLTemplate` handles credentials via its `%u`/`%p` placeholders |
| is a userinfo-bearing `Server` secret elsewhere on disk? | **no — it is already cleartext** in the config store, same root-only directory |

The issue's premise was that the digest is "persisted **and logged**". The logged half does not hold.

### Disposition: accept and document

The FNV-64a brute-force concern is real in the abstract and non-additive in practice. An attacker holding the ownership store also holds the config store beside it, where the same credential sits in cleartext — attacking an unsalted 64-bit digest is strictly harder than reading the neighbouring file.

Option 1 from the issue (fingerprint `RedactURL(Server)`) is the wrong trade here, and the reason is worth recording: it moves **every existing fingerprint**, and a moved fingerprint is indistinguishable from an endpoint change. On the first reconcile after upgrade that raises the #3735 ownership alarm for every record — a real upgrade hazard incurred to close a non-additive exposure.

So this changes only the comment. It states the enforced property, names the test that enforces it, states the `Server` caveat plainly, and records the condition under which the acceptance lapses (if the store ever ships off-box — a support bundle, telemetry, a peer sync) so that change is not made without revisiting this.

### No test added, deliberately

The property was already bound by `TestBackendFingerprintStableAndSecretFree` (#3735), which is **stronger** than anything this issue would have prompted — it also covers `Username`, `TSIGKeyName`, `AWSAccessKeyID`, `SourceAddress` and `Name`. I had written a replacement before finding it; it was strictly weaker, so I deleted it rather than ship redundant coverage.

Worth noting how it surfaced: my first mutation cells were run filtered to the new issue number and would have reported the new test as the only guard. Running them against the **whole package** is what showed the #3735 test reddening on both mutations.

### Validation

Two arity-preserving mutations of `backendFingerprint` (add/drop breaks `authorityFingerprint`'s signature and yields a build break, not a red — my first attempt did exactly that and scored two void cells):

| cell | mutation | build | collected | `--- FAIL` | reds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `p.URLTemplate` → `p.URLTemplate+string(p.Password)` | 0 | 536 | 2 | secret-invariance half |
| M2 | `p.Server` → `""` | 0 | 536 | 2 | endpoint-identity half |

Each localises to one half. `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` clean, zero `--- FAIL`. Diff is one file, comment-only.

## PR #8096 — config: redact the per-feed path on the AST config-read route (#7406) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `docs/7406-feed-url-secret-placement`

Closes #7406

## What #7406 asked, and what measuring it turned up

#7406 argues its residual is unsatisfiable: a secret that **is** a host label or a path segment cannot be redacted by any string rule, because `https://SECRET.dyn.example.com/upd` and `https://api.example.com/upd` are indistinguishable strings. **That is correct** — all four rows reproduce at HEAD, and this PR does not try to close them.

But the reachability question underneath it had not been asked, and asking it found a live leak of the *satisfiable* class on a surface the issue never checked.

## Which leaves can actually carry a secret in the host or path?

Exactly one family. The issue treats all five as equivalent; they are not.

| leaf | credential leaf available? | host/path secret reachable by construction? |
|---|---|---|
| DDNS `server` / `update-server` | YES — `password` / `api-token` | No |
| DDNS `url-template` (generic) | YES — `password`; template carries `%u`/`%p` **specifiers**, not literals | No |
| DDNS `checkip-url` | n/a — public IP echo, no auth | No |
| `archive-sites` | YES — sibling `password` leaf; userinfo handled | No |
| **`feed-server` `url` / `hostname` / `feed-name <f> path`** | **NO — the schema has none** | **YES** |

A `feed-server`'s complete leaf set is `url`, `hostname`, `update-interval`, `hold-interval`, `feed-name <n> path` (`pkg/config/schema_security.go:1293`). With no credential leaf, a subscription key has nowhere to go but the URL — and the provider, not the operator, picks the URL shape. Every DDNS backend by contrast has a dedicated `config.Secret` leaf, which is why `pkg/ddns/README.md` (`f329e0d12`) can tell operators to use the userinfo or query. **That advice does not transfer to feeds**, and the feeds README had no mention of redaction, tokens, credentials or secrets at all.

## The defect this fixes

`feed-name <f> path` is URL-bearing: `resolveBaseURL` joins it onto the feed-server's `url`/`hostname`, so the leaf carries a URL tail. `FeedEntry.MarshalJSON` has redacted it since #6703 — its own doc comment says a `?token=SECRET` query "is the common shape".

The AST route did not. `urlLeafIndices` had no `path` case. Measured before the fix, same config, two surfaces:

```
feed-server et url                 https://feeds.example.com/base?<redacted>   <- agree
feed-server et feed-name bad path  /sub/list.txt?token=SECRETPATHQ             <- AST VERBATIM
```

`RedactedClone` backs the on-box CLI `show configuration` (`pkg/cli/cli_show.go`), the gRPC config RPCs (`pkg/grpcapi/server_config.go`) and the REST config reads (`pkg/api/config.go`), so the token that the REST JSON route redacted was printed in cleartext on all three. This is the **query-string class** — the class #6703's acceptance criteria explicitly cover and `RedactURL` handles correctly — not the unsatisfiable host class.

## The fix

One `case "path"` gated on `feed-server` ancestry, following the doctrine already stated in the `urlLeafIndices` doc block: distinctive leaf names (`url`, `url-template`, `checkip-url`) match unqualified; generic ones (`server`, `update-server`) are context-gated. `path` is generic, so it is gated.

## Tests assert the agreement, not a literal

The two surfaces must agree, so the tests assert *that*, rather than pinning either side to an expected string — a literal would encode which surface is trusted, and here the AST side was the wrong one.

- `TestFeedPathQueryTokenIsRedactedOnBothSurfaces7406` — the token survives neither surface, and both render identically.
- `TestFeedPathWithoutCredentialIsUnchanged7406` — over-reach control: a credential-free path is still rendered verbatim on both. Without it, "redact the whole leaf" would pass the test above while destroying the value operators read.
- `TestFeedPathSegmentSecretIsRenderedOnBothSurfaces7406` — pins the boundary this deliberately does not cross, so a later one-sided "fix" of the path-segment case reproduces exactly the two-surface disagreement being closed here.

## PR #8097 — nat: release the replaced synced session's reservation (#6979 F3) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/6979-f3-release-on-replace`

Part of #6979 — closes **F3** only. F1 and F7b remain open, so this deliberately carries no close keyword.

## The row, and why it survived

F3 reads: *"`upsert_synced_with_origin` removes the previous session and discards `_previous`; the handler then reserves only the new decision. The replaced session's reservation is not released."*

The predicate still holds at the call site (coordinates drifted: the two `_previous` discards are now `install.rs:139` and `:324`). But taking it at face value produces the wrong fix, because **#6528 moved the release inside `reserve_flow`**, keyed on `SourceNatFlowKey` — the ORIGINAL 5-tuple, with no translated field. A same-key re-decision therefore finds the incumbent under the same flow and retires it with RELEASE semantics. Its own comment names F3's defect: *"retire the stale reservation first so we do not leak the old port's bit."*

So a NAT → different-NAT replacement already self-heals. Adding a release at the call site for that case would **double-free the port the new decision legitimately owns**.

## What actually leaks

The retire only runs if the replacement reaches `reserve_flow`. The reserve is gated twice — on `is_peer_synced() && !is_reverse` at the call site, and on `nat.rewrite_src.is_some()` inside `reserve_synced_source_nat_allocation_with_holder`. Three shapes route around it:

1. **NAT → no-NAT** — the active re-evaluates a reused 5-tuple after its NAT rule is withdrawn.
2. NAT → a reverse entry.
3. peer-synced → local-origin (HA activation, `allow_replace_local`).

Each installs the new session while the old port stays reserved with nothing left to free it: delete-sync releases the *current* decision, which no longer names that port. The port is held until the process exits.

## Measurement

Through the real `handle_upsert_synced`, reading `source_nat_pool_statuses().used_ports`, with the installed decision as an **anti-vacuity discriminator** — `used_ports` alone cannot separate "freed" from "the upsert was REJECTED so nothing changed":

| replacement | `used_ports` | installed `rewrite_src_port` | reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| NAT → port 20001 | 1 → 1 | `Some(Some(20001))` | #6528 retires; correct |
| NAT → no-NAT | 1 → **1** | `Some(None)` | **leak** — landed with no NAT, port still held |
| NAT → no-NAT *(fixed)* | 1 → **0** | `Some(None)` | freed |

## The fix

Capture the previous `(decision, metadata)` before the upsert discards it; when the new entry will not re-reserve the flow, run the same teardown pair `handle_delete_synced` uses (`release_source_nat_allocation_for_worker` + `release_nat64_allocation_for_worker`, same holder id). The release sits **above** the `is_peer_synced()` gate so it also covers shape 3.

`new_entry_reserves` is load-bearing in **both** directions:
- Skipping the release when the new decision *does* reserve is what keeps `reserve_flow`'s own eviction from being double-freed.
- Releasing *unconditionally* — the obvious simplification — would drop this worker's holder bit and re-take it on a same-tuple refresh (HA sync reconnect, periodic re-upsert), opening a window for another worker's local allocation to steal the port.

## Tests

Three, all driving the real entry point so deleting the wiring reds them — testing the release helper directly would not. Each asserts a *different* value, so no cell can pass for another's reason:

- `synced_replace_dropping_nat_releases_the_old_reservation_6979_f3` — fail-on-revert; pins `installed == Some(None)` **first** so a rejected upsert cannot make it pass vacuously.
- `synced_replace_changing_nat_port_keeps_exactly_one_reservation_6979_f3` — over-reach control for the #6528 path. `0` here would mean this release double-freed the new decision's port.
- `synced_refresh_with_identical_nat_keeps_its_reservation_6979_f3` — over-reach control for the unconditional-release regression described above.

## Validation

- Rust: `cargo test -- --test-threads=1` → **rc=0, 5014 collected, 0 FAILED**.
- Go: `go test -count=1 ./...` → **rc=0, 0 `--- FAIL`, 0 package FAIL, 0 races**.

## PR #8098 — session: give SessionKey a routing domain (#2387 Track B-P0, phase 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `feat/7160-vrf-session-key`

Phase 1 of the Option-B decision on #7160. **Does not close it** — this is the structural half; the field is not yet populated.

### The defect

Two flows in different routing-instances sharing a 5-tuple collide in the conntrack map. Live under PBR `then routing-instance`: the established-session fast path short-circuits before `ingress_route_table_override`, so tenant B's flow inherits tenant A's cached egress, NAT and **policy** decision — a cross-tenant policy bypass.

### What this does

`SessionKey` gains `routing_domain: u32` (`0` = default instance, so single-VRF identity is byte-identical). All five key transforms **preserve** it rather than defaulting it. That symmetry is what makes the field legal on the key, and is the axis on which it differs from #6928's `ingress_ifindex`/`ingress_vlan_id` — those sit on the session *value* because the reply ingresses on the forward flow's *egress*.

### What this deliberately does NOT do

Nothing populates the field. Every value in the tree is `0`, so **the defect is still live in production** and the commit-time overlap warning remains the operator's only signal. Phase 2 threads `StableRoutingInstanceTableID(name)` through the control plane and onto the wire.

### Correction: phase 2 does not need an HA protocol bump

#7160 says Option B "bumps the HA wire, which makes a release non-rolling-upgradable", and I repeated that in my implementation contract on the issue. **Both quote plan §4d, which plan v5 §0a corrected** — and the correction is already in this repo, in the section directly below the one this PR edits:

> The HA session-sync wire does NOT need a version bump […] it rides as a length-gated trailing **value** field, exactly like #2170 `Generation` […] Interning **domain 0 = the default routing-instance** makes an old peer's omitted field decode to the default VRF […] and `CurrentHAProtocolVersion` never moves.

Acting on the issue text would have broken rolling upgrade for nothing. My first draft of the README section asserted the bump and **contradicted the wire bullet twenty lines below it**; that is fixed, and the guard's failure message now warns the phase-2 implementer by name.

### The doc guard was inverted, not deleted

`vrf_session_identity_doc_guard.rs` asserted `!key_rs.contains("routing_domain")` and fired on this change — which is exactly why the docs are in this PR. Deleting a guard that has just done its job would retire it silently, so instead it now:

- pins that the field **exists** (a revert re-opens #2387);
- **counts** the five preserving transforms — fixing four and missing one is the plausible partial revert, and a search rather than a count would not see it;
- fires when `routing_domain` reaches `src/protocol/`, so phase 2 cannot land without revisiting the docs.

| cell | mutation | collected | build | named FAIL |

| M1 | `reverse_wire_key` zeroes the domain | 4882 | 0 | 1 — transform cell only |
| M2 | field excluded from `Hash`/`Eq` | 4882 | 0 | 2 — the two identity cells only |
| M3 | a third transform zeroed | 2 | 0 | 1 — guard, *"found 4, expected 5"* |

Each localises to the cell that owns the property.

**`cargo fmt` must not be run in this repo.** Pristine `origin/master` has **3054 rustfmt hunks** under rustfmt 1.9.0, so formatting produces thousands of lines of unrelated churn. My first attempt did exactly that: 307 collateral files, which broke the #6592 runtime-view canary and made the diff 3674/2104 instead of 557/23. `git diff origin/master --name-only` against the set of files actually containing my change is what caught it — a scope check is the only gate that is scope-independent.

## PR #8099 — cli: record why the egress FIB hit cannot be zone-corroborated (#7240) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7240-comment`

Comment-only. Does not close #7240 — it records the measured reason that issue cannot be done as filed, so the next reader is not sent at a change that does not work.

The existing comment said the symmetric check awaited "the egress zone's own value … enumerated across the fabric/tunnel override paths". I did that enumeration, built the check on all three surfaces, and **four pre-existing tests went red**. They are right.

```
--- FAIL: TestInterfaceFilterEgressArmMakesColumnNameAnotherInterface6928
    `interface lo.80` must select both sessions through the egress arm, got 0: []
--- FAIL: TestInterfaceFilterReachesRowViaEgressArm6928
--- FAIL: TestMatchesV4_InterfaceFilter
--- FAIL: TestSessionEntryEgressIfaceParity_4650
```

### Why it is structural, not a pending enumeration

**Ingress** — the zone and the `{ifindex, VLAN}` are stamped at the *same instant from the same observation*: the packet arrived on that interface, and that interface's zone is the one policy used. They must agree, so a disagreement is positive evidence of a recycled ifindex. That is the whole mechanism of #6987.

**Egress** — the FIB result and the security zone are *two different derivations*. One answers "which netdev does this route leave by", the other "what zone did policy assign". They legitimately differ for any egress interface that is not a zone member: `lo`, and by construction the tunnel and fabric paths. A disagreement is the normal case, so it cannot adjudicate a recycle.

I had enumerated where `egress_zone` is **written** and concluded it was safe. That was the wrong half — the hazard is that a *correct* egress interface need not belong to the recorded egress *zone* at all. The tests found what the enumeration missed.

### No partial landing is available

- **Filter**: the row becomes unreachable by a filter naming the interface it actually left on. The failing test documents selecting on either direction as intended — *"not a defect"*.

## PR #8100 — cos: make the residual-surplus reset linearizable against refill (#7206 A1-b5-F4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7206-f4-residual-linearizable`

Part of #7206 — closes **A1-b5-F4** only. A1-b1-F6 is the other survivor, so no close keyword. (I re-measured the cohort today: [6 of the 8 rows are already fixed](https://github.com/psaab/xpf/issues/7206#issuecomment-5470687073).)

### The race

`reset_residual_surplus_budget` published `tokens = 0` and `last_refill_ns` as two independent stores. `refill_residual_surplus_budget` claimed the timestamp CAS and then added tokens in a **separate** loop. A reset interleaved between those two steps left non-zero tokens after a completed reset — residual surplus that the reset had just cancelled.

### Why the check runs after the CAS, and only after

A pre-CAS check is the intuitive placement and is what I wrote first. It cannot be the guarantee: a reset can land between that check and the CAS, and **the CAS cannot detect it** — a reset stores `0`, so if the expected `tokens` is also `0` the compare *succeeds* and writes the stale `added` on top of a completed reset. That is exactly the reported failure.

### Mutation testing removed half the fix

I implemented both checks. Each turned out **redundant given the other** — deleting either one alone left the full suite green, because the survivor caught the case:

| cell | mutation | collected | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | `reset` no longer bumps the generation | 4890 | clean | 2 |
| M2 | pre-CAS check removed (both present) | 4890 | clean | **0 — escaped** |
| M3 | post-CAS check removed (both present) | 4890 | clean | **0 — escaped** |
| M4 | post-CAS check removed, now the sole guard | 4890 | clean | 1 |

Two guards where only one is load-bearing read as defence in depth while actually being an untested branch beside a guard nobody could tell was doing the work. So the pre-CAS check is **removed**, and M4 shows the remaining one is bound.

This is the compound-mutation blind spot in miniature: neither single deletion could fail, so only mutating each *in the presence of the other* revealed that my test could not distinguish them.

### Testability

`commit_refill_tokens` is extracted from the refill loop so the guard is reachable from a test **without winning a race**. That matters more than usual here: a threaded probe that simply fails to hit the interleaving returns the same green as a correct implementation, so it cannot be the primary evidence. The concurrent test is kept for livelock and bound checking only, and its doc comment says exactly that.

The positive control is load-bearing too — a `commit_refill_tokens` that never added anything would satisfy the "adds nothing" assertion perfectly.

### Accepted trade-off

Restoring `0` rather than retrying is deliberate: the reset is the newer intent and declared the budget empty as of its own `now_ns`. A legitimate post-reset refill running concurrently can have its tokens dropped — transient (the next refill re-adds them) and erring toward granting *less* surplus, which is the safe direction. Documented in the code.

### Validation

`make test-rust` and `make test-go` both clean, zero failures. Scope is 2 files, zero collateral.

## PR #8102 — dataplane: run the input filter before the embedded-ICMP reversal (#7359) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7359-icmp-reversal-filter-order`

Addresses the **input-filter half** of #7359. No close keyword — the PBR half is deliberately not done; see below.

The flowless embedded-ICMP NAT reversal reverse-translated an ICMP error, queued it toward the internal client, and `continue`d — skipping the interface input filter further down the same arm. A `discard` term did not drop it, a `count` term did not advance, a policer did not meter it.

### Hoisted, not duplicated

The L3 identity and the filter evaluation move **above** the reversal so both consumers share one evaluation. Adding a second call site inside the reversal arm would double-count every counter and re-fire every log term on the flowless path — a worse defect than the one being fixed, and one no single-path test would catch.

### PBR is not in this PR, and that is a decision rather than an oversight

The issue's title covers PBR too, but the two are not the same change. The input filter is an **admission** question and the hoist answers it. `then routing-instance` steers a route lookup that the reversal *replaces* with its own resolution toward the client — threading an override in changes **where the reversed error is routed**, not whether it is admitted. It wants its own review and its own test, so I have left #7359 open for it rather than folding it in quietly.

### Two things about the test

**The fixture nearly produced a false negative.** My first version left `flow_src_addr`/`flow_dst_addr` zero in the metadata. `l3_session_flow_from_meta` returns `None` for an unspecified address — the *reachable* #7055 leg — so `l3_ctx` was `None`, the filter block was skipped on **every** path, and the test failed **against the fixed code**. That reads exactly like "the fix does not work", and I was one step from recording it as one. What separated a fixture defect from a production finding was instrumenting the hoisted block to print whether it was reached and whether `l3_ctx` was `Some`:

```
PROBE7359 reached hoist, l3_ctx.is_some=false
```

Reached, but empty — so the ordering was right and the input was wrong.

**The absence assertion needs a fixture guard.** The ordering cell asserts *no queued forward*, and an absence is satisfied just as well by a fixture that configures nothing. So `the_7359_fixture_actually_attaches_its_input_filter` is kept **permanently** rather than deleted after use: if a renamed snapshot field, a changed family string or a moved ifindex ever stopped the filter attaching, the ordering test would keep passing while measuring nothing.

The ordering test also reuses the #5690 reachability fixture unchanged except for the filter, so the pair shows the filter is what changed the outcome.

### Validation

`make test-rust` and `make test-go` clean.

| cell | mutation | collected | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | move the filter evaluation back below the reversal | 4892 | clean | 1 — `input_filter_discard_drops_the_embedded_icmp_reversal_7359`, and nothing else |

## PR #8106 — session: populate SessionKey.routing_domain from the ingress interface (#7160 phase 2) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7160-phase2-routing-domain`

Closes #7160

## What this does

#7160 phase 1 (PR #8098) put `routing_domain: u32` on `SessionKey`. Nothing set it, so every value in the tree was 0 and the defect was still live in production: two flows in different routing instances that share a 5-tuple collided in the conntrack map, and because the established-session fast path short-circuits before `ingress_route_table_override`, tenant B's flow inherited tenant A's cached egress, NAT and **policy** decision.

**This is phase 2. It populates the field.**

## The number, and where it is decided

`StableRoutingInstanceTableID(name)` — a pure FNV-1a of the routing-instance NAME into `[100000, 999999]`, already gated at commit against collisions — is computed in **Go** (`routingInstanceDomain`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace/routes.go`), shipped per interface on the config snapshot as `InterfaceSnapshot.routing_domain`, and never re-hashed in Rust. Two implementations of one hash in two languages is exactly the "when two spellings must agree" trap, and this number has to mean the same thing on the HA peer.

The band starts above 0, so a named instance can never collide with the 0 that means "the default instance". That is what lets 0 do triple duty: an interface in no instance, a snapshot from an older Go binary, and a peer ingress identity this node cannot resolve.

## The stamp

One site — the poll path's **stage 9b**, immediately after fabric-ingress classification — from the **LOGICAL** (VLAN unit) ingress ifindex, the same identity the zone, filter and pre-routing-NAT paths already use. Every key the descriptor derives (lookup key, installed forward key, reverse companion, index entries) therefore carries one consistent domain.

It runs *after* stage 9 because that is an input, not a detail: a frame that arrived over the fabric link did not arrive on the flow's real ingress interface, so the fabric link's own membership would be a **wrong** answer rather than a missing one. A peer-zone-encoded frame resolves its domain from that zone (`zone_routing_domain`), which is **absent** for a zone straddling two instances — the #6722 "identify exactly one, or nothing" discipline.

`has_routing_domains` is a single-bool gate, false for every deployment with no routing-instance interface membership (including the smoke cluster), which keeps session identity there bit-identical to pre-#7160.

## The correction phase 2 had to make — please read this part

Phase 1's field doc and plan v5 §0a both assert *a flow's routing domain is the same in both directions*, and all five key transforms preserved it on that basis. **Measured against this dataplane, that is false**, and §3 of the plan already says why: the transit route lookup is **not** VRF-isolated — it uses the DEFAULT table unless a PBR term overrides it. So a flow that ingresses on a routing-instance member interface and egresses out of the default instance is a real, *working* configuration whose reply resolves a different domain. Keying the reverse-match index on the forward domain would have blackholed every such flow's replies: a forwarding outage, not a hardening.

The maintainer flagged exactly this on the issue — *"config-derived guarantees the two NODES agree; it does not guarantee the two DIRECTIONS do"*. This is the answer.

So the transforms split, and **both halves are load-bearing**:

| transform | domain | why |
|---|---|---|
| `forward_wire_key` | preserve | another key of the same direction |
| `translated_session_key` | preserve | a reverse entry's own translated alias |
| `reverse_session_key` | preserve | navigates between the two halves of one flow |
| `reverse_wire_key` | **zero** | builds the index a REPLY is looked up under |
| `reverse_canonical_key` | **zero** | same |

The isolation the zeroing would otherwise cost is recovered one layer up: `find_forward_nat_match` walks the (1:N) reverse bucket in **two passes**, preferring a candidate whose forward session carries the reply's own domain and falling back to a domain-agnostic match only when none does. Two contained tenants demux exactly; a non-contained flow keeps forwarding as it did before the field existed. `reverse_match_key` is the one name for the zeroing convention so the index side and the probe side cannot drift. The shared NAT map, being 1:1 rather than 1:N, expresses the same preference as two probes.

**The forward direction — which is where the bypass lives** — is exact: forward lookups go through `key_to_handle` on the full key, so two tenants hold two entries and neither can reach the other's.

## HA: no protocol bump, and no new wire field either

The issue text says Option B "bumps the HA wire"; that quotes plan §4d, which v5 §0a corrected. §0a's finding stands, and phase 2 is cheaper than §0a needed it to be: **the domain does not ride the wire at all.**

It is a pure function of the flow's ingress interface and the config; both nodes run identical config; and #7095 already resolves the peer's cluster-stable ingress NAME into the importing node's own ifindex/vlan. So the importing node **derives** it (`Coordinator::synced_routing_domain`) instead of reading a second number that could disagree with the first. `CurrentHAProtocolVersion` and `SessionSyncWireVersion` both stay put; rolling upgrade is unaffected.

A session whose ingress identity the peer could not name (fabric-redirected, #7096) imports at domain 0 — the pre-#7160 identity — and re-adjudicates through policy after a failover instead of being taken over. A correctness-preserving degradation, not a bypass, and it is stated in the docs.

## PR #8107 — config: hard-reject dangling class-of-service interface references (#7337) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7337-cos-iface-ref-strict`

Refs #7337 — the **Go strict gate** the issue says must land *before* a Rust backstop. No close keyword; the backstop is now unblocked but not done.

The seven `class-of-service interfaces` reference fields were warn-only at commit and then failed OPEN in the dataplane: `forwarding_build/cos.rs` resolves each name with a bare `.get(...)` yielding `None`, with no `Missing*Ref` and no error. The interface materializes no scheduler queues, or a classifier arm contributes nothing — QoS silently degrades to best-effort while the committed config still says the interface is shaped and classified. The operator's only evidence is a warning they saw once at commit time.

### The population is seven, not four

The issue names four. At master there are seven — `scheduler-map`, `output-traffic-control-profile`, the `dscp` / `ieee-802.1` / `inet-precedence` classifiers, and the `dscp` / `ieee-802.1` rewrite-rules. The two added since it was filed leak the same way.

### Why the existing gate did not cover this

`validateClassOfServiceSchedulerMapRefsStrict` validates the **scheduler-map → scheduler** link. This is the **interface → scheduler-map** link. They are the outer and inner halves of one reference chain and only the inner one was gated, so an interface naming a scheduler-map that does not exist at all committed cleanly. Easy to mistake one for the other when grepping — I nearly closed this issue on that basis.

### The no-brick half is load-bearing, and the matrix proves it

Strict on commit, lenient on load/peer-sync per #1960. That is not a formality here: **the mutation that ignores the lenient flag reds five tests besides the one written for it**, because several existing fixtures legitimately load dangling-reference configs. A gate that rejected on both paths would brick an upgrading node carrying a config its previous binary accepted.

### Two judgement calls, stated rather than buried

**`Level` is checked as well as `Units`.** `applyCoSInterfaceLevelBindings` folds an interface-level binding into each *configured* unit before the gates run, so for an interface with units this is redundant — but an interface-level binding on a stanza with **no** configured units is folded nowhere and would otherwise be invisible. It has its own cell; removing the check reds exactly that cell.

**A dangling `ieee-802.1` rewrite-rule is rejected even though that feature is documented inert here.** The gate is about whether the NAME resolves, not whether the resolved rule has a runtime effect. Gating only the enforced references would make commit behaviour depend on an implementation detail the operator cannot see from their config.

### Three existing tests were repointed, not loosened

They asserted the warning these references used to produce. They now compile on the **tolerant** path, where a warning is still the outcome. I did not loosen the shared strict helpers: that would have silently removed the strict check from every other test in those files, which would keep passing while proving nothing about commit behaviour. Two files get a lenient *sibling* helper used only by the fixtures that dangle on purpose.

### Validation

`make test-go` clean; `make test-rust` clean at 5023 collected (no Rust touched).

| cell | mutation | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | gate unregistered | clean | 3 |
| M2 | lenient flag ignored — the #1960 brick | clean | 6 (mine + 5 pre-existing) |
| M3 | `Level` check removed | clean | 1 — exactly its own cell |

Scope checked against the **merge-base**, not the moving `origin/master` ref: 7 files, zero collateral.

One process note: I lost this implementation once mid-work by running `git checkout --` inside a mutation cell while the fix was still uncommitted — the applied-check is meaningless there, and the restore wiped the subject rather than the mutation. Re-applied, then committed *before* mutating.

## PR #8109 — userspace-dp: revalidate established sessions against a changed static input filter (#7212) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7212-static-filter-revalidation`

Implements the mechanism #7212 decided: lazy per-tuple revalidation of an
established session's interface INPUT filter, stamped by config generation.

Does NOT close #7212 — one acceptance bullet remains, tracked as #8108 and
stated below.

## The gap

A purely STATIC address/protocol/port `then discard` attached or tightened after
a session was created was never rechecked, so that flow forwarded until it idled
out. The session-hit fast path re-evaluated an input filter only when its verdict
genuinely varies per packet (a DSCP match, #1430, or a per-packet L4 match,
#2362), and the rotation purge is gated on the same predicate, so a static filter
change matched neither. Junos firewall filters are stateless and evaluated on
every packet, so this was a parity gap as well as a revocation gap.

The obvious symmetry — an interface-keyed clear, mirroring the policy
invalidation that runs at commit — was rejected in #5858 with evidence and is not
re-proposed: it drops PERMITTED flows, and a purged permitted SNAT flow
reinstalls on a DIFFERENT translated port.

## Mechanism

For a static filter the verdict is a pure function of `(ingress interface,
family, 5-tuple)`, all constant for the life of one direction of a session:

* `SessionEntry::filter_revalidated_gen` records the
  `ValidationState::config_generation` this direction's verdict was computed
  under. `install` stamps the generation the worker published for the pass;
  `upsert_synced` stamps `0`, which is never a live generation.
* On an established-session hit whose stamp is stale, the static verdict is
  re-derived ONCE and the entry re-stamped.
* The session is revoked only if the new verdict is DENY.

The re-derivation is side-effect free. `NonRoutingCountPolicy::Never` runs the
SAME walk the counted evaluator runs with counting suppressed on both of its
arms, so the action it returns is that walk's action by construction — there is
no second walk to drift. Counting here would inflate every matched `then count`
term by one packet per PERMITTED session per commit, which is the common case and
would be silent. Only on a DENY does the ordinary counted evaluator run, so the
one newly-denied packet is counted, logged and rejected exactly once.

It evaluates on the flow's 5-tuple ALONE (`TermMatchExtra::default()`), not on
the triggering packet — see "Two defects found in review" below for why that is
load-bearing rather than an optimisation.

## PR #8110 — userspace-dp: carry the tunnel discriminator on the HA session-sync wire [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7188-session-sync-discriminator`

Closes #7188

## The defect

Two RFC 2890 GRE tunnels between one pair of outer endpoints are two sessions
on the active and **one aliased session on the standby**.

GRE is IP protocol 47 and carries no L4 ports, so the two tunnels share a
5-tuple. The helper's own `SessionKey` separates them on a typed
`TunnelDiscriminator` — that is #7188's landed half. The sync path did not carry
it: `build_synced_session_key` hardcoded

```rust
discriminator: Default::default(),
```

and `Default` for `TunnelDiscriminator` is `None` — the *"no discriminator
concept for this protocol"* class, not even `Unkeyed`. So a keyed GRE session
did not merely lose its key across sync; it arrived in the class reserved for
non-tunnel protocols, and **both** records rebuilt to the same key. `install.rs`
opens with an unconditional `remove_entry`, so the second install evicted the
first. After a failover the two tunnels shared one policy decision, one NAT
state, one counter set and one timeout — the exact collapse #7188 exists to
prevent, restored silently by the failover.

## Why this is 30+ files and not a one-line receive-side fix

**Go collapsed the two tunnels BEFORE the wire.** `snapshotDeltaSink` — the
cold-prime bulk window — deduped into `map[dataplane.SessionKey]`, and protocol
47 has no ports, so two same-endpoint tunnels are one Go key. The later delta
silently overwrote the earlier, and the standby was primed with one session for
two tunnels regardless of what the wire carried. A value-only wire field would
**not** have satisfied the acceptance bullet on its own. The dedup key is now
`(session key, discriminator)` and the sink's delete arms take the converted
value, so a close in the same batch retracts only the tunnel it names.

The discriminator itself crosses six hops, each an independent place to drop it:
the helper's JSON delta producer, both binary HA delta frames (**open AND
close** — a close names the session to retract, and for protocol 47 the 5-tuple
names two tunnels at once), Go's `SessionDeltaInfo`, `SessionValue{,V6}`, the
`pkg/cluster` wire (v4 and v6), `SessionSyncRequest`, and the peer helper.

## `0` is RESERVED for "not carried", and is NOT the encoding of `None`

This is the load-bearing detail, and it is a correction to the obvious design.

`serde(default)` and a short length-gated record both yield `0`, so `0` is the
one value a peer produces **without meaning to**. A build that has the field
always states a class, `None` included. Without that separation a peer that
predates the field is indistinguishable from a new peer with

## PR #8111 — nat: refuse a source-NAT identity a peer pool already owns (#6979 F6) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/6979-f6-pool-address-overlap`

Part of #6979 — **F6 only**, and nothing else on that issue. F1, F7b and F3 are already disposed
(measured in the issue's own re-measurement comments); F4 and F5 stay open.

## What actually reproduces, and what does not

F6's second half says a **match-only** rule edit "strands a reservation in an
allocator that can no longer match the flow, while the rule that now owns it is
free to reissue the tuple". Before designing anything I drove three probes
against `origin/master`. Single-address pools, one-port range, so a duplicate is
unambiguous:

| probe | construction | master |
|---|---|---|
| **P1** | pools `a` and `b` both `[203.0.113.1]`; a **match-only edit** narrows r1's `source-address` so flow 2 matches r2 | flow 2 gets the **identical** `203.0.113.1:20000` flow 1 still holds |
| **P2** | the same two pools, **no edit at all** | the same duplicate |
| **P3** | **ONE** pool, the same match-only edit | `Unavailable(AllocatorExhausted)` — **no defect** |

**P3 is what decided the design, and it corrects the finding.** The key's
ignorance of match criteria and zone scope is harmless on its own: a match-only
edit changes none of `(pool name, addresses, port range)`, so the allocator is
reused by `Arc` and its live reservation keeps refusing the tuple. **F6's own
fix suggestion — add match criteria to the key — would have fixed nothing and
broken exactly that carryover**, which is the stranding `drain_allocator_key`
(#7717) exists to prevent. P2 says the edit is not load-bearing either.

What is left is the real defect: **two distinct allocator keys can cover one
pool address**, so that address carries two independent occupancy bitmaps and
neither can see the other's reservations. The comment #7858 left on
`carry_renamed_pool_reservations` names the hazard exactly — "keeping them apart
would give one address two independent occupancy domains, which is the collision
the key exists to prevent" — while two differently-named pools on one address
are that state, live on master.

## Severity, not oversold

- The config is **rejected at strict commit** by the Go #5144 gate
  (`validateNATPoolExternalTupleOverlapStrict` — on address overlap alone; it
  does not consult port ranges). It reaches the dataplane only from a tolerated
  lenient load, a peer sync, an older control plane, or a handcrafted snapshot:
  the same population #6812's aggregate-budget gate exists for.
- The consequence is a duplicate translated identity — two live flows on one
  `(pool address, port)` toward one remote, replies the reverse index cannot
  attribute. Mis-delivery, not a leak.
- What the issue calls "protection in the wrong place" is real but **benign on a
  valid config**: teardown sweeps every pool rule without running its matcher,
  so a stranded reservation is still released. P3 measures that. **This PR does
  not claim to fix a stranded release, because there is not one to fix.**

## PR #8112 — session: restore reverse_wire_key's domain-agnostic reverse-match key (master is red) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7160-restore-reverse-wire-key`

## master is red — one-hunk restore

**#8106 merged one commit short.** A mutation cell that reverts `reverse_wire_key` to preserve the routing domain was applied in the worktree when that PR's `git add -A` ran, and the corrective commit was pushed after the merge had already been taken.

Master's Rust suite fails two cells today, and they are exactly the two that guard this line. Measured on `origin/master` (`c3b152077`), not asserted:

| tree | `cargo test --bin xpf-userspace-dp 7160` |
|---|---|
| master as merged | **17 passed / 2 failed** |
| master + this hunk | **19 passed / 0 failed** |

The two failures are `a_natted_reply_from_outside_the_flows_domain_still_resolves_its_session_7160` and `key_transforms_split_same_direction_preserve_from_reverse_match_zero_7160`.

## What the line does, and why preserving the domain there is wrong

`reverse_wire_key` builds the bucket a **reply** is looked up under. This dataplane routes transit traffic in the **default** table unless a PBR term overrides it, so a flow that ingresses on a routing-instance member interface and egresses out of the default instance — a real, working configuration — has a reply that resolves a *different* routing domain.

Keying that bucket on the **forward** domain makes the pool tuple the server actually replies to unreachable, and the flow breaks. That is a forwarding outage, not a hardening. The isolation the zeroing might seem to cost is recovered one layer up, in `find_forward_nat_match`'s two-pass domain preference — see the `routing_domain` doc on `SessionKey`.

## Diff

One hunk, in `userspace-dp/src/session/key.rs`: `routing_domain: forward_key.routing_domain` → `routing_domain: 0`, with the comment that explains why.

The test is right and the code is wrong. `reverse_wire_key` builds the **reverse-match index** — the bucket a reply is looked up under — and this dataplane's transit route lookup is not VRF-isolated (default table unless a PBR term overrides). ## PR #8116 — session sync: refuse an import whose routing domain cannot be resolved (#7160 follow-up) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-30)

Branch: `fix/7160-sync-domain-failclosed`

Follow-up to #7160 phase 2 (#8106). Addresses the `routing_domain` hazard on the HA sync path.

## The finding

Phase 2 resolves a peer-synced session's routing domain from the #7095 cluster-stable ingress identity rather than carrying it on the wire. That is right for every session whose ingress the sender could *name*. It was wrong for the ones it could not — #7096 fabric-redirected sessions, and any session with no cluster-stable ingress name. Those imported at **domain 0**, and phase 2's own docs called it *"a correctness-preserving degradation, not a bypass"*.

**That claim was wrong.** 0 is not a neutral placeholder on a node that runs routing instances — it is the **default routing instance**. An import filed there sits at exactly the key the domain-agnostic fallback probe in `lookup_shared_forward_nat_match` reaches:

```rust
if let Some(exact) = map.get(reply_key).cloned() { return Some(exact); }
let probe = crate::session::reverse_match_key(reply_key);   // domain -> 0
map.get(&probe).cloned()
```

So a reply that *did* resolve its own domain can match a session that was only keyed at 0 because nothing knew its domain. That is the HA half of the collision #7160 exists to close, and no single-instance test can see it, because there every key is legitimately 0.

The fallback probe is **not** the defect — it is what keeps a non-contained flow's reply resolving at all. Manufacturing wrong domain-0 keys on the sync path was.

## The fix: three states, not two

`Coordinator::synced_routing_domain` now returns `Option<u32>`:

| state | meaning | upsert | delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Some(0)` | the default routing instance — and the **only** domain on a node with no routing-instance membership | import | delete |
| `Some(n)` | a tenant's instance | import | delete |
| `None` | routing instances exist and the request named nothing to resolve one from | **refuse** | proceed at 0 + per-domain sweep |

The two verbs answer `None` differently on purpose: a refused **delete** *leaks* a session, while an over-broad sweep removes nothing the 5-tuple did not already name.

The refusal is `SyncedImportOutcome::RejectedUnknownRoutingDomain`, carrying its own stable reason token (`unknown-routing-domain`) so Go can tell it from a transport failure and from the other semantic refusals, and counted by `synced_import_unknown_routing_domain_total`.

**What refusing costs, stated plainly:** on a VRF deployment a synced session with no cluster-stable ingress name is not taken over, so its flow re-adjudicates through policy after a failover. That is the *same* outcome the old behaviour produced for those flows, minus the cross-domain reachability.

## Tests

A cell that asserted the OLD behaviour by name (`an_unnamed_peer_ingress_imports_at_the_default_domain`) is **rewritten rather than deleted**, and records why its previous claim was wrong.

The new cells drive the real control-socket dispatcher:
- refused, **nothing published**, and counted — on a node with routing instances;
- **still imports** on a single-instance node (the half that keeps this from being a fail-closed regression for every cluster today);
- a **named** ingress still imports at its own domain, so the refusal is scoped to the unresolvable case rather than turning off HA sync for VRF deployments.

## Not done here, and why

Carrying the domain on the sync wire is the *complete* fix — it removes the degradation as well as the reachability. It is not in this PR because Go's `SessionValue` takes its ingress identity from the **BPF conntrack mirror struct**, so a wire-carried domain is a shared C struct change with its own alignment rules. That belongs in its own cut. This change removes the reachability now.

## Observability

The refusal is counted and **exported**: `xpf_userspace_synced_import_unknown_routing_domain_total`. It is the only signal that a VRF cluster is silently not taking over a subset of its peer's sessions, and it is always 0 on a single-instance node — so sustained growth is actionable and a 0 is a real "every synced import resolved its domain" answer.

## PR #8117 — nat: bound the source-NAT overlap index's cost, and stop overclaiming it (#6979 F6 follow-up) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/6979-f6-bound-touches-scan`

Follow-up to #8111, which merged while this was in its gate. Codex's round-2
review of #8111 then landed and found two more of the same class, plus a claim
of mine that was simply false. All of it is here.

## Three cost sites, one shape

#8111 rebuilt the pool-overlap index per **distinct allocator** rather than per
rule, because rules are not bounded by #6812's aggregate budget and pool
addresses are. That fixed the counting pass and the owner pass. Three sites with
the same shape survived:

| # | site | before | after | found by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the **assignment** pass — deciding which rules get the index — scanned every pool-mode rule's full address vector | 1024 rules over two overlapping `/16` pools: **67,108,864** hash lookups at apply | 131,072; the address scan runs once per distinct allocator and the per-rule step is a pointer compare | my own re-check |
| 2 | the **`distinct` dedup** was documented as bounded by `max_pools`. It was not: `PortAllocator::default()` builds a **fresh `Arc` per rule** and every failed pool rule carries one, so D could equal R | **R(R−1)/2** `same_allocator` comparisons | rules whose allocator has zero occupancy slots are skipped — such an allocator can never answer `holds_port` true, so it is not an occupancy domain | Codex round 2, finding 1 |
| 3 | the **counting** pass counted owners per address **occurrence**, so a pool repeating one of its own members became its own peer: `[X, X]` counted 2 | that rule got the index and paid the `SeqCst` fence + a map probe on **every** mint, with no peer present | counting is per distinct allocator; **indexing stays per occurrence**, which is what #8111's round-1 duplicate-position finding required | Codex round 2, finding 2 |

A `#7717` draining pool keeps its **retained** allocator, which has occupancy
slots, so the case that actually matters is still indexed by site 2's skip.

Behaviour is otherwise unchanged: a rule receives the index exactly when its
allocator covers an address another **real** allocator also covers.

## Two cells, each verified to red against the mutation it binds

- **`a_mixed_family_peers_v6_index_is_offset_past_its_v4_addresses_6979`.**
  Codex supplied `index: v4_len + pos` → `index: pos` as a mutation the existing
  eight-cell matrix misses — and it did. Every v6 fixture was v6-**only**, where
  `v4_len == 0` makes it a no-op. The new peer carries a v4 address first, so
  its shared v6 address sits at occupancy slot 1 and the two disagree.
- **`a_pool_with_duplicate_members_is_not_its_own_peer_6979`** for site 3. Only
  the **wiring** can be asserted — the runtime already answers correctly,
  because the same-allocator skip catches it — so that is what it asserts, and
  the assertion says why.

## Three false claims, corrected rather than softened

- The mint-path fast path is `Option::is_none`, not `Vec::is_empty`. Stale from
  the pre-#8111 shape and repeated in four documents.
- The index is *proportional to* the aggregate **address** budget; the dedup and
  assignment passes are bounded by a **different** quantity. Folding them into
  one budget sentence is what let sites 1 and 2 hide.
- I wrote that a bounded deterministic-v4 retry **"is not expressible with the

## PR #8118 — cluster: show when a peer's RG state was substituted locally (#7367) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7367-peer-override-visible`

Refs #7367 — the **second** acceptance criterion only. No close keyword; the first criterion is not addressed and I say why below.

`show chassis cluster status` renders the **post-override** `peerGroups` map, so a peer state *this node substituted* was indistinguishable from one the peer actually reported.

`applyTransferCommitOverridesOnPeerStateLocked` rewrites a peer group's `State` to `secondary-hold` in the **same map that feeds both the election and the operator's view**. One write corrupts both.

That is how #6656 presented as a healthy cluster **on both nodes at once**: node0 printed node1 as `secondary-hold` because node0's own override forced it, node1 printed itself `primary`, and neither render carried anything anomalous — while one node held 33 sessions and 4.6M packets against the other's 1 session and 4.7K.

### The change

`PeerGroupState` gains `StateOverriddenLocally` and an `OverrideReason`. The reason is not decoration: a transfer-out override stays armed until cleared, a commit-grace window expires on its own, and the operator's response differs. **`State` and every election consequence are unchanged** — this only lets the render say which of the two it is.

```
node1    100      secondary-hold                     ...   <- peer reported
node1    100      secondary-hold (local: transfer-out override)  ...   <- this node substituted
```

### What this does NOT do

Criterion 1 — surfacing `rg_active`, VIP presence, or a per-RG session count to distinguish *"primary and carrying traffic"* from *"primary and carrying nothing"* — is **not** addressed. That data lives in `pkg/daemon`, and the only thing comparing RG ownership against VRRP mastership (`CheckVRRPPosture`) is gated off entirely under `private-rg-election`, which is the compiler default. It needs a design across a package boundary, not a render change. The issue stays open for it.

### The test is a pair, and that is the point

A single case cannot show a *difference*. Asserting only the override case passes equally well against a render that appends the suffix unconditionally; asserting only the reported case passes against one that never appends it. Both managers are driven to the **same** `NodeState` first, with that asserted, so the comparison is about the substitution being visible rather than about two different states.

| cell | mutation | build | named FAIL |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | render annotation removed | clean | 1 |
| M2 | override site stops marking | clean | 2 |
| M3 | annotate **unconditionally** | clean | 1 — via the over-reach assertion |

M3 is the one that matters: it shows the fix does not simply mark every row, which a test asserting only the override case would have missed.

### Validation

## PR #8123 — userspace-xdp: assert the two facts #5192's residual decision rests on (#7464) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7464-xdp-align-asserts`

Closes #7464

#5192 item 2 measured the aligned-store fix at **+14,047 processed insns (+1.81%), −1.40 pp of verifier budget** and declined it — in a file with a documented outage, where `08a0bbd7f` blew the 1M cap and took both cluster dataplanes down. That decision is sound. It rests on two facts nothing asserted.

1. **`size_of::<UserspaceDpMeta>() % 8 == 0`.** The store does `bpf_xdp_adjust_meta(ctx, -meta_len)`, so `data_meta = data − 96`, and the whole *"the UB is unreachable on the zero-copy fast path because that path is in fact aligned"* argument needs that offset to **preserve** 8-alignment. The existing size assertion happens to imply it, and the implication was nowhere stated — grow the struct to 100 bytes, update that assertion to 100 (an ordinary, reviewable edit), and the UB moves silently from a generic-XDP portability concern onto the **primary forwarding path** with nothing failing.
2. **`align_of::<UserspaceDpMeta>() == 8`.** The layout block pins the size and six offsets and **no alignment**. The residual is scoped to an 8-byte demand from `config_generation: u64`; a future field raising it widens the residual on every path with no signal.

### The `.o` does not move — and the control is what makes that claim mean anything

```
CONTROL regen (before any edit):  f576dfef5644337fc6f614c35c4555e2  == tracked
AFTER regen (assertions added):   f576dfef5644337fc6f614c35c4555e2  == tracked
```

I ran the control **first**, deliberately. Without it, "byte-identical afterwards" would be consistent with a build that never reproduces the tracked object at all, and would prove nothing about this change.

Exactly **one of eleven** manifest sha entries moves, and it is `userspace-xdp/src/lib.rs` — the source I edited. The object entry does not.

### Gate

| cell | mutation | assertion 1 (`size % 8`) | assertion 2 (`align == 8`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| M-A | `config_generation: u64` → two `u32` (size preserved, demand drops to 4) | holds | **FAILS by name** |
| M-B | `#[repr(C, packed)]` | **FAILS** | **FAILS** |

**Recording the coupling honestly rather than implying two independent guards:** under `repr(C)` the size is always a multiple of the alignment, so **no mutation can fail assertion 1 while assertion 2 holds**. Assertion 1 is not independently falsifiable here. Its value is that it *states* the implication the size assertion only implies — which is exactly what #7464 asks for — and that the two decouple if the `repr` ever changes. I would rather say that than present a matrix that looks stronger than it is.

## PR #8124 — nat: release the NAT reservation a dropped synced delete strands (#6979 F4) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/6979-f4-dropped-delete-strands-reservation`

Part of #6979 — **F4 only**. F5 is measured and dispositioned here but
deliberately NOT fixed; see below.

## The finding's prediction is right about the route it names, and that is the trap

#6979's closing note expects the #6211 holder-set to bound F4 to "that worker's
bit is cleared". Constructed rather than re-read, **it does** — for the route
the finding describes. A worker that passes its command stage and then **stops**
is covered twice: `retire_dead_worker_holders` (#8069, panic) and
`retire_all_worker_holders` (#7092, generation teardown).

The unbounded route keeps the worker **alive**. `push_bounded` DROPS the command
at `MAX_PENDING_WORKER_COMMANDS`, and its return was ignored. Probe at the
parent:

```
PROBE-F4 queue_drops_delta=1      occupied_after_delete=true
PROBE-F4 dead=false               retire_dead_freed=0
PROBE-F4 occupied_after_sweep=true
```

Shared authority is already gone so no replay re-delivers, and no sweep selects
a live worker. The port is held for the life of the allocator — F4's "until
process restart", by a mechanism the finding does not describe.

## The repair

A dropped push runs `release_source_nat_allocation_for_worker` for that worker
id: byte-for-byte the call the worker makes when it processes the command, so
the holder mask empties on the same last-release rule and the port is returned
exactly once.

It cannot **over**-release: the command was dropped, so that worker will never
run this teardown itself, and `release_flow` no-ops unless
`live_by_flow[flow].translated` equals this exact tuple, so a worker whose own
`UpsertSynced` is still queued is untouched.

Only the **forward** key is repaired — the reverse companion's NAT teardown
returns immediately on `is_reverse`, so repairing its drop would call a no-op
and count a repair that did not happen. Measured: it made the counter read 2 for
one stranded reservation.

`session_delete_dropped_released` counts the repairs, wired through
`ProcessStatus` (additive, `serde(default)`; wire fixture regenerated, one
line). **Not repaired:** the same dropped command also costs that worker its
local session-table and BPF map teardown. Shared authority governs which
sessions exist and the process-wide session-map delete already ran, so the NAT
reservation is the part with no other owner.

- **#8126** (`e11433476`) moved this tally row from 17 to **18** to accommodate that same comment.

Source says 17, row expects 18, `shim_index_path_has_one_construction_and_one_lookup` fails again.

### Resolved at 17, keeping the reword

Both fixes were defensible, and the row-move carries the stronger argument *about the tally's design*: it counts comment and doc mentions **on purpose**, because a version that ignored them could be paid off by moving a binding into a macro-generated doc string, and moving a row for a legitimate mention is an action its own failure message explicitly describes.

But that argument is about whether the tally should count prose — not about whether *this* comment needed the token. It didn't; the sentence reads no worse without it. So the tighter bound is free and the row stays where the #5173 measurement put it.

### The collision is the lesson, not either fix

A red master invites more than one agent to fix it at once. "Green separately, red together" applies to two fixes for the **same** red at least as sharply as to two unrelated features — arguably more, because both authors are staring at the same failing test and neither expects a second repair to exist. Checking whether a red is *already being fixed* is now part of fixing it.

## PR #8131 — flow: enforce the tcp-session initial/closing/time-wait timeouts (#7342) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/7342-tcp-session-timeouts`

Enforces `security flow tcp-session initial-timeout`, `closing-timeout` and
`time-wait-timeout`, which #6539 recorded as accepted-only. Closes #7342.

## The split had to come first, and the issue was right about that

`session_timeout_ns` split a TCP close only two ways — RST onto the 2s abort
window, everything else onto ONE post-FIN window described in-source as "the full
30s TIME_WAIT-style window". Junos distinguishes CLOSING (after the first FIN)
from TIME_WAIT (after the close completes), so that single window had to stand
for both leaves. Mapping `closing-timeout` onto it was a guess, mapping
`time-wait-timeout` onto it was an equally arguable guess, and mapping both was
impossible.

The discriminator is a FIN per DIRECTION. Forward and reverse are independent
entries, so each knows whether its own direction FINed;
`propagate_tcp_state_to_companion` already mirrors close state between them and
now mirrors that bit as the companion's peer-side FIN. One FIN is CLOSING, two is
TIME_WAIT, and a RST short-circuits both — an abort has no close handshake to
complete, so the bits are gated on FIN specifically rather than on `is_closing`,
which is FIN **or** RST.

### The field that looks like the answer and is not

`SessionEntry.observed_tcp_flags` appears to give this for free, and building on
it would have been wrong in a way no test would have shown. `account_packet`
OR-folds BOTH directions' flags onto the FORWARD entry **on purpose** (#2749, so
NetFlow's `tcpControlBits` reports the whole flow), so `observed_tcp_flags &
TCP_FIN` is already true after ONE fin. A TIME_WAIT detector built on it puts
every half-closed session straight into TIME_WAIT — **and every single-FIN test
still passes.**

That is also why the load-bearing cell drives TWO FINs from opposite directions.
After the first, both halves are already `closing` (#4109 F17 pulls the companion
onto the close window), so a fixture that stops there shows CLOSING and proves
nothing: the pre-split code produces exactly that. The negative control is a
RETRANSMITTED FIN from one direction — an implementation that counted FINs rather
than tracking direction passes the first cell and puts half-closed flows into
TIME_WAIT whenever a FIN-ACK is lost.

## Why all three, in one PR

"Carry three, enforce two, flip the third later" is not available, and it is
closed **by design rather than by oversight**:
`TestTCPSessionTimeoutsHaveNoWireCarrier_6539` asserted the table and the wire
agree in BOTH directions, so an unenforced leaf that reaches the wire snapshot
reds it. #6539 deliberately made carrier and enforcement equivalent. One additive
wire bump is therefore also one protocol change, one cluster smoke and one
release note rather than two of each.

Branch: `docs/7455-forwarding-table-export-by-design`

Closes #7455

The issue offers two acceptances: implement a per-route forwarding-policy evaluation, or **close recording that xpf models forwarding-table export as a global ECMP toggle by design**. Taking the second — and correcting the `feature-gaps.md` entry that made the first look overdue.

That entry read **"Partial (parsed but not fully wired to FRR)"**, which describes an unfinished implementation. It is neither unfinished nor unwired.

### Measured before writing it down

- `resolveECMP` (`pkg/frr/config_render.go`) reduces the one named policy to **two booleans**: any term carrying `load-balance` sets `ecmpMaxPaths = 64`, and `consistent-hash` selects the hashing mode. No per-route evaluation, no composition rule — because there is no per-route forwarding-policy model to compose into.
- A list carrying more than one policy is **hard-rejected at commit** (`compiler_validate_strict_routing.go`, *"forwarding-table export declares N policies"*), with the error stating it renders as a single ECMP policy, and downgraded to a warning on the tolerant path per #1960.

So the contract is **enforced**, not merely documented, and an operator cannot silently receive chain semantics they did not get. "Nothing is broken today" is accurate.

### The note records why the shortcut is refused

Because it is what a future reader will reach for: OR-ing several policies' terms together would accept the Junos spelling while computing a **different answer than Junos**. That is worse than the current rejection precisely because it is silent — a loud refusal tells the operator their config means something else here; a quiet reinterpretation does not. The issue says the same thing and it deserves to survive the close.

## PR #8134 — nat: a synced import must not fall through to a sibling allocator (#6979 F1 half 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-08-31)

Branch: `fix/6979-f1-pass1-refusal-is-final`

Part of #6979 — **F1 half 1**, the last row.

## The ruling was right in direction and one level too high

You ruled: *a PASS 1 `Refused` returns without falling through to PASS 2; a
`NothingToReserve` must still fall through.* I implemented exactly that and
**re-ran the reproduction. It still reproduced.**

PASS 1 never returned `Refused`. `reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` iterates
its candidate set and, on a pool-owning rule whose allocator declines,
`continue`s to the **next rule**. Both overlapping rules are in PASS 1's *own*
filtered set — so A refused, B accepted, PASS 1 returned `Reserved`, and the
PASS1→PASS2 seam was never reached at all.

The fall-through is **inside the scan**, which is what F1's original text said:
*"it reserves on the first candidate whose allocator currently accepts; a
refusing rule falls through to the next."*

## Both levels ship, because each is inert without the other

- **`reserve_synced_on_first_pool_owner` takes `stop_at_first_owner`.** PASS 1
  passes `true`: its candidate set is already "rules the active could have
  matched" in snapshot order, which **is** the Junos specificity precedence
  (#4161) the active resolves with. So the first candidate whose pool owns the
  translated address *is* the active's rule, and its refusal is the answer.
  Walking on answers a different question — "who will accept?" — and books the
  reservation in an allocator the active never used.
- **PASS 1's `Refused` returns without falling through.** `NothingToReserve`
  still falls through, so interface-mode SNAT (#6751) and genuine config drift
  keep today's behaviour.

**PASS 2 is byte-identical** — the un-narrowed pre-#6211 fallback for an
unresolvable zone pair or drifted config, where "first rule whose pool contains
the address" is the only question available. Refusing there would reject every
import on a standby that has not yet applied a snapshot.

## The counter is bound, not assumed

Your fourth requirement. A coordinator-level cell drives the real import and
asserts `synced_import_reserve_refused_total` increments. If that path did not
reach the counter, the reasoning the whole trade rests on would be false while
every unit-level cell still passed.
