## PR #8511 — dataplane: report per-worker session-volume high water (#7919 instrument) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/7919-session-counter-query`

**Refs #7919.** Adds the measurement the issue has been missing, and nothing else. It does not fix #7919 — it makes the remaining question answerable.

## Why this, and why it is not the per-session query I was authorised to build

#7919 narrowed to one question no surface could answer: **does the owning worker's own session table hold the volume, or does it not?** The two answers point at different defects — a mirror losing a value it was given, versus accounting that never produced one — and every derivation on the issue so far, mine included, reasoned about the *mirror* rather than the source of truth behind it.

I was cleared to add a per-session control-socket verb. I built something smaller instead, because the axis turned out to be per-**worker**, not per-session:

> Measured on the reference cluster with three transit flows — `xpf_userspace_worker_session_table_entries` reads **6 on all six workers** (3 flows × fwd+rev) while the conntrack map holds **3** rows, against a **0-across-the-board baseline** with no transit.

So every worker holds a copy of every session, but only the worker whose packets land accounts for one — the replication types carry no counters field. *"Which workers' tables ever hold volume"* is therefore the whole discriminator, and it needs one number per worker, not a query per session. That is an added status field rather than a new verb, a new round-trip, and a new blocking wait.

The per-session verb stays available if this does not discriminate. **Ping me and I will build it** — I am not closing that option, just not spending it yet.

## What it does

`WorkerRuntimeCounters::session_volume_high_water` — the largest `fwd_packets + rev_packets` this worker has ever seen on a **forward** entry of its own table.

Sampled on the conntrack-mirror refresh walk, which **already** iterates the table on a budgeted slice: one compare per walked entry, **no new iteration**, nothing on the packet path. `refresh_bpf_conntrack_last_seen` now returns a `RefreshSliceOutcome` carrying the cursor it always returned plus the observed max; the cursor contract is unchanged and its existing budget test still binds it.

**A high-water, not a per-cycle max**, deliberately: the walk is budgeted, so one cycle may miss a busy session, and a per-cycle value would read 0 for a worker whose one busy session was simply not in that slice — a zero indistinguishable from *"never accounted"*, which is the exact confusion this exists to resolve.

## Absent is not zero

This is the part that makes it usable as evidence rather than decoration.

The field is **ADDED, never a redefinition** — in a rolling HA upgrade the two nodes run different binaries on one wire, so the new concept takes a new key. An old helper omits it; Go decodes it as `*uint64` and **nil means "this helper does not report it"**. A missing answer read as `0` would assert that a worker has never carried traffic — manufacturing exactly the evidence being gathered.

The helper also skips the key while the value is 0, so a genuine never-observed reading and an old helper are indistinguishable. That is correct: both mean *"no positive evidence of volume"*, and neither is a measurement.

## The consumer ships with it

A record nothing reads is not observability. `xpf_userspace_worker_session_volume_high_water` is emitted per worker and **only when the helper reported it** — no series is the honest encoding of "cannot answer".

## Tests

**Rust** — the slice reports the busiest walked session's volume, with a control that an *unaccounted* table reports 0 so the value cannot be an artefact of walking rather than of volume; plus the wire contract both directions, including an old payload without the key still decoding.

**Go** — the metric carries the value when reported; is **absent** when unreported, with a positive control that sibling worker series *are* emitted for the same status so the absence assertion cannot pass vacuously; and the decoder pins absent→nil with a control that the old payload really decoded.

### Mutations — 5, all killed, each by the intended cell

| # | mutation | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | delete the metric's **CALL SITE** (not its function) | `...IsEmittedWhenReported7919` |
| Q2 | emit unconditionally, so absent becomes a measured 0 | `...IsAbsentWhenUnreported7919` |
| Q3 | rename the JSON key | `...AbsentDecodesToNil7919` |
| Q4 | remove the Rust sampling | `a_refresh_slice_reports_the_largest_session_volume_it_walked_7919` |
| Q5 | drop `skip_serializing_if`, so a 0 reaches the wire | `an_unobserved_session_volume_high_water_stays_off_the_wire_7919` |

## PR #8513 — Warn at commit when a deny pattern cannot fire on a surface [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8189-commit-time-unenforceable-advisory`

## What lands

The unenforceable-deny finding moves from the **authorization path** (logged once per class when someone first makes a restricted call) to **commit output**, where every other #7172 advisory speaks.

Measured on the real commit path before this change, an unenforceable pattern and an enforceable one produced **identical** output — one warning each, the generic `recognized (custom RBAC)` line, no advisory of any kind. Nothing distinguished them.

## Why a registry and not a moved table

The three command tables live in `pkg/grpcapi`, which imports `pkg/config` and not the reverse. Relocating them is not available either: `showTextTopicCommand` is **derived** from `cmdtree.ShowTextTopicCommands()` (#8058), and `pkg/cmdtree` imports `pkg/config` too — so no package holding all three can be imported from `pkg/config`.

Inverting the dependency is the only direction available: a surface registers what it can produce, `pkg/config` reasons over whatever registered. It also makes the honest wording literally accurate — this **is** the registered command set.

`unenforceableDenyPatterns` now **delegates** to the shared predicate instead of keeping its own loop. Two implementations of "can this pattern ever fire" would be two things to keep in agreement, and a commit-time answer disagreeing with the runtime one is the confusion this advisory exists to remove.

The delegation is **scoped to grpcapi's own surface name**, not "any registered surface" — those are the same set only while gRPC is the sole registrant, and an unscoped check would quietly start answering a different question the moment a second appears.

## Every ambiguous case resolves to silence

This is the load-bearing decision, and it follows from the failure direction. If a command is reachable but missing from a table, a pattern matching only it is reported unenforceable — telling the operator **at commit** that a restriction which actually works does nothing. They then remove it or broaden it, and both are worse than the silence being replaced. Moving the finding into commit output *raises* the cost of it being wrong.

So: **no registered surface, or a surface reporting zero commands, emits nothing.** An empty set makes every pattern vacuously unmatched, which would fire the advisory on every config in the field.

## The wording is scoped to what the guards actually bind

It says **"the REGISTERED command set"**, never "the commands this surface can present".

Each of the three tables *is* guarded against its own source in **both** directions. What is **not** guarded is server-table vs client (`cmd/cli/show.go`) — #8058's subject, single-sourced for one of three: `showTextTopicCommand` is derived from `cmdtree`, while `methodCanonicalCommand` and `systemActionVerbCommand` are still hand-maintained literals. The narrower phrase is true of what is checked; the wider one would claim the correspondence nothing checks.

## No fourth drift guard — and that is deliberate

#8189 asks for one, on the premise that *"only the first one currently has a guard"*. **That is false at `origin/master`.** Both named tests carry the reverse direction, and say so in their own comments:

```
authz_command_table_topics_7172_test.go:162  "...does not serve — a stale entry hides an unmapped real verb"
authz_command_table_7172_test.go:109         "Stale direction: an entry for a method that is no longer served."
```

A fourth guard would be a second list of the same fact, and two lists of one fact drift apart. The correction is posted on the issue.

## Validation

`go build ./...`, `go vet`, and the `pkg/config` (97s) + `pkg/grpcapi` (14s) suites green at the rebased head. Both scope halves clean — five files, all mine.

`go test ./...` reports one failure, **`pkg/memlockcensus/TestMemlockCensusMatchesTheTree`, which is PRE-EXISTING and not from this branch.** Verified by running that package on a clean detached worktree at `origin/master` `d3fefa473` with none of these changes present: identical failure, same two rows. It appears to be self-referential — the census flags `census_8371_test.go`'s own `TestMemlockGuardsAreInertHere` and `scanTree` as unregistered memlock-gated guards — and it arrived with #8512, which merged shortly before this branch rebased. Flagged separately; master is currently red on it.

## PR #8514 — test: stop the memlock census matching its own scanner [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8371-census-self-match`

**Master is red from #8512 and this fixes it.** Reproduced on a clean worktree at
`origin/master`:

```
--- FAIL: TestMemlockCensusMatchesTheTree
    #8371: 2 memlock-gated guard(s) exist in the tree but are NOT in the registry:
      pkg/memlockcensus/census_8371_test.go -> TestMemlockGuardsAreInertHere
      pkg/memlockcensus/census_8371_test.go -> scanTree
```

The scanner was censusing itself. Neither row is a guard whose protection is
conditional — the first **calls** `rlimit.RemoveMemlock` to report whether the
privilege exists, the second **greps for the literal**.

## Why the pre-merge suite was green, which is the part worth keeping

`git grep` reads **tracked** files only, and `census_8371_test.go` was still
untracked when `go test ./...` ran in the authoring worktree. **The scanner could
not see itself until the commit landed.**

So the green was real, and it was measuring a tree that stopped existing the
moment the file entered the index. A pre-merge verdict that cannot hold
post-merge, from an instrument whose input is the index rather than the working
tree.

**Generalises:** a scanner reading `git grep`, `git ls-files`, or any
index-backed source must be exercised against a tree where its own files are
**committed**. Run on a dirty worktree, it measures a different population than
CI will.

## The exclusion is pinned in both directions

An exclusion is a hole, and a hole widened by one character stops the census
seeing an entire package — which would leave it trivially satisfied and reading
exactly like a clean tree. `TestTheScannerExcludesItselfAndOnlyItself` asserts:

- the constant names a file that **exists** — an exclusion naming a missing path
  excludes nothing and would go unnoticed;
- it is a single `_test.go` file, not a prefix or directory;
- the scan still finds the tree's guards afterwards;
- no censused row is the scanner itself.

Widening the constant to the directory **reds 2 cells**.

## PR #8516 — afxdp: re-derive the synced reverse companion at reconcile replay (#7209 item 1) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `work/7209-barrier-offlock`

`Refs #7209` — **does not close it.** Both acceptance cells stay
`#[ignore]`d and `sync_session` is still under the snapshot-wide mutex.
This is item 1, shape (ii), which unblocks two of the four blocking calls
scope item 2 wants off that mutex.

## The defect

`synthesized_synced_reverse_entry` has exactly one early return — on
`is_reverse`. There is **no forwarding-dependent `None` arm**, so an import
taken while `Coordinator.forwarding` cannot resolve the reply path does not
degrade gracefully: it builds a companion carrying `NoRoute`, ifindex 0 and
owner RG 0, publishes it into all four shared surfaces, and into the kernel
session map whenever the local-replace guard holds.

Nothing re-derived it. The replay republished `entry.decision` verbatim, and
the only mechanism that ever rebuilt a companion was
`prewarm_reverse_synced_sessions_for_owner_rgs` at RG **activation** — which
a mid-life `apply_snapshot` on an already-active node never reaches. The
wrong reply-path row was permanent for any node that did not subsequently
fail over.

Reachable today on a standby taking bulk sync before its first apply, where
activation repairs it before it matters. It becomes permanent the moment a
reconcile releases the lock — which is why it is item 2's prerequisite.

## The fix, and why the replay is the right place

`reconcile` reaches the replay **after** `snapshot::apply_snapshot` has
assigned `coord.forwarding = new_forwarding`, so the table read there is the
new generation's rather than the emptied one `stop_inner` left. That
ordering is what makes the replay a repair point at all, and it is the same
shape #8171 established for the entries themselves.

## The shape was chosen on measurement, not taste

#7209 left item 1 open between *refuse the companion* and *defer to the
replay*. Implemented as mutations against the full binary suite:

| shape | cells red |
|---|---|
| (i) refuse when the table cannot resolve it | **8** — incl. six pre-existing |
| (ii) re-derive at replay | **1** |

Shape (i)'s extra reds are structural: `synced_import_cap_for`'s `2x` is
load-bearing **because** the companion is returned for every non-reverse
import, so the cap counts ENTRIES at two per admitted forward. Refusing
changes that accounting.

symlink at `traceLogDir` pointing to a directory made it return nil — and the
`O_NOFOLLOW` open then applied to `<target>/<name>`, a real file at the
redirected location rather than a symlink, so it passed too. Root-written flow
telemetry landed in the attacker-chosen directory **with both guards reporting
success**.

Six prior archived reviews marked this confinement "VERIFIED SAFE", and each of
them checked the file.

## Severity, stated so it is not re-filed higher

**Defence in depth, not a live escape.** Planting the symlink needs write access
to `/var/log`, which is `0755` and root-owned; the CLI user supplies only the
*trigger*. Those are two capabilities held by two parties, and the review that
surfaced this conflated them. What the fix buys is converting *"someone already
had write access to /var/log"* from a full trace-redirection primitive into a
failed open.

A **dangling** symlink already failed (`MkdirAll: file exists`), so the case this
closes is specifically a symlink to an *existing* directory — which is what the
fixture builds.

The stat fails closed on any error that is not "absent": an `EACCES` here means
we cannot establish what the path is, and `MkdirAll` would be deciding that for
us.

## The mutation escape is the part worth reading

Four mutations, all killed — but the two that matter **escaped first**, and the
reason was in the test, not the code.

`t.TempDir()` embeds the **subtest name** in its path, the path lands in the
error string, and the subtest is named *"a symlink to an existing directory is
refused"*. So `strings.Contains(err.Error(), "symlink")` was satisfied by the
test's **own name**. Removing the symlink branch entirely still passed, because
the fallback *"not a directory"* error carried the word in its path.

The assertion now keys on `"is a symlink;"` — a phrase containing a space and a
semicolon, which cannot appear in a temp path.

**General form: an assertion on a bare word can be satisfied by the fixture's own
scaffolding.** A fixture that supplies the value the assertion looks for tests
nothing.

## The premise, verified from the code first

The issue names three commands that "should canonicalize but don't". Measured at
`origin/master a5f2f94a4`, with resolving controls in the SAME run so the absence
result is not vacuous:

| command | `Canonicalize` at master | dispatcher actually serves it? | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `show log messages` | `CanonicalUnknown` | **yes** — `showDaemonLog` reads `/var/log/<name>` for a non-numeric first arg | valid defect |
| `show configuration security zones` | `CanonicalUnknown` | **yes** — `cli_show.go` `case "configuration":` joins every remaining word into the config path | valid defect |
| `clear security flow session all` | `CanonicalUnknown` | **no** | **not a defect — see below** |
| *controls:* `show route 10.0.0.0/8`, `show security policies`, `show version` | `CanonicalOK` | — | instrument works |

**Two of the three are real.** And the class is wider than the issue's sample:
**every** `show configuration <stanza> <deeper>` fails — all 16 stanza children,
at more than one depth — and so does **`show log 50`**, the `[N]` form that
node's own `Desc` string advertises.

## Why this is a security bug, not a cosmetic one

`Canonicalize`'s result is not advisory. `evaluateCommandRegex` (`pkg/cli`) fails
closed on anything but `CanonicalOK`, so a legal-but-unresolvable command is
**refused to every login class carrying `allow-commands` / `deny-commands`** —
while an unrestricted class runs it fine. The operator sees a permission error
for a correctly spelled, fully implemented command.

`pkg/cmdtree/README.md` already predicted this exact failure:

> Over-rejection is the risk to watch when touching this, because a caller MUST
> fail closed on anything other than `CanonicalOK`: refusing too much REFUSES a
> lawful command for every operator with a restricted class.

#8304 is that warning coming true.

## The third command is not a defect, and modelling it would be the mirror bug

`clear security flow session all` **is refused by the box.**
`parseClearSessionFilter` delegates to `parseSessionFilterMode(args, true)`
(`pkg/cli/session_filter.go`); its token switch has `case "zone"`, `"protocol"`,
`"source-prefix"` … and **no `all` arm**. The `default:` at `:242` sets
`unknown session filter "all"`, and `hasFilter()` (`:356`) counts
`parseErr != nil` as its **first** term — so the parse error never falls through
to a clear-all.

The tree refusing it is the tree **agreeing with the dispatcher**. Marking it
would assert a command that does not exist — the mirror defect of #8304, and
exactly what #8057's canonicalize-to-self check exists to catch. A test pins it
unresolved so a later "finish the issue" pass cannot quietly add it.

## PR #8520 — firewall: reject a valueless `from` leaf in a filter term [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8480-valueless-from`

Closes #8480

`set firewall family inet filter F term T from protocol` — value omitted — parses
to `Keys=["protocol"]` with no tail and no children. `firewallMatchValues` skips
`""` and returns an empty slice, so `term.Protocols` is empty, and the term reads
an empty match set as **match-ANY** rather than as an error. A stateless
first-line filter widens: `then discard` discards every protocol, `then accept`
opens every protocol.

Security policies have rejected this since #6526 and NAT since #8430. **#8430's
title covers "NAT `match` AND firewall `from`" and only the NAT half shipped** —
this is its unshipped remainder, a consistency gap in an area already hardened
twice.

## Scope is the whole risk, because this gate's failure mode is over-reach

Not every `from` leaf is value-bearing:

| leaf | why it must NOT be flagged |
|---|---|
| `is-fragment` | a presence-only **flag** — `compileFirewall` sets `term.IsFragment = true` and reads no values. The likeliest over-reach, precisely because it *looks* valueless. |
| `flexible-match-range` | carries its operands in **children**, with their own `match-start` / `byte-offset` grammar |

Both have their own control. The gate reads through `firewallMatchValues` — the
same helper `compileFirewall` uses — so gate and compiler cannot disagree about
which leaves carry semantics in their operands.

A leaf written more than once is valueless only if **every** occurrence is: Junos
merges duplicate blocks, so `from { protocol; }` beside `from { protocol tcp; }`
is constrained.

Strict rejects at commit; lenient warns so an already-persisted config still
**boots** (#1960). It walks the AST rather than the compiled `*Config` because
the defect is the *absence* of values — afterwards a valueless leaf and an
omitted one are byte-identical empty slices.

## Validation — the two escapes are the instructive part

| mutation | |
|---|---|
| gate never fires | killed |
| `is-fragment` added to the value set | killed — the over-reach control |
| last-occurrence-wins duplicate handling | killed, **after a fixture fix** |
| prefix-list read via the general helper | **equivalent mutant — branch removed** |

**The duplicate mutation escaped** because the fixture tested only
`protocol; protocol tcp;` — an order that *ends* on the valued occurrence, so
last-occurrence-wins passes either way. The reverse order discriminates; its
absence made the case a fixture that varies the right axis and samples only the
passing point.

## PR #8521 — dataplane: add a read-only per-session counter query (#7919 instrument) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/7919-session-counter-verb`

**Refs #7919.** Adds the read-only per-session counter query — the instrument that separates the two remaining explanations. It does not fix #7919; it makes the question answerable.

## Why a verb, after I argued against one

I previously talked the reviewer out of this in favour of a per-worker aggregate (#8511, merged). That aggregate was the right *axis* and the wrong *instrument*, and building it is what proved so: `session_volume_high_water` is **monotonic over the process lifetime**, so a large value on a worker whose current flow reads 0 may be residue from an earlier flow that worker owned. **Axis and attribution are different properties.** Only a per-session read supplies the second.

Two other candidates were ruled out before adding wire surface:

- **The shared session table can't** — `SyncedSessionEntry` has no counters field. Positive control: `Packets` occurs **0** times in `protocol_ha.go` against **8** and **12** in two sibling files, so the search term is right and the field is genuinely missing.
- **`export_idle_leases` isn't a template** — it returns *data* rather than deltas, but only because idle leases aren't worker-owned. It's a near-miss that would have been adopted by analogy and quietly answered a different question.

## What it does

`session_counters` takes one 5-tuple and reports what **each** worker's own table holds. Broadcast, because every worker holds a copy of every session (measured: `session_table_entries` reads 6 on all six workers for three flows) while only the worker whose packets land accounts for one.

| condition | how |
|---|---|
| **ADD, never redefine** | one new request key, one new response key. The **wire-invariant golden confirms it** rather than my asserting it: the diff is a single added `"session_counter_query": null`, nothing renamed or removed. The response and status fields don't appear in the default specimen at all — both are skipped while empty. |
| **Read-only** | `counters_with_replica_flag` looks the key up without touching the table. Nothing installs, refreshes or expires. |
| **Unsupported ≠ zero** | an older helper's `unknown request type <verb>` maps to `ErrSessionCountersUnsupported`, never to an empty result. |
| **Not hot-path, not periodic** | diagnostic-triggered only; two-phase like `kick_owner_rg_export` (#2962), with the bounded 3 s wait **outside** the `ServerState` lock. |

**The sequence is the ack.** A worker writes its answer fields, then its sequence with `Release`; the reader loads the sequence with `Acquire` before reading the answers. There is no second completion flag that could disagree with it.

## Three states, and none may collapse

- `answered = false` — did not reply before the deadline. **Not an answer.**
- `answered && !found` — replied: it does not hold this session.
- `answered && found` — holds it; counters are its copy's, and `replica` says whether that copy is a peer-synced origin.

A row flattening these into "counters or zero" would answer neither question the verb exists to separate. `replica` is carried because **a replica reporting volume would falsify the premise the whole investigation rests on** — so the answer carries what it would take to notice.

## Why "unsupported ≠ zero" is the load-bearing part

In a rolling upgrade the two nodes run different binaries on one wire, so an old helper refusing this verb is **normal operation**, not a test path. Returning `nil, nil` there would tell the caller *no worker holds this session* — one of the two states the query exists to distinguish. **The failure would look exactly like a finding.**

The Go match is against wording produced by binaries **already released**, whose text cannot be changed retroactively — so it's a wire contract in everything but name, and the helper's exact wording is **pinned on the Rust side** so a reword breaks a test instead of silently downgrading "ask a newer helper" to a generic error.

The classification is **extracted** into `sessionCountersFromResponse` / `isUnknownVerbError`, because the request path has no test seam and an inline choice cannot be bound.

## Mutations — 6, all killed, attribution checked

| # | mutation | killed by |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | predicate matches **nothing** | `TestUnsupportedVerbIsAnErrorNotAnEmptyResult7919` |
| R6 | predicate matches **everything** | `TestAnExecutionFailureIsNotReportedAsUnsupported7919` |
| R2 | return `nil, nil` for unsupported | the unsupported cell |
| R3 | reword the helper's refusal | the wording pin |
| R4 | drop the missing-query refusal | the refusal cell |
| R5 | zero the accessor's counters | the accessor cell |

## PR #8522 — api: export each management listener's state, address and surface [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8195-grpc-listener-visibility`

Closes #8195

The gRPC management listener's state has exactly one consumer,
`show system services` — and that is reached **over the gRPC listener**. When it
fails, the surface that would report the failure is the surface that is down.
That circularity is what this issue is about, and it is why the fix is a metric
scraped over the **separate HTTP listener** rather than another CLI verb.

## Correction to the issue, which shrinks it

The body says the state is on neither REST nor Prometheus. A gauge already
exists: `xpf_management_listener_down`, landed in `ffddaa69d` on 2026-08-27 —
**four days before the issue was filed** — plumbed through a `func() bool` seam
rather than via `sysservices`, which is presumably why the original grep missed
it.

It does **not** satisfy the acceptance, and this is not a "you already have it"
note:

| gap | why it matters |
|---|---|
| bare 0/1, **no address** | an operator cannot tell *which* endpoint failed to bind — the first question asked |
| **HTTP leg only** (`mgmtListenerDown` → `effectiveHTTPListener`) | the gRPC listener is absent entirely |
| **three states collapsed into two** | `StateDisabled` — deliberately turned off — is indistinguishable from `StateListening` at 0 |

So `xpf_management_listener_down` is left **exactly as it is** (dashboards and
alerts reference it) and `xpf_management_listener_state` **adds** what it cannot
express. Add, never redefine.

## Two design choices that carry the weight

**Same snapshot as the CLI.** It is emitted from the `sysservices.Listeners`
snapshot `show system services` renders — deliberately, so the metric and the CLI
cannot disagree about a listener's state. That is the one-renderer-fixed-the-
other-forgotten shape #8258 tracks and #8183 was an instance of.

**Every state gets a series, not only the current one.** A collector emitting
just the active state would make an alert on `state{state="failed"} == 1`
silently un-evaluable while the listener is healthy — the series would not exist,
and an **absent series is indistinguishable from a healthy one** at the point an
alert reads it.

The seam is optional and emits **nothing** when unwired: a zero-value
`Listeners` renders both legs as `StateDisabled`, which is a *claim* (the
operator turned them off) rather than the truth (we do not know), and it reads as
healthy. Same absent-vs-zero doctrine as the #6828 sibling gauges.

## PR #8523 — test(worker): give worker_loop_setup its first test caller [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `test/worker-setup-harness`

`Refs #7209` — the prerequisite that was hiding behind a one-line change.
**No production diff**; this lands the test substrate only.

## `worker_loop_setup` had no test callers. At all.

`worker_loop` and `worker_loop_setup` were reachable only from
`reconcile/bringup.rs`, and the spawn seams that exercise the #5143
readiness barrier substitute **stub threads** rather than the real body.
Verified with a positive control: worker-level fixtures do exist, but they
construct a `BindingWorker` directly and bypass setup entirely.

The consequence is not thin coverage — it is coverage that **cannot fail**.
Every cell over worker setup was green *by construction*.

**Measured on the branch that prompted this:** deleting a load-bearing line
from `worker_loop_setup` passed the **entire suite — 5214 cells, zero
failures** — because nothing ran it. A guard that cannot reach the mechanism
it names is not a guard on it.

## Two design constraints, both forced rather than chosen

* **The harness runs on its own thread.** `worker_loop_setup` opens with
  `pin_current_thread(worker_id)`; pinning a cargo test thread would outlive
  the cell and follow whatever test that thread is next reused for. It also
  matches production, where setup always runs on a freshly spawned worker.
* **It returns observations, not the setup.** `WorkerLoopSetup` owns an
  `Rc<WorkerUmemInner>` and is therefore not `Send`, so it cannot cross the
  thread boundary. The facts a cell wants are reduced inside the closure.

## The positive control is the point

A harness that ran setup but returned *before* the bind partition would look
exactly like coverage while testing nothing — the same failure mode the stub
seams already have. So the first cell asserts something **only the real body
produces**: an explicit per-slot `BindingSetupFailure` for a plan whose map
fds are all `-1`. If it ever goes empty, the harness stopped reaching the
bind and everything built on it is vacuous.

The second cell is its complement, and it exists because the first has a way
to pass for the wrong reason: a body pushing a failure **unconditionally**
would satisfy it. With no plans to bind, setup must report neither a binding
nor a failure.

## PR #8525 — afxdp: saturate the two computed IP length casts in TCP segmentation [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8321-saturate-seg-len`

#8321 findings 19 and 20: the two bare `as u16` casts on computed IP length fields in the TCP segmentation path.

**Reachability — the question the issue said was next, now answered.** `total_ip_len <= mtu` identically (chunk_len is bounded by `segment_payload_max = mtu - headers`). The config layer places no upper bound on mtu (`ValidateIntegerMin(1)`, and its own valueDesc defers to the kernel), which is what made these look reachable. But the mtu reaching the dataplane is **read back from the kernel** — `buildLinkSnapshot` sets it from `link.Attrs().MTU` — so it is whatever the driver accepted, far below 65535 on every interface this dataplane forwards on. Findings 19/20 are mechanism-real and consequence-refuted, the same shape as finding 17.

**The casts change anyway, for an independent reason.** `saturate_len16` already exists with its own test, and these were the only two computed-length casts not using it. A wrap forges a plausible small length; a saturation is wrong on the wire but never mistakable for valid. Uniform costs nothing on any reachable input, and the derivation is recorded in the code so nobody re-derives it a fourth time.

The cell binds the helper at the boundary rather than driving the segmenter, and says why: a segmenter-driven cell could only exercise lengths the MTU permits, so it would pass identically against a bare cast. A control asserts every in-range length passes through byte-identical.

Validation: build clean, new cell passes, 5229 other cells unaffected.

## PR #8528 — harness: let the mouse-latency gate FAIL on a concentrated tail [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8277-concentrated-tail`

#8277. The degenerate-coroutine validity rule is a **fairness** predicate used as a **validity** predicate, which made the gate incapable of returning FAIL on the one shape it exists to detect.

When the tail is *concentrated* — a minority of flows starved while the rest are fine — the starved flows necessarily complete far fewer transactions, so `min < 0.5 * median` fires on exactly the reps that demonstrate the phenomenon. On master `d8a876042` a cell whose loaded p99.9 was 740–1349 ms against a 6.66 ms idle baseline (**111×–202× against a 2.0 gate**) reported `INSUFFICIENT-DATA`, 0 of 15 valid. A *uniform* slowdown still failed correctly — the median moves with the min — so only the concentrated shape was unreachable.

## A narrowing, not a deletion

The rule was written against a real client-side artifact, and deleting it would re-admit that. So the distinction comes from data the run already emits — `attribute_starvation` takes the largest of the three per-coroutine phase maxima:

| dominant phase | meaning | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `read_us` | the echo path — the thing being measured | **RESULT**, rep admitted |
| `sleep_overshoot_us` | timer wake delay in the probe's own loop | client-side, still invalid |
| `drain_us` | local socket backpressure | client-side, still invalid |

Threshold-free on purpose: an arbitrary cutoff is what put this rule in the position of invalidating its own phenomenon, and the separation is two orders of magnitude, not a judgement call.

A rep is admitted only when **every** starved coroutine is echo-attributable — one client-side or unattributable coroutine invalidates it. `coroutine_diagnostics` has **no default**, so a caller that cannot supply it must choose the pre-#8277 behaviour explicitly; making it required broke 11 call sites loudly, which is the point.

## Tests

Every fixture shares one `attempts_per_coroutine` and varies **only the attribution** — the acceptance criterion, and the only shape that can tell the versions apart. Five mutations, all killed:

| mutation | killed |
|---|---|
| unconditional invalidation (old behaviour) | the phenomenon cell |
| delete the rule | 4 client-side/unattributable cells **+ the pre-existing** `test_degenerate_coroutine_min_attempts` |
| drop the unattributable arm | 3 cells |
| wrong phase named server-side | 4 cells, both directions |
| rename the probe.json key format | the schema pin |

**That last one was found by mutation.** Routing the key names through `phase_max_key` moved producer and consumer together, so every behavioural cell stayed green while `probe.json` silently emitted different names — single-sourcing working internally and losing a guarantee externally. The three names are cited in #8277's acceptance and appear in `docs/log/`, so they are now pinned as literals in the test while staying single-sourced in the code.

## Docs

`docs/fairness-regimes.md` gains the section the issue asks for: which tail shapes the gate can and cannot verdict on, how the two starvation causes are separated, and what this does **not** fix — #8259's attribution defect (neither subsumes the other), the `error_rate >= 0.01` rule (same shape, left alone deliberately, with the reason), and the historical `INSUFFICIENT-DATA` cells that are candidate masked FAILs.

**Not cluster-validated.** This changes a pure decision function and its unit tests; a live re-measurement of the surplus fixture is the separate confirmation the issue wants. 36 cells green (27 pre-existing, 9 new).

Closes #8277

## PR #8529 — afxdp: parse the DECAPPED frame in both ICMP-error arms [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8271-icmp-decap-frame`

#8271. `poll_binding_process_descriptor` substitutes an owned decapped inner frame at `stage_native_gre_decap` and rebinds `meta` to it. Two arms then **classified** on `packet_frame` (correctly, at the inner `meta.l4_offset`) and handed their helper `raw_frame` + `desc` — the still-encapsulated **outer** frame — with the **inner** meta. The helper parsed outer bytes at inner offsets.

This is the #1885/#1902 class, not a novel reading: two sibling arms of the same function were fixed for the identical pairing and carry comments stating the rule verbatim. These two were never brought along, and they are reachable on exactly the input those fixes were about.

Both helpers now take the frame they **parse**. `desc` stays the outer descriptor in both — that use (queue/recycle the original UMEM frame) was always correct.

## The wrapper is deleted, not left unused

`try_embedded_icmp_nat_match` existed only to slice the UMEM frame at `desc.addr`/`desc.len` and call its `_from_frame` twin. Its single behaviour was to pair whatever frame `desc` points at with whatever `meta` it was handed, and after the fix it had zero callers. Removing it removes the ability to make the mistake; every caller must now name the frame it means.

## Two cells, because there are two defects — measured, not assumed

With arm 2 fixed and **arm 1 reverted, the entire 5230-cell suite was green** — including arm 2's own new cell. One cell proves one arm. Reverting either arm now reds exactly its own cell and no other:

| revert | red |
|---|---|
| arm 2 (embedded ICMP) | `gre_decapped_embedded_icmp_reversal_reads_the_inner_frame_8271` only |
| arm 1 (NAT64) | `gre_decapped_nat64_icmp_error_reads_the_inner_frame_8271` only |

**The fixtures use a VLAN-tagged underlay deliberately**, which the issue asks for by name. On an untagged underlay the mis-paired read lands on the outer L3 header — a valid version nibble — so the parse proceeds and fails as an ordinary miss. The 4-byte dot1q tag is what turns the same defect into a misaligned slice, so an untagged fixture would pass under the defect for the wrong reason.

**The fail-on-revert result is also the control that the fixtures reach decap.** If the tunnel endpoint did not match the frame's outer destination, `stage_native_gre_decap` would never fire, `packet_frame` would equal `raw_frame`, and both cells would pass against both versions — silently degrading into duplicates of the #5690/#6472 originals they are adapted from. They go red on revert, so decap is firing.

Both arms were verified live at `origin/master` before anything changed; the issue recorded them at `e0748d0c2` and master has moved.

## Scope

Reachability is narrower than #1885's. Arm 2 needs native GRE decap AND an ICMP-error inner AND `allow-embedded-icmp`. Arm 1 needs decap AND an ICMP-error inner AND a configured NAT64 prefix — it is otherwise **ungated**, so its reachability is the wider of the two.

Validation: **5226 cells green** (5224 before + 2 new), build clean. `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/README.md` updated — it named the deleted function.

One note: `cargo clippy` fails on `umem/mmap.rs:208` ("mutable borrow from immutable inputs"). That is **pre-existing on master** — confirmed by running clippy on a clean `origin/master` worktree — and in a file this change does not touch (0 lines of diff). Not addressed here.

Closes #8271

## PR #8530 — config: reject a typo under security flow {tcp,udp,icmp}-session [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8296-flow-closed-world`

## Measured before and after, through `configstore.CheckText`

| authored under `security { flow { … } }` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `aging { early-aegout 10; }` (typo) | REJECTED | REJECTED |
| `tcp-session { rst-invalidate-sesion; }` (typo) | **ACCEPTED** | **REJECTED** |
| `tcp-session { inital-timeout 10; }` (typo) | **ACCEPTED** | **REJECTED** |
| `udp-session { timout 30; }` (typo) | **ACCEPTED** | **REJECTED** |
| `icmp-session { timout 30; }` (typo) | **ACCEPTED** | **REJECTED** |
| every documented valid keyword | ACCEPTED | ACCEPTED |
| `tcp-session { strict-syn-check; }` | ACCEPTED (silently inert) | ACCEPTED **+ advisory** |
| `flooby { wibble 42; }` under `security{}` | ACCEPTED | ACCEPTED *(deliberate)* |

## Why the typo matters, and why the fail direction decides it

The render-back is the trap: `show configuration` is how an operator confirms a
commit took, and it confirms the **text was stored**, not that anything consumes
it. What the typo then does is not uniform:

- `rst-invalidate-sesion` — a **hardening** flag. The typo silently drops a
  protection the operator explicitly asked for. **Fail-open.**
- `timout` / `inital-timeout` — the session falls back to the **default**, which
  is usually **longer** than the value being tightened.
- `no-syn-check`, `no-sequence-check` — relaxations, so a typo fails **safe**.
  Reasoning from those makes the class look benign; they are the wrong examples.

`security flow aging` has rejected its unknown options since #4313. These three
siblings are the same shape and were left open — a partial hardening that
stopped, not a compatibility posture.

## MODEL BEFORE FLIP — the measurement changed the scope

The obvious change is "flip `closedWorld` on the three subtrees". **That is
unsafe as stated**, and the audit is what caught it.

`schemaNode.closedWorld`'s own contract permits a flip only once a subtree is
**leaf-complete**, "otherwise it false-rejects a valid-but-not-yet-modeled
config" — and it names the #2078/#4231 accept-with-advisory knobs as exactly
what a blanket flip breaks.

`security flow tcp-session strict-syn-check` **is** such a knob, documented in
`docs/feature-gaps.md`. It was modelled by **nothing**: absent from `setSchema`,
absent from the compiler, and — contrary to that doc's claim that *"Commit emits
an accepted-only advisory"* — carrying no advisory either. Verified with a
**count**, not a truncated listing: the only Go file mentioning it was a scratch
test I had just written.

So a real Junos keyword committed clean, rendered back, and reached no consumer
— **this issue's own defect, for a keyword the tree documents as supported.**
Flipping `tcp-session` first would have rejected it.

## PR #8531 — config: census the SECOND route by which a leaf redacts [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8258-secret-coercions`

#8258 starting point 3 — and the hole it found in starting point 1, which landed an hour ago in #8527.

## Measured first: point 3 was mostly closed already

All ten custom `MarshalJSON` implementations in `pkg/config` were classified. **Eight** transform by calling `RedactURL`/`redactURLSlice` and are already covered by #8104's URL census. **One** (`SNMPConfig`) is a field-shape alias with no value transform. **One** is covered by nothing, and it is the interesting one.

`SNMPCommunity.Name` is declared `string`. It becomes a `Secret` only inside `MarshalJSON`/`MarshalYAML`:

```go
return json.Marshal(alias{Name: Secret(c.Name), ...})
```

So the typed route redacts it exactly as if the field were declared `Secret` — and **#8527's reflection census cannot see it**, because at the type level it is a plain string. The SNMP v1/v2c community string is the v1/v2c authenticator, so this is not an obscure corner.

## The error, stated plainly

#8527's commit argued reflection beats a source scan because "the population is a TYPE, so reflection enumerates it exactly. No wrapper can hide from it." Reflection is exact about the question it answers; the error was believing that question was the whole population. It is the identical trap #8104's own census comment warns about, arriving from the other direction:

> defining a set as "things that call X" is a CLAIM that X is the only route to the behaviour.

Defining a set as "things whose **type** is X" is the same claim. A conversion is a route the type does not record. I quoted that warning in #8527 and then walked into it.

## The fix

A second census enumerates the conversion route with `go/ast` rather than a regex — `Secret(x.F)` inside a method is a syntactic fact, so it is extracted rather than pattern-matched — and feeds the **same** `astLeafForSecretField` map, so a leaf enrolled by either route gets the same behavioural verdict. The reflection census's reverse check now runs against the **union**; it fired on the new row when the second route was added, which is that check correctly measuring the wrong population.

## The result: still no divergence

`snmp community <name>` **is** redacted on the AST route (`secretIndices` masks the token after `community` under an `snmp` parent). The surfaces agree here too. What changed is that the agreement is now asserted for a leaf no instrument could previously see.

## Sensitivity — four mutations, all killed, each aimed

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| drop the `snmp` ancestor gate from `secretIndices` | kills **exactly** the `SNMPCommunity.Name` behavioural row — proves the new row guards a real redaction |
| break the `go/ast` scan | trips the known-instance guard (the assertion #8527 lacked, and why it shipped blind) |
| remove the mapping row | coercion census fails by name |
| drop the union | reverse check fails by name |

The scan also carries a positive control on itself: fewer than 20 non-test files parsed means it did not read this package, and everything downstream would pass vacuously.

`docs/architecture.md` corrected — its #8258 bullet, written an hour ago, claimed reflection was the population. True when written, incomplete by the time this landed.

Validation: `pkg/config` green (100s), 26 cells across the three census tests, gofmt/vet clean on the new files. (`gofmt -l pkg/config/` flags six other files; all pre-existing on master and untouched here.)

Addresses #8258 starting point 3. Point 2 — drop/permit verdicts across the shim and the userspace helper, the #6534 family — remains, and the issue stays open for it.

## PR #8532 — test: build the session key and its probe by their two production routes (#8262) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `test/8262-key-route-harness`

**Closes #8262.**

## The gap, verified from the code

`cached_entry()` sets `key: test_key()`; the session installs from `entry_for_session.key`; the probe uses `flow.forward_key`, defaulting to `test_key()`. **Both operands of the comparison came from one literal**, so they agreed by construction. That harness could vary every other axis — TX headroom, admission, mirror sampling, validation state — and never touch the axis a key-mismatch bug lives on. Invisible to review, because the tests around it are real and passing.

## What it does now

The key comes from the **frame**: `parse_session_flow_from_bytes`, then the poll loop's own post-parse mutation (`forward_key.routing_domain` from `ingress_routing_domain`). Nothing is copied out of `test_key()` into the probe.

Two seams were missing:

- **`StageSeed::install_key`** — the key the session installs under, when it must differ from the cached entry's. Without it the operands cannot diverge at all.
- **`StageRun::session_lookup_miss_counts`** — the harness computed `lookup_miss_counts()` nowhere, so the counters that distinguish "probe key ≠ installed key" from every other miss were unreadable from a test.

Two cells, because a harness that can only show agreement proves nothing about its own power: a **control** asserting the routes agree (whole `(0,0,0)` tuple, so it is a real baseline) and a **red cell** installing under one route's key and probing with the other's.

## Proof it can fail — the only thing separating it from the old harness

Three mutations, all red:

| # | mutation | result |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | **revert the `install_key` seam — i.e. restore the pre-#8262 harness** | **red cell FAILS** |
| S2 | route helper stops applying the poll-loop mutation | both cells fail on preconditions |
| S3 | fixture loses its routing domain, so the mutation is a no-op | both cells fail |

**S1 is the issue's claim demonstrated rather than argued**: with the old fixture's behaviour restored, the harness cannot express this mismatch.

S3 is worth its own note — without a non-zero domain the two routes cannot diverge, and the cells would **pass while testing nothing**. That is precisely the failure this file is being fixed for, so it is asserted as a precondition rather than assumed.

## A measured result that contradicts the obvious guess

A plain divergent key does **not** bump `lookup_miss_key_mismatch`. It misses with **no handle** — the two keys hash to different slots, so the probe never resolves a handle whose key it could compare. `key_mismatch` is for a *resolved* handle whose stored key disagrees (slab-handle reuse), a different defect.

Measured: `(0,0,0)` when the routes agree, `(2,0,0)` when they diverge.

**This matters beyond the file.** #7919's cluster reading found `session_lookup_miss_key_mismatch_total` at 0 on every worker, and it would be easy to read that as "no key divergence anywhere". It is not evidence of that. The cell records the reason where the reasoning lives, with an assertion that reds if the counters ever behave differently.

## Correction to the issue's motivation

The body says this is *"the reason [#7919's] confirmed mechanism cannot be exhibited below the cluster"* and calls #7919 *"a confirmed key mismatch"*. **#7919 is not a key mismatch** — key-mismatch counters read 0 on every worker, and the mechanism confirmed there (10/10 against a pre-registered protocol) is a multi-worker mirror clobber, which this harness would not exhibit. Recorded on #8262.

The test gap is **independently real** and is what this PR closes; it just is not unblocking a live fix. Flagged so nobody re-derives the link.

## Validation

Rust **5362 passed / 0 failed**; Go **71 packages, EXIT 0**, re-run at the merged head. One file touched, 225 insertions, 2 deletions.

## PR #8533 — dataplane: retain helper crash history across a recovery [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8397-crash-history`

#8397. Nothing kept helper crash history once the helper came back. `restartHelperAfterCrash` wipes the whole record on success, so a helper that crashed four times in the last hour and is healthy now presented a **completely clean crash surface** — and nothing else retained it either, since there was no crash or restart metric.

That is the worst shape a diagnostic can have: the failure is a *disappearance*, and a clean crash surface is also exactly what a healthy helper is supposed to look like. No assertion about the current record can tell the two apart.

## A separate store, not more fields

The wipe is not incidental — the record's contract is "the current crash episode", and that is what makes `LastExitWasCrash`, `RestartPending` and `CrashLooping()` mean what they mean. Keeping some fields across the clear would put two lifetimes in one struct. Preserved as-is.

## The two questions the issue asked to be decided

- **Where it lives:** on the Manager, lost on daemon restart. A daemon restart is a far louder event and already journalled, and the counter crosses that gap monotonically. Persisting diagnostic history adds a durability surface for data whose audience is an operator answering "is this recurring?" in session.
- **Rendered or queryable:** both, minimally. The block is dense, so history contributes **one** summary row; per-episode detail is reachable through `HelperCrashHistory()` for a future verb.

## The row's placement is the load-bearing detail, and I got it wrong first

The crash block returns early on `!LastExitWasCrash && !RestartPending` — correct for every current-episode row, fatal for this one. History exists for the helper that crashed repeatedly and is running **now**, and at that moment both flags are false. A row after the guard renders in every case *except* the one it was written for, and the failure is invisible.

It is emitted above the guard, and `TestCrashEpisodeRowRendersForAHealthyHelper8397` fails if it is moved back — verified by making that move.

## The counter is a counter on purpose

`xpf_dataplane_helper_crash_episodes_total` is monotonic within a daemon lifetime, because every gauge-shaped view reads clean the moment the helper is healthy. `rate()` is the alert; the ring is the follow-up. Emitted **before** the dataplane gate — "has this helper been crashing?" is most worth answering when the dataplane is *not* loaded — and extracted into its own collect method so its three-way distinction is drivable:

| source | emits |
|---|---|
| 4 episodes | 4 |
| 0 episodes | **0**, not omitted — an absent series reads as healthy to an alert exactly as a zero does |
| no source wired | **nothing** — a daemon with no dataplane accessor knows "unknown", not "never crashed" |

The **total is not bounded by the ring**: a daemon that recovered from 40 crashes reports 40 while holding the last 8. "8 crashes" and "at least 8 crashes" are different answers to the question this exists to answer.

## Tests

History survives the wipe (with a control asserting the wipe *actually happened*, or the file would be measuring the wipe not occurring); the ring bounds and drops the **oldest** while the total does not cap; the accessor returns a copy; **no phantom episode before a recovery** — a ring appending on the *crash* would satisfy every other cell while reporting an episode that may still be looping; the row renders healthy **and** crashed, and not at all with no history or unknown crash state; the metric's three-way distinction; and the daemon accessor is nil-safe on both receiver and dataplane, since it is handed over as a method value and called from the collector goroutine on every scrape.

`pkg/fwdstatus/README.md` records the new accessor and why the row sits above the early return.

Validation: `pkg/fwdstatus`, `pkg/api`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace` all green; gofmt and vet clean on every touched file.

Closes #8397

## PR #8534 — proto: add BUSY and carry peer_status on the session list [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8308-peer-status-list`

#8308 — both of #7294's scoped residuals. Each was left open because it is a wire change with its own rolling-upgrade question, and neither should have ridden along inside a rendering fix.

## Two additions, never a redefinition

`PeerFetchStatus` gains `PEER_FETCH_STATUS_BUSY = 4`; `GetSessionsResponse` gains `peer_status` (8) and `peer_error` (9) — the fields the two summary responses have carried since #5320.

The tempting alternative was to narrow `UNREACHABLE` to mean "unreachable or refused" and let the error string carry the difference. That is a **redefinition**, and in a rolling HA upgrade the two nodes run different binaries against **one wire**: the older binary keeps its old reading of the same number, so the nodes would report different things about one event while agreeing on the bytes. The additive choice costs an older client rendering BUSY as the raw integer `4` rather than a word — visibly odd rather than quietly wrong. That is the trade, and it is the right one, because the alternative's failure is invisible.

## Why BUSY

`peer_only_5968.go` returns `codes.ResourceExhausted` when this node declines to ask the peer on admission. **The peer is reachable.** Calling that a partition sends an operator debugging a fabric problem after a network fault that does not exist — and since #8306 fixed the REST wording, REST said `busy` while gRPC said `unreachable` about the same event.

## Why the list surface reported nothing

Not a discarded error — the discarded error was *downstream of a gap in the message*. There was nowhere to put an outcome, so #8306 worked around it by setting `peer_status: "ok"` locally, which meant only "the fetch succeeded". Every arm of `fetchPeerSessions` now records its outcome through the same helpers the summary surfaces use; a list and a summary disagreeing about one peer fetch would always be a bug, so it is single-sourced rather than bound by a test. The page-token arm is `NOT_APPLICABLE`, not `UNREACHABLE` — nothing was attempted and nothing failed.

## Both upgrade directions tested, through real encode/decode

A new-against-new test proves nothing about the window, so these round-trip the wire:

| direction | asserted |
|---|---|
| new server → old client | BUSY crosses as `4`, and explicitly **not** as `3` — which an older client renders "unreachable", the exact misreport this fixes, invisible to that client |
| old server → new client | a response omitting fields 8/9 decodes as `UNSPECIFIED` / `""`, with a control that the older fields still decode so the cell cannot pass against an empty marshal |

**The member numbers are pinned.** Renumbering BUSY to 3 does not fail a test — it fails to *compile* (`duplicate key 3 in map literal`), which is the strongest available form of that guard.

REST reports what the **server** classified, keeping the local `"ok"` only for an `UNSPECIFIED` response so an older peer does not regress below #8306 during the window. The REST cell asserts the two routes **agree** on the word rather than pinning either to a literal — the literal encodes which side you trust, and the defect was that the sides disagreed.

## Validation

`pkg/api`, `pkg/grpcapi`, `pkg/cli`, `cmd/cli` green; `go build ./...` clean. Three mutations killed: a refusal classified UNREACHABLE, BUSY rendered "unreachable" on REST, BUSY renumbered to 3. The regenerated `xpf.pb.go` was checked to be purely additive — no exported method removed, exactly two added.

`pkg/api/README.md`'s #7294 paragraph is corrected; it recorded both of these as open residuals.

Closes #8308

## PR #8535 — test/cluster: a reusable crafted-frame screen probe with an arrival witness [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `feat/8336-screen-probe`

#8336. #8298 was a live security bypass whose cluster reproduction was **not achievable with the obvious tooling** — two measurement attempts came back VOID, both for reusable reasons. This turns those two failures into a procedure.

## The three traps

| trap | why it bites | what the probe does |
|---|---|---|
| **The standard smoke exercises no screen code** | `stage_screen_check` is gated on `has_screen_state()`, and the loss cluster carries no `security screen` config — so a deploy + failover against a screen change is green for unrelated reasons | arms a profile first, disarms on **any** exit, verifies removal on **both** nodes (shared cluster, config syncs to the peer) |
| **The per-reason counter cannot see a parse-error drop** | `extract_screen_info` failing closed yields `ip-malformed`, which — with `syn-cookie` and `icmp-fragment` — is surfaced **only** through the aggregate. There is no label to sample, so a fail-closed drop is invisible **by construction** and the zero reads exactly like "nothing happened" | samples `xpf_screen_drops_total` |
| **Without an arrival witness a zero is unreadable** | a flat aggregate means either the frame never reached the firewall or it arrived and was permitted — only the second is a finding | sends a **witness** frame crafted to trip a per-reason check; its counter moving proves the path is live |

## The verdict is three-valued, and the order matters

VOID is decided **before** the subject is read, in dependency order: an unarmed profile makes the witness meaningless, and a flat witness makes the subject meaningless. A layer evaluating the subject first would report `PASSED` — not dropped — for a frame that **never arrived**. That is the exact false finding both earlier attempts were one step away from.

Four mutations, each red on the cells aimed at it: reordering the witness check, treating an unreadable sample as zero, skipping the armed gate, and summing the two nodes in the disarm check.

## The self-test found a hole in my own layer

Its totality check — *every input class yields exactly one verdict* — caught that an unquoted empty variable at a call site word-splits away, so the function arrives with fewer arguments than its signature and under `set -u` aborts and emits **nothing**. A verdict layer that can emit nothing is the missing-cell defect this file exists to prevent, wearing the file's own clothes. Parameters are now defaulted and short-argument classes are in the totality list.

"Did not move" and "could not be read" stay distinct throughout — an absent metric, a failed scrape and a helper restart mid-probe (a counter that went **backwards**: the two samples describe different processes) all render as "no number", and treating any as zero turns a broken instrument into a clean result.

A VOID run exits 2 and a dirty cleanup exits 3, so a caller checking only the status cannot read "we did not measure" as "nothing was wrong".

**Hermetic**: the selftest feeds literal counter samples — no incus, cluster, network or crafted frames. Wired into `make test-screen-probe-lib` and `scripts/run-selftests.sh` beside its siblings. `docs/engineering-style.md` gains the technique.

**Not cluster-validated**: the driver needs the shared lock and a crafted-frame sender, which is the caller's half. What *is* validated is the decision layer — which is where both earlier attempts actually failed.

Closes #8336

## PR #8536 — nat: release the import-time reservation when the tunnel-remap purge deletes a session [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8138-nat-purge`

## The leak, reproduced on the purge path

The #1873 R-D tunnel-remap purge deletes peer-synced sessions whose stored
`tunnel_endpoint_id` was remapped. It never released the NAT reservation the
coordinator took when it **imported** those sessions.

Measured before the change: **`purged = 1`, `occupied_after_purge = true`.**

`reserve_synced_translation` takes that reservation as `NatHolder::Untracked`,
which contributes **no holder bit**. Every teardown sweep frees by *clearing
bits*, so none can see it, and `delete_synced_session` frees one only on the
#6979 F4 dropped-command route (with a worker id). A session purged before any
worker adopted the reservation has nobody to release it — the `(pool_addr, port)`
is held for the life of the allocator.

## Where the release must be aimed — the part that isn't obvious

`purge_remapped_tunnel_sessions` now takes the forwarding to release against as
a **parameter** instead of reading `self.forwarding`, because the two production
callers hold different states and **one holds nothing**:

| call site | state at the purge |
|---|---|
| `coordinator/reconcile/snapshot.rs` | `stop_inner(false)` has already **DEFAULTED** `coord.forwarding` — no rules, no allocators |
| `coordinator/snapshot_refresh.rs` | purge runs *before* `self.forwarding = new_forwarding`, so it is the live previous state |

Both pass `&new_forwarding`, which is correct for both because `forwarding_build`
carries `iface_nat_allocators` across a rebuild by **`Arc::clone`**
(`mod.rs:657-658`) — the new state's allocators *are* the objects the reservation
was minted against. That is also why the leak is observable at all.

**This is the #8124 hazard.** Driving the release against the reconcile caller's
defaulted state frees nothing *and* increments a repair counter — a repair that
did not happen. That is why it was removed before merge rather than shipped.

## It cannot over-release

`drop_holder_locked` returns early — *keeping* the record — whenever any holder
bit remains, and `Untracked.bit()` is `0`. So a reservation a worker **has**
adopted is left for that worker's own teardown; only a record with `holders == 0`
is freed. The allocator documents this as the deliberate direction: an
under-release leaks a bounded, observable port, an over-release hands a live
worker's `(pool_addr, port)` to a new flow.

## Honest counting

`release_source_nat_allocation` now **returns whether it actually freed
anything** — `release_flow`/`rollback_flow` already computed it and the value was
discarded — so `tunnel_purge_reservations_released` counts *outcomes, not
attempts*. Surfaced as `xpf_userspace_tunnel_purge_reservations_released_total`.

## PR #8538 — userspace-dp: bound the peer-supplied owner_rg_id before filing it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8486-owner-rg-bound`

#8486. `metadata.owner_rg_id` arrives from the peer as a raw `i32` and was filed into the shared owner-RG indexes for **every positive value**.

The buckets are not the cost. The authoritative un-file uses `HashMap::retain`, which is **O(capacity)** and visits empty slots — so removing N keys filed under N distinct ids is **Θ(N²)** of outer-capacity work on the session-control thread.

The Go side bounds RG ids to 0..15 on the *strict* path and downgrades that to a WARNING on the tolerant peer-sync path. The helper is the last line, and it did not hold one.

## Clamp the filing, not the import

The issue's second candidate, and it is the right one. Refusing the import would decline a takeover this node is otherwise fit for — the tolerant path exists precisely because a peer may legitimately run an older or looser config, so a hard refusal trades a bounded memory cost for a **blackhole on failover**. The session is kept and stays usable; only the index entry is skipped.

**The remove path stays permissive (`> 0`) deliberately**, and the asymmetry is the point: anything ever filed can always be un-filed, including under a future tightening. A symmetric bound would strand entries filed under the old one — turning a hardening change into a leak.

## The counter is surfaced, and the tree caught me not surfacing it

An internal counter nothing reads is a claim written into inert code. #6641's `every_counter_accessor_is_wired_into_process_status` failed until the accessor was assigned into `ProcessStatus` — the instrument doing its job on exactly the change that needed it.

**Only out-of-range ids are counted.** The ordinary "no redundancy group" case (id 0, carried by every standalone session) is not a decline; counting it would make the metric read as an attack on every non-clustered box and bury the signal. That distinction has its own cell.

## Mutations — four, all killed, each aimed

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| remove the bound (pre-#8486) | all four |
| reject **everything** — the over-rejection that would silently disable owner-RG indexing and stop a takeover finding the peer's sessions | all four |
| count the no-RG case too | only the counter cell |
| off-by-one on 15 | only the boundary cell |

## One process note

The test module was first registered under an existing `#[path]` attribute, which aliased it to a **different file** — so the new cells never ran and a duplicate registration of the embedded-poll-filter tests passed under the new name. The output said "ok" for tests I had not written. Caught by reading *which* cells ran rather than that something ran.

The status field is additive: `#[serde(default)]` so an older helper decodes 0 rather than failing the whole status parse, and the wire fixture diff was inspected before regenerating — one new key, nothing changed or removed.

Validation: **5232 cells green**, build clean.

Closes #8486

## PR #8539 — nat: make the persistent-NAT forwarding disarm visible at commit [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8447-visible-disarm`

#8447. Adding `persistent-nat` to a rule-referenced source pool on a chassis-cluster member stops the dataplane forwarding transit entirely — rx goes to 0.

**The behaviour is deliberate and documented (#1449)** and nothing here changes it: persistent-NAT leases are helper-local and not HA-synchronized, so the dataplane declines to forward rather than forward with semantics it cannot honour.

**The defect is that it happened invisibly.** Interfaces stay up, the config commits cleanly, and the failure presents as a *connectivity* problem rather than a NAT one. The only surface was `Forwarding supported: false` inside a `show` nobody runs when the symptom is "the link went down" — and this issue spent five rounds of cluster measurement rediscovering a contract the daemon already knew the reason for and threw away.

#8503 fixed the disarm-time silence. This fixes the other two surfaces.

| when | surface |
|---|---|
| **at commit** | a `ValidateConfig` advisory naming the **consequence** — that forwarding stops, that it will look like a link failure, and where to look |
| at disarm | the #8503 WARN (already merged) |
| **continuously** | `xpf_dataplane_forwarding_supported` — what an alert keys on |

An **advisory, not a rejection**: the config is valid, the behaviour is the documented contract, and `chassis cluster` and the NAT stanza commit independently — rejecting would make the standalone case unreachable through a shared config.

The metric reads the **same field** `desiredForwardingArmedLocked` gates on, so it cannot disagree with the arm/disarm decision. Three-way, and the third value is the point: forwarding → 1, disarmed → 0, **no source → no series**. A daemon with no dataplane accessor does not *know* whether forwarding is live; emitting 1 there would turn "we cannot see" into "everything is fine" — the exact reading this issue is about. Reasons are deliberately not labels (unbounded, operator-facing, a cardinality problem).

## The predicate is single-sourced, not mirrored

It moved to `pkg/config` (which `pkg/dataplane/userspace` already imports, not the reverse) and the capability gate now **calls** it. The tree's habit for this shape is to mirror with a comment saying it mirrors — see `deterministicIPv4Enforced`. A mirror is a drift surface whose failure mode is an advisory that stops firing for a config that still disarms forwarding: **silence that reads exactly like safety.**

Both are keyed on the **rule**, not the pool table — an unreferenced `persistent-nat` pool translates nothing, so it neither disarms forwarding nor warns, and the two agree by construction rather than coincidence.

## Mutations — four, all killed, each aimed

| mutation | reds |
|---|---|
| drop the cluster condition | the standalone cell — warning on every persistent-NAT config would train operators to ignore it |
| key on the pool table | the unreferenced-pool cell |
| remove the consequence wording | the actionability assertion |
| make the metric unconditional | the disarmed cell **and** the no-source control |

`docs/ha-failover-status.md`'s "Persistent SNAT Lease Boundary" gains the three surfaces and why the predicate is shared.

Validation: `pkg/config`, `pkg/api`, `pkg/dataplane/userspace`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/cli` all green; `go build ./...`, gofmt and vet clean.

**Does not close #8447.** The issue also carries an unestablished question — whether a *dedicated* pool rule reproduces the outage, rather than only the retargeted catch-all — which needs the cluster.

## PR #8540 — protocol: stop counting path-qualified type positions as struct literals [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8537-literal-guard-paths`

## The defect

`exhaustive_literal_count` finds a struct name followed by `{`, then excludes
non-literals by inspecting the text immediately **before the name** (`->`,
`struct`, `impl`, `for`, `enum`). A path-qualified occurrence defeats every arm:

```rust
fn f() -> crate::ConfigSnapshot {   // pre ends with "::", not "->"
```

so a **return type** was counted as an exhaustive struct literal. Found on the
#8138 branch, where a test helper with that signature — containing no literal at
all, it builds one with `::default()` — tripped the ratchet.

## The fix, and the repair that looks right but isn't

Strip the path qualifier, then apply the **same** arms to what precedes the whole
path.

The obvious alternative — *skip any hit preceded by `::`* — is wrong in the other
direction: `crate::Name { .. }` in **expression** position is a real exhaustive
literal and must still count. That alternative is mutant **G2** below, and the
qualified-literal rows in the fixture are what catch it.

## Why it wasn't cosmetic

The guard is a **ratchet**, so the natural response to a red is to raise the
ceiling — which writes the miscount permanently into the baseline and leaves the
ceiling holding room for a *real* literal nobody will notice. Its failure text
("Add `..Default::default()`") also sends the reader hunting for a literal that
does not exist.

## Seven ceilings tightened — and the headline number is measured, not inferred

| struct | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `ConfigSnapshot` | 15 | **0** |
| `FabricSnapshot` | 8 | 7 |
| `InterfaceSnapshot` | 2 | 0 |
| `MapPins` | 2 | 0 |
| `NAT64RuleSnapshot` | 4 | 3 |
| `SourceNATRuleSnapshot` | 1 | 0 |
| `ThreeColorPolicerStatus` | 2 | 1 |

A 15 → 0 swing is too large to accept on faith, so I checked it against the
source rather than the guard:

- the tree contains **exactly 15** `-> crate::ConfigSnapshot {` return types —
  matching the old ceiling one for one;
- **control:** 60 bare `-> ConfigSnapshot {`, which the pre-fix arms already

## PR #8541 — config: a reversed integer range must not silently disable the check [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-04)

Branch: `fix/8358-range-footgun`

#8358's one real residue. `ValidateInteger`'s body guards its comparison with `min <= max`, so `ValidateInteger(1, 0)` — the shape a caller reaches for when they mean "at least 1" and mis-order the arguments — returned a validator that **accepted every integer**, and nothing said so.

That is the worst shape a check can have: it fails to a value indistinguishable from a healthy one. The leaf has a validator, review sees a validator, `?` completion shows a typed leaf, and the gate does nothing. It would be found the way this class is always found — by an operator committing something absurd that works.

## A panic at construction, not an error at validation

This is a *programming* error, not an operator one. `setSchema` is a package-level var built at init, so a reversed range fails every test in every package that imports `pkg/config`, immediately and unmissably. It cannot reach an operator because it cannot get past a build.

Measured before adding it: all 35+ literal call sites and every named-constant site are well-ordered, so nothing relies on the disable. `ValidateIntegerMin` is the documented "no upper bound" spelling and its own comment says so.

The `min <= max` term in the closure is **kept** rather than simplified — it is what made the case silent, and leaving it beside the panic documents the pairing.

## Mutations

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| remove the guard | the panic cell reds |
| panic **unconditionally** | the whole package fails at init with `ValidateInteger(0, 255) has min > max` — demonstrating both that the guard runs at initialization **and** that its message renders correctly against a real call site |

Boundary covered both ways: a well-ordered range still validates (without which an unconditional panic would satisfy the first cell while disabling every numeric leaf), and `min == max` is allowed and exact — a leaf with one legal value is well-ordered, and panicking on it would be an off-by-one in the guard itself.

## How this was found

#8358 asks for a `ValidateIntegerRange` constructor, on the measured premise that `ValidateIntegerMin` is the only numeric bound the schema can express. **That premise is wrong.** `ValidateInteger(min, max)` is exactly that constructor — **109 sites** against 32 for the Min-only form — already carrying `(1, 65535)` for ports, `(0, 255)` for octet fields, and `(1, 4094)` for VLAN ids, the last being the issue's own worked example of a justified constant.

The search was for the *name* `ValidateIntegerRange`; the conclusion was drawn about the *capability*. Full reasoning is on the issue, including why the 32 Min-only leaves are Min-only deliberately under the reviewed `no-schema-only-caps` doctrine (PR #1845) — which means the issue's item 3 would delete a design decision rather than consolidate a duplicate.

Validation: `pkg/config` green (120s), `go build ./...` clean, gofmt clean.
