## PR #8782 — config: compile snmp community `clients` from the packed spelling [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8778-snmp-clients-failopen`

## The defect

```
set snmp community public authorization read-only clients 10.0.0.0/8   # ONE line  -> clients=[]  ALLOW-ALL
set snmp community public authorization read-only                      # TWO lines -> ENFORCED
set snmp community public clients 10.0.0.0/8
```

**The difference was a line break, and this is a fail-OPEN rather than a lost restriction.** `AllowsSource` documents `len(Clients) == 0` as allow-all (the Junos default), so dropping the allowlist did not narrow it — it **inverted** it. The community answered from every source while the operator's config said otherwise and the commit reported success.

## Two shapes, one defect, different causes

Only measuring the tree showed the second. Flat `set` builds a **chain**, not siblings:

```
community public
  authorization read-only
    clients 10.0.0.0/8        <- CHILD of authorization
```

so a loop over one level of children saw `authorization` and never saw `clients`. The brace-elided hierarchical spelling instead packs every token onto **one node's `Keys`**, where a separate flat-form loop read `authorization` and not `clients`.

**Fixing the Keys loop alone left the flat-set spelling — the one an operator types — still broken.** I assumed one shape, measured, and found two.

The fix walks the chain (descending only through recognised keywords, so a `clients` node's own **value** children are not mistaken for statements) and extends the Keys loop to consume the `clients` run. That run goes to `parseSNMPClients` rather than being parsed inline, so the `restrict` modifier and the #5898 orphan-`restrict` fail-closed path behave identically to the braced spelling instead of being reimplemented beside them.

## The guard asserts the outcome, not an agreement

The obvious cell is *"packed compiles to what braced compiles to"* — and it is **wrong here**: it passes when both spellings are allow-all, which is exactly the regression it would exist to catch. Each spelling is instead asserted to **admit** an address inside the allowlist and **deny** one outside it, which is false of an empty allowlist however the other spelling behaves. *(Constraint: team-lead.)*

Subtests: flat-set one-liner; hierarchical packed; `restrict` under packing; a positive control on the two-line spelling that always worked; and the **second ingestion surface** — `docs/config-schema.md` records that snmp compiles from both `snmp {}` and `system { snmp {} }`, and that a defect has already been reachable from one and not the other, on the spelling our own reference config uses. Both call `compileSNMP` today; the cell asserts that rather than assuming it.

## Validation

Three **production** mutants, each asserted to have run and each caught by exactly the subtest that should catch it:

| mutant | failing subtest |
|---|---|
| drop the chain descent | `flat-set one line` only |
| drop the packed-Keys `clients` case | `hierarchical packed` + `restrict` |
| truncate the clients run | `restrict` only |

0 residual. Full `pkg/config`, `pkg/snmp`, `pkg/api` green; dataplane canaries green; gofmt clean.

Docs updated in the same change — the three spellings, the fail-open explanation, and the guard-shape note that an equality cell is the wrong instrument for an allowlist.

Closes #8778

## PR #8784 — config: opt vpn-monitor into packedStatements, and refuse ambiguous container names [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8768-six-containers`

`security ipsec vpn <v> vpn-monitor destination-ip <ip> source-interface <if>;` collapsed both statements into one node. Opted in, and verified across **every** admitted leaf pair rather than the one it was first reported on. Refs #8768.

## The guard had a flaw, and trying to opt in more containers exposed it

Its fixture registry is keyed by container **name**, and schema names repeat:

```
"proposal"             under ike  AND ipsec
"dead-peer-detection"  under ike gateway AND ipsec
```

If two nodes of one name opt in, the map holds **whichever the walk reached last**, and the leaf enumeration silently describes the wrong container — a guard reporting on a node nobody opted in, while reading as coverage for the one they did.

**So the cell now refuses:** two opted-in nodes sharing a name is a hard failure naming the container. Keying by schema path is the real fix, and is deliberately left until a second node of one name actually needs to opt in — refusing is correct today and doesn't claim a generality it hasn't been tested at.

## Which is why only one of @lane-8526's six is here

`ike proposal`, `ipsec proposal` and `dead-peer-detection` all have **ambiguous names**, so opting them in needs the path-keyed registry first. Its measurement that all three are FIXABLE for one leaf pair each stands; what's missing is the machinery to hold them to *every* pair.

## Validation

Full `go test ./pkg/...` green; canaries and tree-wide `gofmt -l` run regardless of diff scope. **Three containers now opt in, 20 ordered leaf pairs compare equal.**

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| opt in **both** nodes named `proposal` | **red** — `2 container name(s) opt in at MORE THAN ONE schema position: [proposal]` |

I checked **which branch fired**, not merely that something red — the collision check, not the missing-fixture one that would also have failed.

## PR #8786 — config: correct the #8768 opt-in guard's stated reason, which cited a retracted mechanism [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8768-guard-rationale`

The guard's assertions were never wrong. **Its explanation of why they matter was** — and it was landed, in the header comment, two error strings, and most urgently in the **failure message a person sees when the cell reds**. Follow-up to #8768 (closed).

## The retracted mechanism

It claimed `snmp community` demonstrated a leaf-level reader ignoring a correctly-split tail. **It does not.** `snmp community` does not fold at all — `("community","authorization")` isn't in the scope list — so there is no split structure and no reader ignoring one. Its lost `clients` is an ordinary drop at an unadmitted site (#8778).

**I measured that myself and reported it as a correction, then did not re-read my own landed rationale against it.** The hollowed-rationale shape, with the later change made by the same person who wrote the claim.

**So no per-leaf reader divergence has ever been demonstrated**, and the 18-of-18 EQUAL this cell measures is entirely consistent with none existing.

## The justification is a priori, and says so

Opting a container in is a claim about **every** admitted leaf, so every pair must be compared for the claim to be tested. That needs no counter-example and doesn't weaken without one. **Weaker footing than "we found one", and the honest one.**

## The failure message mattered most

It told whoever hit it that a leaf's reader does not take its value from the split structure — **a specific diagnosis for a defect nobody has observed**, which is worse than no diagnosis because its specificity is what makes it trusted.

It now states what the cell **measured** (these two spellings disagree, nothing more) and names the likelier causes to *establish* rather than assume: the fold declining to split on a token outside the modelled grammar, or an under-declared arity — the #8777 case.

**"Multi-ness is not the discriminator" is no longer asserted.** Its evidence was `snmp community clients` diverging, which is not a fold divergence, so the evidence is gone even if the claim may still be true.

The retraction is **recorded rather than deleted**: a guard whose stated reason is a phantom still passes review, and the next reader inherits the phantom.

## Validation

Full `go test ./pkg/...` green, **73 packages**; canaries and tree-wide `gofmt -l` run regardless of diff scope. **Verified by forcing a real divergence** that the new message is what appears and the retracted text does not — a failure string is only correct if you have seen it fail.

## PR #8788 — config: declare `next-header` so an IPv6 term's protocol match survives packing [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8781-next-header-packed`

Closes #8781

`from next-header` is the Junos spelling of the protocol match in a `family inet6` firewall filter. `compileFilterFrom` has handled it since #3307 — which added the switch arm precisely because the criterion *"was silently dropped (the term lost its protocol constraint)"* — but the schema never declared it under `from` in either family.

The packed reader resolves its tail **through the schema** (`packedBodyChildren` → `resolveSchemaChild`) and returns the node's children unchanged when the lookup fails. So #3307 fixed the braced half and left the packed half inert:

```
family inet6 { ... from { next-header tcp; } }   Protocols=[tcp]
family inet6 { ... from next-header tcp; }       Protocols=[]
```

Both commit cleanly on the strict path. **A correctly authored IPv6 term, written in the packed spelling, loses its protocol match entirely and therefore matches every protocol** — the failure direction `docs/config-schema.md` already names for this class (*"a filter term whose `from` was dropped matches EVERYTHING"*, #7457). A term meant to accept TCP accepts everything; a term meant to discard TCP discards everything.

### Worse than #8773, and found by censusing it

#8773's dropped criterion was a **cross-family** spelling — a configuration Junos rejects anyway. Here the dropped spelling is **the one Junos tells operators to write**.

It was found by census rather than observation: enumerate the keywords each compiler switch arm handles, and check whether the schema declares each at that path. That is the cheap way to find the rest of a class instead of waiting for a second symptom.

### The fix, both halves

Declare `next-header` under `from` in both families so the packed reader can resolve it, **and** warn at commit for the cross-family spellings. Declaring alone would make the spellings agree silently; warning alone would not stop the drop.

`CrossFamilyDSCPSpelling` becomes `CrossFamilyMatchSpellings` — a second aliased field joined it, and a DSCP-specific name on a list holding protocol spellings is the kind of stale label that later gets reasoned from. The validator's `want` was derived from the **address family**, which was correct while the list held one field and silently wrong the moment it held two: a field-specific answer computed from a field-independent input. It is now a map from each spelling to its own counterpart, listed in both directions so a third aliased field is a visible edit rather than a silent gap.

### Two census results worth recording

- **A candidate is not a finding.** `then next` was also undeclared and measured **clean**: both spellings leave `Action` empty, so they agree — by both being wrong, which is a different defect and not this one.
- **Enumerate the arms from source, not memory.** A hand-written list of the `then` arms included `sample` and `port-mirror`, which are not compiler arms at all, and reported both as defects.

### Gate movements

Both expected, neither a behaviour change. The #4406 golden moves by the field **rename only** — 12 old keys out, 12 new keys in, every value `null`, zero value diffs, checked field-by-field before regenerating. The #7484 ratchet improves 701 → 703, which that cell calls a good failure.

### Validation

Full `go test ./...` green tree-wide at the merged head; `gofmt -l` clean; four mutations killed, each mutant confirmed **both to have applied and to build** before its verdict was read: removing the inet6 declaration (the defect itself), removing the inet alias, not recording the cross-family protocol spelling, and dropping `next-header` from the counterpart map.

The applied-check is new and earned itself immediately — two earlier mutants whose anchors no longer matched after gofmt reformatting were reported as **ESCAPED on a tree that had never been mutated**. A mutation harness that cannot prove its edit landed reports false escapes, which are indistinguishable from real ones.

## PR #8789 — config: pin the flat `set` spelling of `from next-header` as its own case [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8781-flatset-arm`

Follow-up to #8781 (PR #8788), which fixed the packed hierarchical spelling but whose guard used `NewParser` fixtures exclusively — so it said nothing about what the CLI produces.

CLAUDE.md forbids hierarchical text as a stand-in for a `set` session because the two build different trees. That gap is not hypothetical: on #8778 a fix for the hierarchical packed form left the flat `set` spelling **still failing open**, with a passing hierarchical test beside it, because flat `set` built a chain where the fixture built siblings.

### Measured, not assumed

The flat spelling is fine — `SetPath` builds `from` with a real `[next-header tcp]` child, so the compiler reads it from `node.Children` and `Protocols` is `[tcp]`. The one-line form `from next-header tcp then accept` is **refused at commit**: `next-header` is `multi:true` and absorbs the trailing tokens onto its own Keys. `protocol` behaves identically, so that is long-established multi-value behaviour, not something the #8781 declaration introduced. Both are now asserted, the second with its control.

The assertion is the **enforced outcome** — `Protocols` exactly `[tcp]` — never that two spellings agree. An IPv6 term whose protocol match is dropped matches every protocol, so two dropped spellings agree perfectly while the filter is wide open.

### What this cell binds is recorded in it

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| remove `next-header` from `compileFilterFrom`s arm | **RED** |
| remove the inet6 `next-header` schema declaration | still green |

The flat path never consults the schema, so this binds the **compiler arm**, while the packed path' dependency on the schema **declaration** stays bound by the existing cell. Two paths, two dependencies, one cell each — and the comment says so rather than leaving the next reader to assume the newer cell subsumes the older.

The escaping mutation is reported as a property of the cell rather than fixed: the flat path genuinely does not depend on the declaration, and forcing a red there would assert something untrue about the mechanism.

## PR #8790 — config: key the #8768 opt-in registry by schema path, and land the three it blocked [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8768-path-keyed`

The registry was keyed by container **name**, and names repeat: `proposal` under both `ike` and `ipsec`, `dead-peer-detection` under both gateways. A name-keyed map doesn't fail on that — it holds whichever node the walk reached last and enumerates the **wrong** container's leaves while reading as coverage for the one someone opted in.

The previous cell **refused** on collision, which was correct and blocked three containers. A path is unique by construction, so the refusal is replaced by an address that cannot be ambiguous.

**Six containers now opt in; 94 ordered leaf pairs compare equal.** The three landed: `security/ike/proposal`, `security/ipsec/proposal`, `security/ike/gateway/dead-peer-detection`.

## Tested at two nodes — the generality I declined to assume

| mutation | result |

So two same-named nodes are genuinely distinct rather than aliases.

The first path-keyed version listed every container **twice**. Junos `groups` mirrors the whole schema, so each container also has a `groups/*/<path>` address pointing at the identical node. Deduping by **node identity** and keeping the shortest path as canonical fixes it — the mirror only ever adds a prefix.

That was invisible under name keying, which is a small argument for the change beyond the collisions it was made for.

## PR #8793 — config: traverse into a braced compound-key container, with the 30 measured [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8763-traversal`

Part of #8763.

The brace-elision pass never traversed into a braced `family inet { … }`. For a
node with `Keys=[family inet]` it took `kw=Keys[0]="family"` and recursed with
`schema.children["family"]`, while the node's children belong to `family inet`
(`family.children["inet"]`). **The recursion advanced the schema one level where
the node advanced two**, so every lookup beneath a braced compound-key container
missed and the subtree was never visited — not "declined to fold", never asked.

It bites exactly where the second token is a **child keyword**. `unit 0` is
unaffected: there the second token is an instance arg, and `args` is precisely
what `identity` counts. Every `compoundKey` declaration in the schema is named
`family`, which bounds the surface.

## What this activates, measured pair by pair

30 admitted pairs are reachable **only** below a `family`. They folded nothing
before and fold for the first time after — and "the suite stays green" is not a
measurement of them, because a silently dropped value produces a clean commit
either way.

| verdict | n | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| reads-but-inert | 16 | the packed tail is **already** read; the fold changes nothing |
| recovery | 9 | dropped today; the fold delivers exactly the braced result |
| chain-incomplete | 2 | folds and **still** delivers nothing |
| refused either way | 2 | a live gate rejects the value in both spellings |
| reader defect | 1 | nothing reads it in **any** spelling; pre-existing |

**Nothing hazardous**, and the headline is the opposite of what "30 pairs go
live" suggests: the entire firewall-filter match and action surface —
`from source-address`, `destination-port`, `tcp-flags`, `icmp-type`,
`then policer`, `then forwarding-class`, `then routing-instance` — is **already
read** out of the packed tail, so this traversal activates none of it.

The nine real repairs: `flexible-match-range range`, `filter term`, the four
`flow-server` leaves, `output source-address`, `output flow-server`,
`prefix-limit maximum`.

`flexible-match-range range` is worth naming — **same container, same `from`,
opposite answer from the eleven beside it.** A container-level verdict would have
been wrong for it.

## The instrument is three-way, and that is the point

Comparing packed against braced establishes **agreement**, and two spellings agree
whenever both are wrong: a leaf whose reader ignores the value compiles
identically either way, so an agreement check reports success on a leaf that does
nothing. Every case therefore also compiles a **baseline** with the statement
removed.

## PR #8795 — config: read a brace-elided routing instance's packed body [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8787-instance-type-packed`

## The defect

```
routing-instances { ri1 { instance-type forwarding; } }   1 instance
routing-instances { ri1 instance-type forwarding; }       0 instances
routing-instances { ri1 interface ge-0/0/0.0; }           0 instances
```

Not a dropped property — the **entire instance vanished**, on a commit reporting success.

**The harmful direction is `forwarding`.** `InstanceType == "forwarding"` is what makes the daemon **skip** VRF creation, so a dropped value creates a VRF the operator asked *not* to have and moves interfaces into it — a forwarding and isolation change, not a lost label. **Reachable from a loaded or peer-synced config file, not from flat `set`** (which builds a chain and compiled correctly throughout): the boot and HA-sync paths rather than the CLI.

**Cause:** `compileRoutingInstances` skipped `child.IsLeaf`, and a brace-elided instance *is* a leaf.

## Not fixable by the #8690 normalizer

That pass is scoped per `(container, head)` pair, and the pair it asks for this site is **`("ri1", "instance-type")`** — the operator's *instance name*, not a keyword. No scope entry can name it. Measured both ways: admit-all folds the node, the real predicate cannot be made to.

The packed tail is read with the **same keyword set the braced switch handles**, so the two spellings cannot drift. `interface` consumes its whole run — the #3904 note records that reading only the first value stranded the remaining ports outside the instance (a VRF isolation break), and a single-value packed read would have reintroduced exactly that.

## Two separable halves, and mutation shows they do different work

Removing the schema declarations leaves **every compile assertion passing** — the compiler fix carries that alone. What the declarations do is offer the leaves in completion and `?` help: **2 completions before, 4 after**. Pinned by their own cell so the halves can't be confused. #8785 is why I measured rather than assumed: there, declaring a leaf was expected to fix a drop and did not.

The stale rationale is replaced, not left: *"instance-type and interface are NOT listed here → they become leaf nodes"* was true when written and stopped being true when packed-tail resolution landed.

## The guard asserts absolute outcomes

Never `packed == braced` — both spellings producing zero instances agree perfectly, so an equality cell is green on exactly the defect it exists to catch. Controls: braced and flat-`set` both already worked and must keep working; a bare `ri1;` must **not** become an untyped phantom VRF.

| mutant | fails |
|---|---|
| restore the `IsLeaf` skip | both packed subtests, neither control |
| disable the packed-tail read | both packed subtests, neither control |
| drop both schema declarations | **only** the completion cell |
| drop one declaration | that cell alone |

0 residual.

`gateCoverageFloor` 703 → 705: the #7484 ratchet reported *COVERAGE IMPROVED* and named the new floor — two leaves blind to the spelling gate are now compared, which is the declaration half working.

Full `pkg/config` green; `pkg/routing`, `pkg/daemon`, `pkg/frr` green; canaries green; gofmt clean.

Comparing spellings proves the fold moves the compiled config the way the braced

## PR #8801 — config: carry the IKE identity through a packed gateway body [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/local-identity-arity`

Closes #8796

An IKE gateway whose body is written as a **packed tail** silently loses `local-identity`, and depending on statement order loses the rest of the body with it. All of these commit cleanly on the strict path:

```
braced  gateway gw1 { ... local-identity hostname foo; }   local=hostname/foo ext=ge-0/0/0
packed  gateway gw1 local-identity hostname foo;           local=""/""        ext=""
packed  gateway gw1 local-identity ... external-interface  local=""/""        ext=""
packed  gateway gw1 external-interface ... local-identity  local=""/""        ext=ge-0/0/0
```

An IKE gateway compiled with no local identity does **not** fail closed: strongSwan falls back to the local address, so the tunnel negotiates under a different peer identity than the operator configured — it authenticates as the wrong party or not at all. `remote-identity` has the identical shape and defect.

### Master's fix is incomplete, and this completes it

While this was in flight, master opted the `security ike` gateway into `packedStatements`. That is **one of three decisions**, and alone it changes nothing — measured at master's exact state, all three packed spellings still return `LocalID=""/""`. The security defect is live on master right now behind a change that looks like it addressed it.

| decision | controls | status before this PR |
|---|---|---|
| pair admitted to `compactNormalizeInScope` | **whether** the tail folds | missing |
| `packedStatements` on the container | **how** the folded tail splits | master added it — to one of the two gateway containers |
| `args: 2` on the identity leaves | where each statement **ends** | missing |

Both remaining parts are re-verified load-bearing *on top of* master's change: removing either alone reds the cell. The second gateway container (`security ipsec`) is also opted in — same children, same compiler path, and fixing one of a pair leaves the defect live at a spelling operators reach the same way.

### Declaring the arity alone is inert

Measured byte-identical output. A fix that changed only the arity would have measured as correct on a harness forcing the other two and changed nothing shipped.

The arity hypothesis was **refuted by a control**, not by reasoning: two `args`-declared siblings in one packed tail (`external-interface ge-0/0/0 ike-policy pol1`) also lost the second statement, so a missing arity could not be the whole cause — the tail was building a **chain**, each statement nested under the previous. That control is kept in the cell; it is the only assertion there that catches the chain regressing.

The order-dependence is the diagnostic signature: the **first** leaf decides whether the pass fires, because admission is per `(container, leaf)` pair.

### A coverage trade, recorded rather than absorbed

Declaring `args: 2` moves those four leaves out of the #7484 spelling gate's `args<=1` population; the floor drops to 701. That cell says *"find what stopped compiling rather than lowering this floor"*, so that was done — nothing stopped compiling, four leaves changed declared shape for a correct reason, and the constant now carries the cause. Four spelling-gate verdicts traded for a packed spelling that stops discarding an IKE peer identity.

### Merge resolution

Both conflicts were substantive. The ratchet conflicted (master 705, branch 699) and was resolved by **re-measuring at the merged tree** rather than adjusting arithmetically — measured 701, which happens to equal 705 minus these four leaves; the agreement is the evidence, not the method. Master's #8768 fixture for the container was dropped in favour of this branch's: master's omits `local-identity` and `remote-identity`, so it would have opted the container in and never compared the leaves the opt-in exists for.

### Validation

Full `go test ./...` green tree-wide — 72 packages ok, 0 FAIL, **counted** rather than inferred from an absence of FAIL lines; `gofmt -l` clean; every mutation confirmed to *apply* and to build before its verdict was read.

## PR #8802 — config: create every zone in a bracketed security-zone group [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8794-zone-group`

## The defect

`security-zone [ trust untrust ] { screen edge; }` created only `trust`. **Not a missing body — the later zone was never created**, because `namedInstances` takes `Keys[1]` and discards `Keys[2:]`. The syntax is affirmatively supported (`formatset_container_bracket_6668`, `wantCommit: true`).

## Severity: measured, and it is NOT the reported fail-open

```
policy naming the lost zone   strict REJECTS, naming it
CONTROL two explicit blocks   strict ACCEPTS      <- the miss is the cause
tolerant path                 accepts + 2 warnings, one naming the zone
grouped body's interfaces     land in the SURVIVING zone, not misattributed
```

The Rust `ScreenVerdict::Pass` path is **real but unreachable here** — `screen/tests.rs` calls it *"the legit Pass case"*, but it needs traffic attributed to the missing zone, and that zone has no interfaces. The report inferred the consequence from the shape; the shape is right, the path is not live.

**The harm is ordering:** commit the group before anything references it, and the loss is silent until a later unrelated commit fails pointing at the *policy* rather than at this statement.

## The HA concern dissolves — measuring is what showed it

The worry was that `ConfigTree.Format` emits bare keys, so a provenance-based fix would desync a primary from its standby. But the lexer strips brackets and both spellings parse to **identical trees**:

```
security-zone [ trust untrust ] { ... }   Keys=[..trust untrust] children=1
security-zone   trust untrust   { ... }   Keys=[..trust untrust] children=1
```

There is no provenance to preserve, so a provenance-only fix is impossible and any fix is structural — and a structural fix has both sides of the `Format` → `SyncApply` boundary fanning out identically. **No version fence needed.** A rolling upgrade still differs, but that is the pre-fix behaviour on the old node and errs toward *fewer* zones — the fail-closed direction.

## The discriminator cannot sweep in a packed tail

A group has surplus keys **and a braced body**; a packed tail has surplus keys and **no children**. Disjoint by the same property that separates them in the #8690 normalizer, whose fold requires `len(Children) == 0`. Scoped to zones deliberately — `namedInstances` is shared, and fanning it out globally is a separate decision with its own evidence.

## Validation

| mutant | fails |
|---|---|
| revert the fan-out | both group subtests, neither control |
| fan out only the first name | both group subtests + discriminator |
| weaken discriminator to `len(Keys) >= 3` | **only** the discriminator subtest |

**The safety subtest was vacuous and mutation found it.** Its first version fed `security-zone trust screen edge;` through a compile — and the weakened-discriminator mutant **survived**, because the #8690 normalizer admits `("security-zone","screen")` and pre-splits that tail before `compileZones` runs, so the input never reached the discriminator. It now calls `zoneGroupInstances8794` directly, the only way to put the bodiless shape in front of it.

Guard asserts **absolute outcomes** — both zones exist and carry the profile — never grouped == longhand, since two spellings each producing one zone agree perfectly.

Full `pkg/config` green, canaries green, gofmt clean.

Closes #8794

## PR #8803 — config: complete the interface-unit admission chains, both of them [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8755-chain`

Part of #8755.

A brace-elided interface unit silently lost its address **or** its firewall filter
binding, on a commit reporting success with **zero warnings**. The filter case is a
fail-open: an operator binds a filter, the commit succeeds, no filter is applied —
and it emits **fewer** warnings than the correct spelling, because nothing is left
to warn about. A quieter commit is the signal an operator reads as healthier.

## Two symptoms, two mechanisms

The issue names both losses together and **they are not one defect.** They need
different numbers of chain links — measured, not inferred from the shared shape:

| spelling | links needed | state before |
|---|---|---|
| `family inet address 10.0.0.1/24;` | **one** | `(inet, address)` unadmitted → pass folded **0** times; the statement stayed one node |
| `family inet filter input f1;` | **two** | `(inet, filter)` **was** admitted → folded **1** time, to `family inet` + `filter input f1`, then stopped: `(filter, input)` was not in |

The filter half is the instructive one: **a scope entry existed, it fired, and it
delivered nothing.** Admission is a chain and only the first link was in. #8763
recorded that as `chain-incomplete` rather than leaving it to be rediscovered,
precisely because an admitted pair reads as coverage.

Had the two been treated as one defect, admitting `(filter, input)` would have
"fixed #8755" while the address half stayed broken with a green suite — **the two
symptoms have no link in common.**

## Four pairs admitted, reach checked against the schema

`inet address`, `inet6 address`, `filter input`, `filter output`.

Both heads exist under other containers, and pair scoping is what keeps them out —
checked by walking `setSchema`, not by asking the inventory (a census of divergent
*sites* answers a different question):

- `filter` is also `firewall family inet filter <name>` (args:1, children
  `{term, interface-specific}`) — **no** `input`/`output` child, so
  `(filter, input)` cannot reach it. Exactly two paths each, both the interface unit.
- `inet` is also under firewall, forwarding-options, protocols bgp and rib-group.
  **None** has an `address` child. `(inet, address)` reaches exactly one path.

A head-only rule would have been wrong for both.

## Three-way measurement, absolute assertions

A packed-vs-braced comparison goes green whenever **both** spellings drop the
value — exactly this defect's shape. So every case also compiles a **baseline**
with the statement removed, and the cell `Fatal`s if the baseline already
satisfies the expectation: that would mean the fixture cannot distinguish a
delivered value from a default.

## PR #8804 — config: declare `address` under source NAT pool (#8800) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8800-nat-pool-address`

Closes #8800

`security nat source pool <p> address <a>;` — the brace-elided ("packed") spelling — compiled to a pool with **zero addresses**, while `pool <p> { address <a>; }` compiled correctly.

## Cause

Neither the fold nor an under-declared arity — the two prior causes in this family. **`address` was never declared as a schema child of `pool`.** The compiler has read it since #4521 (multi-value: `Keys[1:]` plus block children), but with no declaration `isBody` is false, so the brace-elision pass was never *asked* about `("pool","address")` and no scope entry could ever have named the site. That is also why it appears in no census: the inventory is built by running the pass, and the pass never saw it.

`pool port-overloading-factor` and `pool routing-instance` were already admitted — `address` was the one missing sibling of an otherwise in-scope container.

## Both NAT pools, not one

The first version of this PR fixed only the **source** pool, and that was a partial fix that read as complete. `compileNATDestination` reads `address` under a **destination** NAT pool too (`parseDNATPoolAddress`, which deliberately walks every token so `address <ip> port <n>` captures both), and that pool declared `children: nil` — the identical defect at the sibling path:

```

packed        addr=""          port=0     strict REJECTS   <- defect
braced-port   addr=10.0.0.5/32 port=8080  strict accepts
packed-port   addr=""          port=0     strict REJECTS   <- defect
```

After declaring it, all four agree and `packed-port` carries both the address and port 8080.

**What hid it is worth stating, because it generalises.** The scope predicate is **pair-keyed**: the `("pool","address")` entry added for the source pool *already* applied to the destination pool. Inspecting the scope list would have shown the pair present and looked correct while this path stayed broken. Only the schema declaration was missing, and only at one of the two containers. Found by asking which other container the same compiler-arm shape appears in — not by a test failing.

## Severity, measured rather than inferred

- The **strict commit path already rejected** the zero-address pool (`... has no pool addresses; the rule commits but the dataplane marks the pool unusable (EmptyPool) and drops it at runtime`). It failed **closed** and was **loud at commit** — no silent commit, no fail-open leak.
- **Flat `set` was never affected** (verified through `SchemaValidate`, not only the compiler).

So this was a config-file-only defect, which is why it is a small change rather than an urgent one.

## Fix — two parts, both required

Declare `address` in `setSchema` so the pass asks, **and** admit `("pool","address")` in `compactNormalizeInScope` so it says yes. Declaring alone was measured to leave the packed spelling still compiling to zero addresses.

A second symptom of the same missing declaration: completion never offered `address` after `set security nat source pool <p>`.

## PR #8805 — cluster: bound the persistent-NAT lease count before allocating from it [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8792-lease-count-bounds`

Closes #8792

`decodePersistentNatLeasePayload` sized its preallocation from the 4-byte record count taken straight off the wire, and the loop's bounds check sat one line **below** the `make()` it was meant to protect:

```go
count := int(binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(buf))
out := make([]userspace.IdleLeaseWire, 0, count)   // sized from the wire
for i := 0; i < count; i++ {
    if off+4 > len(buf) { return out, false }      // correct, and unreachable
}
```

A four-byte frame of `ff ff ff ff` asks for 2^32−1 records of 112 bytes — about 448 GiB — before a single length prefix has been read. Each record costs at least its own 4-byte length prefix, so the body holds at most `(len(buf)-4)/4`; a count above that cannot describe the frame under any encoding and is now refused **before** the allocation.

### Refused rather than clamped, unlike the DHCP sibling

That decoder carries this bound under "the #7175 discipline" — which this function's doc comment already cited — but it separates a wrong *count* from lost *data* and tolerates the former, a tolerance its own cell pins. This one's bool means "decoded **completely**", and a full-set push **replaces** the peer set, so installing whatever fit would delete every lease past the point the sender's count went wrong. The divergence is deliberate and now recorded at both ends.

### What this does not claim

Not that it stops a crash. Whether the oversized allocation is fatal is a property of the **host**: `112 × (2^32−1)` stays under the runtime's `maxAlloc` so no `makeslice` panic is inherent, and under `overcommit_memory=1` the mapping can succeed unbacked and the process survives to discard the frame. The invariant repaired here holds everywhere — a count the body cannot physically hold is rejected before the allocation.

Reachability, stated precisely: a supported **unkeyed** control segment, plus a malfunctioning or malicious **legitimate peer** on a keyed one. No Internet-facing exposure was established.

Worth keeping: the receive loop's `defer` only disconnects. It is not a recovery boundary, so wrapping the decoder in `recover()` is not a fix even where the allocation *is* fatal — a Go runtime OOM is a `fatal error`, not a panic.

### The guard measures the allocation, not only the return values

This is the assertion that earned itself. **A bound applied one line too late produces identical return values** — `ok=false`, zero leases — so an outcome-only cell is green on the defect.

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| bound removed (the original defect) | killed |
| bound moved **below** the `make` (outcome identical) | **killed by the allocation budget alone** |
| checked subtraction reverted | **escaped** |

The third is reported rather than fixed: with the count bounded, neither operand can overflow on any reachable input, so the subtraction form is shape hygiene and not part of the repair. The code says so at the line, so it is not later mistaken for load-bearing.

**The cell deliberately does not use `0xFFFFFFFF`.** A guard whose regression mode is to allocate hundreds of gigabytes does not fail — it takes the suite, and possibly the machine, with it. Every count in it is impossible for its buffer while staying trivially small, so a revert reds in milliseconds. The allocation probe uses `1<<20` (~112 MiB if the bound is bypassed): unmistakable against GC noise, survivable anywhere.

### Docs

`docs/sync-protocol.md` gains the rule rather than the instance — a wire-advertised count is untrusted, the bound is `(len(body)-4)/4`, the check must precede the allocation, the two decoders' answers differ deliberately, and a test for this class must assert the invariant rather than a crash.

## PR #8809 — config: the IPv6 forwarding mode was read from a shape nothing produces [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8797-inet6-mode`

Part of #8797.

`forwarding-options family inet6 mode <flow-based|packet-based>` compiled to an
empty value **in every spelling an operator can write**. The leaf completes, `?`
help describes it, commit returns success, `show configuration` renders it back —
and `ForwardingOptions.FamilyInet6Mode` stayed `""`.

## It was not unread, which is the part that matters

#8797 recorded this as "declared and accepted with no reader", measured with a
baseline-with-the-statement-removed: `braced == baseline`, and `packet-based ==
flow-based`. **Both observations were right and the diagnosis they suggested was
wrong.**

There *is* a reader. `compileForwardingOptions` descended
`FindChild("family") → FindChild("inet6") → FindChild("mode")` — a **two-level**
lookup. But `family` is declared `compoundKey`, so the parser **and** `SetPath`
both produce **one** node with `Keys=["family","inet6"]`; the address family is
part of the node's key, not a child of it.

| spelling | before |
|---|---|
| `family inet6 { mode packet-based; }` (NewParser) | `""` |
| `family inet6 mode packet-based;` (one-liner) | `""` |
| `set forwarding-options family inet6 mode …` (**what operators type**) | `""` |
| `family { inet6 { mode packet-based; } }` | `"packet-based"` |

The one shape that worked is the split form the #2419 census synthesizes and
nothing else emits. **The leaf looked unread because every spelling that could
reach it missed, and the one that hit is not a spelling.**

This is the **same defect as #8763's traversal bug** — a two-level lookup against
a one-node compound key — in a compiler instead of the normalizer. That class has
now appeared in the normalizer, in a guard's own tree walk, and here. The
`compoundKey` shape is the one people model wrongly.

## Testing

Four hierarchical spellings plus the **flat `set`** form — the one that matters
here: it is what an operator types, it went through the broken path, and a
hierarchical-only test would have reported this fixed while
`set forwarding-options family inet6 mode packet-based` still compiled to `""`.

A baseline leg asserts the field is empty with no statement, so a green cannot be
a default. The **value** is asserted, not just presence: `flow-based` and
`packet-based` must compile to *different* values, since them compiling to the
same thing was half the original symptom.

## PR #8812 — config: fan out bracketed groups for device-map and OSPF interfaces [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/device-map-interface-group`

## The defect

`chassis device-map interface [ ge-0/0/1 ge-0/0/2 ] { pci … }` compiled to **one** entry — `namedInstances` takes `Keys[1]` and discards `Keys[2:]`. The second NIC vanished and was governed by `unmapped-interface-policy` instead. Under `manage-down` that brings it **down**, and on bare metal (#1956 §9.6) the console is the only fallback.

## The remedy is NOT "map both NICs", and that correction is the point

A grouped statement shares **one body**, and a device-map body must carry a per-NIC stable identity (`pci` or `mac`). Two NICs cannot share a PCI address, so the grouped spelling **can never be valid**.

```
BEFORE  interface [ a b ] { pci X }   ACCEPTED, entries=1
AFTER   same input                    REJECTED: "PCI address … is bound to both
                                      ge-0/0/1 and ge-0/0/2 — one NIC cannot be
                                      two interfaces"
```

**The fan-out converts a silent misconfiguration into a commit rejection**, by letting the existing duplicate-identity validator *see the second name at all*. Before it, that name did not exist, so no conflict could be detected — the validator was not broken, it was blind.

**My first guard demanded two entries and failed against the correct behaviour.** Reading *why* it failed — the message named both NICs and the shared PCI — produced the right remedy. Adjusting the cell until it passed would have driven the compiler to accept a config that cannot be meant.

## The same syntax wants opposite outcomes on the two containers

OSPF interfaces legitimately share a body (`metric`, `passive`), so `area <a> interface [ a b ] { metric 10; }` must **create** both — and now does (1 → 2).

> Create-N where the body is shareable, **reject** where it must carry a per-instance identity. A fan-out is right in both cases; only the container's semantics say what happens next.

## Scope, deliberate

Five `namedInstances(...FindChildren("interface"))` sites exist. The other two — `nat proxy-arp` and `router-advertisement` — have the same mechanism and **unmeasured** severity, so they are named rather than fixed blind. Unlike #8794's zones, the five enumerate **disjoint stanzas**, so a partial fix cannot produce the compiler-vs-validator disagreement that made the partial #8802 worse than the bug. Checked, not assumed.

Helper renamed `zoneGroupInstances8794` → `bracketedGroupInstances8794`: named for the shape now that zones are not its only caller.

## Validation

| mutant | fails |
|---|---|
| revert the chassis site | device-map cell **alone** |
| revert the OSPF site | OSPF cell **alone** |

0 residual. Guards assert **absolute outcomes** — the grouped device-map is rejected *and the rejection names both NICs*; both OSPF interfaces are created — never grouped == longhand. **The `manage-down` arm is asserted explicitly**, since a cell exercising only the default policy measures the mild half.

## PR #8813 — docs: the dual AST shape is a BRACING choice, not flat-set vs hierarchical [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8808-ast-shape-docs`

Part of #8808.

Three project docs taught that flat `set` produces a different AST shape from the
hierarchical spelling, using `family inet dhcp` as the example:

```
Hierarchical `family inet { dhcp; }` -> Node{Keys:["family","inet"]} with children
Flat `set … family inet dhcp`        -> Node{Keys:["family"]} with child Node{Keys:["inet"]}
```

**The second line is false, and it is false for the example it uses.**

## Measured

```
FLAT  "set interfaces eth0 unit 0 family inet dhcp" ->
  [interfaces] [eth0] [unit 0] [family inet] [dhcp]
HIER  interfaces { eth0 { unit 0 { family inet { dhcp; } } } } ->
  [interfaces] [eth0] [unit 0] [family inet] [dhcp]
```

**Byte-identical.** `SetPath` descends a `compoundKey` container exactly as the
parser does (`ast_edit.go:506`, `:850`, `:999`).

Checked across four shapes — the compound `family`, a **non-compound** chain
(`bgp group neighbor peer-as`), nested containers (`security policy match`), and a
bracketed list — and flat and hierarchical agree in **every one**.

That last point matters. The obvious repair is *"keep the general dual-shape point,
it still holds for non-compound containers."* **It does not.** Flat and hierarchical
agree there too, so correcting only the `family inet` example would have left a
second false statement behind.

## The real axis is bracing — three shapes, not two

| spelling | tree | |
|---|---|---|
| `family inet { dhcp; }` | `[family inet]` + child `[dhcp]` | COMPOUND |
| `family { inet { dhcp; } }` | `[family]` → `[inet]` → `[dhcp]` | SPLIT |
| `family inet dhcp;` | `[family inet dhcp]` | PACKED (#2419) |

A compiler must handle all three. The **SPLIT** form is where a bare
`Node{Keys:["family"]}` with an `inet` child actually comes from — an operator
bracing the family separately, never a `set` command.

## Why a doc line is worth a change

It is false **in the direction that makes people skip a measurement.** It says the
flat surface has a different shape, so a defect proven against the compound shape
reads as inapplicable to `set` input. That inference was drawn during #8763 and the

## PR #8816 — config: NAT pool address must be groupReplace, not leaf-list UNION [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8804-groupreplace-union`

**Fixes a regression that is live on master right now.** Follow-up to #8800 / #8804.

#8804 declared `address` under the source NAT pool with `multi: true`, which made the leaf **leaf-list eligible** — `isLeafListSchema` requires `multi` — so apply-groups switched it from scalar **OVERRIDE** to token **UNION**. An inline `address` then merges with the group's instead of replacing it, and a NAT pool carries an address the operator believed they had replaced.

```
group  address 10.0.0.9/32;   inline  address 10.0.0.1/32;

before #8804   addresses=1 [10.0.0.1/32]   OVERRIDE, correct
after  #8804   addresses=2 [both]          UNION, regression
master today   addresses=2 [both]          still live
```

## The fix is `groupReplace`, and the alternative was measured rather than argued

`groupReplace`'s own contract describes this leaf exactly: *a multi leaf that packs a SEPARATOR onto its value list is not a set, so token-level union/dedup would corrupt it* — citing a port range packing `to`. The NAT pool address leaf packs `to` for a `<low> to <high>` range. Setting the flag reverts it to the safe pre-#4070 OVERRIDE, which is precisely the pre-#8804 behaviour.

The obvious alternative — drop `multi` — is wrong, and three states were measured on master to establish that rather than reasoned about:

| | union regression | existing NAT cells |
|---|---|---|
| master as-is | `addresses=2` **broken** | 0 failing |
| drop `multi` | `addresses=1` fixed | **14 FAILING** |
| add `groupReplace`, keep `multi` | `addresses=1` fixed | **0 failing** |

`multi` governs **flat-set token absorption**, not validation: it is why `set ... address <low> to <high>` and the bracket-list form reach the compiler as ONE leaf. Dropping it leaves `SchemaValidate` accepting every spelling identically — validation is not the property `multi` governs — while silently changing the compiled result, redding #4521, #4422, #5144, #6812 and the deterministic-NAT flat-set family.

**Reasoning from "SchemaValidate is unchanged" to "multi is unnecessary" is the specific mistake this change's comment exists to stop being repeated.** I made it, and the full suite was the only thing that caught it — a targeted run over the cells I had just written passed.

## Why `groupReplace` rather than dropping `multi`, stated for the history

Keeping `multi` and adding `groupReplace` is not merely the smaller change — it is the one that preserves behaviour in both directions. Dropping `multi` would have fixed the merge semantics **by giving up the multi-value spellings**: `address <low> to <high>` and `address [ a b ]` stop reaching the compiler as one leaf. `groupReplace` keeps both working and restores only the scalar-override merge behaviour.

## Reviewer arms attempted, and the scope of the exception

Recorded rather than summarised as "reviewed", because a record that reads stronger than its evidence is the defect class this change belongs to:

- **Codex** — worked on the third attempt (the first hung on stdin; the forwarder subagent returned a job id with no entry in the local state DB). **It found this regression.**
- **AGY** — failed all three attempts on a documented plugin bug (`--print took "--print-timeout" as its prompt`), including with a short focus and with no timeout argument. An infra outage, not a review outcome.
- **Claude SMR** — my own arm; on the parent change it found the destination-pool half.

So: two working arms and one infra outage. Not a clean triple, and this body says so.

## Guard

`TestNATPoolAddressGroupOverride8804` asserts the override **and** carries a degeneracy control: with no inline address the group's value must still be inherited, so the cell cannot pass by apply-groups failing entirely. Its failure message names `groupReplace` and warns off the multi-removal fix, since that is the plausible-looking wrong repair.

Mutation-checked: removing `groupReplace` (i.e. master today) reds the cell; restoring it greens.

## PR #8817 — config: declare `address` under the DESTINATION NAT pool [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8800-destination-pool-address`

Follow-up to #8800, which fixed the **source** NAT pool only. The destination pool has the identical defect and it is **still live on master** (confirmed at `7bff3b595`).

```
braced        addr=10.0.0.5/32 port=0     strict accepts
packed        addr=""          port=0     strict REJECTS   <- defect
braced-port   addr=10.0.0.5/32 port=8080  strict accepts
packed-port   addr=""          port=0     strict REJECTS   <- defect
```

`compileNATDestination` reads `address` here — `parseDNATPoolAddress` deliberately walks every token so `address <ip> port <n>` captures both — but the pool declared `children: nil`. The head was therefore not a schema child, the brace-elision pass was never *asked* about it, and the packed spelling compiled to an empty address. After the declaration all four agree, with `packed-port` correctly carrying both the address and port 8080.

## Severity is LOW and it fails LOUD

The packed spelling is **rejected at commit**, with a message naming the pool and the consequence, so an operator gets a clear error rather than a silent misconfiguration. That is the opposite of the source-pool case as originally reported, and it should not be ranked against the #8781-class fail-opens.

## What made this half invisible — the generalisable part

The scope predicate is **pair-keyed**, so the `("pool","address")` entry added for the source pool *already* covered this path: `inScope("pool","address")` returned **true** here while the path was still broken. **Checking the scope list would have shown the pair present and looked correct.**

That is a blind spot distinct from the pass-driven and position-blind ones in this family, and nastier than either, because the instrument returns **true** rather than zero. A missing entry is visible; a *satisfied* predicate over a still-broken path is not. No test failing would have surfaced it.

It was found by asking which other container the same compiler-arm shape appears in. The cheap general form, which has now caught three defects:

> **When the code names one member of a declared pair, the other is a candidate by construction** — `source`/`destination`, `ike`/`ipsec`, `inet`/`inet6`, `input`/`output`.

## `groupReplace`

Set for the same reason as the source leaf (#8816), and this leaf needs it more: its value list packs `port`, so apply-groups token UNION corrupts the **address** outright rather than merely over-collecting. Measured — inheriting `address 10.0.0.2/32 port 8080;` over an inline `address 10.0.0.1/32 port 80;` compiled the address as `"8080"`. Pinned by `TestDestinationNATPoolAddressGroupOverride8800`.

## Guard changes

- Two packed-vs-braced cells (`address`, `address-port`) plus the group-override guard.
- **#8690 scope arm** gains one entry, hand-measured as that bucket's failure message requires: with a valid value the pass makes packed agree with braced; with a **malformed** value the single-host-address gate still **rejects** under the pass and only the reason changes — so no gate is disarmed. The verdict and its measurement are stored **with the entry**, not only in the commit message, because a hand measurement that lives in a commit message is invisible at the point someone next reads the bucket.
- **#7484 floor 702 → 703**, re-measured at this head rather than derived by adding one, with blind holding at 364.

## PR #8818 — config: the NAT address-range cap rejected on the LENIENT path, so a persisted config could not boot [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `work/8814-nat-range-lenient`

Part of #8814.

`address <low> to <high>` in a NAT pool expands to one address per IP and is
capped at 256. The cap was raised as a **compiler** error inside
`expandAddressRange`, so it fired on the lenient path as well as the strict one:

```
braced, 257 IPs   CompileConfigLenient -> FAILS TO LOAD
braced, 256 IPs   CompileConfigLenient -> loads
```

`CompileConfigLenient`'s own doc says it exists *"so an upgraded node boots
through"*. A braced oversized range **could not boot through, on master, before
any recent change** — #8800 only removed the accident that hid the same failure
for the packed spelling.

The chain is `compileSecurity → compileNATSource → appendPoolAddresses` and carries
no `compileOpts`, so there was no seam at which to downgrade it.

## Why the cap is NOT moved out of the compiler

The issue proposed moving it into a strict validator. Measured, the widest legal
spelling is:

```
address 0.0.0.0/32 to 255.255.255.255/32   ->  4294967296 IPs
```

An expansion with no bound would try to allocate **4.29 billion strings on the
lenient path — the boot path.** That trades a load failure for an OOM.

So the bound **stays** in `expandAddressRange` and only the **error** becomes a
recorded fact — the shape `NATPool.PortRangeInvalidSpec` and
`FirewallFilterTerm.UnknownFrom` (#3307) already use in this package, and the
narrower of the two options you named: **no signature change to `compileSecurity`.**

| path | behaviour |
|---|---|
| strict (commit / commit-check) | REJECTS, naming the cap |
| tolerant (load / peer-sync) | warns; the pool loads **without** that range |

A size failure is separated by sentinel from a **malformed** one. Size has a safe
fallback — omit the range — and malformed input does not, so `low > high`, a
non-IP endpoint, and IPv6 endpoints still fail on **both** paths. A sentinel that
swallowed parse errors would turn this into a silent-acceptance bug, the class the
NAT gate family exists to prevent.

newlines as whitespace and merges every set line into one node, so a measurement
taken through it describes a tree nobody has (#8808).

The cells assert the **recorded field** as well as the address count and the strict
verdict. Recording is what connects the two paths — a fix that loaded leniently but
recorded nothing would leave the strict gate with nothing to reject, and the
address count alone cannot see that.

| oversized reverts to a hard error | KILLED |
| the record is dropped | KILLED |

## PR #8820 — config: land the arity census as a ratchet with its blindness stated (#8807) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `feat/8807-census-guards`

Lands the arity census (#8787's predicate A) as a **ratchet with its own blindness in the failure text and its mutation control in the cell**, rather than as a one-off report. Partial progress on #8807; the positional predicate itself is not built and this says so.

## Why an instrument at all

#8787 ran this census once, fixed some rows, and left nothing behind — so the class can reappear silently. Worse, it recorded the predicate as *"control-validated"* using `pre-shared-key`, a row that **kept firing after #8777 fixed it**, because a *correct* `args: 1` sibling at `security ipsec vpn` matched by name.

> **A control that still fires after its own fix cannot distinguish fixed from broken.**

That is nastier than a control that never fires, because a firing control looks like diligence.

## Container-keying: 12 hits → 6

Each compiler `case` clause is now paired with the innermost enclosing `range ... FindChildren("X")` container and compared only against schema declarations under a node of that name.

**The validation is not the reduction — it is the agreement.** The six rows removed were `preempt`, `inet6`, `match`, `local-identity`, `remote-identity`, `pre-shared-key`: **exactly** the false-pairing and already-fixed sets from the hand adjudication, with no overlap error in either direction. A mechanical predicate independently reproducing a human adjudication is a much stronger result than "it found fewer things".

And `pre-shared-key` dropping out is the specific point: the successor **fixes a named defect in the predecessor**, so the control goes quiet when the defect is fixed.

## Result: 12 hits, ZERO defects

`reject` and `then` were the last two genuine candidates. lane-8015 measured both with an absent baseline and a reachability check: every spelling delivers, a bogus `reject` message-type is a **loud commit rejection** via the `UnknownActions` path rather than a silent drop, and both values reach real consumers.

So the arity-contradiction class is **empty at this head**. That is a result, not a null — and it cost four false-pairing adjudications to establish. The ratchet fired for real to record it:

```
genuine arity candidates FELL to 0 ([]) -- THIS IS A GOOD FAILURE.
Set arityGenuineFloor8807 = 0. Leaving it at 2 gives the next regression that much room to hide.
```

One real residue: **completion under-offers** for both leaves, because the compiler is *ahead* of the schema — the mirror of the #8773 rule. lane-8015 is landing that separately.

## The three properties this guard has to keep

**1. Ratchet, not equality.** The hit set is asserted against a hand adjudication, because a hit is a *candidate* and not a defect — a new one reds with instructions to confirm the site and the declaration are the same path **first**, then measure braced-vs-packed. The genuine count is ratcheted in **both** directions; a drop is a good failure that must tighten the constant.

**2. The blindness is in the failure text, and it has been seen to render.** I forced a real red to confirm it appears — a failure message is only correct if you have watched it fail. It states three limits:

- **Name-keying.** It localises a site only when the container is lexically recoverable; the four remaining false pairings are all sites where it is not.
- **Existence.** In *either* mode it is blind to a leaf undeclared at its own position while declared elsewhere, because it can only pair with declarations that exist. That is the #8800 shape, and **no arity predicate can see it** — it is an existence question.
- **Constant index only.** Found by lane-8015 while checking a row here: `parsePolicyTermInlineKeys` (`compiler_routing.go:1269`) consumes a following token via a *variable* index and is invisible. So a keyword can have sites this predicate reports **and** sites it cannot see, and a row's recorded evidence may describe only the visible half — which is exactly what the `then` row did before it was corrected.

So green means *"no new arity contradiction this predicate can localise"*, never *"the class is covered"*.

**3. The mutation control lives in the cell and asserts both halves in one run.** It re-breaks #8796 by narrowing both `gateway local-identity` declarations and requires the row to appear; requires silence on the unmutated tree; and requires the restore to have restored. **Either half alone is satisfiable by a dead instrument** — one by something that always fires, the other by something that never does. Verified by a meta-mutation: blinding the census reds both cells.

## Residual blindness, stated beside the ratchet

The four unlocalisable sites are unlocalisable for two concrete reasons — a bare `range node.Children`, where the container is whatever the caller passed and is not written at the site (`count`, `reject`, `then`), or a variable bound further up the function (`from-zone`, `interface`, `pool`, `match`). Recovering those needs the **call path**, not a lexical walk, which is the positional predicate #8807 exists to build and the reason it is separate work rather than a bigger regex.

## PR #8826 — config: declare what the compiler already reads, so completion stops under-offering [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/completion-reject-then`

Part of #8807 — the residue its census surfaced. Not a close: that issue is about building the positional predicate.

Two leaves the **compiler reads more of than the schema declared**:

| leaf | compiler | schema |
|---|---|---|
| `firewall … term then reject` | reads a message type from `Keys[1]` **or a child** | declared neither |
| `policy-options policy-statement then` | **iterates this node's children** for the policy default action | declared a bare leaf |

Nothing was dropped, because neither compiler path consults the schema. The symptom went to the other surface — completion and `?` help offered nothing where the compiler accepts something:

```
then reject <TAB>                 n=0  ->  n=14
policy-statement <p> then <TAB>   n=0  ->  n=2   [accept reject]
term <t> then <TAB>  (control)    n=12 ->  n=12
```

### This is the #8773 docs rule running backwards

`docs/config-schema.md` records that adding a schema leaf is a *compiler-behaviour* change, because the packed reader resolves its tail through the schema and an undeclared-but-compiled leaf drops **silently**. Here the compiler is **ahead** of the schema instead, so nothing drops and completion **under-offers**. Two directions, two very different symptoms, one relationship.

### Declared as children rather than `args:1` + enum — on a measurement

The args form adds no leaves and is tidier by the numbers. It was tried: every compiled spelling survives it, and `then reject <TAB>` still offers only `<[Enter]>`, so **it does not fix the defect**. The children form was chosen because it works, and because the compiler already reads the child shape (`then { reject { tcp-reset; } }` compiles today).

### A schema declaration is not monotone, so compilation was measured

Nine spellings captured **before** the change and byte-identical after: bare / packed / braced / child-form `reject`, all three policy-statement spellings, the typo rejection (`then reject nonsense` still refused — that gate is the compiler's `UnknownActions`, not the schema's), and **apply-groups inheritance** of a reject message type, which is the surface where an earlier schema change caused a live regression.

### The guard asserts both halves in one cell

The newly declared paths offer their values **and** the untouched control still offers twelve. A completion guard asserting only `n>0` on the fixed paths is satisfied by a completer that matches everything; one asserting only the control is satisfied by a completer that regressed the fix. **Either alone is satisfied by a stuck answer.**

### Two ratchet movements, both deliberate and explained at the constant

- **`valueMoves` 1 → 0 (tightened).** Its single member was `policy-options policy-statement <*> then` — a leaf whose value demonstrably reached the compiler while the gate could not compare its spellings. Declaring the children emptied the class. A zero here is a claim, not an absence.
- **`flag` 179 → 209 (raised).** The 30 new members are the reject message types (14 per family) and the two default actions. They are enum **values** modelled as child keywords, not configuration leaves: `tcp-reset` *is* the value, so there is no second spelling for a differential to compare, and they can never leave this class however the gate improves — unlike the other 179, where "make them compare" is a real option.

### And the #8807 census ratchet

It landed mid-flight and correctly fired: declaring the `then` children removes that row. The cell asks that a vanished hit be distinguished from a broken instrument, so — **`reject` is still reported by the same run.** Had the glob or schema walk broken, both would have vanished together. `arityGenuineFloor8807` stays 0: `then` was measured *benign*, so resolving it moves the hit count, not the defect count.

### Validation

Full `go test ./...` green tree-wide — 72 packages ok, 0 FAIL, counted; `gofmt -l` clean; both declarations mutated **separately** (different arms) and each kills the cell.

The flat-set cell asserted `serr != nil` — that strict compilation returned **an** error, not that the **range cap** returned it. Both the pool row and the proxy-arp leg had that shape.

`err != nil` is a **proxy** for the property, and a future change can satisfy it without the property holding. If a schema tightening on `to`, a new required sibling, or a validator reordering makes strict reject this input for an unrelated reason, **the cap gate can be deleted and the cell stays green** — pinning "something rejects this line", which is not what #8814 is about.

```
proxy-arp  "NTF_PROXY neighbour per address"
```

Deliberately narrower than `"capped at"`: a future unrelated cap would contain that, and the point is that an unrelated rejection must not satisfy this cell. If a gate's wording changes, the cell fails loudly and a human re-points it — the intended cost. It cannot silently start accepting a different gate's rejection.

With the pool gate mutated to reject with an **unrelated** message — simulating *"cap gone, something else rejects"*:

|---|---|
| OLD (`serr != nil`) | **ok — SURVIVES** |

The failure reads *"strict rejected, but NOT with the range-cap gate"* — the right branch, not a generic red. **A mutant caught by the wrong branch reads as a working guard**, so the branch was checked and not just the verdict.

Its error is now checked in the flat helper. This cell's own assertions (pool non-nil, address count, recorded count, proxy-arp `recorded == 1`) would catch a partial tree **today**, so this is robustness rather than live vacuity — worth doing because a helper of this shape gets copied into a cell with weaker assertions, where the positive control is gone. ## PR #8831 — config: read a packed `security alg <proto>` stanza [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8823-alg-packed`

`security { alg ftp disable; }` compiled to `FTPDisable=FALSE` on a **clean commit**. All four wired protos measure false in that spelling — an operator disabling an ALG gets a success and an ALG still **enabled**.

## A fourth spelling nobody listed is worse than the reported one

Testing the adjacent shape found `alg ftp { disable; }` — proto packed onto `alg`, body as a child — and it does not merely drop:

```
alg ftp disable;          ftp=false  unsupported=[]            silent drop
alg ftp { disable; }      ftp=false  unsupported=[disable]     WRONG advisory
alg h323 { gatekeeper; }             unsupported=[gatekeeper]  WRONG name
```

The #4232 advisory exists to report a proto the dataplane does not wire. In the mixed spelling it named `disable` and `gatekeeper` — a keyword and a sub-statement — **as protocols**. A reader acting on that goes looking for an ALG that does not exist. **An advisory built to catch silent drops was itself silent in one spelling and misleading in another.**

## The remedy was measured, not reasoned

I have twice reached for a remedy without checking what the codebase already does with the shape, so both candidates were run:

| remedy | dns/ftp/sip/tftp | h323 |
|---|---|---|
| schema-side: admit `("alg",<proto>)` | **fixed** | **NOT fixed** |
| compiler-side packed read | **fixed** | **fixed** |

Admitting the pair **cannot** reach an undeclared proto: the pass asks *nothing* for `h323` (measured `asked=[]`) — the #8800 signature — and declaring unsupported protos so it would ask defeats the advisory those declarations exist to preserve.

**So the site is both classes at once** — unadmitted-pair for the four declared, #8800 for the rest — and only a compiler-side read covers both. It mirrors `algDisabled`, which already reads a packed tail one level down, and matches #8795.

The **early return** matters as much as the read: children of a packed `alg <proto>` belong to the *proto*, and letting the old loop also see them is what produced `unsupported=[disable]`.

## Validation

Three mutants, each caught with a **distinct blast radius** rather than a shared red:

| mutant | fails | branch |
|---|---|---|
| revert the packed branch | 10 subtests | value: *"ALG is still ENABLED"* |
| drop the children check | exactly the 4 mixed-spelling protos | value |
| remove the early return | exactly 1 — the mixed advisory | `UnsupportedProtos=[h323 gatekeeper]` |

0 residual. Guards assert the **value**, never that the commit succeeded — every broken cell committed cleanly (`CompileConfig` returned nil for all twelve), so a commit-succeeded assertion is vacuous here **by construction**. Four protos × four spellings, plus the advisory in all three h323 spellings.

**Touches no schema file**, so it is disjoint from the `schema_security.go` region work in flight (#8824, #8825).

Full `pkg/config` green, canaries green, gofmt clean.

Closes #8823

## PR #8833 — config: build the positional predicate, both directions (#8807) [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `feat/8807-positional-predicate`

Builds the positional predicate #8807 specifies and #8787 explicitly deferred — **both directions, with both acceptance controls passing**.

**No close keyword, deliberately.** team-lead owns #8807 and is closing it with a caveat in the closing comment. See "What this does not establish" below — there is a real soundness gap and it should be read before the issue closes.

## Direction 1 — read at P, undeclared at P

The class every keyword-anywhere check passes silently: a head declared *somewhere* but missing at the path the compiler reads it. A head declared **nowhere** is #8787's predicate B and is excluded by design.

**Control (#8800): passes.** Removing the `address` declaration from both NAT pools makes the predicate report `pool / address`; restoring silences it; the restore is asserted so a later cell cannot inherit a broken tree.

5 hits: 3 are **#8825** (a packed `application-set` loses its members), 2 are **benign** — `vpn / gateway` and `vpn / ipsec-policy` compile identically in both nestings. **A candidate is not a finding: assuming would have over-reported by 40%.**

## Direction 2 — declared at P, unread at P (the converse)

The predicate that defeated #8787's predicate C five times. **Control (#8785): passes**, and both halves run — it must report `proposal / description`, and must *not* report `proposal / dh-group`, which the same compiler does read.

9 hits: one is #8785; **eight are pinned as `unmeasured`** under a ceiling that ratchets down and must never rise. "Not measured" is a third state, not a pass.

## Three earlier versions failed, and the failures are in the file

1. **Reusing the arity census's site collector** — the #8800 control **failed**. That collector records only clauses containing a constant `Keys[i]`; the #8800 site reads `prop.Keys[1:]`, a slice. The control caught a predicate that otherwise looked like it worked.
2. **Nearest enclosing `FindChildren`** — 104 hits with obvious noise (`ids-option / ping-death`), because a switch often iterates a *nested* child and the nearest container is then an ancestor.
3. **Requiring the immediate range to iterate that container's DIRECT children** — 5.

Plus a bug in the schema walk: keying `seen` on the node alone meant a node reached under a second container name recorded no children, so that name looked like a container declaring nothing. Keyed on `(node, name)` now; it had manufactured three false hits.

## The filter I rejected, recorded because it is tempting

An **unambiguous-container** filter cuts the converse from 60 hits to 2. It also **excludes the #8785 control itself**, because `proposal` has two schema paths. A filter that kills its own control invalidates everything downstream of it — #8787's recorded lesson about predicate A. The 60→2 reduction looks like a win and is not.

The coverage gate used instead is **not tuned to save the control**: it passes at 50%, 60%, 70% *and* 80%. The threshold was chosen for signal-to-noise (26 hits at 50%, 9 at 70%), and the sweep is in the file so that stays checkable.

## What this does NOT establish

**The #8785 control proves sensitivity, not soundness** — that the instrument fires when it should, never that it fires *only* when it should. Blindness item (5) states the specific hole:

The converse marks a head as READ if any `.Name()` clause at that container names it. **It never checks the clause does anything with the value.** A clause reading into nothing is scored as a read and the row goes quiet — which is #8785's own defect with a clause in front of it. `description` under `security ike proposal` is caught **only because no clause exists**.

That is the same mistake one level up from the `then next` retraction: #8787 called it clean by checking `Action` when the value lands in `NextTerm`. **Checking for the existence of a read rather than for where the value lands.** Answering "unread" properly needs whole compiled results compared with and without the statement, warnings included — behavioural, not AST. **Filed as #8830.**

And the sharper form of the same point: the #8785 control passing is **partly luck about which form #8785 took**. Had it been the clause-that-drops variant, the control would have failed and that would have been visible. A control whose success is contingent on an incidental property of the case it was built from is not measuring what a green run reads as measuring.

All five blindnesses are in the **failure text**, not comments, and were confirmed to render by forcing a real red.

Validation: `go test ./pkg/config/` green; `go build ./...` clean. Every control mutation-checked in both directions.

## PR #8834 — config: refuse an unparseable tcp-mss child instead of silently clamping nothing [MERGED] (merged 2026-09-05)

Branch: `fix/8824-tcp-mss`

Part of #8824 — the half that is not in dispute. See below for the half I deliberately did **not** fix.

`security flow tcp-mss all-tcp { mss notanint; }` committed clean, clamped nothing, and warned nobody.

`selectMSSToken` prefers the `mss` child only when it parses, then falls through to the flat token. That fall-through is correct for the **mixed** shape `gre-in 1400 { mss bogus; }` — the #1979 precedence, where the flat 1400 is what the compiler uses. With **no** flat token there is nothing to fall through to, and returning "no value selected" reported *nothing configured* for a config that plainly configures one. No gate ever saw a token, so nothing refused it.

The asymmetry is what makes it a defect rather than a policy:

```
all-tcp notanint;            REFUSED   (same bad token, flat)
all-tcp { mss 70000; }       REFUSED   (same braced shape, out of range)
all-tcp { mss notanint; }    ACCEPTED as 0    <- only this vanished
```

MSS clamping exists to stop PMTU blackholes on tunnels. A clamp that silently does not happen is indistinguishable from one that was never configured — which is the state the operator believes they have left.

### What I did not fix, and why it is escalated

#8824 also reports that `set security flow tcp-mss all-tcp mss 1350` is refused. Whether that is a defect turns entirely on whether inline `mss` is a **typo** or the **flat-set flattening** of the braced child.

`TestCompactLeafTCPMSSKeywordStillRejected6564` pins the rejection on the former reading — deliberately, with a stated acceptance criterion ("identical in both AST shapes **or** rejected at commit") that "both reject" satisfies. #8824 asserts the latter reading.

I implemented that change, measured it working across every spelling, **and then reverted it.** Nothing in this tree settles the premise: the only in-repo support for either reading is #6564's own reasoning and the copy of it in `docs/config-schema.md` — one source cited twice. A lane that cannot produce evidence for its premise should not overturn a numbered, tested decision on it.

The comment on `tcpMSSOptionNodes` now records the dispute instead of asserting either side, and the new cell deliberately does not cover that spelling.

### What must not change, asserted alongside the fix

Widening acceptance could have taken these with it, so they are pinned: the #1979 mixed-shape precedence (`gre-in 1400 { mss bogus; }` still selects 1400), typo detection (`all-tcp msss 1350` still refused), every previously-working spelling, and `ipsec-vpn` still refused **for its own unrelated reason** — which is also the control proving these refusals are attributable to the value rather than to a blanket rejection.

### Mutations

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| fix removed (silent zero returns) | killed |
| unparseable child **always** wins (breaks #1979) | killed |

The second is the one worth having: it is the *over-fix*, and it passes every assertion about the defect while breaking the behaviour the original fall-through existed for.

### Modularity gate

#7253 fired — twelve lines took `compiler_interfaces.go` from 1498 to 1510 LOC. Recorded in `docs/refactoring-audit-accepted.txt` rather than answered by splitting a 1500-line compiler file inside a correctness fix, which would bury the fix and pair a mechanical move with a behaviour change.
